0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
The message. First Corinthians was written to a gifted, lively and badly divided church, and its answer to every one of that church’s troubles is the same: the cross. The Corinthians had been rescued by a crucified Christ and then had begun to measure themselves by the world’s standards of wisdom, status and power. Paul calls them back: “we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1:23–24). Whatever the question, from quarrelling to the life to come, he brings it back to the gospel he first preached among them and the love it creates.

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul as its author, with “our brother Sosthenes” (1:1); no one seriously disputes it. He wrote from Ephesus, where he planned to “stay … until Pentecost” (16:8), probably in the spring of about AD 54 or 55, during his long ministry there (Acts 19). It was not his first letter to them: he refers to an earlier one that has not survived (5:9), and more correspondence followed, including our 2 Corinthians.

The city. Corinth stood on the narrow isthmus joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each sea: Lechaeum to the west and Cenchreae to the east. Cargoes were hauled across the neck of land to avoid the dangerous voyage round southern Greece, and the trade made the city rich. The old Greek city had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, settled largely with freed slaves, and it became the capital of the province of Achaia. So the Corinth Paul knew was new money: a city of many nations and languages, of merchants and craftsmen, where people rose by patronage and display. Temples to many gods stood in the city and on the great rock of Acrocorinth above it, and much of the meat in the market had passed through them. Nearby the Isthmian Games were held every two years, which is why Paul could speak to them of runners, boxers and a perishable wreath (9:24–27). Centuries earlier the Greek verb korinthiazesthai, “to act the Corinthian”, had become a byword for sexual immorality, and the letter shows how hard the old reputation was to shake.

Paul and the church there. Paul came to Corinth on his second journey, about AD 50, after Athens. He made tents with Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:1–3), preached in the synagogue until opposed, then taught next door in the house of Titius Justus; Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed with his household (Acts 18:4–8). He stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11). When the Jews brought him before the proconsul Gallio, the case was thrown out (Acts 18:12–17); an inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s year in office to about AD 51–52, which makes this one of the firmest dates in Paul’s life. After Paul left, Apollos came and watered what Paul had planted (Acts 18:27–19:1; 1 Corinthians 3:6). The church was mostly Gentile, with Jewish believers among them, and “not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth” (1:26). Not many, but some: a few households were well off, and the gap between them and the rest shows in the letter.

What prompted the letter. Chloe’s people brought word of quarrelling (1:11), and other reports told of worse. Then Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus arrived (16:17), probably bringing a letter from the church with questions, which Paul takes up one by one with “Now concerning” (7:1; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1). The church had split into followers of Paul, Apollos, Cephas and “Christ” (1:12). A man was living with his father’s wife, and the church was proud of its tolerance (5:1–2). Members were suing one another before pagan judges (6:1). Some thought the body did not matter, whether for indulgence or for denial. Some ate in idols’ temples and wounded weaker consciences (8:10). At the Lord’s Supper the well off ate their own meal while the poor went hungry (11:21–22; see meals and reclining at table). Spiritual gifts, especially tongues, had become marks of status. And some denied the resurrection of the dead (15:12). The danger was not persecution from outside but pride, worldliness and confusion within.

How the letter makes its case. After a greeting and thanksgiving that call them “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1:1–9), chapters 1–4 deal with the divisions. Paul sets the folly of the cross against the wisdom of the world (chapter 1), shows that true wisdom is given by the Spirit (chapter 2), presents preachers as only servants in God’s field and builders on the one foundation, Christ (chapter 3), and holds up the apostles themselves, weak and despised, as the pattern (chapter 4). Chapters 5–6 confront sexual sin, church discipline and lawsuits, ending with “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (6:19–20). From chapter 7 he answers their letter: marriage, singleness and divorce (chapter 7); food offered to idols, where knowledge must give way to love for the weak brother (chapters 8–10), with Paul’s own surrender of his rights as the example (chapter 9); order in worship, head coverings and the Lord’s Supper (chapter 11); and spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14), with love at the centre (chapter 13) and the rule that all must build up the church. Chapter 15 defends the resurrection, both Christ’s and ours. Chapter 16 closes with the collection for Jerusalem, travel plans and greetings.

Where it leads: to Christ. Paul resolved “to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (2:2), and the letter keeps that resolve. Christ “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1:30). He is the only foundation (3:11), “our Passover lamb” (5:7), the Rock that followed Israel in the wilderness (10:4), the Lord whose death is proclaimed at his table “until he comes” (11:26), the head of the body in which every member is needed (chapter 12), and the last Adam, raised as the firstfruits of a great harvest (15:20–22, 45). Martin Luther later set this theology of the cross, which finds God in the weakness of Christ crucified, against a theology of glory, which looks for him in success and power; this letter shows why. It ends not in an argument won but in worship: “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (15:57), and in a prayer, “Our Lord, come!” (16:22).

For us. The Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world at the same time. We too are tempted to follow favourite leaders, admire polish and power, treat the body as everything or nothing, use our freedom without regard for others, and prize the gifts that impress. Paul’s answer still stands: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (4:7). A church that remembers this will stop boasting, start loving, and keep working, “knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (15:58).

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the letter. After a greeting and thanksgiving that tell the Corinthians who they are in Christ (vv. 1–9), Paul turns to the first and most pressing of their troubles, the factions, which will occupy him to the end of chapter 4.

The message. Everything you have, you have from God in Christ, so stop boasting in men. The church that quarrels over its favourite teachers was called by God, enriched by God and will be kept by God. It was saved not by human wisdom but by the message of a crucified Messiah, which the world calls foolish and which is God’s own power. Its members were chosen, many of them nobodies, so that no one can boast before him. Christ alone is their wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption, so the only boast left is in the Lord.

Why it was said. Corinth was a boom town full of people climbing the social ladder, where status, eloquence and success were prized (see the introduction). One inscription found there records that a man called Erastus paved a street at his own expense in return for public office, perhaps the same Erastus, “the city treasurer”, who sent greetings in Romans 16:23. The church had brought the city’s habits in with it. Members were lining up behind Paul, Apollos or Cephas as though they were rival schools of philosophy, and measuring one another by speech and knowledge (vv. 5, 12).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul begins with who they are: God’s church, sanctified in Christ and called to be saints (vv. 1–3), richly gifted, and certain to be kept guiltless to the end by the faithful God who called them into fellowship with his Son (vv. 4–9). Then he names the quarrel and exposes it with three questions: is Christ divided, was Paul crucified for you, were you baptised in Paul’s name? (vv. 10–17). He goes to the root in the message itself: the word of the cross is folly to the perishing and God’s power to the saved, a crucified Christ who offends Jew and Greek alike yet is God’s power and wisdom to those he calls (vv. 18–25). Finally he points to the people in the room: God chose the foolish, the weak and the despised, so that no one might boast (vv. 26–29), and gave them everything in Christ (vv. 30–31).

Where it leads. The chapter that begins with a quarrel over men ends with every eye on one Man. Christ is named ten times in its first ten verses; he is the only one crucified for them, the power and wisdom of God in the shape of a cross, and the one who “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (v. 30). And the Lord in whom Jeremiah told Israel to boast turns out to be Jesus (v. 31).

For us. Every church is tempted to follow favourite leaders, admire polish and measure people by status, and every heart wants something of its own to point to. This chapter does not tell us to stop wanting a boast; it gives us a better one. Notice what you reach for when you feel small, and put Christ in its place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church belongs to God before it belongs to anyone in it. Paul writes as an apostle by God’s will, not by his own choice or the church’s vote (v. 1), and he addresses a troubled congregation by what God has made it: his church, set apart in Christ, called to be saints, one part of a worldwide people who call on Jesus as Lord (v. 2). Grace and peace come to them from the Father and the Son together (v. 3). Before any correction, they are told whose they are.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul calls himself an apostle “by the will of God”, and he is not being modest (see the note on v. 1). The same is true of their own standing: they are saints because they were called (v. 2), not because they volunteered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s authority was contested at Corinth by people who preferred Apollos’s polish or Peter’s prestige. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still God’s calling, not human talent. A pastor who rests his authority on his own gifts has little to stand on when people turn against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes with God’s authority, not his own, and the name beside his shows what grace can do with an enemy.

Called by the will of God. Three phrases carry the weight, and each takes something away from Paul: called; by the will of God; and apostle (apostolos), one sent with authority, a man under orders carrying somebody else’s message. He does not say he became an apostle, trained for it, or was appointed by a church; any of those would place the commission in Paul. He puts it outside himself entirely (Galatians 1:15). Whatever else the Damascus road was, it was not a job interview: Paul was travelling with warrants to arrest Christians when he was knocked to the ground and blinded by the very person he was persecuting (Acts 9:3–9). So to a church questioning his authority (4:3; 9:3) he says, in effect: the appointment was not mine to make and is not mine to resign.

Why it matters for this letter. Sixteen chapters of correction are coming, for people who do not want to be corrected. If Paul’s standing rested on his personality, eloquence or track record, they could simply prefer somebody else’s, as they have (v. 12). Resting on the will of God, it makes their preferences beside the point.

An apostle of Christ Jesus. The title is itself a confession of the resurrection. Nobody is sent by a dead man, and Paul’s whole claim rests on having seen the risen Lord and been commissioned by him (9:1; 15:8). Nor did the sending begin with Paul. Christ is himself the Apostle of our confession, sent by the Father (Hebrews 3:1), and on the evening of the resurrection he told his disciples that as the Father had sent him, so he was sending them (John 20:21). Paul’s authority is borrowed: the risen Son extending his own commission through a man he had arrested on a road. That is why it cannot be voted down. To receive the one Christ sends is to receive Christ (John 13:20).

And our brother Sosthenes. This may be one of the quietest miracles in the New Testament. When the Corinthian Jews dragged Paul before the proconsul Gallio and the case was thrown out, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal (Acts 18:17). He held the office Crispus had held before his conversion (Acts 18:8): he led the opposition. We cannot be certain it is the same man, for Sosthenes was not a rare name. But if it is, the head of the opposition became the co-sender of the letter, and the Christians at Corinth opened it to find a name they remembered from the wrong side of a courtroom.

The gospel recruits its opponents. Remember that when you pray for someone who seems entirely closed: the relative who mocks, the colleague who has heard it all. Paul was among the most dangerous enemies the early church had, and Sosthenes may have been another; both names head this letter. The gospel does not merely survive its opponents; it has a long history of enlisting them, because our Lord does not wait to be chosen. He chooses, and he does not need willing material; he makes it willing. Every name at the top of this letter is a trophy of grace.

What it does not mean. Not that apostles in Paul’s sense still exist. The eyewitnesses sent by the risen Lord laid the church’s foundation once (Ephesians 2:20), and their authority continues in their writings: when we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter. Some churches call pioneering missionaries apostles, meaning sent messengers, and the word can bear that (2 Corinthians 8:23), but no one now adds to the foundation or speaks with Paul’s authority.

Is my job a calling in the same sense? Not quite, though it is not nothing. When Paul says “called” of all Christians (vv. 2, 9, 24), he means God’s effectual summons into Christ, the call that saves, the same for the apostle and for you. Paul’s office was a further, unrepeatable commission. Your work, family and church responsibilities are callings in a secondary sense: the place where God has put you to serve him (7:17–24). So you need not hunt for a dramatic sense of vocation before your life counts. The first call, the one that made you his, is already the greatest thing that will ever happen to you; everything else is lived out of it.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However badly they behave, the Corinthians are God’s own church, set apart in Christ, and they share that name with everyone who calls on Jesus as Lord. Paul tells them who they are before he tells them what to do.

To the church of God that is in Corinth. The little word “of” does more work than any other in the sentence. The church (ekklēsia, in the Greek Old Testament Israel gathered before the LORD) belongs to God, not to Paul or Apollos or any faction; it merely has an address. And every reader knew what Corinth was: proud, status-conscious, a city whose name had become a verb for immoral living (see the introduction). “The church of God in Corinth” was very nearly a contradiction in terms, and Paul writes it without a flicker of embarrassment. If God can have a church in Corinth, he can have one anywhere. He planted his holy people in the middle of the city whose name was a byword for vice, and put his name on them before they had learned to behave.

To those sanctified in Christ Jesus. A great deal of Christian anxiety turns on this phrase. “Sanctified” (hagiazō, set apart as holy) is in a Greek form that describes something done to them in the past, with results that continue (6:11). It is not a report on their conduct but a statement of their location: they are set apart for God because they are in Christ, who is holy. To be in Christ is to be joined to him by the Spirit through faith, so that God now deals with you as belonging to his Son (6:17).

Remember who is being described. This church will shortly be rebuked for factions, for a man living with his father’s wife, for lawsuits in pagan courts, for drunkenness at the Lord’s Supper while the poor went hungry, and for chaos over spiritual gifts. Paul already has the report (v. 11), and still calls them sanctified saints. He does not withdraw the title to make them earn it. He states who they are, and then spends sixteen chapters telling them to become it. That order is the gospel. The world says: behave, and you will belong. Paul says: you have been set apart, so live like it.

Called to be saints. In the New Testament “saints” (hagioi, holy ones) is never a rank awarded to the exceptional but the ordinary word for a Christian, and Paul applies it happily to perhaps the worst-behaved congregation in his letters. The question is not whether your record has earned it, but whether you are in Christ. And “called”, here as throughout the letter, means more than invited. It is not an invitation slipped under the door that you may or may not open, but like Jesus at the tomb calling Lazarus by name: a word that creates the response it asks for (John 11:43–44).

Together with all those who in every place call upon the name. Corinth is one congregation inside something worldwide. The Corinthians were inclined to act as a law to themselves, and four times Paul will set their practice beside that of the other churches (4:17; 7:17; 11:16; 14:33). A church that has to be reminded at its very address that it is not the only one has already shown part of its problem.

Grace and peace. The greeting joins grace, a Christian reshaping of the ordinary Greek greeting, with peace, the Hebrew shalom, and both come from the Father and the Son under a single “from”, one source of one gift (Romans 1:7; 2 Corinthians 1:2).

Jesus is the LORD they call on. “Call upon the name” of the Lord is lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where it means to invoke and worship the LORD, Yahweh himself (Genesis 4:26; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13). Paul applies it to Jesus without argument or apology, and in the greeting sets him beside the Father as the giver of grace. He is not arguing for the deity of Christ but assuming it in passing, which says far more about what the earliest church believed than any formal argument would. It arrives disguised as an address label.

Set apart at his own cost. On the night before the cross the Son said, “for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). He set himself apart for the altar, so that a church in Corinth could be set apart for God, once for all.

In everyday life. When you have sinned badly, not a slip but the real thing, do you assume you must work your way back in before you can pray properly? The instinct is common, and it is not the gospel. The letter that says “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified” (6:11) says it to people who were still getting it badly wrong. Go to him today as what he has made you, and ask him to make your life match your name.

If I am already sanctified, why must I still grow in holiness? Because the Bible uses the word in two ways, and both are true of you. Definitively, you were set apart for God the moment you were joined to Christ; that is finished and does not fluctuate (6:11; Hebrews 10:10). Progressively, the Spirit is making your actual life match that status, a lifelong work that is real but never complete in this life (2 Corinthians 3:18; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 13.1–2). The first is the ground of the second, never its reward. You do not pursue holiness to become God’s; you pursue it because you are his. So when you fail, you have not lost the first; you have found another place where the second still has work to do.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus of Greece, with two ports and a mixed, mobile population. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All that the Corinthians have is grace, and God will finish what he began. Paul thanks God for the very gifts they are misusing, because those gifts were truly given in Christ (vv. 4–5) and confirmed the gospel among them (v. 6). They lack nothing as they wait for Christ’s return (v. 7), and they will be kept so that no charge stands against them on his day (v. 8). The ground of it all is God’s faithfulness: he called them into fellowship with his Son (v. 9), the one Person every faction shares.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 is one of Paul’s great texts on perseverance: the saints persevere because God is faithful (see the note on v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge (on how Paul’s thanksgiving corrects them, see vv. 4–5). Now: The same pride can attach to theological sophistication or spiritual experience. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God for the Corinthians because their gifts, even the ones they are misusing, came from God’s grace in Christ.

I give thanks to my God always for you. Paul already holds Chloe’s report (v. 11): the quarrelling, the immorality, the lawsuits, the disorder. He has a list that would justify opening in anger, and the first thing he does is thank God for them. This is not flattery, or a sweetener before the medicine. He is thanking God for what God did, so he can do it with complete sincerity about a church he is about to take apart. Nor does the thanks cancel the correction; he simply refuses to let the problems be the first or the truest thing he says.

Enriched in him. The verb is passive: the wealth arrived as a gift. It belongs to the word family of Paul’s best-known sentence about Christian wealth: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). They are rich because he made himself poor; everything in their hands was paid for by what he gave up.

In all speech and all knowledge. These are the two things that have gone most badly wrong at Corinth: speech, where the trouble over tongues will fill chapters 12–14, and knowledge, which Paul will say flatly “puffs up” (8:1). He thanks God for the very gifts now doing the damage, because they were real gifts.

Tracing the gift to the Giver. When a gift is misused, our instinct is to disparage it. Paul traces it to the Giver, gives thanks, and then spends the letter putting it back in its place. The trouble at Corinth was never that they had too much of God’s grace, but that they had forgotten it was grace. And the Giver did not take it back when they misused it; he sent an apostle to set it right: generous beyond our deserving, and patient beyond our misuse.

How can I thank God for someone without pretending his sin is fine? By thanking God for what God has done in him, not for what he is doing wrong. Paul keeps the two columns separate: thanks for grace in verses 4–9, correction from verse 10. Thanksgiving is not a verdict that the problem is small, but a confession that God is at work even there. It also changes the correction. You will speak more gently, hopefully and accurately to someone whose gifts you have honestly thanked God for that morning, and he is far more likely to hear you, because he can tell you are not his enemy.
verseByVerse.note: The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge, the very gifts they later misused.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gifts at Corinth were God’s seal on the gospel and his provision for the time of waiting until Christ appears.

The testimony about Christ was confirmed among you. The testimony is the gospel Paul preached, and “confirmed” (bebaiōthē) is a word from contracts and guarantees: ratified, made secure. The gifts were God’s signature under the apostolic message, so that nobody could call it one man’s opinion.

Not lacking in any gift. Not that every individual had every gift (12:29–30); the church as a whole lacked nothing. A congregation deficient in love, humility, unity, self-control and basic decency is told it lacks no spiritual gift whatever. Both are true at once: gifting is not maturity, nor evidence of it. That warns the gifted, who may read their usefulness as God’s approval of their character, and relieves everyone else, who may have assumed the gifted must be the godly.

As you wait for the revealing. “Revealing” (apokalypsis) is the drawing back of a curtain on someone already there: Christ’s return in glory. Some Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived (4:8); Paul reminds them they are still waiting (13:8–12). The gifts are equipment for the interval between his going and his coming, provisions for a journey rather than trophies for a cabinet.

Gifts from an ascended King. These were not native talents. When Christ “ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8, citing Psalm 68:18): the gifts are the spoils of his victory, handed out by a King who has gone up to the Father and will come again. So every gift looks back to a Saviour who died, rose and ascended, and forward to the same Saviour unveiled. A gift that becomes a reason to admire its holder has forgotten both ends of its own story.

A lamp at sunrise. The one we wait for is not absent but hidden behind the veil. On that day every gift will be laid down like a lamp at sunrise, because the Light himself will have come, and the tongues that argued at Corinth will have only one thing left to say. The gifts were tokens of his care for the interval; the unveiling will be the Giver himself, seen face to face (13:12).

Possession or equipment? The words “as you wait” would have solved most of the Corinthian problem if they had believed them. A gift held as a possession becomes a measure of standing; standing invites comparison; comparison produces the factions of the next paragraph. A gift held as equipment raises a different question: not “What does this say about me?” but “What is this for?” The same gift, held in two ways, builds a church or splits one.

For the Christian who thinks he has no gift. You watch people who teach, or organise, or know what to say in a hospital room, and find nothing comparable in yourself. But “to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (12:7): not to some; to each. Gifts are usually discovered by serving, not by looking inward. Take the job nobody wants, and see what God does with it.

If the sign gifts have ceased, does God still heal? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting, but that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing or new revelation as signs authenticating a message. God still hears prayer for the sick and often answers it, sometimes through doctors, sometimes beyond them, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). So pray boldly for healing, and give thanks when it comes. Be wary of anyone who claims to heal at will, or to bring a new word from God that binds your conscience; test everything by the Scripture God has already given.

Where Christians differ: do all the gifts continue today? Some hold that the revelatory and sign gifts, prophecy, tongues and gifts of healing, belonged to the apostolic age and ceased once the foundation was laid and the New Testament complete, pointing to the apostles and prophets as a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20) and to the signs as God’s attestation of the apostolic message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Others hold that they continue until Christ returns, reading the perfect of 13:10 as his appearing rather than the closing of the canon, and noting that this very verse ties the gifts to the waiting for the revealing of the Lord, which is plainly not over. This commentary’s view: the first is the better view. The sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message, and with a closed canon God speaks to his church through Scripture, sufficient for all of life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). This is held charitably: both positions are taken by people who love Scripture and submit to it, and what Paul says here, which neither side disputes, is the main thing. Whatever gifts God has given you were given for the waiting, will not be needed when he appears, and were never meant to tell you or anyone else how you are doing (Romans 8:23–25; 1 Peter 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians will be kept to the end, and on the last day no charge will stand against them. Before Paul names a single fault, he tells them how judgment will go for them.

Who will sustain you to the end. The one who sustains is most naturally the one just named, our Lord Jesus Christ (see “Uncertain wording” below), and certainly not the Corinthians. The verb (bebaiōsei) has the same root as “confirmed” in verse 6, the language of a legal guarantee: as God confirmed the gospel among them, he will confirm them to the last day. The comfort is in the plain “will”: not “may”, nor “will, if you hold on tightly enough”, but a promise about something already guaranteed.

Guiltless. The whole verse is built to deliver this word. Anenklētous is a courtroom term: not never having done wrong, but unaccused, with no charge standing and no case to answer. On the day of our Lord, the day of judgment and of Christ’s return, believers will stand without accusation, because Christ’s righteousness is theirs (Romans 8:33–34; Colossians 1:22). Paul’s word for it is justification: the Judge pronouncing a guilty person in the right with him, for Christ’s sake and not for any goodness of his own (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

How can that be true? There is only one way, and the letter says it plainly: “Christ died for our sins” (15:3). The charges are not ignored, waived or dropped for lack of evidence. They were transferred. Every accusation that could be brought against a Corinthian believer on that day was brought against Christ on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, and answered there. Their charge sheet is clean because the charges were written on his.

For the Christian who is afraid of the last day. You believe in the forgiveness of sins in general, and are not sure it will hold for you, because you know things nobody else knows: the thing you have never told anyone, the pattern confessed a hundred times and returned to, the person you damaged who never got an apology. You expect that day to be when it all comes out. But look at what Paul says will be true of you then: guiltless. Not forgiven with a permanent asterisk, not acquitted after a difficult hearing, but no charge standing. The Lord who will sit on that day’s throne is the Lord who bore that day’s charges, and there is no accusation left in the universe that he has not already answered with his blood.

What about people who seemed to be Christians and then walked away? Scripture gives two answers that must be held together. Some who leave were never truly joined to Christ, however real it looked: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). Others are true believers in a long and grievous backsliding, as Peter was for a night and the Corinthians were for a season, and God will bring them home. From outside we often cannot tell which, so we do not pronounce; we pray, keep the door open and keep calling. What you can know is your own case: if you are still coming to Christ with your sins today, that coming is the evidence that he is keeping you.

Where Christians differ: perseverance. Some teach that true believers may fall away and be finally lost. This is the view of Arminian Christians (who hold that saving grace can in the end be resisted and lost), held out of a sincere desire to take Scripture’s warnings seriously. This commentary’s view: Paul says they will be sustained to the end. If it were up to the Corinthians, with all their failings, they would not stand. But God keeps his people. True believers may fall into serious sin, as the Corinthians did, and must be corrected; but God will not let them go (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; Westminster Confession 17.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). The warnings are real, and they are one of the ways he keeps them.

Uncertain wording. “Who will sustain you” most naturally points back to the nearest name, “our Lord Jesus Christ” at the end of verse 7, and that is the reading followed here. But the Greek could also refer to God, the subject of verse 4, and verse 9 grounds the promise in God’s faithfulness. Either way the keeping is God’s work, not the Corinthians’, and the Father and the Son are at one in it.

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s own faithfulness guarantees that he will finish what he began when he called them into fellowship with his Son.

God is faithful. Three short words in the Greek, the floor under everything Paul has just promised and the reason for the confidence of verse 8. The phrase returns at a key point in the letter (10:13).

By whom you were called. The calling is his act: his call actually brought them to Christ and joined them to him. The fellowship is his gift, and the faithfulness that will keep them in it is his character. At no point in the sentence do the Corinthians contribute anything, a remarkable thing to say of a church whose behaviour is about to be dismantled for fifteen chapters. What God begins, he finishes (Philippians 1:6).

Into the fellowship of his Son. Sharing, partnership, common life (koinōnia). They were called not into a religion or a moral improvement scheme but into a shared life with the Son of God, and since every believer shares in Christ, they share in one another. Told in the last line of the thanksgiving that they were all called into partnership with the same Person, the Corinthians should already see how absurd are the factions Paul is about to name (vv. 10–12).

He has never broken a promise. Not to Abraham, waiting twenty-five years for a son; not to Israel, kept through four centuries in Egypt; not to David, whose throne stood empty for nearly six hundred years before a child was born in Bethlehem to fill it. Each promise looked for a long time like one that had failed, and each was kept, at last in the same Person: “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). That Son is the one into whose fellowship you have been called, and the God who kept every word to the fathers will not let go of what he has called.

But what if I let go? A reader who has taken verse 8 seriously will already have asked it. I have let go before; I know how thin my grip is on a bad week, and I have watched people far stronger than me walk away. Paul does not reassure you about your grip. He takes the weight off it altogether and puts it on the character of God. The guarantee is not that you are faithful but that he is, and that is the only guarantee worth anything, because a promise is exactly as reliable as the person making it, and you know what yours are worth. The most dangerous thing in the world is not a God who might abandon you, but a God of infinite faithfulness who has committed himself to you: dangerous, because such a God will not leave you as you are; and safe, for exactly the same reason. That is what “the perseverance of the saints” means: not first their stamina but their preservation; Christians persevere because they are being kept (on the debate, see “Where Christians differ: perseverance” in the note on v. 8).

What does fellowship with Christ look like on an ordinary day? What is his is yours, and what is yours he has taken. His righteousness covers you, his Spirit lives in you, his Father is your Father, and his future is your future; and he has taken your sin, your burdens and your griefs as his concern. You enjoy it by using it: speaking to him in prayer as one who is welcome, listening to him in Scripture, receiving him at his table, and sharing your life with others who share his. It is not a feeling to manufacture but a relationship you are already in, and feelings tend to follow when you act on it.

parallels.desc: the faithful God

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church that lines up behind favourite leaders is tearing the one Christ who died for it. Paul pleads by Christ’s name for one mind (v. 10), says how he heard of the quarrels and names the four slogans (vv. 11–12), and asks three questions that expose them: is Christ divided, was Paul crucified for you, were you baptised in his name? (v. 13). He is glad he baptised few, so that no one could make a party of it (vv. 14–16), for his task was to preach the cross plainly, not to win admirers with eloquence (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions show what happens when a leader’s personality becomes the centre of a church. Paul’s refusal of “eloquent wisdom” is not a dislike of learning (see the note on v. 17).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and on travelling orators: you attached yourself to an impressive teacher and measured your standing by his. The Corinthian factions were the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity culture is the modern version: a church that divides over which tradition’s champion to follow is repeating the Corinthian mistake (on following a preacher online in place of your own pastors, see vv. 12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pleads, by the one name they all share, for a church that speaks with one voice instead of tearing into rival parties.

In the flow. With verse 10 the body of the letter begins. The factions run to the end of chapter 4, and Paul answers them not with a plan for managing the church but with the cross (1:18–2:5), the Spirit’s wisdom (2:6–16), and a right view of ministers as servants (3:1–4:21).

I appeal to you. Paul does not command, though as an apostle he could; he pleads (parakalō). And he pleads by the name of Christ: by his authority, and by the one name in Corinth that belongs equally to every person he is writing to, which is exactly his point. Christ has been named ten times in the first ten verses. Before Paul mentions a single faction, he has filled the room with the one Person they all share.

No divisions. “That all of you agree” is literally “that you all say the same thing”: one voice instead of rival slogans (v. 12). Divisions (schismata, schisms) are tears, the word used of a torn garment (Mark 2:21): not a difference of opinion but the sound of fabric giving way. The church had not yet split into separate congregations, but there were cliques and rivalries. And the fabric is a body (12:12–27); a tear in a body is not untidiness but a wound.

United in the same mind. Mended, put in order (katartizō), the word used of fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). This is not a demand that every Christian hold identical views on every question. Paul makes room for genuine disagreement on disputable matters such as food and days (Romans 14), and this letter spends chapter 8 on a question where believers landed differently. What he wants is a church so fixed on the same Lord that no rival loyalty can organise a party.

Chloe’s people. Probably members of her household or business, perhaps slaves or freedmen travelling between Corinth and Ephesus: exactly the witnesses a status-conscious congregation would discount. Paul takes the report seriously and says openly where it came from. He will not build a rebuke on gossip he cannot attribute.

One loaf, one name. Paul does not ask them to manufacture a unity they lack, but to stop tearing one they already have. They were all baptised into the one name of Christ; they all eat from one loaf, which is a sharing in his body (10:16–17); they are all members of the one Christ (12:12). That unity was made at the cross, where he broke down the dividing wall in his flesh and created one new people in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–16). A party at Corinth is not a difference of taste but a hand raised against something Christ died to make.

Not a seam showing. On the night he was betrayed, with the cross a few hours away, the Lord Jesus prayed for people who did not yet believe in him, that they would all be one, as he and the Father are one (John 17:20–21). Corinth was inside that prayer, quarrels and all, and so is every divided congregation since. The Son has never asked the Father for anything in vain. His church still tears, and he still mends it, and on the last day there will be one flock and one Shepherd (John 10:16), with not a seam showing.

What does this ask of me on Sunday? Your church probably has a fault line: a leadership dispute, a music argument, two families who no longer speak. Four things are asked of you, none of them dramatic. Refuse the party: every division needs recruits, and declining to take a side is a positive act, not cowardice. Stop repeating it: much of what tears a congregation is not the original disagreement but its retelling, and the sentence that begins “I probably shouldn’t say this” has done more damage in more churches than any heresy. Speak to the person, not about them, as Paul does here at some cost. And keep eating together: this letter treats a shared table as a declaration that we are one body (10:17), and people who eat together find it much harder to caricature each other.

Unity is not the same thing as quiet. A call for unity is not a call to suppress genuine concern, and “you are being divisive” is the standard reply of anyone who wishes an uncomfortable question would go away. Paul opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11). Nor does unity ever mean covering up sin or abuse; this letter demands that serious sin be dealt with openly (5:1–13). The unity commanded here is unity around the crucified Christ, so the test is whether what divides your church is Christ or preference. If a congregation splits over the gospel, that is a grief and may be a necessity. If it splits over anything else, as it usually does, Paul’s plea applies without qualification.

When is it right to leave a church? Rarely, and never casually. There are real reasons: the gospel itself is denied or obscured; serious sin or abuse is protected instead of dealt with; you are required to act against Scripture; or you have moved away. Preference about style, music or personality is not one of them, and even real concerns should first be raised humbly, privately and with the elders (Matthew 18:15); abuse or any crime, though, is not a matter for a quiet word, but for the proper authorities, at once. If you must go, go openly and peaceably, without recruiting others or leaving a trail of grievance, and join another faithful church promptly. Leaving Christ’s people altogether is never an option Scripture offers.
verseByVerse.note: Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business who had travelled to Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians were rallying behind rival leaders, and Paul’s three questions show that this tears apart the one Christ who alone died for them and owns them. Even the party that claimed Christ himself is rebuked.

Each one of you says. Literally, “I am of Paul”: I belong to him. Each name is a real attraction. Paul’s party was probably the loyal old guard, proud to follow the founder. Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24–28), was the polished speaker, a considerable draw in a city that paid to hear orators. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name; his party, perhaps Jewish believers, claimed the leading apostle of the Twelve, with a prestige Paul could not match.

Or “I follow Christ”. Perhaps the most dangerous party, because it looks like the right answer, and it is rebuked with the others (on whether it was a party at all, see “Uncertain wording” below). It is the claim to have risen above the mess: “I have no time for your teachers and your squabbling church; I have Christ directly, and need nothing else.” It sounds like maturity and is a subtler form of the same pride, for it has still turned Christ into a party badge, and done it by using his name to look down on his people.

Good material, bad division. As far as we can tell, nobody is teaching error. Every one of these men is a genuine servant of God, and Paul will insist that Apollos and he are simply servants through whom the Corinthians believed (3:5). That is what makes it so hard to see from inside. A congregation dividing over false teaching at least knows what it is doing; one dividing over preferences believes it is defending something important.

Is Christ divided? Three questions follow, and each is a hammer. Has Christ been split up and shared out among factions? If the church is his body, a factional church is a dismembered Christ, a grotesque image, and meant to be. There are not four Christs for four parties. Every believer at Corinth has the whole of him, so no group holds a portion the others lack. To divide the church is to tear him.

Was Paul crucified for you? Here is the only credential that could justify a Christian naming himself after someone. Loyalty of this depth belongs to a person who died for you, and exactly one person qualifies. Paul is not being modest. The Corinthians have offered him something he has no right to receive, and he refuses to head a party.

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? Baptism names your owner. To be baptised into someone’s name is to be publicly transferred into his possession, and every Corinthian was baptised into the name of Christ, whoever stood in the water with him. The questions are absurd and the answers obvious: only Christ died for them, and they belong to him alone.

For the one who has withdrawn into a private faith. You have been hurt by a church, or simply exhausted by one, and have quietly withdrawn: you love Christ, read your Bible, and have concluded you can do without the rest. Nothing here doubts the hurt, and a church that damaged you owes you an apology it may never offer. But look where the fourth slogan sits. Paul does not set it above the others as the one healthy option; he puts it in the same sentence and lets the same three questions fall on it, because Christ has attached himself to a body, and no one can take the Head and decline the rest of him. The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you” (12:21).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should have no preferences among teachers, or that denominations are always sinful. Paul rebukes no one for learning more from Apollos than from Cephas, and churches that hold distinct convictions about baptism or church order are not his target. The sin is boasting in a human leader and treating your own side as the measure of who really belongs (3:21). A loyalty has become party spirit when you can no longer gladly receive Christ’s gifts through someone outside it.

Can I just listen to my favourite preacher online instead of my own church? Listen to him gladly, but not instead. Christ gives his gifts through the gathered church you actually belong to: the pastor who knows your name, the elders who will visit you in hospital, the table you share, the people who can see your life and speak into it (Hebrews 10:24–25; 13:17). A celebrity preacher cannot shepherd you, and will never know if you drift. And comparing your pastor unfavourably with a man edited for an online audience is exactly the Corinthian habit Paul is rebuking. Thank God for both, and give your loyalty to the local body where Christ has placed you.

Uncertain wording. The fourth slogan, “I follow Christ”, is hard to place. It may describe a fourth group, perhaps people who claimed a direct line to Christ that set them above any human teacher; some take it instead as Paul’s own retort to the other three. We know too little about the groups to be sure. The likeliest reading is the one followed here: it is a fourth slogan, since Paul puts it in the same sentence as the others, and “Is Christ divided?” falls on it as on them.
verseByVerse.note: Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is glad he baptised so few at Corinth, so that no one could turn his baptism into a badge of belonging to Paul.

I thank God that I baptized none of you. He is not disparaging baptism (see the note on v. 17). What he is glad about is narrower and shrewder. Paul probably left most baptisms to others, and the fewer people who could claim a personal bond with him through baptism, the fewer could build a party on it.

Crispus and Gaius. Those he remembers were people of standing. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue (Acts 18:8), probably the most prominent convert in the city. Gaius later hosted the whole church (Romans 16:23). Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, southern Greece (16:15–17). These are exactly the people a personality cult would gather round, and Paul knows it. The parenthesis about Stephanas is the sound of a real man dictating a real letter and remembering something halfway through.

I do not know. A man writing Scripture admits, in Scripture, that he cannot remember. The worry this raises assumes that inspiration means dictation, God using Paul as a pen, which is not what Scripture claims for itself: Luke opens his Gospel by describing research and eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). The Spirit so guided and guarded what these men wrote that the result is precisely what God intended to say, without suppressing their vocabulary, temperament or memories (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). This verse truly asserts that Paul, as he wrote, was not certain whether there had been others; nothing false is affirmed. And a forger inventing an apostolic letter would hardly leave his author groping after a detail and correcting himself mid-sentence.

Not in my name. Baptism belongs to Christ because what it pictures belongs to him: to be baptised into his name is to be publicly marked as joined to him in his death, burial and rising (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12). No apostle died or rose for the Corinthians, so no apostle may have his name written over their baptism. Crispus the synagogue ruler and Gaius the wealthy host went down into the water on the same terms as the poorest believer beside them, with nothing to bring, buried with a crucified Lord and raised with him into one body (12:13).

I was baptised as an infant and have since come to faith. Should I be baptised? On the view this commentary holds, yes: the baptism the New Testament describes is the public confession of a believer, and since you did not make that confession as an infant, the step of obedience is still before you. That is no slight on your parents, who very likely acted in faith and love, nor a judgment on paedobaptist churches, which are true churches of Christ. Talk it through with your pastor or elders, read the passages for yourself, and act with a clear conscience. If your church holds the other view, raise it humbly; godly Christians differ here, and love must govern the conversation.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) argue from household baptisms (here, and Acts 16:15, 33) that believers’ children should be baptised, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise, which like circumcision includes children (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39; Colossians 2:11–12). This commentary’s view: the New Testament never mentions an infant in any household baptism. The text here does not say who was in the household or how old they were, but at the end of the letter this same household is described as devoting themselves to serving the saints (16:15), which describes believers old enough to serve. Elsewhere the households baptised are households that heard the word and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8), and baptism in the New Testament follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12). So this commentary holds believer’s baptism (1689 London Baptist Confession 29), while warmly recognising paedobaptist brothers and sisters as faithful Christians who read the covenant differently.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s commission was above all to preach the gospel, and to preach it plainly, because clever rhetoric would hide the power of the cross. On this sentence the argument turns from the factions to the message itself.

Christ did not send me to baptize. This sounds wrong at first: the risen Christ sent his apostles to make disciples, baptising them (Matthew 28:19). But Paul cannot mean he was against baptism. He was baptised himself as soon as his sight returned (Acts 9:18), he has just named people he baptised (vv. 14–16), and his teaching on what baptism signifies (Romans 6:3–4) is among the richest in the New Testament.

But to preach the gospel. “Not this but that” is a Hebrew way of stressing priority, meaning “that before this”: God says through Hosea, “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6), though he had commanded the sacrifices. Christ sent Paul chiefly to preach (euangelizō, to announce good news); baptising was not the centre of the assignment, and did not need an apostle’s hands.

The Great Commission was given to the church. In Matthew’s Greek there is a single command, “make disciples”; baptising and teaching describe how it is done, and the church obeyed it together, never assuming each apostle must perform every part in person. Jesus set the pattern: he did not baptise, but only his disciples (John 4:2). Paul was sent to the Gentiles “to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light” (Acts 26:18), a planter of churches for whom preaching was the part only he had been sent to do: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (3:6). So he is not contradicting Matthew 28 but describing his place in obeying it. Disciples are made first by the announcement of Christ crucified, and baptism follows faith, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:41).

Not with words of eloquent wisdom. Literally “wisdom of word” (sophia logou): clever rhetoric and human philosophy. In Corinth travelling orators, the sophists, were celebrities, paid for their performances, judged by their style, compared and followed by rival fans. To preach the cross in that style is to enter the competition, and the moment you do, the audience starts assessing the performer. They may leave impressed; they will not leave humbled and changed.

Lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. The verb (kenoō) is the one used in Philippians 2:7 of the Son’s glorious self-emptying; here the emptying is a disastrous one. The cross can be hollowed out not by attacking it but by the way it is presented: a preacher can leave every doctrine formally intact and still drain it of power, simply by making the message a vehicle for the messenger. Two things can produce a response to preaching, the speaker’s persuasive skill and the Spirit of God working through the message of a crucified Saviour. Both produce visible results; only one produces conversions. A herald carries a message that is not his own, and the moment he becomes interesting in his own right, the message has a rival.

The weakness is the method. God arranged it so on purpose. He could have chosen a method that rewarded eloquence, and the gospel would have travelled the ancient world on the strength of its orators. Instead he chose a message no skill can make respectable, a crucified man, so that when it saves anyone at all, no one can mistake whose power did it. And the crucified Lord at its centre needs no polish from us, because he is himself the power of God, and his cross has never once been emptied by anything but our attempts to improve it.

What it does not mean. Not that preachers should be careless or dull, or that learning and clear speech are bad. Paul argued and reasoned (Acts 17:2; 19:8), was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and plainly took great trouble over words. A muddled sermon is not thereby more spiritual; it is merely worse. Preachers must not rely on technique, or try to make the gospel attractive by hiding its offence.

Does it matter who baptised me? No. A baptism does not take its value from the minister’s reputation, from how well you knew him, or from whether he later disgraced himself. You were baptised, as every Corinthian was, into the name of Christ (v. 13), and that name is the whole of it.

How can I tell whether I am moved by the preacher or by Christ? Ask what you take home. If on Monday you remember chiefly how good the sermon was, the turn of phrase, the story, the cleverness, the preacher may have become the subject. If you remember Christ, what he has done and what he asks of you, and find yourself praying about it, the message has done its work. Another sign is what happens when the gifted preacher is away: if you stay home, you were following him. None of this means preferring dull preaching. Pray for your pastor to be clear, and for yourself to listen for the Lord behind the voice.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators were admired like celebrities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God saves through the message the world thinks foolish: Christ crucified. The word of the cross divides its hearers into the perishing and the saved (v. 18), as Isaiah foresaw God overturning the wisdom of the wise (v. 19). The world never found God by its wisdom, so God chose to save believers through preaching (vv. 20–21). Jews want signs and Greeks want wisdom, and a crucified Messiah offends both, yet to those God calls he is God’s power and God’s wisdom (vv. 22–24), for what looks like God’s foolishness and weakness outdoes all human wisdom and strength (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross

Luther distinguished a theology of the cross from a theology of glory, and 1:18–25 is its clearest ground. The theology of glory looks for God in power, success and wisdom that make sense on human terms. The theology of the cross finds God revealed in weakness, foolishness and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross was never a fallback plan but God’s plan from eternity, the place where his justice and his love were both satisfied in the same event and in the same Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Crucifixion was the ultimate mark of shame and criminal status. The early Christians were staking their standing and their lives on an executed man. Now: The pressure is to make the gospel more palatable: to lead with Jesus as life coach rather than sin-bearer, with personal fulfilment rather than atonement. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age, and the answer is still to preach it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message of the cross sounds like nonsense to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is God’s own saving power. Isaiah foresaw God overturning the wisdom of the wise, and at the cross he did it.

In the flow. “For” links verse 18 to verse 17: if the message itself is God’s power, dressing it up can only hide it. From here to 2:5 Paul sets out three exhibits of one truth, the message (1:18–25), the people God called by it (1:26–31), and the preacher who brought it (2:1–5), each weak by the world’s measure and full of God’s power.

The word of the cross. Not the cross as an event, but the message about it, spoken aloud by somebody: God saves people through an announcement, and the announcement is about an execution. Folly (mōria) is nonsense; it later gave English the word moron. To the perishing the cross is not merely unconvincing but idiotic, and Paul says so without defensiveness, because he expects it. A message the natural mind found reasonable would not be this message.

Those who are perishing … us who are being saved. Both describe something still going on: two directions of travel, and the same message lands differently depending on which road you are on. And the cross is not merely a message about power; it is God’s power at work, saving people (Romans 1:16).

For it is written. The quotation is from Isaiah 29:14, about people who honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from him, and about the wise men of Judah who thought they could manage the Assyrian crisis by clever alliances. Their wisdom perished, not because it lost the argument, but because God did something it had never reckoned with.

God has done this before. He gave Abraham a son at a hundred, brought Israel out of Egypt with no army, and brought them home from Babylon by a pagan king’s decree; every time, the experts had established that it could not be done (Isaiah 55:8–9). Then the pattern reached its centre. The scribes and chief priests of Jerusalem and the officials of Rome examined Jesus, weighed him and disposed of him, and on their own terms they were right: he died. On the third day God raised him, and every calculation that had finished him was overturned. There Isaiah’s word came true at full scale.

When your family thinks it is beneath you. You have a brother, or a daughter at university, or a colleague, who is not hostile but kind and faintly embarrassed on your behalf, as if you were an intelligent person with one inexplicable exception. This verse tells you three things. It is predicted: you have met exactly what Paul said would happen. It is not that you explained it badly: Paul explained it better than you, and the folly verdict came in anyway. And, which changes how you pray, the difference between the two responses is not intelligence. Both hear the same words; what separates them is which road they are on, and that is God’s business. So answer as well as you can, kindly and without heat, and then pray for him, because what he needs is not a cleverer you but an opened eye.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is irrational or that Christians should despise thinking; this letter is itself a sustained piece of careful argument. The foolishness lies in the content, a crucified Saviour, not in the minds of those who believe it. We are to be always ready to give a reason (1 Peter 3:15), and simply not shocked when the reason is found absurd.

Does “being saved” mean I am not saved yet? You are saved, you are being saved, and you will be saved, all at once. The moment you trusted Christ you were justified, forgiven and adopted, and that can never be undone (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8). Now God is working that salvation out in you, freeing you from sin’s power day by day (Philippians 2:12–13). At Christ’s return he will complete it, raising your body and removing sin altogether (Romans 13:11; 1 Peter 1:5). Your salvation is not uncertain; it is unfinished, and the one who began it will finish it.

parallels.desc: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world’s best minds never came to know God by their wisdom, so God chose to save those who believe through a message the world calls foolish.

Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Each names a recognised professional: the Greek philosopher (sophos), with an explanation for everything; the scribe (grammateus), the Jewish scholar of the law; and the debater (syzētētēs), the professional arguer who could take either side and win. Between them they stand for every route by which the ancient world thought truth might be reached: reason, expert study of Scripture, and skilled speech. The form is borrowed from Isaiah’s taunts, “Where then are your wise men?” (Isaiah 19:12; 33:18): the language of a battlefield after the fact, when the confident men who explained beforehand why it would go the other way are nowhere to be found.

Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? By the cross God showed all human wisdom to be foolish in the matter of knowing him. He did not argue with it. He simply did what it said could not be done, and left it standing in the empty field.

Two wisdoms. The sentence contains two wisdoms, and everything turns on keeping them apart. It was God’s wisdom that arranged matters so that human wisdom, with all its philosophy and religion, would not find him (Romans 1:21–22); the failure was not an accident God worked around but the design, so that salvation would be by grace (on the phrase, see “Uncertain wording” below). To know God here means more than knowing that he exists. It means knowing him as he is and trusting him, the knowledge Jesus calls eternal life (John 17:3), which philosophy and religion never reached.

Why would God arrange such a thing? Not because knowledge of him is unavailable: the creation broadcasts it so plainly that nobody is left with an excuse (Romans 1:19–20). The barrier was never a shortage of evidence, but that the mind doing the looking is not neutral. We do not merely fail to find God; we suppress what we find, because the God who is actually there is not one we would have chosen, and he does not leave us in charge. The problem is moral before it is intellectual, which is why more information alone has never yet converted anybody.

The folly of what we preach. So God closed the route that would have let the clever arrive first, and opened one anybody can walk, and it was his good pleasure. “What we preach” (kērygma) is the content of the message, not just the act of preaching. Paul does not say God saves through folly, but through the message the world files under nonsense. Of all the ways he could have saved, he delighted in the one that leaves no one out for lack of brains or breeding, and lets no one in because of them. His means is preaching, and what he asks is believing; neither requires a degree.

The Son who makes the Father known. If the world could not know God through its wisdom, how is he known at all? Jesus answered in a prayer that reads like a commentary on this verse. He thanked his Father for hiding these things from the wise and understanding and revealing them to little children, and said that no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11:25–27). The road closed in verse 21 has one door, and the door is a Person. That is a mercy with a wide reach: if philosophy were the road, the woman running a household on no sleep and the man whose schooling ended at fourteen would be shut out; instead a professor and a child stand at the same distance from the door. What we preach is not a better philosophy but Christ, the only one who has seen the Father and made him known (John 1:18).

Then what about people who never hear the gospel? Scripture is plain that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, and faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:13–17; Acts 4:12). Creation and conscience leave everyone without excuse, but they cannot tell anyone that God has given his Son for sinners (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). That is why this is a missionary verse: it pleased God to save through preaching, so the church must send preachers. We need not fear that God is unjust; the Judge of all the earth will do right, and those who perish are judged for the light they had and rejected. Infants who die in infancy are in a different case: we hold that elect infants are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on that mercy, and on the Lord who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

Uncertain wording. “In the wisdom of God” can be read in two ways. It may mean the wisdom God displayed in creation and in his dealings with the world, all around people and yet not leading them to know him (Romans 1:19–21); or God’s wise purpose, which ordained that the world would not find him by its own wisdom. Both are true to Paul, and the phrase may hold both. The second fits the flow of the sentence best and is the reading followed here: God in his wisdom ordered things so that salvation would come through the message received by faith, not as a prize for human cleverness.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews want power and Greeks want wisdom, and a crucified Messiah offends both, yet to those God calls he is exactly the power and the wisdom of God. The same message that trips one hearer and amuses another saves a third.

For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom. Two cultures, each with its own test of what counts, and the cross passes neither. Many Jews wanted miraculous proofs of power (Matthew 12:38; John 6:30), not unreasonably: God had authenticated Moses with plagues and Elijah with fire, and they were waiting for a Messiah who would do something visible about Rome. Greeks sought wisdom: a philosophy that satisfied the mind, beautifully argued.

But we preach Christ crucified. Paul gives neither. The verb is present: he kept doing it. He did not lead with the resurrection to soften the entrance, or translate the cross into something more presentable; he went into the most status-obsessed city in Greece and announced an executed criminal. “Crucified” is in a Greek form that describes a past event with lasting effect: the risen Christ is for ever the one who was crucified. The cross is the heart of the message, not an embarrassing detail.

A stumbling block to Jews. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels. For Jews it also meant God’s curse, for a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). A crucified Messiah was not merely a failed one but a contradiction in terms. Paul’s word is skandalon, scandal: not an intellectual objection, but something you trip over and go down.

And folly to Gentiles. The Greek objection was different and just as total. Crucifixion was not a subject for polite society; Cicero said the very word “cross” should be kept far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts, eyes and ears. Worshipping a crucified Jew was not merely false but tasteless, too grotesque to merit a rebuttal. One of the earliest surviving pictures of the crucifixion is a mocking graffito scratched on a wall in Rome, showing a man worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, and the caption: “Alexamenos worships his god.”

But to those who are called. Then the sentence turns. Not to those who worked it out, or were open-minded or better educated, but to the called: summoned by God in a way that brings them to faith. To one hearer Christ crucified is a stumbling block, to another nonsense, and to a third the identical message is the power and wisdom of God. Nothing about the sermon changed. What changed was that God called them.

Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The cross does not abolish the Jewish hunger for power or the Greek hunger for wisdom; it satisfies both, in the last place either would have looked. They wanted power: here is the power of God that saves, in a man led out after a flogging, whose crossbeam a passer-by was forced to carry (Mark 15:15, 21). They wanted wisdom: here is the wisdom of God that planned salvation, in an event that looks like the collapse of every plan, the wisdom by which a holy God is just in forgiving sinners (Romans 3:26).

The wisdom of God with nails through it. He could have come with the signs they demanded; he had done greater things with a word, and twelve legions of angels were his for the asking (Matthew 26:53). He chose instead the one form of death designed to make a man contemptible, and went to it deliberately, in public, outside a city wall, between two criminals, for people who were at that moment shouting for it. The Jews asked for a sign and were given the only one that could save them. The Greeks asked for wisdom and were handed the wisdom of God with nails through it. There has never been a moment in the history of the universe when God looked less like God, or was more fully himself (Colossians 2:14–15).

Our own two hungers. Our age has the same two: a faith that works and a faith that is intellectually respectable. They are right to want power and wisdom, but both demands can be ways of staying in charge of what God must be like. The cross refuses both on our terms and meets both on God’s.

If only the called believe, why should I evangelise or pray? Because the call comes through the preaching. God does not call people in a vacuum; he calls them through the message of Christ crucified, spoken by ordinary believers (Romans 10:14–17). The effectual call is not a reason to stay silent but the reason to speak with hope: you cannot produce faith in anyone, but God can, and he has chosen to do it through words like yours. So pray, because the calling is his; and speak, because the calling comes by the word. Without the effectual call, evangelism would be hopeless. With it, no one is beyond reach.

Where Christians differ: the general call and the effectual call. Many Christians, Arminians among them (those who hold that God’s grace enables every hearer to believe but can be finally resisted), understand God’s call as an invitation that grace makes it possible to accept or refuse; they want to guard the genuineness of the offer and human responsibility, and those are real concerns. This commentary’s view: the gospel is genuinely offered to all who hear it, and all are commanded to believe (the general call). But Paul here speaks of those who are called as distinct from the rest who hear and stumble. This is the effectual call, God’s inward work by the Spirit that makes the gospel powerful in the elect, so that they come freely (Romans 8:30; Westminster Confession 10.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1). The first can be refused, and constantly is. The second is God doing in a man what the man could not do in himself. The difference between those who believe and those who mock is God’s calling, not human cleverness.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels; for Jews, a crucified man was under God’s curse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What looks like God’s foolishness and weakness at the cross is wiser and stronger than anything human beings can do. Paul borrows the world’s verdict in order to overturn it.

The foolishness of God is wiser than men. Read flatly, the sentence is close to blasphemy, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing: very well, call it foolishness. Set the cross against the accumulated wisdom of the human race, every philosophy, every ethical system, every scheme for making people good, and ask which of them has actually dealt with guilt: not managed it or explained it away, but dealt with it. The wisest scheme the world has devised leaves a man with his record and his conscience intact and no remedy for either. What the world calls foolish removed the record.

The weakness of God is stronger than men. The cross looked like weakness: the Son of God helpless, mocked, dying. Rome’s machinery of force was used that Friday to full effect, and it worked: the man died. Three days later he was alive, and nothing in Rome’s armoury could put him back in the tomb. By the cross God defeated sin, death and Satan (Colossians 2:15). What was at work there was not weakness with a good result but strength of a kind the world had no name for. He saves by dying. He reigns from a cross. He conquers by being conquered.
