Into your own weakness. We assume God works through our strong points, where we are competent and impressive, and that our weaknesses are the parts of us he has to work around. This verse says the opposite about him, and Paul will later say the opposite about himself: it was in his weakness that Christ’s power rested on him, which is why he stopped asking for the thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

So should I not bother developing my abilities? No. Your abilities are gifts from God; develop them and use them gladly (Matthew 25:14–30). The point is where you put your trust. Strength used in dependence on God is a tool in his hand; strength trusted instead of God is an idol, and he will often break it. Weakness is not a virtue in itself; it is the place where we stop pretending and lean on him, which is why he does so much there. Work hard, and pray as one who knows the results are his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God chose nobodies, so that the only boast left is in the Lord. Paul tells the Corinthians to look round their own church: few were educated, influential or well born (v. 26). God chose the foolish, the weak and the despised on purpose, to shame the proud and show that rank counts for nothing with him (vv. 27–28), so that no one can boast before him (v. 29). Everything they need, wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption, is theirs in Christ, and it is God who put them in him (v. 30). So Jeremiah’s word stands: boast in the Lord (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Boasting and Grace Alone

Verses 28–29 carry the logic of grace into the life of a church: when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors and people the world overlooks, the only boast left is in the grace that did what merit never could (see the note on vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social ladder was steep: citizens over freed slaves over slaves, the educated over the illiterate, patrons over clients. The church crossed every one of those lines, and the crossing came from the gospel of the cross. Now: A church that quietly copies the class and status lines of its surrounding culture denies in practice what it confesses in its creed. The cross makes a community where the only boast is in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians themselves are the proof of God’s method: he chose mostly ordinary people, and did it on purpose, to shame those the world admires.

Consider your calling, brothers. Look at it (blepete). Paul has argued the point theologically for eight verses; now he tells them to check it against the evidence in their own congregation.

Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards. Literally “according to the flesh”: judged as the world judges. The three terms were the usual measures of status in the ancient world, education, influence and birth, which decided where you sat and who returned your greeting. Many of the Corinthian believers were probably slaves, freedmen and workers. But Paul says “not many”, not “none”, and the church proves that too: Crispus and Gaius (vv. 14–16), and Erastus the city treasurer (Romans 16:23). The gospel is not a movement of the poor that shuts out the comfortable; God saves treasurers as well as slaves. But they were the exceptions, and everybody in the room knew it.

What the critics said. The outside world knew it too. More than a century later the pagan critic Celsus was still sneering that Christianity was a religion of wool-workers, cobblers and laundry-workers, who would say nothing in front of educated men but got hold of children and women in back rooms. He meant it as a demolition; he was describing what Paul says God did on purpose.

But God chose. The verb comes three times in verses 27–28. God chose the people the world overlooks, on purpose: not to bypass the strong but to shame them, by the simple fact of the outcome. When people who could never have found God by wisdom are plainly full of God, the whole apparatus of wisdom stands exposed as useless for the one thing that finally mattered. Nor is it a new policy. He picked a childless couple to found a nation, a shepherd boy over seven older brothers, a young woman in a village of no reputation to carry the Son of God, and fishermen and a tax collector to take the gospel to the world (1 Samuel 16:7; Luke 1:52; Matthew 11:25).

The Lord came by the same road. When God sent his own Son, he sent him this way too: born to parents who could offer only the poor family’s sacrifice of two birds (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8), raised in a town people sneered at (John 1:46), known in his own village as the carpenter (Mark 6:3), and in the end despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3). The church at Corinth looked like its Lord. God did not choose weak people in spite of having a strong Saviour; he chose them because his Saviour came weak, and the shaming of the wise that began in a manger was finished on a cross.

Without a trace of embarrassment. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The Son who could have gathered the wise and the well-born round his throne has filled his house with wool-workers and cobblers, slaves and freedmen, and people like us, and he presents them to his Father unashamed: “Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13). The world looked at the church in Corinth and saw a back room full of nobodies. The Father saw the brothers and sisters of his Son, chosen before they were born, called by name, and already his.

For the ordinary Christian. You are not a leader, you have no platform and no obvious gift, your life has been spent on work nobody records, and you have settled into believing that the real work of God is done by others and your part is to make up the numbers. The verse is not a description of your limitations but of God’s preference. He did not accept the unimpressive because nobody better applied. He chose them, for a reason that has nothing to do with their inadequacy and everything to do with what he intends to show.

Isn’t Christianity just a crutch for the weak? Celsus has had many heirs. In the nineteenth century Friedrich Nietzsche made the charge with real brilliance: Christianity, he argued, was a revolt of the weak against the strong, the resentment of people who could not win on the world’s terms and so declared weakness a virtue. In softer form it is among the commonest objections today: faith is a crutch for those who cannot cope. Paul concedes a surprising amount of it: look round the room; not many of you were strong. But he does not let the strong off so lightly. Everyone leans on something: a career, a reputation, a body that still works, a bank balance, the good opinion of the right people. The question is never whether we lean but whether what we lean on will hold. Nor is the gospel the resentment of the weak. At its centre stands the one truly strong person in history, who chose weakness, not because he could not win, but to lift people who never could. Christianity is not for people too weak to face life. It is for people who have stopped pretending to be strong, and that, if we are honest, includes everyone.

Should the church then not bother reaching the educated and influential? It should reach everyone; Paul reasoned with philosophers in Athens and spoke before governors and kings (Acts 17:22–31; 26:1–29). “Not many” is not “none”, and the gospel is for the powerful as much as the poor. What this verse forbids is courting people for their status, giving the rich man the good seat (James 2:1–4), or thinking the church will be strengthened chiefly by attracting impressive people. A church that seeks only the influential has forgotten how it began. Reach everyone, honour everyone, and expect God to fill his house mostly with people the world overlooks.

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose the nobodies to bring the somebodies to nothing, so that no one can ever boast before him. Here is where the chapter has been heading: salvation leaves no room for human credit.

Low and despised. The language intensifies: not merely the foolish and weak now, but the low (agenē, without family, of no birth) and the despised (exouthenēmena, treated as nothing).

Even things that are not. Then a phrase that goes past every social category: ta mē onta, the things that do not exist, people whose names are on no list and whose absence would alter nothing. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank this was no metaphor: a slave was hardly a person in the eyes of the law. Things that are not are the nobodies; things that are are the somebodies. God uses nobodies to bring the somebodies to nothing (katargeō), showing that their rank counts for nothing with him. The phrase is God’s signature, for he “calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). When he builds a church out of nobodies, he is not making the best of poor material, but doing what he has always done, in the way he has always done it.

The God who raises the dead. Romans 4:17 sets the two halves of God’s method side by side: he gives life to the dead and calls into existence what does not exist. Paul goes on to say where that power was finally shown: in the God who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:24–25). At the cross the world counted Christ among the things that are not, a dead man in a borrowed tomb. On the third day God called him out of it. The church of nobodies at Corinth is the same power at work again: people the world counts as nothing, raised with Christ into a life the somebodies of Corinth could never buy.

So that no human being might boast in the presence of God. This is the purpose of election: God’s free choice, before the foundation of the world, of particular people to be saved in Christ, grounded in his own love and not in anything he found in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). If he chose people for their wisdom, power or birth, or saved them by achievement, effort or sincerity, somebody would arrive with a contribution and a reason to be pleased with himself. By choosing nobodies, he excludes all boasting (Romans 3:27; Ephesians 2:8–9). When Isaiah, a prophet and a master of words, saw the Lord high and lifted up, he did not mention his gifts; he cried woe to himself, a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:1–5). Nobody boasts in that light, and the only people who can stand there are people brought in by grace. When heaven is finally full, there will be one figure in it who is not there by grace, and every voice will be occupied with him: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:11–13).

What it does not mean. Not that God chose people because they were lowly. Lowliness is not merit either. God chose freely, and the lowliness of those chosen displays that freedom.

For the one who feels like a nothing. Some readers struggle not with pride but with the settled sense of being a nobody: years that produced nothing anyone could point to. This verse is addressed to you. The nothings are what he chose (see vv. 26–27), and he chose them to bring to nothing the things that are. He is not collecting the overlooked to keep them safely at the back, but deploying them to dismantle everything the world has been impressed by. That is not a consolation prize. It is a commission.

If no one may boast, is it wrong to feel pleased with something I have done well? No. Paul himself rejoices over the work God did through him (15:10; 2 Corinthians 1:12). There is a right gladness in work well done, a child well raised, a kindness that landed. The difference is where the credit goes. Boasting before God treats the thing as my ground of standing, my reason to be accepted, my proof that I am better than others. Gratitude receives it as his gift, worked through me, and gives him the praise. A simple check: can you rejoice as much when God does the same through someone else? If so, you are probably giving thanks, not boasting.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the Corinthians were hunting for in teachers and status is already theirs in Christ, and it was God who put them in him. Christ himself is their wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.

Because of him you are in Christ Jesus. Literally “from him” (ex autou): God is the source of your being in Christ, not your searching. Union with Christ is God’s work, and every gift that follows arrives by that route.

Who became to us. Paul does not write that Christ gives us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, but that he became them to us. You do not receive four parcels dispensed from a distance; you receive him, and he turns out to be all four. That is the cure for Corinth. They were shopping: wisdom from Apollos, status from their gifts, standing from their faction. The shopping was over before it began. Everything they were assembling piecemeal was already theirs in one Person.

Wisdom from God. The city was full of wisdom for sale, and true wisdom stood in front of them in Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Not that a Christian knows more about everything, but that he knows the one thing on which everything finally depends: who God is, and how a guilty man may stand before him.

Righteousness. Christ is our right standing before God: his righteousness is counted to us, which is justification (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Not that God has made you a good person and now accepts you, but that in Christ his record is credited to you and yours charged to him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: it comes from outside you, reckoned to you rather than produced in you, and so not subject to how your week has gone. It answers the question underneath all religion: how can I possibly be right with God? You cannot. He became it for you.

And sanctification. Christ is our holiness, the word of verse 2. In him we are set apart for God before ever we begin to grow holier, and from him we receive the Spirit who makes us holy (on how the status and the growth fit together, see the note on vv. 2–3).

And redemption. Release (apolytrōsis), especially release secured by a ransom, as when a slave or captive was set free. Christ is our release, bought with his blood (Ephesians 1:7). It looks back to a price paid, and forward to a deliverance not yet complete, when the body itself is set free at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

The whole of a Christian’s life. Side by side they cover the whole of a Christian’s existence: wisdom for the mind that could not find God, righteousness for the guilt that could not be removed, sanctification for the life that could not be cleaned, redemption for the body that will not last. All in one place, and that place is a Person. The wisdom has a face; the righteousness has hands with holes in them; the sanctification was purchased by a man who took our sin on himself; the redemption cost the Redeemer everything he had. There is nothing a soul requires that is not, at this moment, at the right hand of the Father in a body that still bears the marks of what it cost to obtain it.

If Christ is my sanctification, do I need to make any effort? Yes, and gladly. Paul tells the same Corinthians to flee sexual immorality, to discipline the body, and to be steadfast and immovable (6:18; 9:27; 15:58). Christ being your holiness does not make you passive; it makes your effort hopeful. You work out your salvation because God is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13), and the Spirit you received from Christ is the power by which you fight. The difference from religion is the direction: you strive not to become acceptable but because you are accepted, and every step of growth is drawn from him. Effort without Christ is self-improvement; Christ without effort is a misunderstanding.

Where Christians differ: imputed righteousness. Some deny that Christ’s righteousness is counted to believers, saying instead that God makes us righteous inwardly and accepts us on that basis. This commentary’s view: Christ became our righteousness. Our right standing with God is not our own inner goodness but Christ’s obedience counted to us, received by faith alone (Romans 4:5–6; 5:19). Sanctification, which follows, is the inward renewal, distinct from justification but never separated from it. Those who hold the other view, including the Roman Catholic Church, rightly insist that grace really changes people, and Paul agrees; he simply will not let the change become the ground of our acceptance. Both are found in Christ, so the one who has Christ has both.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s Greek does not make plain how the four nouns relate. The ESV’s wording, “wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption”, reflects a common reading: Christ became our wisdom from God, and that wisdom consists in the three that follow. Others read four gifts side by side. The first fits the chapter well: the wisdom the world could not reach turns out to be not a philosophy but a rescue.

parallels.desc: the LORD is our righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since everything comes from God in Christ, the only boast left is in the Lord, and the Lord is Jesus.

As it is written. Paul cites Jeremiah 9:24 in shortened form, and the full sentence is the whole argument of this chapter written six centuries earlier: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me” (Jeremiah 9:23–24). Set wisdom, might and riches beside verse 26, wise, powerful, of noble birth, and you see why Paul reached for it. He has been preaching Jeremiah’s sermon to Corinth; the grounds of human boasting have not altered, only the words.

Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord. The verse does not say “stop boasting”. The instinct to have something to point to, some answer to whether your life amounts to anything, is not removed when a person becomes a Christian but redirected; Paul glories freely in the cross (Galatians 6:14). The question is never whether you will glory in something, but in what. And Jeremiah’s right boast is not an achievement but that you understand and know the LORD. Even the boast is not about you.

The LORD is Jesus. In Jeremiah the one to be known is the LORD, the covenant name later generations would not even pronounce. Paul condenses the sentence to “boast in the Lord” and applies it, without a syllable of explanation, to the crucified man he has been preaching since verse 18. The Lord in whom we boast is the Lord Jesus, Yahweh come in the flesh.

The name will bear the weight. The chapter that began with people boasting in Paul, Apollos and Cephas, in their own eloquence and knowledge and rank, ends by taking every prop away and putting a single name in the empty space. And the name will bear the weight. Wisdom fades, might is buried and riches pass to someone else, but the Lord we boast in has been raised from the dead and will never die again (Romans 6:9). Nothing that happens to us can make him less worth boasting about. A church with nothing to bring him has been given the one boast that will still be true on the last day, and still ringing after it.

In the flow. Boasting runs through the whole letter (3:21; 4:7; 5:6), and the next paragraph applies the same rule to the preacher himself (2:1–5). A church that has learned to boast only in the Lord has nothing left to build a faction with.

In everyday life. Recall the last time you felt diminished and what your mind reached for to restore itself: a qualification, a child doing well, a theological position more rigorous than the other person’s. Whatever you reached for is your boast, whatever you would say in church, and time can take every such thing from you. It cannot take the boast Jeremiah names.

What does boasting in the Lord sound like in real life? It sounds like telling people what God has done rather than what you have done: how he found you, carried you through the illness, answered a prayer, forgave a sin you thought unforgivable. It sounds like giving the credit away when you are praised, not with false modesty but with honest thanks, and speaking of Christ with the warmth you would use for a person you admire. And on the bad days it sounds like this: “I have nothing, but I have him.” Boasting in the Lord is not a religious technique. It is what people naturally do about the thing they treasure most.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,<sup>2</sup>To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus,<sup>5</sup>that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—<sup>6</sup>even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you—<sup>7</sup>so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>8</sup>who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>9</sup>God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.<sup>10</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment.<sup>11</sup>For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.<sup>12</sup>What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.”<sup>13</sup>Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?<sup>14</sup>I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,<sup>15</sup>so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name.<sup>16</sup>(I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)<sup>17</sup>For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.<sup>18</sup>For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.<sup>19</sup>For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”<sup>20</sup>Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?<sup>21</sup>For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.<sup>22</sup>For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom,<sup>23</sup>but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles,<sup>24</sup>but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.<sup>25</sup>For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.<sup>26</sup>For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.<sup>27</sup>But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;<sup>28</sup>God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,<sup>29</sup>so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.<sup>30</sup>And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,<sup>31</sup>so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

keyVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter. The factions of vv. 10–17 grew from judging the gospel and its preachers by the world’s wisdom; here Paul shows that the message itself turns that measure upside down, and the rest of the chapter, the crucified Christ and the church of nobodies, unfolds it. The same words that sound like nonsense to one hearer are God’s saving power to another, which is why the church can never improve the message by dressing it up.

1.reflection:
Paul calls a badly behaved church “sanctified” and “saints”, and promises they will be “guiltless” on the last day, before he corrects anything (vv. 2, 8). Why do you think he starts there? How does it change the way you face your own failures, and the way you correct others?

The Corinthians said “I follow Paul” or “I follow Apollos” (v. 12). What are the modern equivalents, in our own church or online, and how do Paul’s three questions in verse 13 answer them?

Verses 18–25 say the cross looks foolish and weak to the world. In what ways are we tempted to make the gospel more impressive or acceptable, and what is lost when we do?

God chose people the world overlooks, so that no one could boast before him (vv. 26–31). What do you reach for when you want to feel that you count? What would it look like this week to boast in the Lord instead?

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 carries on Paul’s answer to the factions (1:10–4:21). Chapter 1 dealt with the message and the people God chose; now Paul turns to the preacher, and to the wisdom he preached.

The message. The gospel of Christ crucified is not too simple for clever people but too deep for them: God’s own wisdom, which no one can know unless his Spirit shows it. So Paul would not dress it up, for faith built on a speaker’s skill rests on the speaker. And this wisdom belongs to no elite: everyone who has the Spirit has the mind of Christ.

Why it was said. The Corinthians admired polished speakers, found Paul unimpressive beside Apollos, and liked to think of themselves as the spiritual and mature (see the introduction). Paul answers: his plainness was a decision, and true wisdom is not something anyone climbs up to.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul recalls his arrival (vv. 1–5): no lofty speech, only Christ crucified, preached in weakness and fear, so that their faith would rest on the Spirit’s power. Yet the gospel is not against thinking (vv. 6–9): it is God’s wisdom, hidden and settled before the ages for our glory, which the rulers missed when they crucified the Lord of glory. It comes only by revelation (vv. 10–13), from the Spirit who searches the depths of God and taught the apostles their very words. So the natural person cannot accept it, the spiritual person discerns it, and Isaiah’s unanswerable question is answered: “we have the mind of Christ” (vv. 14–16). Few passages say as much about how God makes himself known, gave us Scripture and opens our minds to it.

Where it leads. God’s hidden wisdom turns out to be a crucified Person. Israel’s title for God, the King of glory, belongs to a man nailed up outside a city wall (v. 8). And the Spirit comes out of the depths of God not to show us a God behind Christ’s back but to show us Christ, and give us his mind.

For us. Rest your faith on God’s power, not on polish. If you are afraid to speak of Christ, so was Paul. When you open your Bible, or speak to someone who finds the cross foolish, ask the Spirit for what you cannot supply. And remember that the mind of Christ is a servant’s mind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith must rest on God’s power, not on a preacher’s skill, so Paul came to Corinth with nothing to offer but Christ crucified. He refused the orator’s lofty style (v. 1) because he had resolved to make the crucified Christ his whole message (v. 2). He came weak and afraid (v. 3), and what convinced his hearers was not persuasive technique but the Spirit’s power (v. 4), so that their faith would stand on God and not on him (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s plain preaching is not only a pastoral strategy; it comes from what he believes. The power of the gospel is the Spirit working through the word of the cross, not the preacher’s skill, the brilliance of the argument or emotional pressure on the audience. The preacher is the instrument, not the cause. If people are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything the preacher can add.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth the travelling orator was a celebrity who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee and move on (see the note on vv. 3–5). Now: The modern pressure is to make church “compelling” through production values, platform charisma and emotional manipulation. Paul’s answer is not to be deliberately dull, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came to Corinth with one message, Jesus Christ crucified, and deliberately refused to dress it up. His plain preaching was a decision, not a lack of skill.

When I came to you. Paul goes back to his first visit (Acts 18:1; see the introduction), before Apollos came with more polish. “And I” ties this to the end of chapter 1: a foolish message, unimpressive converts (1:26–31), and now an unimpressive preacher. From first to last the power was plainly God’s.

Lofty speech. Superiority, excellence (hyperochē): the elevated style of the professional orator.

I decided. I reached a verdict (ekrina): Paul did not drift into a plain style; he chose it. A popular reading says he had tried philosophy at Athens (Acts 17), failed, and arrived at Corinth chastened. It is probably wrong: Luke does not present Athens as a failure (Acts 17:34), and Paul still quotes a pagan poet in this letter (15:33). This is a settled resolve about content.

The centre that governs everything. “Nothing … except Jesus Christ and him crucified” cannot be taken woodenly: this very letter deals with lawsuits, marriage, idol food, worship, gifts and the resurrection. The cross was not one topic among many but the lens for all of them. When the Corinthians squabble over food, Paul ends with the brother for whom Christ died (8:11); when they abuse the Supper, he takes them back to the night he was betrayed (11:23). Every practical problem in this church is finally settled at a cross.

And him crucified. Not Jesus Christ alone, who could have been made respectable as a great teacher or moral example, but him crucified. Without the offensive part you have a religion the world can admire, but one that saves nobody. All the wisdom of God is gathered into that one event: the Son of God lifted up on a Roman cross, bearing the sin of the world. A preacher may spend his life on it and never reach the bottom; we will spend eternity on it and never tire.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul preached only on the crucifixion: he taught the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), all of it flowing from the cross. Nor is it an excuse for despising learning; the man writing it was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3) and is in the middle of a sustained argument. And a church taught only how justification works, never how to be a husband, handle money or forgive, is not fed the way this letter feeds.

What is the message of Christ crucified? That Jesus, the eternal Son of God made man, lived the perfect life we have not lived, and died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing the punishment our sins deserved, so that God is just in forgiving us (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). That he was buried and raised on the third day, proving the payment accepted (15:3–4). And that everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven, counted righteous and made a child of God, freely, contributing nothing. If you can say that clearly to a friend, you can do what Paul did at Corinth.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “the mystery of God” instead of “the testimony of God”; the ESV notes this. Either way, the content is God’s message about Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came weak and afraid, without the orator’s techniques, so that the Corinthians’ faith would rest on God’s power and not on him.

Weakness, fear and trembling. Do not make this more dignified than it was. Paul had just been beaten and jailed at Philippi, run out of Thessalonica and Berea by mobs, and politely mocked at Athens (Acts 16:22–17:34). He arrived alone. During that stay the Lord said to him in a vision at night, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent” (Acts 18:9–10). You do not say that to a man who is not afraid. Paul is not embarrassed by his fear; he argues from it.

Not in plausible words. Persuasive (peithos): the techniques of rhetoric designed to win an audience. Travelling orators were the celebrities of cities like Corinth, judged on voice, bearing and style, paid for their performances and followed by admirers. Paul refused to compete on their terms.

Demonstration of the Spirit. A proof that settles a matter (apodeixis, a technical term in rhetoric). Paul claims something better than persuasion, and locates it outside himself: the Spirit’s power, convicting hearts, bringing new birth, and in the apostolic ministry accompanied by signs (2 Corinthians 12:12; 1 Thessalonians 1:5).

Resting on God’s power. This is the point, and it is about foundations. A faith produced by a persuasive man lasts as long as he stays persuasive, and a cleverer speaker can undo it, as had begun to happen at Corinth; if he falls, those who built on him find nothing underneath. Faith that rests on God’s power stands.

Weak in him. Paul’s trembling was not an accident the message happened to survive; it matched the message. The gospel he carried was about a Lord crucified in weakness who lives by the power of God, and Paul says that he and his companions are weak in him too, yet live with him by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). A swaggering herald of a crucified King would contradict his own announcement. The preacher’s weakness was a small copy of the weakness of the cross, and the power that raised Christ from the dead was at work in both.

Fear is not disqualifying. It is easy to assume that God uses the confident, and that you would be useful if you did not go dry-mouthed when the conversation turns to Christ. The founding missionary of the Gentile world arrived at Corinth shaking. The Lord who stood by a frightened apostle in the night and said “Do not be afraid” stands by every trembling witness, and the faith he builds rests on him, so it cannot fall.

What does the Spirit’s demonstration look like today? Chiefly what it looked like at Corinth: people convicted of sin, turning to Christ and being changed. The church itself was the proof: idolaters, thieves and drunkards washed, sanctified and justified (6:9–11). In the apostolic period the Spirit also confirmed the message with signs, and this commentary holds that those sign gifts belonged to that foundational time, because Scripture presents them as the marks that authenticated the apostles and their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians believe they continue; both agree that the greatest miracle has never ceased, a dead heart made alive through a plain message. Look for that, pray for it, and do not despise it because it is quiet.

Textual note. The King James Version’s “enticing words of man’s wisdom” follows later manuscripts; the earliest lack “of man’s”, and the sense is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel is the deepest wisdom there is, and only God’s Spirit can make it known. Paul does speak wisdom among the mature: not the wisdom of this passing age but God’s secret plan, settled before time for our glory (vv. 6–7), which the rulers missed when they crucified the Lord of glory (v. 8). No human faculty could find it; God has revealed it by his Spirit, who alone knows God’s thoughts (vv. 9–11). Believers have received that Spirit to understand God’s gifts, taught in words the Spirit gave (vv. 12–13). So the natural person cannot accept these things, while the spiritual person discerns them (vv. 14–15), for we have the mind of Christ (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the main ground for what is called the inward witness of the Holy Spirit. Calvin rested the believer’s certainty about Scripture not on outside proofs but on the Spirit’s own witness in the heart, and Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned, the Spirit alone reveals them, and he has been given to those who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for polished rhetoric over Paul’s plain preaching was at root a preference for a wisdom they could judge by their own natural abilities. Now: It is tempting to judge the gospel by academic or cultural standards, as if the question were whether Christianity can hold its own in a university seminar. Good reasons matter, and defending the faith serves evangelism, but cannot replace it: only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory (see the note on v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is not too simple for the wise: it is God’s own wisdom, planned before time for our glory and opened to all who have his Spirit. After a chapter and a half of demolishing the world’s wisdom, Paul says the Christian message is wisdom after all, just not of a kind the world can recognise or reach.

Among the mature. Not an inner circle trusted with deeper material, as in the mystery religions. The word (teleioi, the grown-up) means all who have the Spirit and accept the gospel, as opposed to the natural person (v. 14): not a rank but an age, for Paul’s contrast a few lines later is between adults and infants in Christ (3:1), one family at different stages.

The sting. And there is a sting. The Corinthians thought themselves the mature elite. Paul says “among the mature we do impart wisdom”, and a few lines later tells them he could not do it with them, because they were still on milk and squabbling like children (3:1–3): a rebuke delivered by holding the door open and observing that they cannot yet walk through it.

Doomed to pass away. The rulers of this age, who crucified Jesus (v. 8), are being brought to nothing with the age they rule.

A hidden wisdom. Literally, “God’s wisdom in a mystery” (mystērion). In Paul’s hands a mystery is never a puzzle to be solved but a secret God has decided to tell (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:4–6), and to the whole church, not to a few. And the secret has a name: God’s mystery is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:2–3), “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27).

Decreed before the ages. Predestined, determined beforehand (proorizō). The cross was not God’s recovery from an unexpected disaster but the plan made in eternity, before there was anybody to be saved by it (Ephesians 1:4; Revelation 13:8).

For our glory. Not merely our rescue: God meant not simply to get us out of trouble but to bring us somewhere, to share the glory of the Christ who is in us (Romans 8:30; Colossians 1:27), with a body raised imperishable, in glory, in power (15:42–43). Before there were stars, the Father, the Son and the Spirit had settled the cross and set their love on a people to bring to glory. The wisdom the rulers could not see was older than their thrones, it will outlast them, and its end is a company of sinners shining with the glory of the Son who died for them.

The right side of history. Every age believes its leading minds have finally seen clearly; ours speaks of the right side of history, which makes disagreement look not merely mistaken but backward. Nearly a century ago the historian Herbert Butterfield warned against what he called the Whig interpretation of history, reading the past as a steady climb towards ourselves. Paul had watched Roman justice, the temple’s leadership and the crowd’s common sense agree about Jesus, and all be wrong about the question that mattered most (v. 8). That should humble the confident of every party, traditionalist and progressive alike. The Christian does not need history’s verdict, because history is not the judge. It has a Lord, who was once on its losing side, nailed up outside a city wall, and the verdict that lasts was given on the third day.

In everyday life. If God settled this before the ages, the thing you are most anxious about is happening inside a plan complete before the world was made. That does not tell you how it will go. It tells you that it is not being improvised, and that the decree which reaches back before time reaches forward to a glory you have not yet seen (Romans 8:29–30).

Does “for our glory” put us at the centre instead of God? No. Our glory is a share in his: being made like Christ, seeing his face, reflecting his likeness (Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18), the glory of a mirror catching the sun, not of a lamp lit by itself. And the whole plan is to the praise of his glorious grace (Ephesians 1:6, 12, 14). God’s glory and our good are not rivals: he is most glorified in giving his people the greatest gift, himself, and we are most glad receiving it. So long for the glory to come without embarrassment; it is God’s idea, and all his doing.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world’s rulers did not recognise God’s wisdom when it stood in front of them, and so they crucified the Lord of glory. Yet their blindness served the very plan they could not see.

None of the rulers. They thought they were getting rid of a troublemaker; they were carrying out God’s plan (on who the rulers are, see below).

Was the cross a blunder? If they had known, they would not have done it. Did Satan, then, miscalculate, so that better-informed powers would have prevented the atonement? The New Testament’s answer is one of the most important things to grasp about how God governs the world. Peter puts both halves in one sentence at Pentecost: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The plan was fixed, and the men who executed it were lawless and guilty; neither half cancels the other. The Jerusalem church prays the same: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined (Acts 4:27–28). They freely did what they wanted. What they wanted had been decreed.

Blind because they were evil. So the ignorance was real, and they are to blame for it: they were blind because they were evil, and God used that very blindness. It is the pattern of Joseph and his brothers written across the history of the world: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The devil got exactly what he wanted, and it destroyed him: through death the Son destroyed the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).

The Lord of glory. Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts (Psalm 24:7–10; 29:3). Paul gives that title, without explanation, to a man his readers knew had been flogged and nailed up between two criminals. The one they crucified was God the Son. The phrase is stunning and exact: because Christ is one person with two natures, divine and human, what is true of either nature may be said of the person.

Coming down would have lost us. The King of glory came to his own gates and they did not lift up their heads; they crucified him. He made the wood and the iron in the nails, and kept the hearts of the men who drove them beating through every hour of it. And he did not come down, because coming down would have saved him and lost us (John 1:10–11). His glory was never brighter than in that hour (John 12:23; 17:1).

When someone has wronged you. You need not believe that what was done to you was good, or that the person meant anything but harm. The cross shows that God can make evil serve him without its ceasing to be evil: the worst act in history is the one he used to save the world. So bring it to the cross. Do not call the evil good, and do not tell yourself God was absent. Tell him what was done, and then, when you are able, say with Joseph: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” It may take years before you see how.

Did God die on the cross? The person who died was God the Son, so in that sense yes, and the Bible says so (Acts 20:28). But he died in his human nature, not his divine nature: his body died and his human soul was separated from it, while his divine nature, which cannot die, did not cease, and the Trinity was never broken apart. This is no technicality: the one who bore your sin was God himself, so the sacrifice has infinite worth, and he truly died as a man, so he could stand in a man’s place. Only one who is both God and man could do both.

Uncertain wording. Who are “the rulers of this age”? Some take them as the human authorities: Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin. Others take them as the spiritual powers working behind them (Ephesians 6:12). The best reading is probably both: the New Testament shows Satan working through named human beings at exactly this point (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What no one could ever see, hear or imagine, God has now made known by his Spirit, who knows God through and through.

No eye has seen. This sentence is often quoted alone, at funerals and on cards, to say that heaven is beyond imagining, and that turns it inside out. Verse 10 completes it: God has revealed these things. Quoting verse 9 without verse 10 makes Paul say the opposite of what he wrote.

Three faculties ruled out. The quotation closes every route: what we can see for ourselves (eye), what others tell us (ear), and the most we could ever imagine (heart). That leaves one possibility: God had to say it himself.

Prepared for those who love him. Salvation in Christ now as well as glory to come. Isaiah had prayed for God to rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1); when he did, many eyes saw Jesus and many ears heard him, and still they did not see who he was. When Peter confessed him as the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but his Father in heaven (Matthew 16:16–17). That is this verse in a single scene: the thing prepared is Christ, and only God can show him.

Revealed to us. Unveiled (apokalyptō). “Us” means first the apostles, through whom God gave the revelation that became the New Testament, and then all believers who receive it.

The depths of God. “Searches” does not mean the Spirit is exploring a God he does not yet fully know; it is the language of complete access to God’s inmost thoughts. Only someone who is himself God can know the depths of God: strong evidence that the Spirit is God.

The same Spirit in ordinary believers. That Spirit is given to ordinary believers. So a person with no education can read a page of Scripture and genuinely meet God there, while a hostile expert reads the same page and finds nothing but literature.

The one person who has been told. At a graveside we need not say we cannot imagine what has happened to the one we loved, because God has told us: that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8); that the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16); that this perishable body will put on the imperishable (15:53); that he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The Christian at a funeral is the one person in the room who has been told. God did not leave us guessing; he sent his own Spirit out of his own depths to tell us what he has prepared.

What it does not mean. Not that we know everything about heaven; much remains unseen (1 John 3:2). But the heart of God’s plan is revealed.

Is the Holy Spirit a person or a power? A person, and God. Only a person searches, knows, teaches and can be grieved (v. 13; Ephesians 4:30), and only God knows the depths of God. Not an influence sent out from God, like warmth from a fire, but the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son, who comes to live in believers himself. So we call him he, not it, and may pray to him, worship him and rely on him, knowing that his delight is to point us to Christ (John 16:14).

Uncertain wording. “As it is written” introduces Scripture, but the words are not an exact quotation of any one Old Testament verse. The closest is Isaiah 64:4, with echoes of Isaiah 65:17; Paul seems to be quoting loosely and drawing passages together, and the exact source is not certain. The meaning is clear either way: what no human faculty could reach, God has given.

parallels.desc: from of old no one has heard or perceived

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God’s Spirit knows God’s mind, and God has given that Spirit to believers so that they can grasp what he has freely given them.

The spirit of that person. An ordinary analogy that settles a great deal. No one can know what you are thinking unless you tell them; someone who has lived beside you for thirty years can still be surprised. There is a room in every human being that only God sees into (Psalm 139:1–4).

So also the Spirit of God. Scale that up. If one creature is closed to another, there is no route from outside into the inner life of God: the cleverest investigator stands at a door with no handle on his side. Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. The Spirit is one with God, sharing his inner life, yet a distinct person who reveals (v. 10) and teaches (v. 13).

Not the spirit of the world. The outlook of fallen humanity, absorbed simply by living here, and behind it perhaps the spirit at work in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2): instincts about what matters, what success looks like, what is faintly ridiculous. It can assess a career or a reputation, but has no equipment for the things of God.

But the Spirit who is from God. The door has been opened from within (Romans 8:9). God has not merely sent information about himself; he has given the one person who has always been inside, to ordinary believers in a quarrelsome congregation in a port city.

Freely given. The things graced to us (charizomai, from the same root as grace). Here is the double gift: God gives, and then gives the capacity to know what he has given. Without the second, the first would sit unrecognised, like a deed in a language its owner cannot read.

What has been freely given? The rest of the New Testament lists the gifts. Forgiveness: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace” (Ephesians 1:7). A new standing: righteous before God in Christ, not on probation (1:30). A new name: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, so that we call him Father (Galatians 4:6). A future: a body raised imperishable (15:42). And beneath them all, the Giver himself. Paul uses the same verb in Romans: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Having given the costliest thing, the Father will hold back nothing smaller. And these are given, not lent or sold: you did not deserve them, and you do not lose them by having a bad week.

All that the Father has is mine. Jesus described this verse before Paul wrote it. On the night before the cross he said that the Spirit of truth would glorify him, taking what was his and declaring it to them, and that all the Father has is his (John 16:14–15). The things freely given us are the Father’s things, held by the Son and opened to us by the Spirit. The Spirit never shows us a God behind Christ’s back; every depth of God he opens has Christ at its centre.

In everyday life. When you pray, do not only ask for what you lack. Thank him, one gift at a time, for what he has already put in your hands.

What it does not mean. Not that believers have private revelations beyond Scripture. The Spirit helps us understand what God has given and revealed in his word.

If I have the Spirit, why does my Bible reading so often feel dry? Because the Spirit’s help is not the same as excitement. His work is to make you understand and believe what is there, and he often does it slowly, like rain soaking into soil rather than a flash flood. Dryness can come from tiredness, distraction, unconfessed sin, or a season in which God teaches you to keep going by faith. Keep reading; ask his help before you open the page; read slowly, and talk to him about it as you go (Psalm 119:18). The passage that seemed dull on Tuesday is often the one that holds you up on Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles passed on God’s truth in words the Spirit himself taught them, not in words of human cleverness.

Words taught by the Spirit. The claim goes a step further: the Spirit gave not only the message but the wording. This is a key text for verbal inspiration (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). God did not give the apostles a general impression to dress in whatever language came to hand, which is why Scripture can be studied at the level of a single word. If only the ideas were inspired, the words would be packaging.

The promise of the upper room. This rests on Jesus’ promise that the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send in his name, would teach them all things and bring to their remembrance all that he had said to them (John 14:26), and guide them into all the truth (John 16:13). So the New Testament is not the church’s memories of Jesus, slowly improved. It is Christ keeping his word to teach his people through the men he sent, and to hear them is to hear him (Luke 10:16).

Real men, God’s words. The human authors were not suppressed: Paul’s Greek does not read like Luke’s, and this letter shows its author unable to remember whom he baptised (1:16). The Spirit used real men, styles and limits included, and the result is exactly what he intended. The Spirit who searches the depths of God bent down to teach fishermen and a former Pharisee the very words to write, so that a farmer in any century could hold God’s speech in his hands.

Scripture interprets Scripture. One possible rendering of the last clause, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (see below), describes something Christians do constantly, whether or not Paul meant it here: an obscure verse is read in the light of a clear one (Westminster Confession 1.9). So the reader of the whole Bible understands any part of it better than one who knows three favourite chapters very well.

If the very words are inspired, which translation is the real Bible? Inspiration belongs strictly to the words as the prophets and apostles first wrote them in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. But God has preserved those words with remarkable care, and a faithful translation is truly the word of God to you, because it carries what God said (Westminster 1.8; 1689 1.8). Good modern translations differ mostly in style and readability, not doctrine. So read a reliable translation with full confidence, compare another when a verse puzzles you, and know that no doctrine of the faith hangs on a disputed reading.

Where Christians differ: inspiration. Some say the Bible contains God’s word but that its words are merely human, and may contain errors. This commentary’s view: Paul says the words, not only the ideas, were taught by the Spirit. Scripture is God-breathed in all its parts, without error in all it affirms, while using the personalities and styles of its human authors (Westminster 1.4–5, 8; 1689 1.4–5, 8). The Spirit did not dictate mechanically, but guided the writers so that what they wrote was exactly what God intended.

Uncertain wording. “Interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual” is genuinely difficult. The Greek is compressed (pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes): literally, combining spiritual things with spiritual. It may mean explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people (the ESV text), comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, or expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words; the ESV notes these alternatives. The direction of the argument is not in doubt: the Spirit’s truths are conveyed in the Spirit’s words and received by the Spirit’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without the Spirit, a person cannot welcome the things of God or see them for what they are; they look foolish to him. The problem is not intelligence but spiritual life.

The natural person. One of the hardest sayings in Paul. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos, soulish, living only by natural human life) has everything natural birth supplies and nothing more: someone without the Spirit. He may be a brilliant philosopher.

Does not accept, and not able. Paul says two things about him. He does not accept (dechomai) these things: he may understand the words, but the gospel seems foolish to him (1:18). And he is not able (ou dynatai): a lack of ability, not just of willingness, the more uncomfortable claim. They can only be discerned (anakrinō, examined, judged) rightly with the Spirit’s help.

Stating it carefully. Paul is not saying that unbelievers are less intelligent, or cannot give an accurate account of Christian doctrine; many do it better than most churchgoers. Such a person cannot receive these things as true and desirable, because he has nothing in him that can see them, like a man born blind hearing a colour described. Sin damages not only the will, so that we will not come, but the understanding, so that we see nothing worth coming for. And the root is moral rather than intellectual: the cross looks foolish to a man not because he has thought hard and found a flaw, but because he is estranged from the God it reveals.

The teacher of Israel. Jesus met this verse in person. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, was as learned and devout as the natural man ever gets. Jesus told him that unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3), and pointed him to the Son of Man lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14–15). The cure is not a better argument but new birth (regeneration), the Spirit giving life to someone dead in sin, as little earned as his first birth (Ephesians 2:4–5; Titus 3:5), so that he looks at the crucified Christ and lives.

The face you had found foolish. You were the natural person once: unwilling, unable, and sure the cross was foolish. Then the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” shone in your heart, to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the face you had found foolish became the one you love most. The same Spirit can open any heart, and the hardest case you know is not too hard for him.

Then why say anything to anybody? If my brother-in-law cannot receive it, what am I doing at Christmas dinner? The answer is that God has appointed the message as the very means by which he gives the ability. He does not wait for people to become able; he sends the preacher and makes them able. Luke records it in one line about a businesswoman at Philippi, Lydia: Paul spoke, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14). Two things happened; only one was Paul’s. Ezekiel, told to preach to a valley of dry bones, the least promising congregation in Scripture, is not asked whether they can respond. He is told to prophesy, and while he prophesies the bones come together (Ezekiel 37). The preacher’s job was never to produce life, but to speak while God produced it. So this verse makes evangelism bearable. Your relative is not persuaded by evidence he cannot fault not because you argued badly, but because argument was never the missing ingredient. Keep speaking when the door opens, and ask God by name for the one thing you cannot supply (2 Corinthians 4:4–6).

Is this not just a way of saying that anyone who disagrees is blind? Paul does not use it to avoid arguments: this letter answers objections at length and lists the witnesses to the resurrection (15:3–8). Reasons matter, but they are not enough, because the deepest resistance to the cross is not in the head. A sceptic can test that honestly: “If the gospel were true, would I want it to be?” Whoever finds the answer is “no” has learned that his problem is not only the evidence. Many honest doubters do want it to be true and still struggle; to them we owe patience and good reasons, and they may bring their doubt to God in prayer.

If unbelievers cannot understand, how can God hold them responsible? Because their inability is not like a missing limb; it is the inability of a heart that does not want God. A man who hates his brother so much that he cannot forgive him is not excused by his cannot; the cannot is the guilt. So the natural person cannot receive the things of God because he loves darkness rather than light (John 3:19–20; Romans 1:18–21). No one will stand before God and say he wanted Christ but was not allowed; everyone who wants him may come (John 6:37). The wonder is not that some are lost but that any are saved.

Where Christians differ: total inability. Some teach that unbelievers have the natural ability to receive the gospel if they choose to, and God’s grace only assists them; many Arminian Christians hold instead that God’s grace restores to every hearer the ability to accept or refuse. Both views are held by sincere believers who want to honour human responsibility. This commentary’s view: Paul says the natural person is not able to understand the things of the Spirit. Sin has darkened the mind and enslaved the will (Ephesians 4:18; Romans 8:7). This is total inability: not that unbelievers are as bad as they can be, but that they cannot turn to God by their own power. Only the Spirit, by regeneration, opens the heart (Acts 16:14; Westminster Confession 9.3, 10.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 9.3, 10.2).
verseByVerse.note: The “natural person” is someone without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A person with the Spirit can weigh all things in God’s light, while the world without the Spirit is in no position to pass verdict on him. The point is not the Christian’s superiority but the world’s incompetence in this particular court.

Judges all things. The spiritual person (pneumatikos) is anyone who has the Spirit: every true believer, not a superior class (see the note on vv. 6–7). “Judges” is the word of verse 14: discerns, examines, evaluates. This is no claim to be right about politics or medicine or his own motives. He is given the capacity to see what the world is, what a life is for and what the cross means, which no natural brilliance supplies.

Seeing everything by the cross. What does he see that others miss? Paul’s own letter answers. He looks at sin tolerated in a church and sees Christ our Passover lamb, sacrificed (5:7); at the human body, and sees a temple of the Spirit, bought with a price (6:19–20). He judges all things because he measures all things by Christ crucified.

Judged by no one. The natural person cannot properly evaluate the spiritual person, any more than a blind man can judge colours. And the one who sees most clearly of all, who judges all things perfectly and is judged by no one, is the Lord Jesus himself, who was judged by the world’s courts and condemned, so that we might stand uncondemned in his.

A sentence often abused. It has been misused by leaders to place themselves beyond accountability, by teachers to dismiss every objection as unspiritual, and by ordinary Christians who do not wish to be corrected: “You are not in a position to assess me; I am spiritual.” It has protected a great deal of harm. The letter itself shows it cannot mean that: Paul pronounces judgment on a Corinthian believer’s conduct (5:3), and tells them to weigh one another’s prophecies (14:29) and settle disputes between brothers (6:5). Believers are not above correction; it is unbelievers who are not qualified to judge spiritual truth.

When your family thinks you have thrown your life away. Think of the son who turned down the career for the mission field, the woman whose relatives regard her faith as a phase she should have outgrown, the man his colleagues have filed under harmless and rather sad. On this subject, Paul says, they are not competent to reach a verdict. That is not arrogance: they are assessing a spiritual matter with instruments that do not reach it, and their conclusion tells you about the instruments, not about you.

In everyday life. The world’s opinion of your faith is not the final word; your brother’s opinion of your behaviour very often is. To use this verse against correction from other believers turns a sentence about the world’s incompetence against the people God gave you to correct you. When you last felt that people do not understand you, was your critic outside the faith, or a Christian who loves you and had noticed something true?

Does “judges all things” mean Christians should have a strong opinion on everything? No. The spiritual person discerns the things of God: what is true about God, sin, Christ and the life that pleases him. On the many questions Scripture does not settle, from investments to much of politics and science, a Christian may be no wiser than his neighbour, and should say so. Discernment shows less in opinions than in seeing ordinary things in God’s light: recognising an idol in a good thing, noticing pride in your own heart, hearing the gospel distorted. It grows by soaking in Scripture (Hebrews 5:14), not by speaking first.

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can reach God’s mind by his own wisdom, yet believers have been given the mind of Christ. Paul closes the argument with a question from Isaiah and an answer that ought to be impossible.

Who has understood the mind of the Lord? The quotation is Isaiah 40:13 (also Romans 11:34), and its setting matters. Isaiah has just described a God who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighs the mountains in scales, and asks: “Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?” The Greek translation Paul quotes renders “Spirit of the LORD” as “mind of the Lord”. The expected answer is “nobody, ever”: no human can know God’s mind by his own wisdom, much less teach him.

But we have the mind of Christ. A breathtaking claim. In Isaiah, the mind of the Lord is the mind of Yahweh; Paul equates it with the mind of Christ. We cannot reach God’s mind, but we have Christ’s mind given to us by the Spirit: his way of thinking, revealed in the apostolic gospel. “We” means first the apostles, then all believers who receive their teaching. The unreachable has been given.

Nobody has instructed him. Nobody has instructed him, improved his plan, or contributed a single thought he did not already hold. Then he came, unrecognised, and was crucified by the men he was dying for. And he has given his own mind to a Corinthian church that could not stop arguing about preachers, and to every frightened preacher and ordinary believer since. “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33–36).

What it looks like. It can be recognised: to begin valuing what he values and to be unimpressed by what once impressed you: to look at a difficult person and see someone he died for, to ask what would be honest rather than advantageous, to feel the pull of the poor and the unimportant in a way that has no natural explanation. It grows, because someone else’s mind has been given to you.

The mind of Christ is a servant’s mind. Paul at once turns this on the Corinthians, whose jealousy showed they were thinking like the world (3:1–3), and the phrase is still used to end arguments. Your convictions are not automatically his, and the phrase is no weapon against other Christians. Elsewhere Paul describes the mind of Christ not as superior opinions but as an attitude: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:5–8). A man who appeals to “the mind of Christ” chiefly to win arguments is describing something else.

How do I grow in the mind of Christ? By keeping company with him where he speaks. Read the Gospels and watch how he thinks: whom he notices, what angers him, what he refuses, how he prays. Let Scripture correct your instincts, especially where it surprises you, and ask the Spirit to renew your mind (Romans 12:2). Practise it in small things: choose the lower place, forgive quickly, speak the truth kindly, serve someone who cannot repay you. Spend time with mature Christians in whom you see it. Growth is slow, and often noticed only looking back, but sure, because the one who gave you his mind is at work to form it in you.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom.<sup>2</sup>For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.<sup>3</sup>And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling,<sup>4</sup>and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,<sup>5</sup>so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.<sup>6</sup>Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away.<sup>7</sup>But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.<sup>8</sup>None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.<sup>9</sup>But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”—<sup>10</sup>these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.<sup>11</sup>For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.<sup>12</sup>Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.<sup>13</sup>And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.<sup>14</sup>The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.<sup>15</sup>The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.<sup>16</sup>“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

keyVerse.quote: For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the centre of the chapter and of the whole letter. The rest of the chapter explains why Paul could be content with so plain a message: the crucified Christ is God’s own hidden wisdom, planned before the ages and made known only by the Spirit. Every problem the Corinthians brought him would be settled in the light of this one Person and this one event.

2.reflection:
Paul says he came to Corinth “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (v. 3), and preached plainly so that their faith would rest on God’s power (v. 5). Why does it matter what our faith rests on? What tempts us, as a church or as individuals, to rely on polish, personality or performance instead?

The rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, yet in doing so they carried out God’s plan (vv. 7–8; Acts 2:23). How does this help you think about evil done to you, or suffering you cannot explain?

Verses 10–14 say that only the Spirit can open a person’s eyes to the things of God. How should that shape the way we read the Bible, and the way we speak to friends and family who find the gospel foolish?

“We have the mind of Christ” (v. 16). What would it look like for that to show in your thinking and choices this week? How can the phrase be misused, and how does Philippians 2:5–8 guard against that?

3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 completes Paul’s answer to the divisions that began at 1:10. He has set the folly of the cross against the wisdom of the world (chapter 1) and shown that true wisdom is given only by the Spirit (chapter 2); now he applies both to the quarrels over leaders, before holding up the apostles themselves as the pattern in chapter 4.

The message. The church is not yours to divide, because it is God’s: his field, his building, his temple. Its leaders are only his servants, Christ is its only foundation, and God himself will judge what is built on it. So stop boasting in men. You are far richer than your factions: all things are yours, because you are Christ’s.

Why it was said. The Corinthians thought themselves spiritual and wise, and had lined up behind favourite teachers: “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos” (v. 4). In a city where people rose by attaching themselves to impressive patrons (see the introduction), they were ranking preachers like celebrities, and the church was splitting along those lines.

How the chapter makes its case. Their jealousy and strife prove they are still infants, behaving just like everyone else (vv. 1–4). In a farming picture, Paul planted and Apollos watered, but only God gave the growth, so the workers are nothing, one in purpose, and each paid for his labour (vv. 5–9). In a building picture, Christ is the only foundation, and the Day will test by fire what each builder has put on it (vv. 10–15). That building is God’s temple, holy because his Spirit lives there, and he will destroy whoever wrecks it (vv. 16–17). So the wise must become fools, and no one may boast in men, for everything is theirs already (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. The chapter opens by calling the Corinthians babies and ends by handing them the world, life, death, the present and the future. Nothing in them changed between the two; what makes the difference is whose they are. Christ is the foundation God laid, the Lord whose Day will test every work, the true temple in whom God came to live among us, and the heir of all things, who shares his whole estate with people who had done nothing to deserve it.

For us. Every church is tempted to follow personalities and to measure ministry by results. This chapter asks what we are building, on what, and for whom, and it sets us free from rivalry: no one needs to borrow glory from a leader who already belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Quarrelling over leaders shows that a church is still immature, because it has forgotten that both the work and the growth are God’s. Paul could feed the Corinthians only milk, and their jealousy and strife prove they are still infants, behaving like everyone else (vv. 1–4). Paul and Apollos are only servants, each doing what the Lord assigned: one planted, one watered, and God gave the growth (vv. 5–7). So the workers are one, each paid for his labour rather than his results, and the church belongs to neither of them: it is God’s field and God’s building (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated point that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Neither Paul nor Apollos converted a single soul. So a minister cannot take credit for results, cannot treat apparent fruitlessness as simply his own failure, and cannot be ranked against another minister as if their different “results” measured their different abilities.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions measured Paul and Apollos by their outputs, and Paul refuses that measure (see the note on v. 8). Now: Paul’s answer still stands: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God who gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
