verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had to treat the Corinthians as spiritual babies, and years later they still were. They were truly in Christ, but not yet ready for anything beyond the first truths of the gospel.

Not as spiritual people. The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual (pneumatikoi), wise and mature; they had the gifts, the knowledge, the tongues. Paul takes the label off them in his first sentence. Of the flesh (sarkinos) means made of flesh: still governed too much by the old ways of thinking. Infants (nēpioi) are babies.

Milk, not solid food. Milk is the first truths of the gospel; solid food, deeper teaching and application (Hebrews 5:12–14). When Paul first came, milk was all they could take, and that was normal. But solid food never means leaving the cross behind: the Christian who moves on from the cross has not advanced; he has wandered off.

Even now. What stings is not that they were immature when he arrived, as everybody is, but that years have passed and nothing has changed. An infant is delightful. A man who has been an infant for years is a tragedy.

Growing up into him. Both words matter. “In Christ” means their place with God rests on him, not on their progress; a slow believer is as safe as a mature one, and a baby in a father’s arms is no less his child for being unable to walk. “Infants” means this life is meant to grow: no longer tossed about by every wind of teaching, but growing up in every way into Christ, the head (Ephesians 4:14–15). Maturity is not becoming more impressive, which is what Corinth wanted, but more like Jesus. The milk and the solid food are the same Christ crucified (2:2), taken in more deeply until he is formed in us.

In everyday life. Ask what you were like ten years ago in the one area where you are hardest to live with: your temper, your tongue, your resentment. Growth shows up there, and the best judge of it is whoever shares your house. If you are not growing, your standing in Christ has not slipped; ask the Spirit for growth and feed on his word (1 Peter 2:2).

How would you know? Here the people most confident of their maturity are the ones who lack it. Paul’s test, in the next verse, is jealousy and strife (v. 3), not knowledge: the Corinthians were enriched in all knowledge (1:5), and it had not made them adults. One can gather information about God for thirty years and remain a toddler.

How do I move from milk to solid food? Less by learning harder doctrines than by practising what you already know: the mature are those whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant practice (Hebrews 5:14). Read the whole of Scripture steadily; sit under faithful preaching and ask how it applies to you; obey what you were last convicted about; spend time with older believers whose lives show the fruit. Above all, let the gospel go deeper. Mature Christians do not need the cross less; they see more of it, and it shapes more of them.

Where Christians differ: the carnal Christian. Some teach two kinds of Christians: spiritual Christians, who have surrendered to Christ as Lord, and carnal Christians, who have accepted him as Saviour but live permanently as if unconverted. They usually want to explain real Christians who are struggling, and they are right that believers can be immature. This commentary’s view: Paul is rebuking immaturity in true believers, not describing a permanent, acceptable category. The real contrast in these chapters is between the natural person, who does not have the Spirit at all (2:14), and the believer who has the Spirit and is not yet living like it. All true believers have the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and are being changed (2 Corinthians 3:18), though at different speeds, and Christ is received as both Saviour and Lord. A profession of faith that never produces any change is not saving faith (James 2:17; 1 John 3:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21). That warning is not aimed at the believer who grieves over slow growth: the grief itself is the Spirit’s work.

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jealousy and quarrelling show that a church is still living by the flesh, however gifted it is. By that ordinary measure the Corinthians were behaving no differently from the unbelievers around them.

Still of the flesh. Here the word is fleshly (sarkikos): governed by sinful human nature, and the measurement is startlingly ordinary. Jealousy (zēlos) is the heat of being unable to be glad at another’s advantage; strife (eris) is the quarrelling that follows. Not exotic wickedness but the ordinary weather of a church committee, yet in Paul’s list of the works of the flesh these two sit beside idolatry and sorcery (Galatians 5:20). We rank them low because they are respectable.

Behaving only in a human way. Literally, walking according to man: the sharpest phrase in the verse. The church was running on the ordinary principles of competitive Corinth: rank, rivalry, the instinct to join the winning side. Nothing was happening there that could not be seen in a trade guild or a political faction. The Spirit had been given to them, and you could not tell from the outside.

The measure they never thought to use. The Corinthians measured maturity by tongues, knowledge and impressive teachers. Paul measures it by whether they can get on with each other, which is what Jesus said would mark his disciples to a watching world: their love for one another (John 13:35). The love chapter will say it again: gifts without love are noise (13:1–3).

Was Paul crucified for you? Paul has already given the cure, in the questions that opened his argument: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1:13). Rivalry needs a scoreboard, and at the cross there is none: everyone stood there with the same debt and was bought with the same blood. Envy shows that my worth has come to depend on my ranking, so every rise in someone else feels like a fall in me. The cross settles a believer’s worth outside every ranking, in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and a person whose worth is settled there can afford to be glad when others are blessed. The love that replaces envy has a measure, given on the night he was betrayed: “just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34). Envy wants another person’s place; Christ gave up his own for people who had wronged him.

There is no envy in God. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand; the Son delights to glorify the Father; the Spirit does not speak on his own authority but takes what is Christ’s and makes it known (John 3:35; 16:13–14). The life of God has always been glad giving, with no rivalry in it, and that Spirit is given to us to replace our envy with his love.

In everyday life. Name the person in your church whose success you find hardest to be glad about, whom you are slightly relieved to hear criticised. There, on Paul’s measurement, you are still an infant. That is not said to condemn: a diagnosis is the first mercy. Confess the jealousy to God by name, knowing he forgives it (1 John 1:9), and pray for that person’s good today (James 3:14–16).

Is every disagreement in church fleshly? No. Christians can disagree honestly, and Paul himself argues hard in this letter. What makes a disagreement fleshly is its spirit: envy, the need to win, taking sides around personalities, contempt, refusing to listen, spreading the quarrel. Could you pray warmly for the person you disagree with, and be glad if God blessed him? A disagreement held in love, aimed at the truth and the good of the church, is not strife; one that has become about me is.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “and divisions” after “jealousy and strife”, which is why the King James Version reads “envying, and strife, and divisions”. The meaning is unchanged.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ranking Christian leaders is worldly, because they are only servants through whom God brought you to faith. Paul asks not who they are but what they are, and answers with one humble word.

For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? Paul now names only himself and Apollos, perhaps the two who had worked in Corinth. A church divided this way looks exactly like everybody else (v. 3).

What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Paul says “what”, not “who”: he asks what job these men do, not how important they are. He refuses to be a celebrity.

Servants through whom you believed. One word: diakonoi, servants, often the one who waits at table, who brings the food and is not the reason anyone came. The Corinthians have organised their church around a debate about waiters. “Through whom” means they were only the channel: the faith came from God.

As the Lord assigned to each. Even the differences they quarrel over were handed out by the Lord: Apollos’s polished speaking and Paul’s founding of the church are facts about what God gave each man, not reasons to prefer him. You cannot build a hierarchy out of gifts that were distributed rather than earned.

The Lord who waits on us. The greatest servant of all came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), and took the towel to wash his disciples’ feet. And the Lord who assigned is Christ: grace was given to each one according to the measure of Christ’s gift, and the ascended Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers to his church (Ephesians 4:7–11). To boast in one of them is to quarrel over a friend’s gifts while forgetting the friend. They believed through these men, but in him, and he sent the men. When we stop arguing about the waiters, we see at the head of the table the Master who first waited on us.

Comparison is an argument with God. You hear a gifted preacher and come away diminished or quietly competitive; another ministry flourishes while yours does not. Paul’s cure is not to try harder at humility but to remember the word “assigned”: envying another person’s gift is, underneath, an argument with God about what he chose to hand out.

Why do we need someone to follow? In the 1970s the psychologist Robert Cialdini and his colleagues noticed that American students wore their university’s colours more often after their football team had won, and said “we” more readily about a victory than a defeat: basking in reflected glory, they called it. We attach ourselves to a winner, a preacher, a party or a brand, because a little of their shine seems to fall on us and our own worth feels too thin. That is the hunger beneath “I follow Paul”: borrowing significance from someone more impressive. The gospel turns it round: the Lord of glory attached himself to us at our lowest, and is not ashamed to call us his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). You need not bask in anybody’s light when the Son of God has chosen to be known as your brother.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers deserve no honour. Elders who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17). But they are servants, not masters.

What if I really do benefit more from one preacher than another? That is natural and not sinful; God gives different gifts. Receive the help gratefully. The danger is preference turned partisan: belittling the other preacher, staying away when your favourite is not speaking, treating your liking as a measure of spirituality. Thank God for the servant who feeds you best, and be fed gladly by the others, for all bring food from the same Master’s kitchen.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God can give spiritual life, so the preachers he uses are nothing beside him. Paul planted and Apollos watered, but the growth was God’s work from start to finish.

I planted, Apollos watered. Paul brought the gospel to Corinth first (Acts 18:1–11); Apollos came later and built up the young church (Acts 18:27–19:1). But God gave the growth. In Greek, “planted” and “watered” are finished actions, while “gave” is ongoing: God was causing the growth all along.

What no farmer can do. A farmer can prepare the ground, sow, water and weed, and a lazy farmer produces a poor crop. But no farmer has ever made a seed germinate; life is not among the things he supplies. That is the exact shape of Christian ministry. Preaching, hospitality, patient friendship, years of prayer: all worth doing well, and not one of them can produce spiritual life in another human being.

Neither is anything. Literally, neither of them is anything at all: Paul gives his own life’s work the value zero in the column that matters. Not that the work was pointless, for each will receive wages (v. 8), but that he could not supply the one thing needed, the life itself. And if both men are nothing, the argument is over.

A growth that is from God. Jesus used the same picture: the seed sprouts and grows, the sower knows not how (Mark 4:26–27). The body, holding fast to the Head, grows with a growth that is from God (Colossians 2:19): the life of the risen Christ flowing into his members. A preacher can describe Christ; only God can make a dead heart alive together with him (Ephesians 2:4–5).

Laid in the ground like a seed. The God who gives the growth gave the first growth of the new creation on a Sunday morning: his Son was laid in the ground like a seed, and God raised him, the firstfruits of a harvest still coming in (15:20). Every believer since belongs to that harvest. God did it for his Son, he does it again each time a sinner believes, and he has never once needed his gardeners to be clever.

For those who have prayed for years. This is the verse for the parent whose adult child has walked away, the wife whose husband remains politely unmoved, anyone who has explained, invited, wept, watched nothing happen, and begun to suspect the failure is theirs. You were never able to give the growth, and neither was the apostle Paul. That does not make your planting and watering worthless. God ordinarily uses such means, for people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). So name the person to God, ask him for the one thing only he does, and go on planting. This verse removes a burden you were never given and could not carry.

If God gives the growth, should a church bother to plan, train and evaluate? Yes: farmers who trust God for the harvest still plough straight furrows. Paul planned his journeys, trained co-workers and thought hard about how to reach people (9:19–23); such things are part of faithful planting and watering. What the verse rules out is thinking that the right method guarantees results, measuring faithfulness by numbers, or taking credit when things grow. Plan carefully, work hard, and pray as people who know that without the Lord nothing will come up at all.

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Planter and waterer serve one purpose, and God will pay each for his toil, not for his results. There is no gap between them for a faction to occupy.

He who plants and he who waters are one. Literally, they are one thing (hen eisin): one in purpose, serving the same Lord, aiming at the same harvest. The Corinthians made them rivals.

Wages according to labour. Each worker will be rewarded by God, not according to success, which belongs to God, but according to labour (kopos): toil, the kind of work that wears you out. Results were never the servant’s to produce, so they cannot be his measure. The Corinthians compared outputs, as every generation since has done with attendance figures and reach. God notices the toil nobody saw, and on the last day he will say to servants with very little to show, “Well done, good and faithful servant”, and welcome them into his own joy, as though that joy were their wages, when it was his gift all along.

My recompense is with my God. The Lord Jesus walked this road first. In Isaiah the Servant of the Lord says that he has laboured in vain and spent his strength for nothing, yet his right is with the Lord and his recompense with his God (Isaiah 49:4), and the New Testament hears that Servant’s voice in Christ (Luke 2:32, echoing Isaiah 49:6). By the measure of results his ministry ended badly; he left the verdict with his Father, and the Father answered by raising him and giving him the nations. Every servant who labours with little to show stands where his Master stood, and is paid by the same God.

For the faithful who saw little. The missionary who gave forty years to a hard field for a handful of converts; the village pastor while the church in the next town filled up; the mother whose children do not believe. Each may have concluded the life was wasted. The arithmetic is wrong: results were never the thing being weighed. The Lord who gives the growth does not charge his servants for the growth he chose not to give.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by labour. Salvation is a gift (Romans 6:23), and Paul will shortly say that the man whose work burns is saved anyway (v. 15). What is paid for is not your entrance but your labour, and even the reward is God crowning his own gifts.

Will some believers have more in heaven than others, and will that not cause envy? Scripture does speak of differing rewards (Luke 19:17–19; 2 Corinthians 5:10), but never of rivalry. Every believer will have all of Christ and be perfectly satisfied, as a small cup and a large cup may both be full, and with sin gone we will rejoice in every other believer’s reward as gladly as in our own, since each will display God’s grace. In the vision of Revelation the elders cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Whatever we receive, we will give back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church belongs to God, not to its leaders: they are his workers, and the people are his field and his building. “God’s” comes three times in one short verse.

God’s fellow workers. Paul and Apollos labour side by side in a field that is not theirs, and that is no demotion. The dignity of Christian work never came from our importance to it, but from whose work it is.

You are God’s field. A field is not divided into plots belonging to different farmers. The Corinthians have been marking out territory in ground that belongs to somebody else.

God’s building. Paul switches pictures, and not carelessly. A field is forgiving: if a crop fails you sow again. A building goes up in a fixed order, every course resting on the one beneath; the stakes have risen.

I will build my church. When Jesus first promised the church, he said: on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). My church: it is his. I will build: he is not a distant patron funding the work but the builder on site, using his servants as his tools. So every true addition to the building, every person brought to faith and every life built up, is work he is doing.

What it does not mean. A church is not a voluntary society belonging to its members, a platform belonging to its minister, or a heritage belonging to the families who have been there longest. None of them holds the title deeds; God does.

Then who makes the decisions in a church? Christ does, through his word, and every church structure is a stewardship under him. Christians differ on how that works out, through elders with the congregation’s consent, a congregational vote, a presbytery or bishops, and faithful believers hold each view from Scripture. Whatever the order, this verse applies: leaders are servants answerable to the owner, members are workmen and not shareholders, and every decision should begin with the question, what does the Lord of this field want? A meeting that forgets that question has forgotten whose meeting it is.

Uncertain wording. “God’s fellow workers” (synergoi) can be read in two ways: workers alongside God, sharing his work, or fellow workers who belong to God, labouring together in his field. The Greek allows both. The context, which stresses God’s ownership and the workers’ smallness (v. 7), favours the second. Either way, the work is his.

parallels.desc: the planting of the LORD

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ is the only foundation, so everyone who builds on it must take care how he builds, because God will test the work and defend the building. Paul laid the foundation, Jesus Christ, and no other can be laid (vv. 10–11). What others build on it, lasting or worthless, will be shown for what it is on the Day, when fire tests it: good work is rewarded, while the builder of worthless work loses it and is saved only as through fire (vv. 12–15). And the building is God’s holy temple, where his Spirit lives, so whoever destroys it God will destroy (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

In a city full of pagan temples, Paul claims that the living God now lives, by his Spirit, not in a building of stone but in a community of flawed, quarrelsome people. This is the new covenant fulfilment of the Old Testament temple: God with his people, through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were more than social trouble: the factions were demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live (see the note on vv. 16–17). Now: That gives church unity a weight that mere niceness cannot: we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus Christ is the one foundation God has laid for his church, so everyone who builds on it must take care how he builds. Paul laid it by God’s grace; others now build on it, and they will answer for their work.

According to the grace of God given to me. Paul neither boasts nor pretends to a modesty he does not feel: he states his skill and says where it came from, grace, in the same breath (15:10).

A skilled master builder. The master builder (architektōn) lays the foundation and hands the site on to others: to Apollos, and every generation of teachers since.

Take care how he builds. This warning governs the rest of the chapter. It is addressed first to teachers, but everyone in a church is building something, and the question is how.

No other foundation. The foundation is not open for discussion. Christ crucified, as preached by the apostles, is the only foundation (Isaiah 28:16; Ephesians 2:20), and a church built on anything else is not a church of God. Everything a church is depends on who he is and what he did. Its peace with God rests on his death for sinners; its life on his resurrection; its message is his gospel; its hope is his return. Take any away and nothing else can bear the weight; there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:11–12). Even Paul did not choose it: God laid it, before any of us arrived, the only surface able to take the weight of what is built on it: a stone rejected by the builders, chosen by God, and precious to everyone who believes.

How foundations shift. Churches rarely announce a change of foundation. They shift by degrees, always onto something good: their history and families; a personality, as at Corinth; a cause; an experience; a doctrinal system held so tightly that Christ becomes a topic within it. Each can coexist with an impeccable statement of faith. Ask how long it would take anyone in your church to notice if Christ were quietly no longer at the centre (Matthew 7:24–27).

What should I look for in a church? First, the foundation: is Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, clearly at the centre of what is preached, sung and prayed, and is the Bible taught faithfully as God’s word? Then the building: is the gospel shaping how people live and love one another, are baptism and the Lord’s Supper observed, is there loving care and discipline, are the leaders godly and accountable? Style, size, music and programmes come far lower. No church is perfect; look for one built on Christ and trying, imperfectly, to build well, and commit yourself to it.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the Day of Christ’s return, God’s searching judgment will show what each person’s work for him was really made of. Some work is lasting like gold, some flimsy like straw, and only the fire will tell which is which.

Gold or straw. Six materials, in two groups of three. Gold, silver and precious stones were what David gathered for the house of God (1 Chronicles 29:2); wood, hay and straw, the stuff of huts thrown up quickly. They stand for sound or shallow ministry, and what matters is what happens to them in fire: wood, hay and straw do not merely char, they vanish.

The Day will disclose it. The Day is Christ’s return and judgment (1:8; 4:5). Now the difference is largely invisible: a big straw building can impress more than a gold one, and two ministries can produce identical statistics while made of entirely different substances. A life of visible activity, admired at the time, may turn out to have been made of hay.

Revealed by fire. Fire here is a picture of God’s searching judgment (Malachi 3:2–3; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), and it tests the work, not the person’s salvation. “What sort” means its quality, not its quantity. The fire is what the holiness of God does to everything that comes near him, for our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29). Nothing false can stand in the presence of the Holy One, and nothing true has anything to fear from it.

Tested by the one it rests on. Paul calls it the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:8), so the one who examines the building is the one it stands on. The fire asks one question of every piece of work: does it belong on this foundation? Whatever came from Christ, his truth taught, his love shown, work done by his Spirit for his name, shares the nature of the stone beneath it and stands. Whatever came only from us, our cleverness, our ambition, our need to be seen, burns.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only full-time ministers will be judged. Paul speaks first of teachers in the church, but the principle applies to every believer’s service.

In everyday life. Take anything you are doing for God this week and ask whether you would still do it, and as carefully, if nobody ever knew you had done it (Matthew 6:1–4). No one’s motives are wholly pure, even in his best work; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and for his sake the Father accepts the imperfect work of his children (Romans 5:19; Westminster 16.6).

What makes a work gold? Paul gives no list, and we should not invent one, but the letter supplies the direction. Work in which everything depends on Christ crucified, not merely mentions him. Work done in dependence on the Spirit rather than technique, aimed at people’s good rather than the builder’s standing (the very thing gone wrong at Corinth), and done in love, since gifts exercised without it are nothing (13:1–3).

Will my sins be exposed in front of everyone on that Day? What this passage says will be revealed is your work, so that it can be rewarded or lost. If you are in Christ, your sins were judged at the cross; there is no condemnation left (Romans 8:1), and God has cast them behind his back (Isaiah 38:17; Micah 7:19). All will give account, and hidden things will be brought to light (4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:10), so believers should live seriously. But whatever is shown of a believer on that Day will be shown as a sinner fully forgiven, and its point will be the glory of the grace that saved him, not his shame.
verseByVerse.note: Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up.

parallels.desc: like a refiner’s fire

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Work that survives the fire will be rewarded; a believer whose work burns loses it all, yet he himself is saved. His salvation is secure because it rests on Christ, not on what he built.

A reward, or loss. Two outcomes, stated without softening: faithful work is rewarded (Matthew 25:21); otherwise a lifetime’s labour goes up in smoke.

He himself will be saved. The builder is a true believer, and his salvation rests not on his work but on the foundation, Christ, whose work on the cross is finished and cannot burn. Paul adds no conditions. Christ passed through the fire of God’s judgment first, so that no believer will ever be consumed by it: our works may burn; he will not, and we are in him. This verse was never meant to be read by an anxious Christian as a threat.

But only as through fire. Like a man escaping a burning house with nothing but his life. He is out and alive, and everything he spent forty years accumulating is behind him in the flames: saved, but with empty hands. That is sobering enough without additions: a Christian can reach the end, undoubtedly saved, with nothing to show for his life. Paul writes this to warn us off such a life while there is time.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faithfulness does not matter, since we are saved anyway. Loss of reward is real loss, and there is shame in it (1 John 2:28). But the way back is open while you live, as the next paragraph says.

I have wasted years. Is it too late to build with gold? No. While you live you can start building with materials that last. The thief on the cross had hours, and Christ welcomed him. Paul himself spent his early years destroying the church, and then laboured more than all the apostles by the grace of God (15:9–10). God asks not how late you started but whether you are faithful now. Confess the wasted time, refuse to waste more on regret, and give yourself to what lasts: loving people, teaching truth, serving in Christ’s name. Work begun late in faith is still gold.

What is the reward? Its heart is the Lord’s own commendation (4:5; Matthew 25:21), with wider service in the age to come and an imperishable crown (9:25). Salvation is the same for every believer; reward is not, and even the reward is grace (Revelation 4:10).

Where Christians differ: purgatory. The Roman Catholic Church has used this passage to support purgatory, a place of temporal purifying punishment after death for believers before they enter heaven. It became a principal text for that doctrine, and the reading is not foolish: there is a fire, there is a Christian, and he passes through it and comes out saved. This commentary’s view: the passage does not teach purgatory. The fire tests works, not people; verse 13 says so twice. What burns is the work; the man is not being purified but rescued from a blaze consuming what he built. It happens on the Day of judgment, not over a period after death, and nothing suggests duration, degrees or satisfaction for sin. And it concerns the work of teachers, not punishment for sins. Behind that lies the deeper reason: Christ became our righteousness (1:30). If the cross dealt with sin, there is nothing left for a fire to deal with; if a fire is still required, the cross did not finish. Christ’s sacrifice fully paid for his people’s sins, so there is no punishment left for them (Hebrews 10:14; Romans 8:1). At death, believers go immediately to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

parallels.desc: a brand plucked out of the burning

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is God’s holy temple, the place where his Spirit lives, and God will destroy anyone who destroys it. To tear a congregation apart is to attack the house of God.

Do you not know. Paul uses the phrase ten times in this letter, always with an edge: you have been told, and have forgotten. “You” is plural: the congregation together is God’s temple (in 6:19 it will be each believer’s body). And temple here is naos, the sanctuary itself, the house where God dwelt.

In a city full of temples. Corinth had temples to Apollo, to Asclepius, to Aphrodite on the mountain above the town (see the introduction). Paul tells ordinary people meeting in somebody’s dining room that the living God lives among them. The temples on the skyline are empty.

And that God’s Spirit dwells in you? As the glory-cloud filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11), so God’s Spirit lives among his gathered people. The church is where God is.

God will destroy him. The same verb comes twice (phtheirō, ruin, corrupt): you ruin it, he will ruin you. This is not the poor builder of verses 12–15 but someone who tears the building down by factions, false teaching or corrupting influence. So a church split is not a management problem; it is demolition work on the house where God lives, and he defends his property.

Holy. Not because the members are impressive, for Paul has just called them infants, but because of who lives there. You may think very little of your congregation; God has chosen to live in it.

Something greater than the temple. The church is God’s temple only because of Christ. Jesus, something greater than the temple (Matthew 12:6), called his own body the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). The Spirit in the church was poured out by the exalted Lord (Acts 2:33), and the church is a temple because it is joined to him: built on him as cornerstone, it grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–21). To tear at the congregation is to tear at the body of Christ.

The glory walked the roads of Galilee. The God whom heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain (1 Kings 8:27) once filled Solomon’s temple with a cloud. Then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and the glory walked the roads of Galilee (John 1:14). Now by his Spirit the same holy presence has made its home among forgiven sinners in an ordinary room, and guards it as jealously as he ever guarded Zion. The Holy One is not far off. He has moved in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer who causes trouble will lose salvation. The person in view is not someone who has been difficult, held an unpopular position or raised a hard question, but one set on wrecking the church, who shows he was never truly of it (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and is among the means God uses to keep his people.

In everyday life. Recall your last conversation about someone in your church who was not present: was it building, or quietly taking something down? Much demolition in churches is done a sentence at a time, by people who would be horrified to hear it. Where you find it, confess it to the Lord who bought this house, and go and build (Ephesians 2:21–22).

Is this verse about looking after my body? Not directly. It is often quoted against smoking or overeating, but here the temple is the gathered church. Paul does call each believer’s body a temple of the Spirit three chapters later, about sexual immorality (6:18–20), and caring for your body honours God for that reason. But this verse applies first to how you treat your church: your words, your loyalties, your influence.

Is it not harsh for God to destroy someone over trouble in a church? If the church were a club, perhaps. But it is the place where the holy God lives, among people he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). A father who stopped someone setting fire to the house where his children slept would not be harsh; he would be unloving if he did not. The warning comes in advance, while there is time to turn back. God’s severity here is the other side of his love: he will not let anyone tear down what his Son died to build.
verseByVerse.note: “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boasting in human leaders is foolish, because those who belong to Christ already own everything. The world’s wisdom, which ranks teachers and admires cleverness, is folly to God, so whoever thinks himself wise must become a fool in order to be truly wise (vv. 18–20). Then Paul turns the slogans round: you do not belong to Paul or Apollos; they belong to you, together with the world, life, death, the present and the future (vv. 21–22). All of it is yours because you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from Him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great lists of what it means to be in Christ: because believers are joined to Christ, they share in all that is his (see the notes on vv. 21–22 and v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming a third of the apostolic inheritance when they could have had the whole (see the note on vv. 21–22). Now: A Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing. The traditions are real and valuable, and they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
To become truly wise you must give up the world’s wisdom and accept being thought a fool, because God sees straight through human cleverness. The factions were the world’s wisdom (1:18–2:16) in action, and Paul now draws the threads together.

Let no one deceive himself. The danger of the clever, and the hardest to detect, because the deceiver is entirely trusted by the deceived.

Become a fool. To become wise, you must accept being thought a fool by the world, by embracing the message of the cross (1:18–25). This does not mean you stop thinking. It means agreeing that your own mind, however good, cannot find its way to God, and receiving from him what you could never have worked out. For some it costs more: the academic, the man used to being the most informed person in the room, is asked to walk into the kingdom by a door marked fool.

A permanent posture. Nor is it a door you pass through once. Becoming a fool is a lasting posture: letting Scripture correct your ways of thinking rather than trimming Scripture to fit them. Every serious reader meets passages that offend his instincts, and then either he bends or the text does.

He catches the wise. From Job 5:13: God traps the clever in their own schemes. There is a fine irony here: Paul is quoting Eliphaz, one of Job’s comforters, whose confident wisdom God himself exposes before the book ends (Job 42:7). The man who said it was caught by it. Yet Paul introduces the line with “it is written”: Scripture records Eliphaz faithfully, mistakes and all, and this sentence is true.

The thoughts of the wise. From Psalm 94:11, where the psalmist writes “the thoughts of man”; Paul sharpens it to “the wise”, since that is the group in question at Corinth. Futile (mataios) means empty, leading nowhere. God does not merely contradict the clever; he knows their reasoning goes nowhere.

Wisdom with a name. The wisdom beyond that door is not a better philosophy but a person. Christ became to us wisdom from God (1:24, 30). To become a fool in order to be wise is to stop trusting the wisdom you brought and to receive him instead: the crucified Lord whom the rulers of this age did not recognise (2:8). The world’s wisdom could not find God. God’s wisdom came looking for us, and hung on a cross.

Should Christians study at university or work in science and scholarship? Yes, gladly. All truth is God’s truth, and Christians have done some of the finest thinking in history in every field. Daniel learned the literature of Babylon without bowing to its gods (Daniel 1:17). This verse forbids not learning but letting learning sit in judgment over God. So study hard, and take your faith into the lecture room rather than leaving it at the door. Find Christian friends who will help you think, and when a teacher’s claims clash with Scripture, test them humbly and patiently, remembering that the fear of the Lord is where wisdom starts.

parallels.desc: he catches the wise in their own craftiness
the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not boast in human leaders, because in Christ everything already belongs to you, the leaders included. Paul does not say you have nothing to boast about, but that you are far too rich to boast in men.

So let no one boast in men. The conclusion of chapters 1–3. The Corinthians are fighting over scraps, and Paul’s answer is to show them how rich they are.

For all things are yours. A glorious reversal. You said, I belong to Paul. Paul says: no, Paul belongs to you.

Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas. The very men the factions were dividing over (Cephas is Peter), all given to serve you (Ephesians 4:11–12). The faction was a self-imposed poverty, each clinging to a third of an inheritance that was entirely theirs.

Or the world. Then the list jumps. The world is yours, for the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13): not that you hold the title to anything now, but that nothing in the world is finally against you: all of it, even its losses, is put to work for the good of those who love God, and the whole of it will be theirs in the new creation (Romans 8:28; Revelation 21:7).

Or life or death. Life is yours: a gift to be used, not a burden to be got through. Then a word nobody would put in a list of assets: death. The last enemy has been so defeated that it now serves the believer, the servant that carries him home to Christ (Philippians 1:21). What everyone organises life around avoiding has become a possession.

The present or the future. This month, with its unresolved situation, belongs to you as much as the coming glory, and all of it works for your good (Romans 8:28, 38).

The heir of all things. None of this is ours by nature. Scripture names one heir of all things, the Son, through whom God made the world (Hebrews 1:2), and we are heirs only as fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). Through his own death Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death and delivered those who through fear of death were held in lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:14–15). Death is ours because it was first his, and he walked out of it. The whole inventory, apostles, world, life, death, present and future, is the estate of Christ, settled on the people he has made his own.

Not a prosperity gospel. “All things are yours” has been used to claim that God promises believers health and wealth now. But death is on the same list. Paul writes to a mostly poor church (1:26) and is about to say that the apostles themselves are hungry, poorly dressed and homeless (4:11).

In everyday life. If you feel spiritually poor, name what you think you lack: standing, security, a future, someone in your corner. Then read the list again. It is possible to be an heir of everything and live like a man counting coins, and the only thing that has to change is that somebody tells you what is in the account (Romans 8:32; Psalm 24:1).

If death is mine, why am I still afraid of dying? Because death is still an enemy, the last one (15:26), and dying can be hard; Jesus himself wept at a grave and was in anguish in Gethsemane. Fear of dying is not unbelief; it is being human in a fallen world. What Christ has removed is the sting: death can no longer separate you from God, condemn you or keep you (15:55–57; Romans 8:38–39). So bring the fear to him honestly, read what he has promised about the other side, and remember that he has gone through death ahead of you, and will be with you in it.

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things are yours only because you belong to Christ, and Christ himself belongs to God. These words hold the chapter together and give the true slogan: not “I follow Paul”, but I am Christ’s.

Owner and owned. You are not the top of the chain, and that keeps “all things are yours” from becoming a fantasy of self-importance: you own everything, and you are owned. A man who says “I am Paul’s” has swapped an infinite estate for a small allegiance (see vv. 21–22).

And Christ is God’s. Christ, as the Son and Mediator (the one who stands between God and us), belongs to God the Father and serves his glory (11:3; 15:28). Read carelessly, it sounds like a demotion, as the fourth-century Arians (who taught that the Son was created) argued.

Equal in nature, ordered in relation. The church’s answer, set out at Nicaea, is that Scripture speaks of the Son in two ways. As to his being, he is fully and equally God: this same Paul calls him the Lord of glory (2:8) and applies to him the covenant name, the LORD, from Jeremiah 9:24 (1:31). As to his mission, he willingly took a place of submission: sent by the Father, doing the Father’s will, and at the end handing the kingdom over to the Father (15:24–28). The submission is not evidence of a lesser deity (John 14:28; Philippians 2:6–11); it is the shape divine love took when it came to fetch us.

He has never stopped giving. A squabbling congregation was handed the world, life, death, the present and the future, not because it had grown up but because it belonged to Christ. And Christ did not seize his place; he received all things from the Father, gave them away to us, and at the end will hand the kingdom back, so that God may be all in all (15:28). There is no grasping in the Godhead. Everything the Son has, he has from the Father; everything we have, we have from the Son; and the whole vast movement runs outward from a God who has never needed anything and has never stopped giving (John 17:10).

What does it mean in practice to belong to Christ? It means your life is not your own: your time, body, money, gifts and future are his to direct (6:19–20). That is a claim, and also a comfort: because you are his, he feeds, guards, corrects and keeps what belongs to him (John 10:27–29). Your identity is settled not by your job, politics, tribe or failures, but by whose you are, and every other loyalty, to family, church, nation or leader, is real but held under him. When you are unsure what to do, ask the simple question: what would my Owner want?

3.text: <sup>1</sup>But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ.<sup>2</sup>I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,<sup>3</sup>for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?<sup>4</sup>For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human?<sup>5</sup>What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.<sup>6</sup>I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.<sup>7</sup>So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.<sup>8</sup>He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.<sup>9</sup>For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.<sup>10</sup>According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it.<sup>11</sup>For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.<sup>12</sup>Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw—<sup>13</sup>each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.<sup>14</sup>If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward.<sup>15</sup>If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.<sup>16</sup>Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?<sup>17</sup>If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.<sup>18</sup>Let no one deceive himself.
