keyVerse.quote: For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the centre of the chapter and of Paul’s answer to the factions. Leaders come and go, and they are only builders; the foundation was laid by God, and it is Christ himself. A church that rests on him has every reason for unity and none for boasting in men, and a believer who rests on him is safe even if his work burns (v. 15).

3.reflection:
Paul measures spiritual maturity not by gifts or knowledge but by the absence of jealousy and strife (vv. 1–4). Why is that such a revealing test? Whose blessing do you find it hardest to be glad about?

Paul calls himself and Apollos “servants” and says God alone gives the growth (vv. 5–9). How should that change the way we think about preachers, about results, and about years of praying for someone who has not yet believed?

Verses 10–15 picture a fire that tests what each person has built on Christ. What do you think makes a piece of work gold rather than straw, and how does the promise that the builder “will be saved” (v. 15) keep this from becoming a threat?

“All things are yours … and you are Christ’s” (vv. 21–23). Which item on Paul’s list, including death, do you find hardest to believe belongs to you, and what difference would it make this week to believe it?

4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 brings to a close Paul’s long answer to the factions that began at 1:10. Having set the cross against the world’s wisdom and shown that preachers are only workers in God’s field (chapters 1–3), he now holds up the apostles themselves as the pattern.

The message. Stop ranking God’s servants and stop boasting, because you are not the judge and you have nothing you did not receive. In this age the Christian life is not a throne but the way of the cross, and the Lord looks in his servants not for impressive talk but for faithfulness and the power of a changed life.

Why it was said. The Corinthians judged Paul and Apollos as their city judged orators, by polish, status and success (see the introduction), and thought themselves already rich and reigning. Some were saying Paul would never dare come back (v. 18).

How the chapter makes its case. Ministers are servants and stewards, of whom only faithfulness is required, and their only judge is the Lord at his coming, who will expose every motive and give each his praise (vv. 1–5). So there is no ground for boasting, since everything was received (vv. 6–7). Then, with irony, Paul sets their imagined reign beside the apostles’ real life: condemned men in the arena, hungry, beaten and homeless, blessing those who curse them, the scum of the world (vv. 8–13). Finally irony gives way to tenderness. As their father through the gospel he asks them to imitate him, sends Timothy to show them how, and leaves them to choose whether he comes with a rod or with gentle love (vv. 14–21).

Where it leads. Every line of the apostles’ portrait was drawn first in Christ: the faithful Son over God’s house, the Judge who will praise his servants aloud, the condemned man led out before the crowds, struck with fists, treated as refuse outside the city, praying for those who crucified him. And the chapter ends with a King who has every right to come with a rod, yet comes in meekness, because the rod has already fallen on him.

For us. Ask by what standard you measure your leaders, other Christians and yourself, whose verdict you are living for, and whether you expect the crown without the cross. Then take Paul’s question home and let it end your comparing: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Only the Lord can judge his servants, so the church must stop judging and boasting. Paul and Apollos are Christ’s servants and stewards, and faithfulness is all that is required of them (vv. 1–2). Neither the Corinthians’ verdict nor even Paul’s clear conscience settles that; the Lord will, when he comes and brings every motive to light, and then he will commend each one (vv. 3–5). Paul has applied all this to himself and Apollos so that the church will keep within Scripture and stop puffing up one teacher against another, for everything they have was a gift (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pass judgment early on himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism. The final judgment has not yet been given, so every present judgment, including our verdict on ourselves, is provisional. On the freedom this brings, from both false confidence and false despair, see the note on vv. 3–4.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were judging Paul and finding him wanting, not by faithfulness but by eloquence and visible success. Now: Judging ministers by attendance, public approval or conference invitations is the modern version. A minister who shapes his ministry around his peers’ praise has chosen the wrong judge.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ministers are Christ’s servants, entrusted with his gospel, and the one thing required of them is faithfulness. They are not celebrities to be ranked, but servants managing goods that belong to someone else.

As servants of Christ. Corinth followed and ranked its orators, and the church had begun to treat its teachers the same way (see the introduction). Paul offers two humbling words instead. The first means an assistant or attendant (hypēretēs): the officer who carries out a superior’s orders, the synagogue attendant who handed Jesus the scroll and took it back (Luke 4:20). The assistant does not set the orders, and nobody cheers him by name. And they are servants of Christ, not of the Corinthians, who were treating their ministers as hired entertainers. A man who takes his orders from Christ cannot also take them from the people who prefer him.

Stewards of the mysteries. The second word is steward (oikonomos): the household manager, very often a slave, who ran the estate, kept the accounts and gave out the stores to the household (Luke 12:42). He handled a great deal of wealth and owned none of it, and he could not alter the terms on which it was given out. A mystery, for Paul, is not a secret for insiders but something God once kept hidden and has now announced (2:7).

The mystery is a person. The thing announced has a name: God’s mystery, which is Christ (Colossians 2:2). So what the steward carries out of the storeroom is Christ himself, crucified and risen, offered whole to everyone in the house. A steward fails if he hands out something else in his place, however attractive: himself, a method, a mood, a cause. He succeeds when the household is fed with Christ, whether or not anyone remembers who served it.

Found faithful. Then the single criterion. Not gifted, effective or admired, but faithful (pistos), trustworthy with what is not his. A steward is assessed not by how much the household admired him, but by whether the accounts balance when the master comes home. And the Master of this household, the only one in it who owns anything, is the one who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). He was faithful over God’s house as a Son (Hebrews 3:6), and he has never once mislaid a single thing his Father gave him (John 6:39).

What it does not mean. Ministers are not a priestly class who dispense grace through rituals; they are stewards of a message, not keepers of a sacred store only they can unlock. Nor are gifts and effectiveness worthless; God gives gifts to be used. None of them is the test.

In everyday life. Ask what you would change if you genuinely believed it was not yours: the money, the diary, the children. The change is usually not in how hard you work but in whose interests you are working (Luke 12:42–44). None of us will be found perfectly faithful. Christ was, in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a steward who has failed may come back to his Master unafraid and begin again.

Is this only about pastors? No. Paul speaks first of himself and Apollos, but every Christian is a steward of something (1 Peter 4:10): money, time, a gift, a position, a family, a confidence someone trusted you with. The parable of the talents is told to ordinary disciples, and its verdict is not well done, good and successful servant, but good and faithful (Matthew 25:21). The mother at home with small children, the man in an office no one will ever write about, the elderly saint who can only pray: each will be asked the same single question.

How do I know I am being faithful? Faithfulness is rarely dramatic. You do the task you were given, not the one you would have preferred. You do it the same way when nobody is checking, because the Master sees in secret. You use what was entrusted to you instead of burying it for safety (Matthew 25:24–27). You keep your word in small things: “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10). And you keep the accounts honest, owning your failures, because a steward who hides a loss has stopped trusting his master. None of this earns a place in the house. You are there already, brought in by the faithful Son, and faithfulness is fruit his Spirit grows in you (Galatians 5:22). Pick one small duty no one will notice this week, and do it well, for him.

What should I look for in a pastor, then? Faithfulness before flair. Does he preach what Scripture actually says, including the unpopular parts? Does he live it, at home and in private as well as on the platform (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he point to Christ rather than to himself? Is he the same man in a small meeting as in a large one? You may thank God for a gifted speaker. But a church that rates its ministers by charisma alone is repeating Corinth’s mistake, and usually ends up with stewards who behave as if they owned the house.

What if a faithful minister’s church stays small? Then he has not failed. Scripture is full of faithful servants with thin harvests. Noah was a herald of righteousness, and eight people entered the ark (2 Peter 2:5); Jeremiah preached for forty years to a nation that did not listen. God wants his house full, but growth is his work (3:6–7), and the steward answers only for what is in his hands. Pray for your pastor, and do not measure him by a scale the Lord does not use.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither the Corinthians’ verdict on Paul nor even his own settles whether he is a faithful servant: the Lord is his judge. That frees him both from living for approval and from endlessly putting himself on trial.

A very small thing. The Corinthians were comparing Paul unfavourably with other teachers. “Judged” is anakrinō: examined, cross-examined, as in a preliminary hearing. “Human court” is literally “a human day”, set against the Day of the Lord (3:13). Their opinion is not worthless, but it is not the verdict: the court they had set up has no authority to decide the case.

Not even myself. He sets aside his own verdict too. This is not low self-esteem but accurate self-knowledge, since no one has full access to his own motives. His conscience is clear about his ministry among them: no doctrine watered down, no money taken, no flattery used.

But I am not thereby acquitted. Acquitted is dedikaiōmai, from the great word of justification, here in its courtroom sense: declared in the right. Conscience can be wrong, blind or badly taught, and the heart lies not only to others but to its owner (Psalm 139:23–24; Jeremiah 17:9). Paul is not saying his salvation is uncertain, but that his faithfulness as a servant will be assessed by the Lord, who alone sees the motives Paul cannot see in himself.

The Lord who judged him faithful. The Lord who judges Paul is the Lord Jesus, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22), and Paul knew his Judge before he stood before him. Years later he wrote that Christ Jesus our Lord had judged him faithful, appointing him to his service, though he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (1 Timothy 1:12–13). The Judge’s first word to Paul was spoken on the Damascus road, in mercy, to a man with blood on his hands. And that Judge was himself cross-examined in a human court, at night, by men with no right to judge him, and kept silent, leaving his case with the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

The court that never adjourns. In most societies of the past you were told who you were: a son, a farmer, a member of this family and village. The philosopher Charles Taylor has pointed out that modern people are expected instead to create their own identity, which makes us more dependent on recognition, not less, because a self we have built needs someone to confirm that it is worth something. So the court Paul refused to sit in has never been busier: the performance appraisal, the count of likes beneath a photograph, the parents we are still trying to impress at fifty. The moralist tries to win the verdict by being good and the achiever by being impressive, but both are standing in the dock. Paul has walked out of that courtroom, not because he has stopped caring or has acquitted himself, but because the only Judge whose ruling counts met him in mercy. Identity is not achieved and then defended for life. It is received from the One who judges, and for those in Christ his judgment fell on the cross.

What it does not mean. Ministers are not above accountability. Elders can be rebuked for sin (1 Timothy 5:19–20), and churches must test what they hear (1 Thessalonians 5:21); but the final evaluation of a servant belongs to Christ, and ministers should not live for human approval. Nor is self-examination pointless: Paul commands it before the Lord’s Supper (11:28). Examine yourself, by all means; just do not mistake your findings for the Judge’s verdict.

In everyday life. Bring to mind the last criticism that stayed with you for days, and the last praise you replayed, and ask what authority you granted to each. When the voice in your head starts its familiar hearing, acquitting you too quickly or condemning you without mercy, you may say to it what Paul said: you are not the judge either.

If a clear conscience does not acquit me, how can I have any assurance? This verse can land on an anxious Christian like a sentence of condemnation, so a guard is needed. Paul’s point is that the verdict is not his to give, in either direction: he refuses to acquit himself and equally refuses to condemn himself. Both are the Lord’s business, and the Lord has already spoken about those in Christ: there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Assurance rests not on the quality of your self-examination but on Christ’s finished work and God’s promise, sealed to you by the Spirit (Romans 8:16). To people whose hearts accused them John wrote that God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:19–20).

So should I ignore criticism? No: listen to it, but do not bow to it. The Lord often uses others to show us what we cannot see (Proverbs 27:6). Ask whether it is true, whether it agrees with Scripture, and whether people who love you are saying the same. If it is true, repent and be grateful. If it is false, let it go without bitterness, because the one who said it was never your judge. Taking criticism seriously is humility; treating it as a verdict is slavery to opinion, and leaves you either crushed or defensive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not pass verdicts on people’s hearts now; wait for the Lord, who alone sees them and will bring everything to light when he comes. His verdict, not ours, is the one that will stand.

Before the time. The fault Paul names is not judging as such but its timing: a verdict delivered before the evidence is complete and the Judge has taken his seat. The Corinthians were ranking their ministers before the court had sat.

Not a ban on all judging. This verse is often quoted to shut down any moral assessment. But one chapter later Paul pronounces judgment on a man’s conduct (5:3), tells the church to judge those inside it (5:12), and asks whether they cannot settle a dispute between brothers (6:5). What it forbids is the verdict only God can reach: on another person’s heart and final standing. You may say that an action is wrong; you may not say what a man is before God, or what he was really after. It is the difference between “what he said was untrue” and “he is a liar through and through”; between “this decision was unwise” and “he only did it for the credit”. The first is observation. The second is a ruling on the purposes of the heart, and that is reserved for God.

Before the Lord comes. God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The man is Jesus, who was himself condemned by a hasty human verdict. Until he comes, everything is only a preliminary hearing.

Things now hidden; purposes of the heart. Not necessarily evil things, but everything hidden from human view, including the reasons behind what was done in the light. Purposes are counsels, motives (boulai). Two ministers may do the same thing, one for Christ’s glory and one for his own, and from the pew they look identical. The charity done to be noticed will be disclosed, and equally the kindness done anonymously, the temptation resisted in private, the prayers no one heard.

Commendation from God. Here the verse becomes unexpectedly wonderful. The Day will expose every heart, and Paul expects the outcome for God’s servants to be epainos, praise spoken aloud: not a bare acquittal but commendation, from God, to each one. It is the master in the parable saying “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21), and it is from God that praise matters (Romans 2:29). That God should forgive us is grace beyond calculation. That he should then intend to praise us, having himself supplied everything he is praising, is something else again. Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts. The judgment Christians most dread is described here as the occasion on which their Father speaks well of them out loud (1 Peter 1:7), and the universe will see that grace was never merely enough to save; it was enough to glorify.

In everyday life. Catch yourself this week at the moment you move from “that was unkind” to “she is that sort of person”, and stop at the first sentence. And if your motives are questioned unfairly, or your faithfulness goes unseen, take heart: the Lord who sees in secret has a word of praise prepared, and nobody else’s verdict can cancel it.

Will everything I have hidden come out on that day? Scripture says plainly that nothing will stay hidden (Luke 12:2–3; 2 Corinthians 5:10), though it does not tell us how. But for the believer two things are certain. Your sins were already judged in full at the cross, so whatever comes to light then comes to light as forgiven, and no charge can be laid against God’s elect (Romans 8:33). And the emphasis of this very verse is not exposure but commendation. For those in Christ the Day that uncovers everything is the Day of their Father’s praise. You need not dread it; you may long for it.

Is it wrong to want God’s praise? No; it is the right ambition, and Paul holds it out as a motive. What is wrong is wanting people’s praise instead of God’s (John 12:43), or wanting his praise as a wage that puts him in our debt. Jesus told his disciples to give and pray in secret, so that the Father who sees in secret would reward them (Matthew 6:4, 6). Children of a good father want to hear him say “well done”, and he wants to say it. Every good thing he will praise in us, he first put there.

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has used himself and Apollos as the example so that the Corinthians will keep within Scripture and stop boasting about one teacher against another, since everything they have was given to them. Pride in a gift pretends it was never received.

For your benefit. “Applied” (metaschēmatizō) means Paul has transferred the lesson to himself and Apollos as the worked example, so that he need not name the leaders the Corinthians were actually quarrelling over. It is a pastor’s tact: he puts himself and his friend, two men plainly not rivals, in the dock, so that no one in Corinth is humiliated by name.

Not beyond what is written. What is written is Scripture, which Paul has quoted again and again in chapters 1–3 (1:19, 31; 2:9; 3:19–20). The Corinthians’ factions, rankings and worldly standards of eloquence had no warrant in anything God has said. The lesson holds in every age: stop at the line, and do not build convictions on ground Scripture has not given you (on the phrase itself, see the box below).

Puffed up. Swollen with air (physioō): Paul’s favourite word for this church, six times in the letter and only once elsewhere. Nobody was boasting in himself outright; they boasted in their teacher. It is a respectable form of pride, because it feels like loyalty, but it really claimed that I, who chose the better teacher, am the better Christian.

For who sees anything different in you? Verse 7 has humbled proud Christians for centuries: three questions, and no way through them. Who has made you differ from the person you feel superior to? The expected answer is nobody, except God.

What do you have that you did not receive? Nothing whatever. Not your intelligence, which was in your genes before you could form a preference. Not your upbringing, your country, the family that told you about Christ, the health that let you work, or the temperament that makes you easier to like. Not your knowledge, which came from teachers and books others wrote. Not your faith, the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8), nor your salvation, planned before the world began. This is the doctrine of grace pressed down to the level of daily pride. Augustine said it was this very verse that finally convinced him that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift.

Why do you boast as if you did not receive it? Such pride is not merely unattractive; it is a false claim, presenting a gift as an achievement. At bottom it is a refusal to be in anyone’s debt, even God’s, whereas grace invites us to live gladly in his debt for ever, a far happier place to live. And it removes the ground for comparison. Ranking yourself against another Christian on gifts you were both handed is like two beggars quarrelling over which was the more distinguished for having been given a coat.

Boast in the Lord. The list of things received has a summit: Christ, who became to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1:30–31). The greatest thing any Corinthian had received was not a gift or a teacher but Christ himself, and in him a righteousness never theirs to earn. Pride in a teacher boasts in a man who was only a servant, and forgets the Lord who was given to us whole. Even the Son gives away what he received: “The glory that you have given me I have given to them” (John 17:22). Glory passes from the Father to the Son, and from the Son to sinners who had nothing, and heaven will be full of people who received everything and boast in no one but the Giver.

Didn’t I earn what I have? Our culture says that anyone can make it who works hard enough, so the successful quietly conclude that they deserve their success. The philosopher Michael Sandel, in The Tyranny of Merit, has argued that this belief breeds smugness at the top and humiliation at the bottom, where people are told in effect that their failure is their own fault, and that it forgets how much of anyone’s success rests on things nobody earns: a talent the market happens to reward, a home where someone read to you. Paul goes further: even the effort was given, the discipline, the health, the mind that could learn. That is why the gospel offends the self-made and the self-righteous equally; both want to say, I did this. Grace says that the best gift of all, a right standing before God, was earned by someone else entirely. Whoever grasps that cannot despise the one who has less, and need not envy the one who has more.

What it does not mean. Christians may use books, confessions and creeds, as long as they serve and agree with Scripture; Paul himself handed on what he had received (15:3). Nor does verse 7 mean that gifts are imaginary. False modesty denies the gift and so dishonours the Giver as surely as pride does.

In everyday life. The next time you feel the small inner lift of being further on than another believer, ask Paul’s question. What is left when the pride collapses is not humiliation but relief, gratitude, and a strange new warmth towards the person you were just measuring (Romans 12:3; John 3:27).

Does this mean I should not feel good about hard work? No. Paul worked harder than all the apostles, and in the same breath said it was not he but the grace of God that was with him (15:10). Gladness is not boasting; the difference is where it goes. Pride stops at itself: look what I did. Gratitude travels on: look what God has given and done through me. When someone praises your work, thank them simply, and in your heart hand the praise straight on to the One it belongs to.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Some churches hold that tradition or church authority has equal standing with Scripture, and so add doctrines Scripture does not teach. This commentary’s view: Not going beyond what is written expresses the principle the Reformers called sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority for faith and life. Teachers and traditions are useful servants, but nothing may be required of Christians as necessary that is not taught in Scripture or drawn from it by good and necessary consequence, that is, what plainly follows from what it says (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6, 1.10).

Uncertain wording. “Not to go beyond what is written” is one of the most puzzling phrases in the letter. The Greek is very compressed, with no verb, and Paul seems to be quoting a saying the Corinthians knew: perhaps a proverb, or a schoolroom phrase about tracing letters without straying outside the lines. What is clear is that “it is written” is Paul’s usual formula for Scripture, and the clause that follows ties the phrase to pride in leaders. The likely meaning: keep to what God has said, and do not invent standards of your own by which to rank his servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In this age the way of Christ is the cross, not the throne. With irony Paul mocks the Corinthians’ belief that they are already full, rich and reigning (v. 8), and sets beside it the apostles’ real condition: put on show last of all, like condemned men in the arena before the world and the angels (v. 9); fools, weak and dishonoured for Christ’s sake (v. 10); hungry, beaten and homeless, working with their hands, answering curses with blessing, and treated as the scum of the world (vv. 11–13). Those who follow a crucified Lord walk the road he walked.
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Age We Live In

The Corinthians’ problem was not only social pride but confusion about which age they were in (see the note on v. 8). In this time between Christ’s comings the Christian life is shaped by the cross. Suffering, weakness and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but a share in Christ’s own path, in which resurrection comes through the cross, not around it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Behind verse 9 is the arena (see the note on v. 9). Paul had been beaten and imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the modern form of Corinthian triumphalism (see the note on v. 8), and Paul’s hungry, homeless fools for Christ’s sake stand against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
With biting irony Paul exposes the Corinthians’ belief that they had already arrived, full, rich and reigning, while their apostles still suffered. Their mistake was not hoping too much, but claiming the glory before its time.

Already you have all you want! Three exclamations, all irony. “All you want” is korennymi, to have eaten your fill, and the repeated “already” names their error: they believed they had arrived. Rich in gifts and knowledge (1:5), they had turned the gift Paul thanked God for into a status. A congregation can be genuinely blessed and use the blessing as evidence that it no longer needs anything, least of all correction.

Without us you have become kings! They behaved as if they were already reigning, as believers will in the age to come (6:2–3; Revelation 5:10), and as if they had got there without the apostles. Their boast may also have echoed a well-known saying of the Stoic philosophers, that the truly wise man alone is rich and alone is a king, and Paul turns it back on a church that prized wisdom. He does not deny that Christians are rich; all things are theirs (3:21–22). What he denies is the timing. The inheritance is certain, and it has not yet been paid out.

Holy irony. Scripture is not embarrassed by sarcasm: Elijah suggesting that Baal might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27), the Lord himself on men who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Matthew 23:24). Irony serves when someone is so pleased with himself that a straight statement will simply be absorbed. But it is a sharp tool, never for sport, and Paul says why he used it: not to shame them but to warn his beloved children (4:14).

Would that you did reign! Then the irony breaks, and the wistfulness is real: I wish the kingdom had come, because I am hungry and cold, and if you were really reigning, so would I be. They live as if the promised future were already here, and so think they no longer need the way of the cross.

The order of the King’s own road. The Corinthians wanted the crown without the cross, and their King went the other way. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus asked, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). Suffering first, then glory, is the shape of his story (1 Peter 1:11). He reigns now until all his enemies are under his feet (15:25), but his people share his reign as they share his life, by first sharing his sufferings (Romans 8:17). And he is not keeping his throne to himself: the one who conquers, he says, I will grant to sit with me on my throne (Revelation 3:21). Paul’s wish will be granted after all. The crowns are real, the date is fixed, and the King who will give them out won them by wearing a crown of thorns.

What it does not mean. Believers are not left with nothing now. We have every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), and the kingdom has truly arrived in Jesus, but the full glory is future. Christians live between what Christ has already done and what he has not yet completed, and Corinth forgot the “not yet”.

So is it wrong to pray for healing or provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14). God often heals and provides, and we should ask boldly and thank him gladly. What this verse rules out is the teaching that health, wealth and victory are guaranteed now to anyone with enough faith, so that suffering becomes a sign that something has gone wrong with you. That is the Corinthian error in modern dress, and Paul’s answer is the next five verses, listing what the apostles were enduring while the Corinthians reigned (4:9–13). Ask God for good things; do not tell him he owes them to you before the time.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come.

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has put his apostles on show in the lowest and most shameful place, like condemned men led out last to die before a watching world and watching angels. That is where the King’s servants stand in this age.

Last of all. The imagery is from the arena. At the end of a day at the games the condemned were brought out, with no weapons and no chance, not to compete but to die in front of people; condemned prisoners were also paraded last in a Roman triumph, on their way to execution. Either way, God has put the apostles in that last place.

Like men sentenced to death. Condemned to die (epithanatios). Paul faced death every day (15:30–31) and was always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake (2 Corinthians 4:11). The Corinthians are reigning as kings; their founding apostle describes himself as the closing act of an execution. Those are not two styles of Christianity. One of them mistakes what age we are in.

A spectacle. A theatre (theatron). Paul assumes that what happens to Christians is watched by the unseen world of angels, who long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), and to whom God’s manifold wisdom is being made known through the church (Ephesians 3:10).

The first man on that stage. The apostles were not the first to be put there. When Jesus died, all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle went home beating their breasts (Luke 23:48). He was the condemned man led out last, stripped and lifted up where the whole city could see, and his servants stand where he stood: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). Yet on that first stage the spectacle was turned inside out. The man the crowd watched die was disarming the rulers and authorities, putting them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The condemned man at the end of the procession was the Conqueror leading it, and every follower made a spectacle for his name walks in a victory parade, not a funeral, on a road that ends where his ended: on a throne.

A lit stage. That puts a strange dignity on the least impressive Christian life. The believer quietly humiliated for his faith is on a lit stage, watched by beings who understand what they are looking at: a creature who is losing and is not bitter, who blesses the people taking everything from him and does not stop trusting God. That is the life of the crucified Christ in his servant.

Are there still apostles like the ones God put on display? Not in the sense Paul means here. An apostle in this sense was a witness of the risen Christ, commissioned by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), part of the church’s foundation, which is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). The word is used more loosely of messengers sent out by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25), and missionaries today stand in that line. But no one now can meet the qualifications of the Twelve and Paul, or claim their authority; their teaching is in Scripture, and that is how their office continues. And notice the mark Paul gives here: not a platform and a following, but being led out last into the arena, the very opposite of what many who claim the title today look like.

Are angels really watching me? Scripture says they are, though not how much they see or understand. They rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and learn the wisdom of God by watching the church (Ephesians 3:10). That is meant not to make you self-conscious, as if performing, but to tell you that your faithfulness is not wasted. When you forgive someone who has not apologised, or keep trusting God in a hospital corridor, it is not happening in an empty room.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena at the end of the games.

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In each contrast the apostles take the worse half, because following a crucified Lord looks foolish, weak and dishonourable to the world.

Fools for Christ’s sake. Paul is not claiming that Christians are unintelligent, nor recommending eccentricity for its own sake. The foolishness comes entirely from the message: it is what you look like when you have staked everything on a crucified man, in a world that measures by power and success (1:18).

Weak, and in disrepute. Paul came to Corinth in weakness and fear and much trembling (2:3); the Corinthians think they are strong, and that very sense of strength is their weakness. Dishonoured (atimos): they had managed to be respectable in Corinth and confident in church at once. Paul’s implication is quiet and pointed: if the message is genuinely offensive, how have you avoided all the offence?

Outside the camp. Each thing Paul takes for himself, folly, weakness and dishonour, was borne first by Christ. His own family said he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). He was crucified in weakness (2 Corinthians 13:4). He died the death Rome kept for those it most despised, outside the city gate. Hebrews draws the conclusion: let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13). The disgrace is not a detour from following Jesus. It is where he is.

The question that has not aged. Convictions can be held so that they cost nothing. But this verse is also for the Christian already paying in small ways: the colleague whose views are treated as a harmless quirk, the relative the family has kindly decided has become a bit much. That is not persecution as the early church knew it, and should not be dressed up as martyrdom, but it wears people down because it is so ordinary. Being thought a fool for Christ’s sake is not a sign you have handled things badly, but that you are walking where the apostles walked.

How do I know whether I am a fool for Christ or just foolish? Ask what the offence is attached to. If people think you odd because you will not lie for the company, because you go to church, because you believe Jesus rose and is the only way to the Father, that is the foolishness of the cross. If they think you odd because you are harsh, preachy, careless about your work or quick to take offence, that is your own foolishness, a burden to the gospel, not a badge (1 Peter 4:15–16). Paul was courteous, hard-working and wise in how he spoke (Colossians 4:5–6). If they reject you, they should be rejecting Christ in you, not the rough edges round him.

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s credentials as an apostle are not his successes but his sufferings: hunger, blows, homelessness, hard manual work, and a settled habit of answering abuse with blessing.

To the present hour. The list is deliberately physical, and current. “Buffeted” is kolaphizō, struck with the fist, the very word used when Jesus was struck in the high priest’s house (Matthew 26:67). The apostle carries in his body the bruises his Lord received first.

Working with our own hands. Educated Greeks looked down on manual work, and the speakers who toured Corinth were paid handsomely for talking. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3; 20:34), and part of the Corinthian embarrassment was simply social: their founder had calloused hands. He accepted it so as not to put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (9:12).

When reviled, we bless. The heart of the passage: no retaliation, no campaign to set the record straight, and no passivity either. To bless is actively to ask God’s good for the man who has just insulted you; to endure is to stay put under pressure; to entreat (parakaleō) is to speak kindly and keep the door open towards someone spreading lies about you. It is what Paul had been taught: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28). And it is what he knew of his Lord, who when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and who from the cross asked the Father to forgive the men who had nailed him there (Luke 23:34).

Scum of the world. Then the two ugliest words available: what is left in the bucket after cleaning, and what is scraped off (see the box below). To prove to a church impressed by success that he is a genuine apostle, Paul produces not his visions or the churches he planted but his hunger and his ruined reputation. And there was One who was truly treated as the refuse of all things, taken outside the city and put to death so that others might be made clean.

In everyday life. These responses can be learned, because the Spirit of the Christ who blessed his executioners lives in you. When somebody misrepresents you and your answer is drafted at once, Paul’s three verbs are the alternative: ask God to do that person good, by name; stay where God has put you rather than withdrawing in a sulk; keep speaking to them rather than about them (Romans 12:14, 20–21; 1 Peter 3:9). And pray this week for Christians treated as the refuse of the world in places where faith can still cost a life.

Does blessing those who revile me mean I must let people abuse me? No. Paul is describing how to answer insult, slander and persecution for the gospel’s sake: with blessing instead of revenge. He is not telling anyone to remain under abuse at home, at work or in a church. Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when he was about to be illegally beaten (Acts 22:25), and when his life was threatened he escaped (Acts 9:25). Abuse should never be tolerated, and the right response includes getting to safety, telling those who can protect you, and reporting crimes to the authorities, who are God’s servants for that very purpose (Romans 13:4). You can pray for God’s good for an abuser, and refuse to retaliate, from a place of safety. Blessing is not the same as staying.

Should pastors then work for a living instead of being paid? Not necessarily. The Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (9:14), and Paul accepted gifts from other churches (Philippians 4:15–16). He chose to work in Corinth so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money in a city full of paid speakers (9:12, 15–18). Some ministers rightly work a trade; others are rightly supported by their churches. The principle is not the payslip but the heart: a minister must never preach for gain, and a church must never let its minister go in need.

Uncertain wording. The two words translated “scum” (perikatharma) and “refuse” (peripsēma) both mean the dirt removed in cleaning. Such words were also used of the lowest outcasts, whom some Greek cities drove out or put to death in a time of disaster, as if to carry away the city’s pollution. Whether Paul has that custom in mind is uncertain; the words were also ordinary terms of contempt, and that may be all he means. Either way the sense is clear: the apostles were treated as the most worthless thing there is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s hard words are a father’s love, and he longs to come to them gently. He writes not to shame but to warn his beloved children, for through the gospel he became their father (vv. 14–15). So he urges them to imitate him and sends Timothy to remind them of his ways in Christ (vv. 16–17). Some have grown arrogant, thinking he will not come; he will, and will test not their talk but their power, for that is what God’s kingdom consists in (vv. 18–20). Whether he comes with a rod or with gentleness is up to them (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Fatherhood and Learning by Imitation

Paul’s fatherhood rests on the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). His aim is to shape their lives, not to control them. Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living picture of the gospel he preached (on what they are to copy, see the note on vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Paul’s absence some at Corinth had grown arrogant and dismissed him. Timothy is sent to show by his life what Paul had taught. Now: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1) is among the most demanding things a minister can say, and among the most necessary. Disciples need examples, not only doctrines, and a church with correct theology but no Christlike character has missed the point.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s hard words come from a father who loves them: he brought them to new birth through the gospel, and no other teacher can take that place.

Not to shame but to admonish. The irony stops. It came not from injured pride but from a father who could not get through to his children. Shaming and admonishing look similar and are opposite in intent. Shame attacks the person, to make him feel small, and produces compliance or resentment but never growth. Admonition (noutheteō, to put in mind, to warn and counsel) attacks the problem. It aims at change, and it can only be received from someone the hearer is sure loves him.

Countless guides. Literally ten thousand. The word for guides is paidagōgoi: the household slave who walked the children to school, kept them out of trouble and enforced the rules (Galatians 3:24). Useful, necessary, and not a parent; Paul is not sneering at the many teachers, but naming a different kind of bond.

You do not have many fathers. Guardians can be replaced; a father is unique. Egennēsa: I fathered you. The man through whose preaching you were born again cannot be replaced by a better speaker; the polished man may teach you more, but he will never be the one who told you first. Yet behind the father in Christ stands the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope (1 Peter 1:3), and every spiritual father is only a midwife at a birth God brings about.

Those whom I love. Paul’s order, hard words first and love stated plainly, is the risen Christ’s own. To a church that said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, almost exactly the Corinthians’ boast (4:8), Jesus gave a rebuke as sharp as anything in this chapter, and then explained it: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:17, 19). The one who rebukes his churches is the one who died for them, and his warnings come from the same heart as his wounds.

What it does not mean. Paul does not claim authority over their faith in place of Christ: not that we lord it over your faith, he says, but we work with you for your joy (2 Corinthians 1:24). He is a father in Christ, through the gospel, and the life he passed on was never his own.

How to correct someone. Paul speaks the hard thing first, without softening it, then makes the affection explicit: beloved children. We go wrong either way: the love assumed and never stated, so the rebuke lands as shame; or the love stated at such length that the correction never gets said. Does the person you need to correct know, because you have told them, that you are for them? Paul could call the Corinthians puffed-up infants playing at kings because they had watched him work with his hands among them and knew what he had spent on them (2 Corinthians 12:14–15).

What if the person who led me to Christ later fell away or hurt me? Then grieve, but do not doubt what God did. The new birth is God’s work, not the messenger’s, and God can use a cracked vessel to carry living water (Philippians 1:15–18). Your faith rests on the Christ that person pointed to. If that person sinned against you, you are not bound to stay close or to pretend nothing happened, and any harm done should be dealt with honestly. But you may still thank God for the gospel you heard through them, and pray that he would restore them.

Where Christians differ: calling ministers father. Jesus said to call no one on earth your father (Matthew 23:9), yet Paul calls himself their father. Some use this to justify the title Father for priests. This commentary’s view: Jesus forbade giving any human the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs only to God. Paul is describing a relationship, not claiming a title or rank. He brought them to new birth through the gospel and cares for them with a father’s love (1 Thessalonians 2:11; Philemon 10). The word describes affection and responsibility, not a priestly office, and he uses it to plead, not to rule. The verse gives no warrant for making Father an honorific for ministers. Many who use the title mean by it the pastoral affection Paul describes, and the point is not to scorn them but to keep the Father in heaven without a rival.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guides” was used of the household slave who took charge of children on their way to school.

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges the Corinthians to copy his Christlike way of life, and sends Timothy to show them what it looks like.

Imitators of me. It sounds presumptuous, but Paul supplies the qualification later: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). They are to copy not his personality but his direction: he is following Christ, and he asks them to go the same way. Children learn by copying their father; our discomfort with the sentence may say more about us than about him.

What he is asking them to copy. He has just described it (4:9–13), and it is not his eloquence, authority or success, but the lower place, manual labour, being thought a fool, and blessing those who revile you. Nobody builds a personality cult on that material. And many of these believers could not read, so Christianity was passed on the way a trade is, by watching somebody do it; few people become patient by reading about patience.

I sent you Timothy. Paul’s spiritual son (1 Timothy 1:2) was on his way (16:10), bringing not new doctrine but a reminder of Paul’s ways (hodoi, paths) in Christ. He sends not just a letter but a man formed by the very pattern under dispute: an argument can be sent in a letter; a way of life has to be shown by a person.

Everywhere in every church. Paul had no special teaching for Corinth; he taught the same in all the churches (7:17; 11:16; 14:33). Corinth is no exception: one gospel and one pattern of life, the same everywhere.

Christ’s before it was Paul’s. Every item on that list was Christ’s first. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58); he worked with his hands as a carpenter (Mark 6:3); he took the lowest place and washed feet; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). Paul’s life is a copy because Christ lives in him (Galatians 2:20), producing his own humility and love in Paul’s ordinary days by his Spirit. That is why the appeal is not arrogant: Paul is not asking them to become like Paul, but like the Lord they can see, imperfectly but truly, in him.

Is it arrogant for me to say “follow my example”? Not if it is said in Paul’s spirit and about Paul’s pattern. Every parent, elder and older believer is already being imitated; the only question is whether they will own it. Elders are told to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and older women to train younger women by their lives (Titus 2:3–5). You need not claim perfection. You can say: watch how I bring my failures to Christ, how I handle money, how I speak about people who are absent. That is not boasting but the honest admission that Christianity is caught as well as taught.

What if there is no one in my church I can imitate? There almost certainly is, but the people worth imitating are rarely the most visible. Look for the faithful rather than the impressive: the couple who have quietly loved each other for forty years, the widow who prays, the man who never speaks badly of anyone. Ask to spend time with them. Read the lives of faithful Christians from the past, too (Hebrews 13:7). And remember that the final pattern is Christ himself, to whom every human example only points.

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some have grown bold because they think Paul will not come back; he will, and he will test whether their fine talk has any of God’s power behind it.

Some are arrogant. Puffed up again, and the cause was distance: people behave differently when they think they will not have to face the person concerned. Some were saying Paul would not dare return, and the confidence had grown that always grows in the absence of the one who might answer back.

If the Lord wills. Paul simply announces that the absence is temporary (16:5). “If the Lord wills” is not an empty phrase but the settled habit of a man who knows his plans happen only if God allows them, the instinct James insists on: you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). A man who says that about a journey has settled who runs the world, in his diary and not only in his theology.

Not talk but power. Talk (logos) is the impressive speech Corinth prized; power (dynamis) is the real working of God’s Spirit in a life. He is coming to see whether the gospel they discuss so fluently has produced what it always produces where it is real. Jealousy and strife were the evidence of the flesh (3:3), and gifts without love are nothing (13:1–3), so the power he will look for is whether they have begun to love each other (see vv. 20–21). The Lord’s own word is never empty talk: he spoke, and the world was made; he speaks, and the dead hear his voice and live (John 5:25).

My master is delayed. Jesus described this exact arrogance. A servant says to himself, My master is delayed, and begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards, and the master comes on a day he does not expect (Matthew 24:48–50). Puffed-up confidence grows wherever the Lord seems far away, and the cure is the same: the one who is absent is coming, and a church lives well only as the household of a returning Lord.

In everyday life. A man can talk about grace fluently for thirty years and be no easier to live with. So ask those who live with you, not those who hear you teach, whether they see love, patience and holiness behind your words, and ask God for the power, which only his Spirit supplies.

Must I always say “if the Lord wills”? It is not a formula to attach to every sentence; Paul often speaks of his plans without it (16:8). It is an attitude of the heart that should show in how you plan. Make plans, work hard at them, and hold them with an open hand, knowing that you do not know what tomorrow will bring (James 4:13–16). What matters is that you would not be shocked, or bitter, if God redrew the map.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s kingdom shows itself in changed lives, not fine words, and the Corinthians must choose whether Paul comes to discipline them or to love them gently.

The kingdom of God. God’s rule, present now through Christ and the Spirit, shows itself not in eloquent religious talk but in changed lives (Romans 14:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). Speaking well about God proves nothing.

Not a demand for the spectacular. “Power” here must not be used to demand signs and wonders as proof of a genuine church. The power this letter has described is the power of God that saves through a message about an execution (1:18), that will raise the dead (6:14), and that turns a jealous congregation into people who love each other. That is not less than miraculous; it is simply harder to photograph.

Shall I come to you with a rod? Paul leaves it as a question rather than a threat. The rod is a father’s rod of discipline (Proverbs 13:24), and it is real: Paul has apostolic authority and will use it, as chapter 5 is about to show. A father who can never be firm is not being kind, and a church that can never act is not being loving.

Or with love in a spirit of gentleness? Gentleness (prautēs) is meekness, strength under control. Both the rod and gentleness are love, but gentleness is what Paul longs to use, and the choice is not his. He has put it in their hands: what do you wish? It is the strangest kind of authority, a man with the right to compel, asking, and it is how God deals with his people throughout Scripture: he warns before he acts, and the warning is itself the mercy, given so that the rod need not be used. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die (Ezekiel 33:11)?

In the flow. Verses 20–21 bring to rest the first great section of the letter, begun with the plea that there be no divisions (1:10), and the mention of the rod leads into chapter 5, where Paul must deal with a sin the proud church had tolerated (5:1–2).

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. Paul’s gentleness is borrowed. Writing to this same church later, he opens his sternest section: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1). The King entered his capital mounted on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), and called the weary to himself because he was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). The kingdom’s power does not cancel that gentleness; it travels in it. When Paul hopes to arrive with love and a gentle spirit, he hopes to arrive looking like his Lord.

The rod has already been spent. The One who had every right to come with a rod to a world in open rebellion came instead as an infant, worked with his hands, was reviled and blessed, and was made a spectacle last of all. The only rod that has yet fallen in full fell on him: he was pierced for our transgressions, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The King holds all power, and he comes to his people in gentleness, because the rod has already been spent on his own back.

In everyday life. Is there a correction God has been making gently, through a verse that keeps coming back or a friend’s word, that you have been putting off? Respond while it is still the gentle word. And if you have authority over others, follow Paul’s order: warn clearly, show your love plainly, give time to respond, and only then use the rod, and even then with sorrow rather than satisfaction.

Does God still come to his children with the rod? Yes, but always as a Father, never as an executioner. The Lord disciplines those he loves, and the discipline of believers is not punishment for sin, which Christ has already borne, but training in holiness (Hebrews 12:5–11). It can come through hardship, the exposure of sin, or the discipline of the church; it is painful, and always for our good. The quickest way to be spared the rod is to respond to the word: when God speaks gently, listen.

Is church discipline really loving? It is, when done rightly, as the next chapter shows. Discipline is meant to bring a sinner to repentance, to protect the church, and to honour Christ’s name (5:5–7). It must be carried out by the church in a patient, ordered way (Matthew 18:15–17), with humility and with the aim of restoring, not removing. A church that never disciplines is not kinder; it leaves people to wander into danger unwarned. But discipline must never be harsh, hasty or used to protect leaders, and it never replaces calling the police when a crime has been committed.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.<sup>2</sup>Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.<sup>3</sup>But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself.<sup>4</sup>For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.<sup>5</sup>Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.<sup>6</sup>I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another.<sup>7</sup>For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?<sup>8</sup>Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!<sup>9</sup>For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.<sup>10</sup>We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.<sup>11</sup>To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless,<sup>12</sup>and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;<sup>13</sup>when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.<sup>14</sup>I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children.<sup>15</sup>For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.<sup>16</sup>I urge you, then, be imitators of me.<sup>17</sup>That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.<sup>18</sup>Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you.<sup>19</sup>But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.<sup>20</sup>For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.<sup>21</sup>What do you wish? keyVerse.quote: What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
keyVerse.note: This verse is the chapter’s, and the whole opening section’s, answer to Corinthian pride. Gifts, teachers, faith itself and above all Christ were received, so there is nothing left to rank ourselves by and no one to boast in but the Giver. The question humbles, but it also frees: someone who has received everything can stop comparing and start giving thanks.

4.reflection:
Paul says the one thing required of stewards is that they be found faithful (v. 2). By what standards do we tend to judge ministers, other Christians and ourselves, and what would change if faithfulness were the measure?

“What do you have that you did not receive?” (v. 7). Think of the things you are most tempted to be proud of. How does seeing each one as a gift change the way you treat people who have less, or more?

The Corinthians acted as if they were already reigning, while the apostles were hungry, beaten and despised (vv. 8–13). Where do Christians today expect the crown without the cross, and how does Christ’s own road answer that?

Paul asks whether he should come “with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness” (v. 21). How do you respond when God corrects you gently, and how can we correct one another in a way that is plainly loving?

5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Where we are. Paul has spent four chapters on the church’s quarrels and pride. Now he turns to what he has heard about their life, and chapters 5–6 deal with sexual sin, church discipline and lawsuits: the same pride showing in new places.

The message. A church that belongs to Christ, its Passover lamb, cannot be proud of the sin he died to remove. When someone who calls himself a brother persists openly in serious sin, the church must grieve, not boast, and act together in the Lord’s name to put him outside its fellowship, not to be rid of him but to win him back. Its holiness is not something it achieves; it is what the church already is in Christ, and it is to live like it. Those outside are not the church’s to judge: God judges them, and the church’s word to them is the gospel.

Why it was said. A member was living with his stepmother, a union forbidden by the law of Moses and scandalous even in Corinth, and the church was proud of its broad-mindedness (see the introduction). They had also misread an earlier letter of Paul’s, and the misreading had become a reason to do nothing: strict on paper with the whole immoral city, relaxed in practice with one of their own.

How the chapter makes its case. First the scandal, and the deeper scandal of a congregation that boasts where it should mourn (vv. 1–2). Then the verdict: the gathered church, with the power of the Lord Jesus, is to hand the man over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved (vv. 3–5). Then the reason, drawn from Passover: a little leaven works through the whole lump, so clear it out, because you are unleavened already and the Lamb has been sacrificed; and keep the feast with sincerity and truth, not malice (vv. 6–8). Last, the scope: Paul never meant them to leave the world, only to stop treating a professing brother in open sin as if all were well, for God judges those outside (vv. 9–13).

Where it leads. At the centre of the New Testament’s plainest teaching on church discipline stands not a rule but a Lamb. Christ, the Lamb without blemish, died at Passover so that judgment would pass over a leavened people and make them new dough (v. 7). The closing words, “Purge the evil person from among you”, once ended in a stoning; now they end in an exclusion with the door left open, because the one who was not evil was led outside the gate and died there in the sinner’s place (Hebrews 13:12).

For us. Churches still fail both ways: by an indulgence that calls itself grace, and by a harshness that forgets the goal is a man saved. This chapter asks for grief instead of pride or outrage, for discipline that keeps the door open, and for each of us to search our own house for the leaven we have learned to live with, not least the respectable malice that no church ever disciplines. We clean the house not to earn the Lamb, but because he has already been sacrificed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church that belongs to the Passover Lamb cannot boast about the sin he died to remove. The scandal is a man living with his stepmother; the worse scandal is a church proud of tolerating it when it should be mourning (vv. 1–2). Paul calls for action by the gathered church in the Lord’s name, handing the man over to Satan with his salvation as the aim (vv. 3–5). Then he gives the reason: tolerated sin spreads like leaven through dough, so clear it out, as people already made unleavened by Christ our Passover lamb, and keep the feast in sincerity and truth (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

Calvin grounds church discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the church’s holiness is not its own achievement but a share in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the last word against the sinner; it is meant to bring him to repentance (see the note on v. 5). A church that will not discipline, in the name of grace or of avoiding conflict, is less gracious than it thinks: it lets unrepentant sin spread through the whole body, and it withholds from the sinner the painful mercy of being confronted.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The church’s pride may reflect the influence of members with status and polish who had turned gospel freedom into permissiveness. Now: A church afraid to confront unrepentant sin can end up shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A member is living openly with his stepmother, and the church, instead of grieving, is proud of its tolerance. Paul calls them to mourn and to remove him.

Actually reported. The word can mean “actually” or “generally”: the thing is common knowledge, talked about across the region. “Sexual immorality” is porneia, the broad word for any sexual sin outside marriage.

Not tolerated even among pagans. This is the sting: it breaks not only the law of Moses but the standards of pagan Corinth. Roman law prohibited such a marriage outright, and Cicero treats a comparable union inside a family as a crime almost beyond belief. The church of a city famous for vice had managed to be more permissive than the city.

His father’s wife. Not his mother but his stepmother, the father probably dead or divorced; the law of Moses forbade it explicitly (Leviticus 18:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). “Has” describes something going on now: a settled relationship, perhaps living together or even married, not a single lapse.

And you are arrogant! Here is the real subject of the chapter: not the man, but the congregation. They were not ashamed but proud, puffed up, the word Paul has used against them all through chapter 4. Probably they prized a theology of freedom they were pleased with: the body did not matter spiritually (6:12–13), grace could accommodate even this, and a church that took it in its stride proved how far beyond ordinary scruples it had travelled. There is still a tolerance that presents itself as maturity and is actually cowardice with a theology attached, and underneath it is usually a hunger to be the church nobody could call narrow. But a church that needs the world’s approval more than its Lord’s has already chosen whose verdict it fears (Galatians 1:10).

Ought you not rather to mourn? The verb is the one for grieving a death (pentheō). Serious sin in a church usually draws one of two other responses: the Corinthians’ way, to absorb it, explain it and be relaxed about it; or the commoner way, outrage, gossip, the energetic circulation of the details, and a certain relish. Paul asks for neither, but for the grief of people standing at a graveside. Outrage is pleasurable, which is why it is so popular; indifference is comfortable; grief can be neither faked nor enjoyed. It is the only one of the three with any love in it: you do not grieve over someone you were not attached to.

Removed from among you. Mourning does not replace action; it is the only right soil for it, the sorrow of people who love the man and the Lord too much to pretend.

Proud of what the Lamb died for. The Corinthians were boasting about the very kind of sin for which Christ, their Passover lamb, was sacrificed (v. 7). A church that thinks grace makes sin small has forgotten what grace cost. Their only glory was a crucified Saviour (1:30–31), and no one can glory in the cross while being proud of the sins that put him there. Nor is mourning a gloomy alternative to joy. It is the posture Christ himself blessed: those who mourn “shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). The God who asks his church to mourn over sin mourned over it first. He loves his church too much to let her be proud of what is killing her, and his holiness and his tears are not two different things.

What it does not mean. Not that the church should expel members for every sin; all believers sin, every day. Church discipline is for serious, open sin persisted in without repentance, after patient warning (Matthew 18:15–17).

Why was the woman not disciplined too? Almost certainly because she was not a member of the church. The church is responsible for those inside it, and God judges those outside (vv. 12–13). That does not make her sin less serious or put her beyond the gospel; it means the church’s formal discipline applies only to those who profess Christ and have joined his people. Toward her, as toward every unbeliever, the church’s task is to proclaim the gospel and pray.

What should an ordinary member do when there is a scandal in the church? First, do not spread it: talking over the details with people who are not part of the solution is gossip, however concerned it sounds (Proverbs 16:28). Second, pray, both for the person caught in the sin and for the leaders who have to handle it. Third, if you know something your leaders need to know, tell them directly and privately. Fourth, check your heart: aim for the grief Paul asks for, not the interest or superiority that comes so easily. And if the sin is a crime, especially any abuse, it must be reported to the police; the church’s discipline never replaces the law.
verseByVerse.note: “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it, and Roman law condemned it too.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has already reached his verdict, but it is to be carried out by the gathered church, acting with the Lord’s own authority.

Absent in body, present in spirit. Paul is with them in thought and concern, and also in authority: his apostolic word travels in the letter being read aloud (Colossians 2:5). He can pronounce judgment from a distance because the facts are not in dispute: a man is living with his stepmother in plain sight.

When you are assembled. Yet the verdict waits for the gathered congregation; even an apostle with unquestioned authority does not remove the man by letter. Discipline in the New Testament is a corporate act of the church, and this cuts both ways: the congregation cannot hand it to the minister and then complain about him, and a leader who decides a case privately and announces the outcome finds no support here. The steps the Lord laid down in Matthew 18 end the same way, with “tell it to the church” (Matthew 18:17).

With the power of our Lord Jesus. Two things make such a gathering more than a disciplinary hearing: it meets in the name of the Lord Jesus, on his authority, not its own; and it acts with his power. That is the promise attached in Matthew: “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20), in its context a guarantee given to a church doing this very thing, and the most sobering reason for doing it carefully. It does not make a church’s vote infallible. It means that when a congregation acts by his word, the warning the man receives is not only from his neighbours but from his Lord (Luke 10:16).

Who actually carries out discipline, the elders or the whole church? Christians organise this differently, and honest believers disagree. Congregational churches, including many Baptists, read this verse and Matthew 18:17 as giving the final act to the gathered membership, guided by its elders (2 Corinthians 2:6 speaks of a punishment “by the majority”). Presbyterian churches see the elders acting for the congregation as its representatives. Others mix the two. The common ground is wide, and it is the point of this verse: discipline is never one man’s act; it is done before the Lord with his authority, it involves the church, and it is done openly and carefully, not in secret.

Uncertain wording. Verses 3–5 are one long sentence in Greek, and it is not certain which part “in the name of the Lord Jesus” belongs to: the assembling (as the ESV takes it), Paul’s judgment, or the handing over in verse 5. The meaning hardly changes: verdict, gathering and act all stand under the Lord’s name and power.

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is to put the man out of its fellowship into the world where Satan rules, so that, feeling what his sin costs, he may repent and be saved on the last day.

Deliver this man to Satan. Paul’s own closing words, “so that his spirit may be saved”, show that this alarming phrase does not mean damnation. The letter has been describing two spheres: the community where Christ dwells by his Spirit (3:16), and the world outside, which lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19; Ephesians 2:2). To be excluded from the assembly is to be put out of the first into the second: removed from the protection, fellowship, Lord’s Table and prayers of God’s people, and left in the open. Paul uses the same phrase once more (1 Timothy 1:19–20).

For the destruction of the flesh. Most likely the sinful nature, the appetite itself, allowed to run to its own bitter end (see the box at the end of this note). A man shielded from the consequences of what he is doing will continue; a man left to feel what it costs may come to his senses, like the prodigal, who needed the pigs before he wanted the father (Luke 15:14–17).

So that his spirit may be saved. This clause governs everything. The church is not washing its hands of a man but using the last means God has given for reaching him, when everything gentler has failed. Excommunication, the formal removal of a professing believer from a church’s membership and the Lord’s Table, is in the New Testament not the opposite of seeking someone’s salvation but an instrument of it: the surgeon’s knife, used with the intention of a cure.

The day of the Lord.
