In this letter it is the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Paul has promised this church that Christ will sustain them to the end, guiltless in that day, because God is faithful (1:8–9). That is what makes so severe a step thinkable. The church can put a man outside its fellowship without putting him outside the reach of Christ, because his salvation never rested on the church’s grip. The Lord leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost (Luke 15:4). Discipline is the church’s part; bringing the sheep home is his. And the Judge on that day will be the Shepherd who went looking.

What happened next. No treatment of this verse is honest without the sequel. Writing later to the same church, Paul deals with a disciplined man, perhaps this one, though commentators are divided. The discipline had worked, and Paul told the church to forgive and restore him, “so that we would not be outwitted by Satan” (2 Corinthians 2:5–11). Here Satan is the instrument God uses to bring a man home; there he gains if a church will not let a repentant man back. The second failure is the commoner one.

The guard against cruelty. This text has been used to justify real cruelty: shunning as punishment, families broken apart, people pursued for years, the machinery of control. The test is Paul’s stated purpose, the man’s salvation. A church that disciplines without longing for the person’s return, without a route back, without telling him plainly what repentance would look like and how gladly he would be received, is not doing what this verse describes, and has no warrant from it.

Can a true Christian be put out of the church? Yes. Paul’s hope for the man’s spirit suggests he may be a genuine believer in serious, stubborn sin, and true Christians can fall grievously for a time, as David did (Westminster 17.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3). But God does not let his own go, and the discipline of his church is one of the ways he makes them feel the misery of their sin and turns them home. So the doctrine that God keeps his people to the end does not make discipline unnecessary; discipline is one of the means by which he keeps them. Whether a particular person is truly born again is finally known to God, and will be shown by whether he returns.

Can someone who has been put out ever come back? Yes, and the church should long for it; the door in this passage opens both ways (2 Corinthians 2:7–8). Real repentance shows itself in turning from the sin, not merely in regret at the consequences, and then the church should welcome the person as the father welcomed the prodigal, without suspicion or endless reminders of the past.

What if I was disciplined unfairly? Churches are made of sinners, and they can be wrong: acting hastily, without proper process, for things Scripture does not condemn, or to protect their leaders. If that has happened to you, remember that it is the Lord who judges you (4:4); a wrong human verdict does not change your standing before God. Seek to understand what was said, examine yourself honestly before the Lord, and, if you can, ask for a review or talk with wise believers outside the situation. If reconciliation is impossible, it is right to find a faithful church elsewhere. And ask God to keep you from bitterness, which can do more harm than the injustice.

Where Christians differ: church discipline. Many churches today never practise discipline, thinking it unloving or judgmental; others practise it harshly, for minor issues. This commentary’s view: Church discipline is commanded by Christ and the apostles (Matthew 18:15–17; 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15; Titus 3:10). It is one of the marks of a true church, alongside the preaching of the word and the right use of the sacraments (Belgic Confession 29). Its purposes are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church and the honour of Christ (the Westminster Confession 30.3). It should be done carefully, in stages, with love and prayer, and only for serious, persistent, unrepentant sin.

Uncertain wording. “For the destruction of the flesh” is genuinely disputed. Some take it to mean physical suffering, even death, like the judgments in Acts 5 or later in this letter (11:30). Others take “flesh” (sarx) in Paul’s usual moral sense, the sinful nature. The goal is clear, “that his spirit may be saved”; how Paul pictured the means is not. The moral sense fits his usual wording, and his stated purpose that the man be saved, far better, and is the likely meaning.
verseByVerse.note: To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, where Satan rules, in the hope that he will repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tolerated sin spreads through a whole church as leaven works through dough, so get rid of it: you are already God’s clean new people, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed.

Your boasting is not good. A church that is congratulating itself while one of its members destroys himself has its eyes in the wrong place.

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. A proverb Paul also uses in Galatians 5:9. Leaven was not dried yeast from a packet but a lump of old fermented dough kept back from the last baking and worked through the new. It works invisibly and completely: you cannot put a piece in one corner and keep the rest unaffected, and once it is through the dough there is no taking it out. That is why Paul will not let this pass as one man’s private business.

How the leaven spreads. The danger is not that everyone will commit that particular sin, but that the standard moves. Once something serious has been publicly accommodated, it becomes the new floor. How do you raise a small matter in a church that has swallowed a large one? One unaddressed case produces not one hypocrite but a congregation in which nothing can be said about anything, and the young believer watching learns that its words about holiness are not meant.

Cleanse out the old leaven. Then Paul reaches for Passover. Before the feast every Jewish household removed all leaven from the house (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7), and in later practice this became a search by lamplight through every room for any crumb. The picture may have been in season: Paul was writing from Ephesus some weeks before Pentecost (16:8), perhaps close to Passover itself. Not a general resolve to be purer, but a search, room by room, because a lamb was about to be killed.

As you really are unleavened. This clause shows how the New Testament’s commands work, and it reverses how we naturally think. Not: purify yourselves in order to become clean; but: you are unleavened, so get the leaven out. In Christ they are already sanctified (1:2), washed and claimed as God’s own (6:11), and the command is to let the house match the owner. A son is not told to behave well so that he can join the family; he is told to behave like the family he belongs to (Ephesians 5:1). A Christian who reverses the order will spend his life trying to earn what he was given at the start.

Christ, our Passover lamb. Everything in the chapter rests on this clause. Behind the first Passover stood a night in Egypt: a lamb killed in every house, blood struck on the doorposts, and death passing through the streets and passing over every door where the blood was (Exodus 12). Nobody inside was safer because of his character; the blood was on the door or it was not. Every Passover afterwards was a rehearsal, with a lamb on the table that could never take away sin. Then John saw Jesus by the Jordan and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). He died at Passover (John 19:14; the Gospels date the Last Supper in ways not easy to align, but all four place his death at the feast), and not a bone of him was broken, as the law required of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; John 19:36). The lamb was always him. Centuries of suppers pointed at one afternoon outside Jerusalem, when the blood went on the doorposts of the world.

Nothing a search by lamplight would find. There was never any leaven in him. The Passover lamb had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5), and the Son of God lived the one human life in which a search by lamplight would find nothing. Then he gave that spotless life for a leavened people, and his righteousness was counted as theirs (2 Corinthians 5:21). The Lamb without spot has made a stained people into new dough, and he will present them to himself without blemish at the last (Ephesians 5:27).

What does it mean that Christ is our Passover lamb? That he died in our place, so that the judgment we deserved passed over us. The firstborn in a blood-marked house was spared not because he was innocent but because a death had already taken place in that house. So at the cross God’s just judgment against our sin fell on Christ, our substitute, and all who shelter under his blood by faith are spared (1 Peter 1:18–19; Romans 3:25). And Passover began a journey out of slavery: Christ’s blood frees us from the guilt of sin and brings us out from its rule.

What it does not mean. Not that we keep the Jewish Passover or must clear our kitchens of yeast. Christ has fulfilled it. The Lord’s Supper is the new covenant meal (11:23–26), and the old leaven we put away is sin, not bread.

In everyday life. Is there one sin you have quietly accommodated, a habit, a resentment, a way of handling money or truth, that you no longer fight because it has become the floor? Leaven is never content with one corner. Go looking for it the Passover way, room by room, and bring it to Christ. A sin you are still fighting is not the floor but the battle, and the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17). You are not cleaning the house to earn the lamb; the lamb has been sacrificed, and that is why you clean.

Textual note. The King James Version’s “sacrificed for us” follows later manuscripts; the earliest lack “for us”, though the verse plainly means it.
verseByVerse.note: Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since the Lamb has been sacrificed, the Christian life is a festival, to be kept not with the old leaven of malice and evil but with sincerity and truth.

Let us therefore celebrate the festival. An unexpected way to finish a paragraph about excommunication, and it shows how Paul understood the Christian life. The Passover lamb was killed, and then came the seven days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Exodus 12:15–20): a week of feasting flowing out of the sacrifice. Christ has been sacrificed, once, finished; what follows is not a fast but a festival, and the festival is now.

Malice and evil. Then a surprise. After seven verses on gross sexual immorality, the leaven Paul names is malice: kakia, ill will, the settled wish for someone’s harm; and evil, ponēria, active wickedness. He names the sin the congregation had not thought to look for, the sin of the respectable, and the malice was general: it had helped make the church proud rather than grieving. It is possible to be scrupulous about the sins one has no appetite for.

Sincerity and truth. Against that Paul sets eilikrineia, sincerity, unmixed, with nothing hidden underneath; and alētheia, truth, the match between what a person is and what he appears to be. That makes the cleansing far more searching than the removal of one man. A church can conduct discipline impeccably and still be full of this leaven, putting out the immoral member and keeping its factions and long-running grudges.

The feast he set at Passover. It was on the day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed, that Jesus took bread and said it was his body, given for them (Luke 22:7, 19). The old feast ended at that table and the new began there. Paul is speaking to people who gather at the Lord’s Supper, where the bread is a participation in the body of the true Lamb (10:16), and he will rebuke them for bringing their divisions to that very table (11:17–22). No one can bring a grudge against a brother to the meal at which Christ gave himself for both of them.

What does malice look like in ordinary life? Rarely like open hatred. More often it is the small pleasure when someone you dislike stumbles; the story that makes another person look slightly worse; the grudge kept fed by rehearsing it; the cold silence that punishes; the joke with an edge: wanting, even a little, for someone else not to do well. Paul lists it among the things to put away (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8), and the way to put it away is to replace it: ask God for that person’s good, speak well of them when they are absent, and forgive as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32).

How can holiness be a feast when it feels so hard? Because what you put away is stale bread, and what you are given is better. The fight against sin is real and can be painful, but it is the struggle of someone clearing the table for a banquet, not of a prisoner breaking stones. Every sin you put away was a thief at the feast, taking your joy. The Lord who commands holiness spread the table, and he invites you in the words of the old prophet to come, buy and eat without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). Duty and delight are not opposites here.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church is to judge its own members, not the world. Paul’s earlier instruction to avoid the sexually immoral never meant cutting off unbelievers, which would mean leaving the world (vv. 9–10). It meant refusing ordinary fellowship, even at table, to anyone who calls himself a brother and lives in open, unrepentant sin, whether sexual, financial or of the tongue (v. 11). Outsiders answer to God; insiders the church must care for, and that care sometimes means removing them (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside (vv. 12–13) sets the scope of church discipline. The church is not called to police the world but to keep its own fellowship true. Its mission to the world is the gospel, and its care for its own members is part of what makes that witness credible.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. They managed to be withdrawn from the world and undisciplined within at once. Now: Churches still drift into one or the other. Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s earlier instruction to avoid the sexually immoral never meant cutting off unbelievers, for that would mean leaving the world.

I wrote to you in my letter. Paul had written to Corinth before this, and that letter is lost (see the introduction). “Associate” means to mix together with: close, ongoing fellowship.

In the flow. Having told the church to put the man out (vv. 2–8), Paul closes off the obvious way of dodging the command. His distinction between inside and outside carries into chapter 6, where the Corinthians do the reverse, taking insiders’ disputes to outsiders to judge.

Not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world. They had apparently taken his instruction to mean everyone in Corinth, perhaps deliberately, so that it became impossible and could be ignored.

The greedy and swindlers. The greedy always want more, at others’ expense; swindlers are robbers and extortioners, people who grab. Paul sets sins of money and of worship alongside sexual sin, so we may never treat sexual sin as the only kind that counts. A church that would discipline adultery but never greed has not read this verse.

Out of the world. In that city a rule of no contact with immoral people would empty the market, the workshop, the street and most families; you would have to leave the world altogether, as some groups have tried to do. The Lord prayed not that his disciples be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one in it (John 17:15). He was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, an insult that simply described how he spent his time (Matthew 11:19). He ate at their tables, touched their lepers, let a woman of the city weep on his feet, and was never once stained. His holiness was not the fragile kind that has to hide but the kind that heals what it touches. And Paul will soon tell this church to accept dinner invitations from pagan neighbours (10:27).

Strict and open in the wrong places. They were rigorous, in theory, with outsiders who had never professed anything, and relaxed about a member living in public sin. A church can still be indignant about the sins of the surrounding culture and unable to have a hard conversation with one of its own.

Can I have close friends who are not Christians? Yes, and you should; Jesus did, and friendship is one of the main ways the gospel travels. Scripture warns against being bound to unbelievers in ways that pull you from Christ: being unequally yoked (2 Corinthians 6:14), which applies most clearly to marriage, and letting bad company corrupt good morals (15:33). So ask of any friendship: am I drawing them toward Christ, or are they drawing me away from him? Am I free to speak of Christ, and to say no to sin, in their company? If the answers are good, enjoy the friendship and pray for your friend.

Does a lost letter mean part of the Bible is missing? No. Paul, like any pastor, wrote much that was true and useful and not meant to be Scripture: notes, arrangements, greetings, earlier instructions (see the box at the end of this note). You can open your Bible with full confidence that it is the complete word God meant you to have.

Where Christians differ: the lost letter. Some argue that if an apostolic letter was lost, the New Testament canon must be incomplete. This commentary’s view: Not everything an apostle wrote was meant by God to be Scripture for the whole church in all ages. God, in his providence, preserved exactly the books he intended to be the canon (the Westminster Confession 1.2, 1.8; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.2, 1.8). The canon is closed and complete, sufficient for all faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The lost letter’s point is preserved here anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must not carry on ordinary fellowship, even at table, with someone who calls himself a Christian while living in open, unrepentant sin.

Anyone who bears the name of brother. These are the decisive words: not the immoral of the world, who have professed nothing, but the person inside, who calls himself a Christian and whose life publicly contradicts it.

Reviler and drunkard. Paul adds two names to his earlier list. Between the idolater and the drunkard stands the reviler, the man with a vicious tongue, a verbal bully, in the same list as the man in verse 1, with greed beside them both. A congregation will act on a sexual scandal and yet tolerate a reviler for thirty years.

Not even to eat. In that world a shared table was the public sign of acceptance, friendship and common life (see meals and reclining at table). The reference probably includes the church’s own meal, where the Lord’s Supper was taken, as well as ordinary social meals. The man is to find the fellowship he has enjoyed closed to him, precisely so that he notices something is wrong and feels the seriousness of his sin (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

The name of brother. The name this man bears was not his to invent. Christ is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11): he took their flesh, died for them, and made them one family with himself as the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). This man wears the family name of the Son of God while living in the very things the Son died to free him from, and expects the family to say nothing. Withdrawing fellowship refuses to let Christ’s name be used as a cover, and calls him back to the Brother whose name he bears. The table from which the unrepentant are kept back is the Lord’s own, and he keeps his place at its head, waiting for every wandering brother to come back, with a robe and a ring and a fattened calf.

About the unrepentant, not the struggling. Two guards are essential. First, nothing here touches the Christian who is fighting a sin and losing, ashamed, confessing and failing again. He is a candidate not for this passage but for Galatians 6:1, restoration in a spirit of gentleness. The sin Paul describes is settled, public and defended: the man has made up his mind to go on in it and expects the church to accept that. If you are reading this with a guilty conscience about a sin you hate, this verse is not about you, and your hatred of the sin is itself a sign of the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:22–25).

The church’s table, not the family’s bonds. Second, this concerns the church’s corporate fellowship, not the duties of a parent, a child or a spouse, and it is no licence to destroy natural bonds. Of a similar case Paul gives the tone: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3:15). That sentence should govern the whole practice, carried out by the church’s proper process, never by one member’s private decision to shun someone. The aim is to withdraw the signal that everything is fine, while leaving no doubt that he is wanted back.

In everyday life. Pray for anyone you know who calls himself a Christian but lives in open sin, and ask whether your friendship has quietly signalled to him that everything is fine. Only those who grieve over the sin can be trusted to confront a brother; anybody who finds it satisfying should not be doing it (Galatians 6:1).

Must I stop having meals with a grown-up child who professes faith and lives in serious sin? No. Paul is speaking of the church’s fellowship, not the bond between parent and child, which God himself made. Go on loving your child, having them in your home and caring for them. What changes is that you cannot pretend all is well with their walk with Christ. Speak honestly, more than once but not at every meal; pray without ceasing; keep the door wide open. If the church has acted, support its discipline by not treating it as unimportant, while showing your child that your love has not moved an inch: warn him as a brother.

Am I a “reviler” if I lose my temper? Not in Paul’s sense. Every Christian sins with his tongue (James 3:2), and a believer who loses his temper, is grieved, apologises and fights it is not the person in this list. The reviler’s pattern of life is verbal abuse: he habitually belittles, demeans, intimidates or rages at others and sees nothing wrong with it. That is serious enough to call for discipline, and especially serious in a home, where words can be a form of abuse. If you recognise yourself, do not wait to be confronted: confess it to God and to those you have hurt, seek help, and put it away.

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is to judge the conduct of its own members, not the world, which God himself will judge. So Paul closes with the old command to remove the evil person from the community.

For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Paul settles the jurisdiction in a sentence. It is not the church’s job to discipline unbelievers, who answer to God directly. This is not indifference to the world’s sin, which the same apostle describes at length in Romans 1; it is a recognition that the church has not been appointed the world’s magistrate. Our commission to those outside is announcement, not enforcement: we tell them what God has done in Christ. Their accounts are not ours to audit.

Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? “Judge” here means to assess conduct by God’s word and act on it, not to condemn anyone eternally. Belonging to a church is not a private arrangement between a believer and God; it is joining a family that has promised to watch over one another.

God judges those outside. Unbelievers are in God’s hands, and he will judge them rightly at the last day. A running commentary on the sins of people who never claimed to be anything else is energy spent in a court that is not ours.

Purge the evil person from among you. The closing citation is a refrain from Deuteronomy (17:7; 22:21), used when Israel had to remove a serious offender, often by death. Paul keeps the seriousness and changes the penalty. The church is not a state, holds no sword and executes nobody; what it can do is exclude. The new covenant form is as grave as the old and far more merciful: a man put outside the camp can come back, and a man stoned outside the camp cannot. Discipline in the New Testament is a death sentence reduced to a temporary exclusion, with the door left unlocked.

Outside the gate. That mercy comes from the sacrifice Paul has just named: Christ, our Passover lamb (v. 7). The church need purge nobody with a stone, because the death the covenant required has already been died, by someone else, once. In Deuteronomy the evil is taken outside the camp and the people are made clean. And there was a day when someone was led out of the city, in the name of the community’s purity, and executed outside the walls between two criminals. He was not the evil person. He was the only one in the story who was not, and he went out anyway, in the place of the man in verse 1, the arrogant congregation in verse 2 and every reader of this page. “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

The God who brings outsiders in. God judges those outside, and every one of us was once outside: separated from Christ, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). The Judge of outsiders is the God who brings outsiders in: in Christ Jesus those who once were far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). The church judges its own only because it is a family of former outsiders, and the Father who welcomed them has room at his table for many more.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be silent about sin in society. They may and should speak for justice, for the unborn, for the poor and for marriage, and vote and serve as citizens. But church discipline applies only to church members; the church does not try to govern the world by it.

How does this fit with “Judge not”? They are about different things. In 4:5 Paul forbids verdicts on the hidden purposes of the heart, which only the Lord can see. Jesus forbids the hypocrite’s fault-finding, and tells him to take the log out of his own eye so that he can see clearly to help his brother (Matthew 7:1–5). Here Paul requires the church to deal with the open, unrepentant conduct of someone who claims to be a brother. Christians must not judge hearts; they must judge conduct by Scripture, inside the church, humbly and for the sinner’s good. Nor does a church that does this claim to be better than the person it disciplines: every member, the leaders first, stands under the same word as a forgiven sinner, and the one who restores another must keep watch on himself, lest he too be tempted (Galatians 6:1).

So how should I treat a non-Christian who lives in the sins on Paul’s list? With love, honesty and patience, as someone who needs the same Saviour you needed. Do not expect him to live by a standard he has never accepted, or make his morals the first subject you raise. His deepest problem is not his behaviour but that he does not yet know Christ, and the gospel is what changes behaviour. Be his friend, be honest when he asks what you believe, and pray for him. If he comes to faith, he will come under the church’s care and its call to holiness, and find, as every Christian has, that the Lord who calls us to purity also gives the power for it (6:11).

parallels.desc: so you shall purge the evil from your midst

5.text: <sup>1</sup>It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife.<sup>2</sup>And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.<sup>3</sup>For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing.<sup>4</sup>When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,<sup>5</sup>you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.<sup>6</sup>Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?<sup>7</sup>Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.<sup>8</sup>Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.<sup>9</sup>I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—<sup>10</sup>not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.<sup>11</sup>But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.<sup>12</sup>For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?<sup>13</sup>God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”

keyVerse.quote: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this verse. The church is told to clear out sin because of what it already is, unleavened, and it is that because of what Christ has done: the Lamb has been sacrificed. Grief over sin, discipline that seeks a man’s return, and the feast of sincerity and truth all flow from this one sacrifice.

5.reflection:
The Corinthians were proud where they should have mourned (v. 2). Why is grief harder than either indifference or outrage when a fellow believer falls into serious sin, and what would it look like in your church?

Paul says the aim of discipline is “that his spirit may be saved” (v. 5). How should that aim shape the way a church carries it out, and the way it receives someone who repents (2 Corinthians 2:7–8)?

The leaven Paul names in verse 8 is not immorality but malice. Where might malice, or another respectable sin, have quietly become the floor in your own life or church?

Paul does not tell us to leave the world, but to deal honestly with those inside the church (vv. 10–12). How can you keep close friendships with unbelievers while being honest with fellow Christians, and how does Christ, “our Passover lamb”, shape both?

6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 ended with a church that would not judge a sinning member inside it (5:12). Chapter 6 shows the same church handing its private quarrels to judges outside it, then returns to sexual sin, closing the first half of the letter before Paul answers their questions (7:1).

The message. You belong to Christ, body and all, so live as people who do. Future judges of the world should not drag one another before pagan courts; better to suffer wrong than to beat a brother. People washed from their old sins must not go back to them. And the body is not an appetite to be fed wherever convenient: it is meant for the Lord, will be raised, is joined to Christ, is the Spirit’s home and was bought at a price. So glorify God in it.

Why it was said. Members were suing one another in courts where status usually won (see the introduction), and others excused visits to prostitutes with slogans that made sex as neutral as a meal (vv. 12–13). In both, a church proud of its wisdom and freedom was living by the standards of its city.

How the chapter makes its case. The lawsuits (vv. 1–8): those who will judge the world and angels can settle trivial cases; going to unbelievers shames a church that boasts of wisdom; a lawsuit between brothers is already a defeat, and some of them were the cheats. The hinge (vv. 9–11): the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom, and some of them had been exactly that until they were washed, sanctified and justified. The body (vv. 12–20): Paul corrects the slogans and shows what the body is: for the Lord, to be raised, a member of Christ, joined by sex to another, so flee; a temple of the Spirit, bought with a price.

Where it leads. Every argument rests on Christ. The saints judge only because they are joined to the Son of Man, who was himself condemned by an unrighteous court. He suffered wrong and did not sue. Sinners are washed and justified in his name. God raised his body, and he has made ours his limbs and his Spirit’s home, at the price of his blood. The chapter ends not with a prohibition but with a calling: glorify God in the body for which Christ gave his.

For us. We too settle quarrels in public and call our bodies our own. “You are not your own” sounds at first like the end of freedom, but it is the most hopeful sentence here: you belong to a Master who paid everything for you and does not throw away what he has bought.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lawsuit between believers is a defeat whoever wins, because it brings the world’s way of settling scores into the family of God. Paul argues from the saints’ future to their present: those who will judge the world and even angels can settle trivial cases (vv. 1–3); to hand them to unbelievers shames a church that boasts of its wisdom (vv. 4–6). Better to suffer wrong than to sue a brother, and worse still that some of them were the ones doing the wrong (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul argues here from the last things, from what is coming: “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2). What believers will be shapes how they behave now. Those who will share in Christ’s judgment at the end (Daniel 7:22; Revelation 20:4) already have, by their union with him, a dignity that makes taking small disputes to pagan courts absurd.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Paul refuses the framework: the cross makes a community in which being willing to absorb loss shows more strength than winning in court. Now: Paul’s question, “Why not rather suffer wrong?”, still cuts against every instinct.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians who will one day share in Christ’s judgment of the world should be able to settle their own small disputes, not hand them to pagan judges. Paul argues from the greater to the lesser, and the greater is the saints’ own future.

In the flow. Chapter 5 closed with a question: “Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?” (5:12). The Corinthians did the opposite: they would not judge the immoral man inside, and handed their own quarrels to judges outside. Verses 9–11 join the two failures: those who wrong their brothers and those who live in sexual sin are on the same list, and offered the same washing.

A grievance against another. The word means a matter, a case: a civil dispute, probably about property or money (v. 7).

Does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? To dare (tolmaō) is to have the nerve: Paul opens with astonishment, not argument. “The unrighteous” is not name-calling but his standing term for those outside Christ, and the point is competence. Unbelieving judges can apply Roman law; they cannot ask what love requires, or what the cross makes fitting between two brothers. The saints can.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? The first of six times in this chapter Paul asks, “do you not know?” (vv. 2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19): he assumes they were taught it. Its roots are in Daniel’s vision, where the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:18, 22, 27), and in the Lord’s promise that his followers would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4). At the last day believers will share in Christ’s judgment, not on their own authority but because they are united to him by faith, so that what is his is shared with them: his death counts as theirs, and so will his reign (Romans 6:5; 2 Timothy 2:12).

Are you incompetent to try trivial cases? The word for trivial is the smallest available: everyday disputes, tiny beside the last judgment. People appointed to share in the final judgment cannot claim to be unqualified to sort out a disputed debt. That exposes the real problem, which was not competence: at least one party did not want a fair settlement. He wanted to win, and the court was where winning was available.

The setting. Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt, and the man with connections and a hired advocate generally won (see the introduction). Suing a brother used your position against someone with less of it, bringing into the church the very means by which the powerful kept the weak in their place (1:26).

One like a son of man. In Daniel’s vision one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and a kingdom; then judgment is given for the saints of the Most High (Daniel 7:13–14, 22). Jesus took that title as his own (John 5:22, 27). The saints judge only because they belong to him: where he sits, those in him sit (Revelation 3:21), with a dignity borrowed from his. He was judged by an unrighteous court so that they might sit in a righteous one. A man who will share the throne of the Son of Man was asking a pagan magistrate to settle a debt between two of Christ’s own people.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use the courts, or that crimes should not be reported (see on vv. 7–8). Paul is speaking of civil disputes between believers.

In everyday life. If you have a dispute with a fellow Christian, go to them first, and then to wise believers, before going public (see the note on vv. 4–6). And ask whether you want a resolution or a verdict: would you accept an outcome in which nobody was declared right? The Corinthians preferred a venue that would produce a loser.

What about legal processes that are not one brother suing another? Paul condemns suing a fellow believer over a private grievance without first letting the church settle it. An insurance claim, the legal formalities of a divorce that has biblical grounds, probate and similar matters are not in view. And if a fellow member refuses every attempt at reconciliation and church judgment, the case changes (see the box “Where Christians differ: may a Christian ever sue a Christian?” at the end of the note on vv. 7–8). Even then, verse 7 still asks whether it might be better simply to suffer the wrong.

Does “the saints will judge the world” mean believers decide who is saved? No. Salvation and condemnation belong to God alone, and Christ is the Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Scripture does not say how the saints share in his judgment; most likely, united with Christ, they will reign with him and agree with and take part in his verdicts, as the twelve are promised thrones (Matthew 19:28). It is no licence to pronounce on anyone’s destiny now. Its purpose here is to show how great their calling is, and how small their quarrels look beside it.
verseByVerse.note: Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were a way for the powerful to win status.

parallels.desc: judgment was given for the saints of the Most High

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers will share in judging angels, so they can certainly settle the ordinary disputes of this life. Paul mentions it in passing, as something he had already taught them.

Do you not know that we are to judge angels? Most likely the fallen angels, whom Peter describes as committed to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment, and Jude in the same terms (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Believers will have a part in their sentencing. Angels are older than we are and, as Peter says, greater in might and power (2 Peter 2:11). The Corinthians were being intimidated in a provincial courtroom by men with money; they are destined to sit in judgment on beings beside whom a Roman magistrate is nothing.

Matters pertaining to this life! Money, property, contracts, boundaries. Paul uses the vast claim not to make them feel important, since the whole letter assaults their self-importance, but to make their behaviour look absurd. A man who believed he would share in the judgment of angels would find it hard to keep up a two-year grievance about a boundary wall.

Made for a little while lower than the angels. How could creatures of dust judge beings of a higher order? The answer is a man. The Son of God did not take hold of angels but of the offspring of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16): he became one of us, not one of them. Hebrews applies Psalm 8 to him: made for a little while lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:7–9). In him human nature has been seated far above all rule and authority (Ephesians 1:20–21), and the powers that have terrorised the human race since Eden will one day stand before the Lamb, with his people seated beside him. The saints will judge angels for one reason only: they are joined to the Man on the throne. Not one of them deserved it. All of them will have it.

Will we judge the holy angels too? There is no hint of that. The holy angels have never sinned, and they serve God’s people now (Hebrews 1:14). Some think “judge” here also includes ruling, so that redeemed humanity, in Christ, will have a place of honour over the whole created order. Scripture gives no details, and it is wise not to build theories on one sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking a fellow believer before pagan judges shames the church: it shows that its boasted wisdom cannot help two brothers, and it fights in front of the very people it exists to reach. The church should be able to settle these matters itself.

Those who have no standing in the church. Literally those counted as nothing (exouthenēmenoi): in the ESV reading, the pagan judges, whose values the church does not share and to whom it does not look for wisdom (for another reading, see the box below). Why hand them your family quarrels?

I say this to your shame. Earlier he wrote, “I do not write these things to make you ashamed” (4:14). Here he does.

Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers? The irony would have stung. This church prided itself on its wisdom, knowledge and eloquence (1:5; 3:18); now Paul asks them to produce one wise man for a practical purpose, and evidently they cannot. That is always the test of real wisdom. Wisdom that can discuss the deep things of God and cannot help two brothers settle a debt is not wisdom in any sense the Bible recognises. The wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy; where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, it is not wisdom at all (James 3:14–17).

But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers? A second shame: brothers fighting in public, before the people the church exists to reach. A Corinthian pagan would have seen a movement claiming that its God had reconciled enemies and made one body of Jew and Greek, slave and free, and then two of its members in the basilica, arguing about money with the same lawyers and tactics as everybody else. Every claim the church made was being tested in that courtroom, and failing.

The mind of Christ. Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1:24), and we have the mind of Christ (2:16). Wisdom, in this letter, has the shape of a cross. A church with the mind of Christ ought to be full of people able to settle a dispute between brothers, because the gospel itself is the story of a quarrel settled at the cost of the one who was in the right: God, whom we had wronged, bore the cost of making peace with us. The wise man Paul is looking for is not the cleverest member, but the one who thinks like the cross.

The modern courtroom. Congregations now split in public, and Christians savage one another online before thousands, over matters two people of goodwill could have resolved in an afternoon. The watching world does not weigh the arguments. It concludes that their message of reconciliation does not work.

What it does not mean. Church leaders do not have the power of a civil court. The church can mediate and advise, and discipline members who refuse to be reconciled. It cannot fine, imprison or enforce, and it must never try to handle crimes itself.

What does settling a dispute inside the church look like in practice? Not a court, but wise people the parties agree to be bound by. First the two talk privately (Matthew 18:15). If that fails, they bring in one or two mature, impartial believers, often elders or people they both trust, and agree in advance to accept their counsel. Some use trained Christian mediators or arbitrators, whose agreements can also be recognised in law. The aim is not merely a ruling but reconciliation, with honesty about wrongs on both sides.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verse 4 allows two readings. The ESV takes it as a question about the pagan judges, as above. Older translations, the KJV among them, read it as a command, perhaps ironic: appoint even the least regarded members of the church to judge. The question is more likely, since Paul goes straight on to ask whether no one among them is wise enough to settle a dispute (v. 5). Either way, the church should settle these matters itself.

parallels.desc: able men to judge the people

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lawsuit between believers is lost before it is decided; it would be better to accept the loss, and worse still, some of them were the ones doing the cheating. Whoever wins in court, the church has already lost, because love has already failed.

Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Two questions that cut against the instincts of every age. The words are blunt, be wronged, be cheated: a real injury and a real loss, not one to pretend away. Paul proposes that a Christian might choose to absorb it. That is not weakness but a different way of counting the cost. The litigant had calculated that the disputed sum was worth more than the brother; a man shaped by the cross reaches a different total. It is the Sermon on the Mount applied to a courtroom: if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well (Matthew 5:39–40). Better to lose money than to lose a brother and dishonour Christ.

But you yourselves wrong and defraud. Paul turns from the plaintiffs to the defendants. Some of them were the cheats, defrauding their own brothers, perhaps using the courts to do it.

He did not take us to court. Jesus is the one man who never wronged anyone and was wronged by everyone. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). Defrauded of his clothes at the foot of a cross, he did not sue; tried by an unrighteous court, he did not appeal. He suffered wrong not because he could not defend himself, but because he was buying back the very people who had wronged him. We were the ones who defrauded God of the honour we owed him, and he did not take us to court. He took our place in it.

In everyday life. This cuts both ways. If you have been wronged, could you absorb it without keeping a running account, as Christ keeps none against you (Colossians 2:14)? And does anyone have a legitimate grievance against you: money owed, a promise not kept, an advantage taken because you could? Put it right this week. Both men in the courtroom may need to repent (Romans 12:17–19).

A guard against misuse. This passage has been used to do real harm. It concerns property and money disputes between Christian brothers, and cannot be stretched into a rule that Christians must never use the law without contradicting Scripture and Paul himself. Paul invoked his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged (Acts 22:25) and appealed to Caesar rather than be handed over (Acts 25:11), and he calls the civil authority God’s servant, who bears the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). So this text says nothing against reporting a crime, protecting a child, a victim of abuse or assault going to the police, or an employee taking a genuine grievance to a tribunal. Any leader who quotes “why not rather suffer wrong?” to persuade a victim to stay silent and keep it in the church has taken a verse about a money dispute and used it as a lid. That is the opposite of what the passage intends, since its whole point is that the strong should stop using their advantage against the weak.

Does suffering wrong mean I must let someone go on cheating me? No. Absorbing a loss rather than suing a brother is not enabling ongoing wrong. You may forgive a debt and still decline to lend again, or let go of a grievance and still end a partnership with someone dishonest. You may, and sometimes must, warn others or bring the matter to the church, so that the person is called to repent and others are protected (Matthew 18:15–17). Love does not pretend that wrong is right. It simply refuses revenge, and cares more about the brother’s soul and Christ’s honour than about winning.

How do I absorb a wrong instead of fighting it? Not by pretending it does not hurt. Name the loss to God honestly, as the psalmists do. Then remember the size of your own debt. The servant forgiven ten thousand talents had no case against the man who owed him a hundred denarii: “And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33). Hand the account over: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). The matter is not dropped; it is moved to a better court. Decide not to collect, and keep deciding it when the memory returns: no retelling the story for sympathy, no small revenges. And do the person some good, even a small one, as the Lord did you (Romans 12:20–21). The strength comes not from a firmer will but from a fuller heart: if Christ is your treasure, what you lose cannot take what you most need. And if he bore the whole weight of the wrong you did him, you can bear a smaller one for his sake.

Where Christians differ: may a Christian ever sue a Christian? Some say never, under any circumstances. Others say the courts are open to Christians like anyone else. This commentary’s view: Paul’s rule is that disputes between believers should be settled within the church, and that it is often better to accept loss than to sue a brother. But this assumes both parties are willing to submit to the church. Where a professing believer refuses church correction, he is to be treated as an unbeliever (Matthew 18:17), and there may be cases where legal protection is necessary, especially for the vulnerable, or where crimes are involved. Abuse, violence and fraud should be reported to the authorities whom God appointed to punish evil (Romans 13:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A warning and a welcome. The unrighteous, those who live unrepentant in sins of every kind, from sexual sin to greed and slander, have no share in God’s kingdom, and no one should be fooled into thinking otherwise (vv. 9–10). Yet some of the Corinthians had lived exactly so, and the description is now in the past tense: they were washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The three verbs of v. 11, washed, sanctified, justified, cover the whole of what God does in saving a sinner, and all three are the work of Father, Son and Spirit together (see the note on v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street: not distant behaviour but the lives many in the congregation had lived before the gospel reached them. Now: Every church contains people whose past is on this list (see the note on v. 11).

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whose lives are given over to sin, of any of the kinds on this list, have no share in God’s coming kingdom, and no one should be fooled into thinking otherwise. The list is wide enough to leave no one looking down on anyone else.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? English hides a link with verses 1–8. “The unrighteous” (adikoi) is the word used for the pagan judges in verse 1, and “wrong” in verse 8 is its verb, adikeō: you are behaving like the people you took your case to, and you know where they are heading. To inherit the kingdom is to share in God’s coming reign, eternal life in the age to come. “Will not inherit” does not mean less reward but no share at all, and it describes those whose lives are characterised by these sins, unrepentant: they show that they are not God’s people.

Do not be deceived. Someone was deceiving them, probably with the message that grace and freedom are so complete that how you live does not matter if you have knowledge or gifts. It is a lie, and it is still being told.

The sexually immoral and adulterers. The sexually immoral are those who commit any sexual sin outside marriage; adulterers are those unfaithful to their marriage.

Nor men who practice homosexuality. The ESV notes that the two Greek terms refer to the passive and active partners in consensual homosexual acts. Malakoi, literally soft ones, could in sexual contexts denote the passive partner. Arsenokoitai combines arsēn (male) and koitē (bed), literally male-bedders, and appears to have been coined from the Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where both words appear in the prohibition of a man lying with a male. Together they cover both roles, and Paul uses them of homosexual acts generally.

Thieves and the greedy. Only three of the nine items are sexual. Alongside them sit theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse and dishonest dealing: sins present in every congregation and rarely preached with this seriousness. A church that reads the list as a description of outsiders, or of one particular group, has misread it.

The kingdom is the Son’s inheritance. Before it is ever ours, the kingdom belongs to Christ. God has appointed the Son heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and no one inherits anything except by being joined to the Heir: we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The list is not an entrance exam; it describes lives that show no sign of belonging to the Heir, because no one can be joined to Christ and live contentedly in the things he died to remove. So the question it presses is not “Have I been good enough?” but “Am I his?” The astonishing thing is not that the unrighteous are excluded, but that anyone is admitted: the Son was counted among the unrighteous for them, and the King gives his inheritance to the disinherited. And the respectable person who has kept clear of every item is no nearer the kingdom if he trusts his record rather than the Heir; Paul counted his own spotless record as loss in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:7–9).

Temptation is not practice. If you are a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction and is not acting on it, who has perhaps fought this for years, told almost nobody, and reads this verse with dread, you are not the person described here. To resist a desire is not to live by it. The man in this list is not fighting; he has settled into his sin, while a believer who fights is doing what the gospel produces in those it washes (v. 11). The same holds right along the list: being tempted to greed is not greed. Paul warns not against the presence of a struggle but its absence: the comfortable conviction that a person may practise what he likes and inherit the kingdom anyway. That is the deception behind “Do not be deceived” (Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:5–6).

Can a true believer fall into these sins? Yes: David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and the man in chapter 5 was a member of this church. But Paul describes a way of life, not a single fall, and the believer who falls is brought back to repentance, as David was (Psalm 51). What cannot be true of someone born of God is that he goes on in these things, unrepentant, to the end (1 John 3:9–10). The warning is real, and the God who keeps his own to the end keeps them through warnings like this one, not in spite of them.

How should I treat a gay friend or family member? With the love and honesty you would show anyone on this list, which includes you. Keep the friendship, keep eating together, keep listening; Jesus was a friend of sinners. Do not make one sin the whole of the person or the first thing you talk about. Their greatest need, like yours, is Christ, not first a change of behaviour. If they ask what you believe, tell them gently and truthfully, including what you believe about your own sin and need of grace. And if a Christian friend confides that they experience same-sex attraction, count it an honour that they trusted you, keep their confidence, and walk with them.

Where Christians differ: homosexuality. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative relationships, such as pederasty or prostitution, not loving, committed same-sex relationships. This commentary’s view: The terms Paul uses draw directly on Leviticus, which forbids homosexual acts as such, without reference to exploitation, and he names both partners rather than only the exploiter, which an argument about exploitation would not require. Elsewhere Paul grounds his teaching in creation (Romans 1:26–27), and Jesus defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman (Matthew 19:4–6). The historic Christian teaching is that sexual relations belong only within marriage between a man and a woman. This must be held with deep compassion. Same-sex attraction is a real and often painful experience, not chosen, and believers who experience it and live faithfully are brothers and sisters to be loved and supported. Homosexual sin is listed alongside greed, drunkenness and slander, sins all of us need forgiveness for. And verse 11 shows the gospel’s welcome to all.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind “men who practice homosexuality” refer to the passive and active partners in homosexual acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people on that list can be made new, and in Corinth many had been: washed, set apart for God and declared righteous, all through Christ and by his Spirit.

And such were some of you. Four words in the Greek change the temperature of the chapter. The most severe list in the letter describes the people he is writing to. And the tense carries the good news. Paul does not write, “Such are some of you, but you are forgiven.” He says the description has stopped being true.

But you were washed. Three verbs follow, each describing something done to them. Washed: cleansed from sin’s filth. A man may believe he is forgiven and still feel unclean; this word is aimed at exactly that.

You were sanctified. Set apart as holy to God, his own possession, once for all: an accomplished fact, not a target, as in his greeting to “those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1:2). Daily growth in holiness follows, but it grows out of this: they already belong to God.

You were justified. Declared righteous before God: the legal word. Their guilt is removed and Christ’s righteousness is counted as theirs, so no charge can stand against them (Romans 5:1; 8:33). “Sanctified” comes before “justified”, but this is not an order of events: all three happen together at conversion, and Paul seems to move from what is most felt to what is most decisive.

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. All three verbs hang on that name. Christ became to us righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1:30): what was done to them is what he is for them. They were justified because he was delivered up for their trespasses and raised for their justification (Romans 4:25), washed because his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and the Spirit makes it theirs. Nothing here was self-administered.

He has never once suggested he overpaid. The washing cost the blood of the Son of God. He did not tidy up the guilty; he bought them, knowing every item on the list, and he has never once suggested he overpaid. The Father chose, the Son shed his blood, the Spirit applied it, and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves became saints. Such were some of us. But we were washed, and the God who washed us will never call us dirty again (Titus 3:3–7; Romans 8:33–34).

The verse for the person carrying a past. Think of the years you do not talk about, the pattern you were in before Christ found you, which surfaces at three in the morning to tell you what you really are. Paul does not say it was not serious. He says it is past, that three things have happened to you since, and that none of them depends on your assessment of yourself. The accusing voice says what you were is what you still are. You answer not by denying your history but by naming its tense. Such were some of you. You were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified.

Does “such were some of you” mean that the old desires disappear? Paul describes a changed standing and direction: those sins are no longer who they are. He does not promise that temptation ends. Some believers find old desires greatly weakened; many, including those who experience same-sex attraction, go on being tempted and go on fighting, and that fight is the normal Christian life (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:17), not evidence that the gospel has failed. And “you were washed” points to the cleansing of the new birth (Titus 3:5), which baptism pictures (Acts 22:16) but does not itself accomplish. Reformed Christians, Baptist and Presbyterian alike, agree on that, though they differ over whom to baptise.

Should a church welcome people with pasts like these? Yes, with open arms, because the church at Corinth was made of them. A church shocked by former thieves, addicts, adulterers or people who have lived a gay life has forgotten what it is: every member is a former something. Welcome does not pretend sin does not matter; it tells the truth Paul tells here, that Christ washes and changes sinners, and then walks with people as he changes them. If your church would struggle to welcome someone with a story like those in verse 9, ask what that says about how you understand your own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your body belongs to the Lord, so sexual immorality is never a private or trivial matter. Paul quotes the Corinthian slogans that excused it and corrects them: freedom must not master you (v. 12), and the body is not a mere appetite but is meant for the Lord and will be raised (vv. 13–14). It is a member of Christ, and sex joins it to another, so union with a prostitute contradicts union with the Lord (vv. 15–17). Therefore flee (v. 18), for the body is the Spirit’s temple, bought at a price, made to glorify God (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul grounds sexual ethics in the resurrection: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The resurrection of the body is the ground of a Christian ethics that takes the body seriously (see the notes on v. 13 and vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a prostitute was widely accepted in Corinth, part of the city’s social and sometimes religious life. Some Corinthians may have thought it religiously meaningless and biologically natural. Now: The sexual ethics of any age follow from what it thinks the body is. Paul’s answer is that the body is the Spirit’s home, bought at the cross and bound for resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian freedom is real, but whether a thing is permitted is not the only question: a believer must also ask whether it helps, and whether it is becoming his master. Paul lets the Corinthian slogan stand and puts two limits round it.

All things are lawful for me. Almost certainly a Corinthian slogan, perhaps Paul’s own teaching on freedom twisted into a licence. He does not deny it; he refuses the idea that freedom is the only question worth asking.

In the flow. Sexual immorality headed the list in verses 9–10, and Paul returns to it because the Corinthians had arguments ready to excuse it. This theology of freedom also lies behind the pride of 5:2, and the slogan returns over food offered to idols (10:23).

But not all things are helpful. Helpful means beneficial, of real advantage. A thing may be entirely permitted and still be a bad idea. “Is this allowed?” is the question of a man looking for how much he can get away with; “Is this helpful?” is the question of a man who wants to get somewhere.

But I will not be dominated by anything. The second limit goes deeper, with a wordplay. The slogan says all things are exestin, permitted, within my authority; Paul will not be exousiasthēsomai, brought under the authority of, anything: the same root turned round. A man who insists he is free to do a thing, and cannot stop doing it, is not describing liberty. He has only found religious words for his slavery.

The one man nothing mastered. Only one person has been completely free in Paul’s sense: Jesus had authority over all things, and nothing had authority over him. Hungry after forty days in the wilderness, he refused to turn stones into bread at the devil’s suggestion, because man does not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:2–4). He had authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again (John 10:18), and he used it not to please himself but to give himself (Romans 15:3). The Corinthian used his liberty to feed his appetite; Christ used his to go to the cross.

In everyday life. Is something permitted starting to master you: your phone, food, entertainment, alcohol? Instead of arguing that it is allowed, put it down for a month. If it goes without much difficulty, the freedom was real. If you find yourself negotiating, it has authority over you (2 Peter 2:19). That is no reason for despair; finding the chain is the first step to having it broken: bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and ask the Lord who sets captives free to do it.

What are the things God has left free? The many matters Scripture neither commands nor forbids, which older writers called things indifferent: what you eat and drink in moderation, your leisure, your music, which job you take. In these you have real freedom, and other Christians must not bind your conscience with rules God has not given (Romans 14:1–4; Colossians 2:20–23). But even here Paul gives three questions: is it helpful, to me and to others? Is it mastering me? And, as he will add, does it glorify God (10:31)? Freedom is a gift to be used for Christ, not a boundary to stand as close to as you can.
verseByVerse.note: The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth, which Paul quotes and then corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The body is not a mere appetite to be fed however we like; it belongs to the Lord, and the Lord is committed to it.

Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food. Another slogan, still in use: hunger is met with food and nobody calls that a moral matter, so sexual desire may be met wherever convenient, and matters no more than a meal. Behind it lay a common Greek belief that the body was unimportant beside the soul.

And God will destroy both one and the other. Food and stomach belong to this passing life (on whether these words are still the slogan, see the box below). Paul grants that, but rejects the Corinthian conclusion that what we do with the body does not matter.

The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord. The body is not like the stomach. It is not one organ among many but the whole person as a bodily being, and it belongs to the Lord.

And the Lord for the body. Not only is the body for the Lord, which we might have guessed; the Lord is for the body. God is committed to your physical self, not tolerating it until the real you is released at death. He made it, he took one himself, he redeemed it, and he intends to raise it. He ascended in that body, and a man with scars in his hands is seated at the right hand of the Father. The God who made dust into Adam will not abandon the dust of his people.

A doctrine of the body. A faith whose central claims are an incarnation, a bodily resurrection and a new creation cannot regard flesh as an embarrassment. That is why New Testament sexual ethics are never arbitrary restrictions: they follow from what the body is.

Does God care about my sleep, my health and how I treat my body? Yes, though not as our culture worships the body. If the Lord is for the body, what you do with yours is never spiritually neutral: not the sleep you refuse it, nor the contempt some Christians feel for their own bodies and mistake for humility. Rest is a gift (Psalm 127:2), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). But the body is not an idol to be perfected; it is a servant to be cared for and offered to God (Romans 12:1). Look after it as you would look after something precious lent to you by a friend.

Will we have bodies in eternity? Yes. At death a believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, conscious and at rest, while the body waits in the grave (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). At Christ’s return the body will be raised, the same yet transformed, imperishable and glorious like his (15:42–44; Philippians 3:21), to live on a renewed earth. That is why the body matters now: it is not a husk to be thrown away but the seed of what will be raised.

Uncertain wording. Greek has no quotation marks, so we cannot be sure where the slogan ends. The ESV gives “and God will destroy both one and the other” to Paul, conceding that food and stomach are temporary. Many think those words belong to the slogan: the body will perish anyway, so what we do with it does not matter, which Paul answers with the resurrection (v. 14). Either way the meaning is the same: food and stomach pass away, but the body is meant for the Lord and will be raised.

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The body has a future, for God will raise it as he raised Jesus, and it already belongs to Christ as one of his limbs, so it must never be joined to a prostitute.

And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. The power that brought Jesus out of the tomb will be applied to your physical self; what will stand in the new creation is not a disembodied spirit but a raised person (15:20–23), and what will be raised matters now. Meanwhile the risen Christ does not hold his people at arm’s length. He has made their bodies his own limbs, and he will not lose a single one of them.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Members (melē) is the ordinary word for limbs and organs, not a metaphor for belonging to a club. The believer is united to Christ, body as well as soul, as a hand is joined to a body.

Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Deliberately blunt. Prostitution was common in Corinth, sometimes connected with temples, and banquets and festivals often ended with it. To have sex with a prostitute is to take what belongs to Christ and join it to her. Paul refuses to let the sin be pictured as a private transaction between two people in a room; Christ is not absent from it. The Christian does not leave his union with the Lord at the door and pick it up on the way out; there is no such door. Whatever a believer does with his body, he does as a limb of Christ.

Never! One of Paul’s strongest negatives, for a suggestion too appalling to argue with.

The modern form. Today the same transaction is pornography: another human being reduced to a function on a screen, private, deniable and available at any hour, and defended as nobody else’s business: it harms no one, it is only an image. Paul’s answer is that the Lord is present, because the man watching is a limb of Christ. And the image on the screen is a person too, often exploited, sometimes trafficked, made in God’s image and used as a product.

In everyday life. Before you click the link or enter the room, ask the plain question: am I about to take a limb of Christ here? Then use those limbs for him today: hands that help, eyes that look on others with honour, feet that go where love sends them (Romans 6:12–13; 12:27).

If I have fallen into this, has Christ let go of me? No. That is precisely why it matters what you take him into: he does not withdraw when you sin. It is a heavier thought than shame, and more hopeful, because shame tells a man what he is and leaves him there; this tells him whose he is. The argument for purity here is not that you are dirty and must clean yourself up, but that you are joined to Christ, now, in the body. So come back to him at once, confess it plainly (1 John 1:9), and take practical steps against it (see the note on v. 18). His hold on you is the ground of your fight, not the prize for winning it.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sex unites two people whether they intend it or not, so union with a prostitute contradicts the deeper union every believer already has with the Lord. This is why the comparison with food fails: sex does something eating never does.

He who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her. “Joined” is kollaō, glued, cleaved to. Sex is never merely physical; even a casual encounter unites two persons.

The two will become one flesh. Genesis 2:24, the charter of marriage, spoken in Eden before the fall: God designed sexual union to seal the lifelong covenant of husband and wife (Matthew 19:5–6). Paul applies it to a paid encounter with a stranger. God built the bond into the act, and it does not wait for the intentions of the people involved. Neither of them meant a union. A union occurred.

Why casual sex is not casual. Sex can never be what every generation insists: a thing done with the body alone and walked away from. Paul’s claim is not merely that casual sex is unwise, though it is, but that there is no such thing. Outside marriage the act still joins two people, and then the bond is torn. People find that someone they were assured meant nothing is lodged in them years later: something was joined that was designed not to come apart.

But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him. The same verb, “joined”, is used of both unions, set side by side to show they cannot go together: the believer, already joined to Christ, proposes to be joined to somebody else. One spirit with him means that the Holy Spirit who rests on Christ lives in the believer, so that Christ’s own life flows into his, as the vine’s life flows into the branches (John 15:5). That union is deeper than marriage; it is the reality to which marriage itself points (Ephesians 5:31–32). The Bridegroom has bound himself to his people with a bond that no sin can dissolve and no death can break. Sexual immorality sets up a rival union.

A rival intimacy, and a greater one. So Paul’s final answer to sexual sin is not a rule but a union: closer than the one being contemplated, permanent where that is momentary, satisfying at a depth the other cannot reach even when it delivers all it promises. This fight is usually lost not for lack of information but because we want the sin. Purity that is only refusal is a starvation diet, and starvation diets do not last. The Christian is not asked to want less, but to notice that he is already joined to Someone, and to want that more, the only appetite strong enough to displace the other (Psalm 63:1–5).
