What it does not mean. Not that a sexual encounter creates a marriage. It means sex has a meaning that cannot be emptied out, which is why it belongs in marriage.

I have a sexual past. Am I bound for ever to the people I slept with? No. The union is real and its wounds can be real, but it is not a marriage and it does not own you. Christ’s union with you is stronger, and his blood washes every sin of the past (v. 11). Confess it, receive his forgiveness as fully as he gives it, and ask him to heal the memories and attachments that remain; it often helps to talk with a wise pastor or a biblical counsellor. Many believers with painful sexual histories go on to know deep joy in Christ, and in a faithful marriage. The past is real, but it is not the strongest bond in your life.

What if I was sexually abused? Then you did not sin; you were sinned against. Paul is speaking of what people choose to do with their bodies, not what was done to them by force or manipulation. Nothing done to you without your free consent has joined you to your abuser in the sense of this verse, and none of the guilt is yours. Your body remains a member of Christ and a temple of his Spirit, and he is not ashamed of you. Please tell someone safe, seek help, and, where a crime has been committed, report it. Christ, who was himself stripped and shamed by cruel men, stands with the wounded, and he promises to bind up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3).

parallels.desc: they shall become one flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The right response to sexual temptation is not to argue with it but to run, because this sin is committed with the very body that belongs to the Lord. Sexual sin is not the worst sin, but it is unique in its relation to the body.

Flee from sexual immorality. One word, the whole strategy, and the tense is continuous: keep fleeing, as a habit, not an emergency measure. Elsewhere Christians are told to stand and resist (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:13); here, standing your ground to prove you can is how people lose. The model is Joseph, who does not debate with Potiphar’s wife. He runs out of the house and leaves his garment in her hand (Genesis 39:12; 2 Timothy 2:22). It cost him his reputation and his liberty, and it was the right decision.

The sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Drunkenness and gluttony also harm the body, but act on it from outside. In sexual sin the body itself is given to another and becomes one flesh with it (v. 16), so the sin is committed with the very body joined to the Lord (vv. 15, 17). It defiles his temple, and the damage lands on the one who commits it (on the difficult clause “every other sin … is outside the body”, see the box below).

Sin in the body, borne in his body. The sin Paul singles out is committed in and against the body, and the remedy God provided came in a body too: he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness (1 Peter 2:24). Every sexual sin of every believer was carried to the cross and judged there, and that is where the power to flee comes from. A Christian does not run in order to make himself clean, but because that sin has already been condemned in his Lord’s body, and the life open to him is life to righteousness.

What fleeing looks like. The battle is often now a device in a pocket. Resisting only at the moment of temptation, with willpower when it is least available, late, tired, alone, discouraged, is rarely won for long. Fleeing happens earlier, in arrangements made in advance. The decision is taken at ten in the morning, not eleven at night: the filter installed, the device out of the bedroom, the friendship that has begun to warm quietly cooled before anyone has said anything they cannot unsay. And it means telling somebody. Sin that has to be reported to a friend on Thursday loses much of its power on Wednesday.

Does fleeing mean avoiding everyone of the opposite sex? No. Paul worked closely with women in the gospel (Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3), and Jesus spoke alone with a Samaritan woman. Fleeing is not fear of people but wisdom about situations: sensible boundaries about privacy and secrecy, about emotional intimacy with someone not your spouse, about the moments and places where you know you are vulnerable. Treat older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). The aim is honour toward others, not suspicion of them.

What if I keep falling, even after I have tried to flee? Then do not stop fleeing, or coming back to Christ. Repeated failure tempts you to conclude either that you can never change or that it does not matter; both are lies. Confess it to God, who is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Tell a mature Christian and let him help you see where the battle is really being lost, usually earlier than you think. Strengthen the barriers, and seek help, from a pastor or biblical counsellor, if it has become an addiction. Many have walked out of long patterns of sin by God’s grace, often slowly. The Spirit who lives in you is stronger than the habit.

Uncertain wording. “Every other sin a person commits is outside the body” is genuinely difficult. Some think Paul is again quoting a Corinthian saying (every sin is outside the body) in order to contradict it. Others take it as his own statement that sexual sin is unique in its relation to the body. The second is more likely and is followed above; either way Paul’s conclusion stands, that sexual sin is a sin against one’s own body.

parallels.desc: Joseph fled

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your body is the dwelling place of God’s Spirit and the purchased possession of Christ, so it is not yours to use as you please but his to glorify. The chapter ends not on a prohibition but on what the body is for.

Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you. Earlier the temple was the congregation (3:16); here it is each believer’s body. Naos is not the whole complex of courts but the inner sanctuary where God dwells. The argument is not that your body is impressive, but that Someone lives there. In Israel the inner sanctuary was the most guarded place in the land: only the high priest might enter, once a year, and never without blood, or he would die (Leviticus 16:2, 34). That holy God now lives in every believer’s body, which should make us tremble as well as rejoice. Sexual sin brings the Holy One into the brothel.

Whom you have from God. The Spirit is God’s gift (2:12). You did not earn him, so no believer can claim to be too unworthy to have received him.

You are not your own. Five words that cut across the deepest assumption most people hold, the opposite of the modern slogan “my body, my choice”: a claim on the one thing everyone keeps back for himself. The sceptic hears in it the end of freedom. But no one is truly his own: everyone is ruled by something, an appetite, an ambition, the opinion of others (Romans 6:16). Everyone will have a master; what matters is whether your master gave his life for you.

For you were bought with a price. “Bought” is the language of the slave market: somebody paid, and the payment transferred ownership. The price was the cross: not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9). Your new master bought you to set you free, which makes this the most reassuring sentence in the chapter. If you are not your own, you are not finally at the mercy of your failures, your assessment of yourself, or your capacity to hold on. The body you have treated badly, the self you are ashamed of, the life you suspect you have wasted: none of it is yours to write off, because none of it is yours.

So glorify God in your body. Hands that work honestly, a tongue that blesses, arms that pick up a child, a body spent in service and eventually worn out in it: this is what the verse asks for, and the Spirit who lives there works it.

At home in jars of clay. The true temple once walked the streets of Jerusalem: Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, destroyed on a cross and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). From that exalted Lord the Spirit was poured out (Acts 2:33), and the God who had filled the house on Mount Zion moved into people who had been on the list in verse 9, washed, sanctified, justified, and now inhabited. The Spirit of the living God has made his home in jars of clay, and he will not leave until he has raised them in glory.

Isn’t it nobody’s business what consenting adults do? For many today that is the whole of sexual ethics. It rightly guards against coercion, but it is a thin account of something so powerful, and very close to the Corinthian slogan this chapter answers: the body is for appetite, and appetite is private (vv. 12–13). The historian Kyle Harper (From Shame to Sin) has shown how revolutionary the Christian alternative was. Roman sexual morality was organised around status: a free man could use slaves and prostitutes without disgrace, so long as he respected free families. The church held slave and free, man and woman, to one standard, and told the most powerful men in the empire that the bodies of the weakest were not theirs to use. Christianity has always disappointed two kinds of people. To the libertine it says sex is too significant to be casual; to the prude it says the body is too good to be despised, since it is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body (v. 13). Both are answered by the same Saviour, who gave his body for ours and will raise ours like his.

Does this verse forbid smoking, tattoos or unhealthy food? Its first meaning is narrower: sexual immorality. But the principle reaches further, because the body is not ours; we care for it as God’s, and other texts plainly forbid drunkenness and gluttony (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:20–21). What the verse does not do is settle every question of habit or appearance; the ban on tattoos in Leviticus 19:28 belonged to Israel’s separation from pagan mourning rites. Where Scripture does not forbid, Paul’s own test from verse 12 applies: is it helpful, and am I being mastered by it?

If I am not my own, must I let others do what they like with my body? No; the very opposite. You belong to Christ, not to anyone else. No husband, wife, boyfriend, employer or church leader owns your body or has the right to use, hurt or control it. Belonging to Christ is your protection. If someone is abusing or coercing you, it is right to say no, to get to safety and to seek help, including from the police. The Lord who bought you at the cost of his own blood is not indifferent to what is done to his temple, and he calls his church to protect the vulnerable, not to hand them back.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “and in your spirit, which are God’s”; the shorter reading is original. The addition is true, but Paul’s point in this chapter is deliberately about the body.
verseByVerse.note: “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market.

keyVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
keyVerse.note: Here the chapter’s arguments meet. The lawsuits and the slogans both came from people who acted as though they belonged to themselves; Paul answers that they belong to the God who lives in them and the Christ who bought them. The last command is not “do not” but “glorify God”: the body is for worship, because it was redeemed at the cost of his.

6.reflection:
Paul asks, “Why not rather suffer wrong?” (v. 7). When have you found it hardest to let go of a wrong done to you, and how does Christ’s treatment of us make it possible? Where would doing so be wrong, because someone vulnerable needs protecting?

The list in verses 9–10 includes greed, drunkenness, reviling and swindling alongside sexual sins. Why is it important that a church reads it as a description of all of us, and how does “such were some of you” (v. 11) change the way we welcome people with hard pasts?

Paul answers “All things are lawful for me” with two questions: is it helpful, and is it mastering me? (v. 12). Is there something permitted in your life that has begun to master you, and what would it look like to bring it into the light?

Verses 13–20 say the body is for the Lord, will be raised, is joined to Christ and is the Spirit’s temple. How does this change the way you think about sex, about rest and health, and about the body you may be ashamed of? What is one way you could glorify God in your body this week?

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 opens the second half of the letter. Paul now turns from reports about the church to the letter it had written him (“Now concerning …”), and its first question, straight after his warnings about sexual sin in chapter 6, is about sex, marriage and singleness.

The message. Whatever your situation, married or single, widowed, deserted, slave or free, it is the life the Lord has assigned you, and you can belong wholly to him in it. Marriage and singleness are both his gifts, neither is holier, and the aim of everything is “undivided devotion to the Lord” (v. 35).

Why it was said. Some in Corinth had swung from the immorality of chapter 6 to the opposite error: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman” (v. 1), even within marriage. Roman society meanwhile pressed everyone to marry and produce heirs, and a “present distress” (v. 26) bore down on the church (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul answers the slogan (vv. 1–9): husband and wife owe themselves to each other on equal terms; singleness is a gift, but those who burn with desire should marry. On divorce (vv. 10–16): believers must not separate, and in a mixed marriage the believer should stay, for he makes the home holy, but is not enslaved if the unbeliever leaves. Then the principle beneath it all (vv. 17–24): remain with God in the condition in which you were called, whether circumcised or not, slave or free, for all were bought with a price. Finally the unmarried, the engaged and widows (vv. 25–40): the time is short and this world is passing, so singleness frees a person from divided concerns; yet whoever marries does not sin. All through, Paul distinguishes the Lord’s command from his own judgment, refusing to bind consciences where God has not.

Where it leads. Behind every line stands Christ: the Creator who made marriage and blessed a wedding, the single man whose life lacked nothing, the Bridegroom who never deserts his bride, the Lord who took a slave’s form and bought us with a price, the risen one whose coming makes the time short. Married or single, every believer is already betrothed to him, and the wedding is coming.

For us. No one in this chapter is in the wrong place, and no one is second-class. The question is not how to change your situation before you can serve God, but what undivided devotion looks like in the life he has given you now.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Both marriage and singleness are good gifts from God, and within marriage husband and wife owe themselves to each other on equal terms. Paul answers the ascetic slogan from their letter: marriage is God’s provision against immorality (vv. 1–2), in which each spouse gives the other a claim on their body (vv. 3–4), so that abstaining is only brief, mutual and for prayer (v. 5). He himself prefers singleness, but it is a gift, and gifts differ (vv. 6–7); so the unmarried and widows do well to stay as they are, but those who burn with desire should marry (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

The Reformers read 1 Corinthians 7 as honouring both callings as gifts of God, neither superior in itself (on the medieval view they resisted, see the box “Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier?” at the end of the note on vv. 6–7), and Luther’s own marriage was a public statement that marriage is not a second-class state.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics may have shared the same low view of the body that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6, turned the other way (see the note on vv. 1–2). Now: Sexuality is still treated either as a dangerous force to be suppressed or as an identity that cannot be questioned. Paul makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant promises, and not the last thing about anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is God’s good provision, not a lower road for the less spiritual: because sexual temptation is real, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Paul quotes a slogan from the Corinthians’ letter and begins at once to correct it.

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote. Here the letter changes shape. Paul turns from reports about the church (1:11; 5:1) to the letter it had sent him (see the introduction), and “now concerning” marks each new topic (7:25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1, 12). He takes their questions in order, as a pastor answers a letter from people he loves.

Not to have sexual relations. Literally “not to touch a woman”, a polite expression for sexual relations. Because Paul is quoting their letter, this is very probably their slogan, not his, which is why the ESV puts it in quotation marks (older translations such as the KJV print it as Paul’s own words). It was the watchword of ascetics, who thought holiness lay in denying the body, even within marriage. Paul spends the rest of the chapter qualifying it. Read as his own view, it turns the chapter into a grudging concession to marriage, and much unhappy teaching about sex has been built on that misreading.

Two errors that are really one. Chapter 6 dealt with a party for whom the body did not matter because it was disposable, so do what you like with it; here is a party for whom it did not matter because it should be denied, so give it nothing. Both despise the body God made and Christ redeemed, and Paul refuses both (6:13). The ascetic error has a pull of its own, for giving up good things can feel like a holiness we have earned. But rules like “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” have no value against the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:21–23), and no one is made acceptable to God by refusing what he gave.

Because of the temptation to sexual immorality. Literally “because of immoralities”, plural: the many forms of it on every street of a port city like Corinth. Enforced abstinence inside marriage would not produce saints but sin, and God does not treat that lightly: he will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous (Hebrews 13:4). Marriage is his holy provision, not a loophole.

His own wife, her own husband. “Have” probably means have sexual relations with, within marriage. The two halves match exactly: one wife for one husband, each belonging to the other in the same way, before Paul has even begun to argue.

The Lord who went to a wedding. The ascetics thought they honoured Christ by despising what he had made. But when the Pharisees asked Jesus about marriage, he took them back to the beginning: the Creator made them male and female, and the two shall become one flesh (Matthew 19:4–6). He was defending his own handiwork (John 1:3). And he began his signs at a wedding in Cana, turning water into wine so that the feast would not fail (John 2:1–11). He is not a cold lawgiver measuring how little pleasure his people can survive on, but the Creator who gives his children all things richly to enjoy, and the Redeemer who bought the whole of them, body included.

Realism without shame. Paul does not ask the Corinthians for a purity they will not sustain. In effect he says: you are not made of iron, you live in Corinth, and God has provided for this. There is no shaming in it, of married or single, and he will not bind anyone’s conscience where God has not (1 Timothy 4:1–5).

What it does not mean. Not that the only reason to marry is to avoid sin. Scripture gives marriage many purposes: companionship, for it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18); children (Genesis 1:28); a living picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32); and the prevention of immorality. Paul is answering a specific question, not writing a full theology of marriage.

Is sexual desire itself sinful, then? No. Desire for one’s husband or wife is part of the good creation: the man and his wife were naked and not ashamed (Genesis 2:25), and the Song of Songs celebrates married love without embarrassment. What is sinful is desire turned toward someone who is not your spouse, or desire allowed to rule rather than serve. God has given this desire a holy place, and pretending to be above it does not make a person more spiritual; it makes him more vulnerable.
verseByVerse.note: From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The ESV notes that “to have sexual relations” is literally “to touch.” The quoted saying was probably a slogan of some at Corinth.

parallels.desc: it is not good that the man should be alone

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In marriage husband and wife each owe themselves to the other, on exactly equal terms. Neither body is a private possession to be withheld, and neither is a thing to be seized.

Conjugal rights. Literally “what is owed”: the language of debt, an obligation each spouse owes, not a right to be seized. In a world where a man’s desires were assumed to be the point, Paul begins with what a husband owes, and then “likewise the wife to her husband”: complete mutuality.

The wife does not have authority over her own body. “Have authority” (exousiazō) is the verb Paul used in 6:12, where he refused to be dominated by anything. In marriage each gives the other a claim on their body. In the Greco-Roman world this first half was unremarkable: a wife’s body was understood to be at her husband’s disposal.

Likewise the husband. The second half was startling. A husband’s body was his own; his liberties outside the marriage, with slaves, prostitutes and mistresses, were assumed and largely unpoliced. The single word “likewise” gave a wife the same claim on her husband, with the same force, that he had on her. So the passage cannot be a charter for a husband’s demands: whatever it grants him it grants her in the same sentence.

The mind of Christ in marriage. The obligation is to give; neither spouse is anywhere given permission to take. That is the mind of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–7). The husband who loves his wife as Christ loved the church follows a Lord who handed over his own body for his bride. A debt owed and gladly paid: that is the shape of the cross carried into the most private room of a Christian home.

What it does not mean. Not that either spouse may force or coerce the other: love does not insist on its own way (13:5). These verses have been quoted to wives, usually by husbands and occasionally by pastors who should have known better, to argue that a woman has no right to refuse, that her consent is not required, that saying no is a sin. They will not carry the weight. The framing is mutual throughout, and even abstaining must be by agreement (v. 5). A man who uses verse 4 to override his wife’s no has turned a verse about mutual self-giving into a lever, and ignored the half of it that binds him.

If this verse was used against me, what do I do? First, hear it plainly: forced or pressured sex in marriage is not what Paul is describing, and it is not your duty to submit to it. It is a sin against you, and where it involves force or threat it is also a crime; you are not to blame for refusing it. Tell someone you trust, a pastor or elder, a wise friend, a doctor or counsellor, and if you are in danger, seek safety first and contact the authorities. A church that hears this should protect you, not send you back to explain yourself. And if you have carried guilt for years because a verse was twisted against you, lay it down. The Lord who wrote these words binds up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3), and he never handed anyone a lever.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Married couples must not withhold themselves from each other, except briefly, by mutual agreement, for prayer. Abstinence in marriage is an exception with an end date, not a higher state.

Do not deprive one another. “Deprive” (apostereō) means rob or defraud, the verb Paul used of the Corinthians cheating their brothers in the law courts (6:7–8). Withholding yourself from your spouse is a kind of theft. It is common in an unhappy marriage and rarely named: deniable, wordless, and able to last for years while both pretend nothing is happening. Paul calls it fraud.

By agreement for a limited time. The one exception has three conditions. By agreement: both, freely, never one spouse deciding for the other. For a limited time: with an end agreed in advance, not an indefinite drift. “That you may devote yourselves to prayer”: a season of special prayer, not leverage or punishment, or the slow drifting apart such withdrawals often are. Then “come together again”: Paul assumes the resumption.

So that Satan may not tempt you. Paul names the danger without embarrassment. A marriage in which this has lapsed has a door left open, and there is somebody who tries doors. And he says not “because of your sin” but “because of your lack of self-control”: a statement about how human beings are made, offered without condemnation.

A Bridegroom who does not defraud. Why is withholding called robbery? Because marriage was made to show something: “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). A husband and wife who give themselves to each other tell a true story about a Bridegroom who never holds himself back. Christ does not ration his love to his church or go quiet in a grievance. He gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he gives himself still (Hebrews 7:25). A marriage that defrauds has stopped telling that story; a marriage that gives goes on telling it.

Two readers, two words. To the one who has been quietly withholding, perhaps for reasons that felt justified, hurt, exhaustion, a grievance never resolved: this verse does not ask you to comply resentfully, which Paul asks for nowhere, but to stop carrying on the argument in silence and to have it in words. To the one who has been going without and has begun to feel foolish for minding: it is not foolish; a verse of the Bible exists to say that this matters. And pray together, even briefly, even awkwardly: Peter tells husbands to live with their wives in an understanding way, so that their prayers may not be hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

What if one of us cannot, through illness, pain, trauma or age? Then this verse is not a rule to be enforced against a suffering spouse. Paul addresses the deliberate withholding of a gift that could be given, not the inability to give it. Where there is illness, pain, the after-effects of childbirth, depression or past abuse, love will be patient and gentle, will seek medical and pastoral help, and will find other ways of tenderness. A husband who presses an unwell or traumatised wife is not obeying this verse; he is breaking the one before it. And the spouse who goes without for such reasons should take that longing honestly to God, and to a pastor or biblical counsellor if needed, rather than let it harden into resentment or wander elsewhere.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “fasting and prayer”; the earliest have prayer alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wishes everyone shared his freedom as a single man, but he will not make his preference a rule, because marriage and singleness are each a gift from God.

A concession, not a command. Paul tells them how much weight to give what he has just written, as he does all through the chapter (vv. 10, 12, 25). Most likely “this” is the permission to abstain for a time for prayer (v. 5): allowed, not required. Some take it more broadly of the marriage counsel in general. Either way, he will not bind consciences where God has not.

I wish that all were as I myself am. Paul was unmarried as he wrote; whether he had never married or was a widower, he does not say. He found singleness a freedom for ministry, because the single person can give the Lord undivided attention (vv. 32–35).

Each has his own gift from God. This sentence stops Paul turning his preference into a rule. The word is charisma, a grace-gift, the word he uses of the Spirit’s gifts in chapter 12. Marriage and singleness are not one gift and one deficiency, but two gifts, differently distributed. God hands out lives as the Spirit hands out gifts in the church, to each one individually as he wills (12:11), with no one forgotten and no one given the wrong thing. A married Christian is not the standard of which single Christians are a variation, and a single Christian is not waiting in a corridor for real life to begin. Both have been handed something.

Both gifts meet in Christ. The surest proof that singleness is no deficiency is the life of Jesus. The one perfectly whole human being who ever lived never married, and his life lacked nothing; he was full of grace and truth (John 1:14). It was Jesus who first spoke of a gift like this (Matthew 19:11–12). Yet this single man is also the Bridegroom, and the Bible’s story closes with his wedding (Revelation 19:7; 21:2). He honoured the one state by living it and the other by making it the picture of his love.

What it does not mean. Not that singleness is a gift only for those who feel no desire. Single Christians are often told they must have the gift and therefore should not mind, so that wanting marriage becomes a failure to accept their gift. But Paul calls the state itself the gift, given by God for now, to be used for him. The single Christian who longs to be married has forfeited nothing: he is wanting something good that he does not have, the ordinary experience of married and unmarried alike.

Can a life without sex be a full life? Our culture finds it hard to imagine, and pities those who go without as repressed or missing out; churches have often agreed in their own way, treating marriage and children as the real Christian life and singleness as a waiting room. Paul overturns both. The historian Peter Brown has described how the cities of the Roman world, where death came early, pressed their young people to marry and produce heirs: your body was owed to the city’s future. The early Christians’ honour for the single life was, among other things, a declaration of independence from that demand. A single woman in the church was not a failure to provide heirs but a full member of a family that grows by new birth. No one’s future now depends on their own line continuing. It depends on a risen Lord, whose life every one of his people, married or single, will share for ever.

How do I know whether I have the gift of singleness? If you are single today, you have it today; that is what Paul means by gift. It is not a hidden feeling to detect in yourself, a question that only breeds anxiety. The question is the one Paul puts in verse 17: what life has the Lord assigned me now, and what does faithfulness in it look like? You may pray for marriage, look for it wisely and gladly receive it if God gives it; that too would be his gift. Some find over years that God has given them a settled freedom in singleness (Matthew 19:11–12), and may embrace it with joy. Neither path needs to be decided on a feeling.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier? The medieval church came to treat celibacy as a higher, more spiritual state, and required it of clergy. This commentary’s view: Paul values singleness highly, but he calls both singleness and marriage gifts from God. Neither is holier. Forbidding marriage is described as a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and church leaders may be married (1 Timothy 3:2; 1 Corinthians 9:5). The Reformers rightly restored the honour of marriage, including for ministers. Each believer should seek to serve God in the calling he has given.

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unmarried and widowed do well to stay single, but those who burn with desire should marry, and there is no shame in it.

To the unmarried and the widows. “The unmarried” may mean widowers here, paired with widows, or all unmarried people. Paul repeats his preference, again as counsel rather than command.

If they cannot exercise self-control. The word is used of athletes in training (9:25). There is no virtue in a heroic celibacy you cannot sustain.

Better to marry than to burn. Some have taken “burn” of the fire of judgment, but the sense is almost certainly the ordinary one: consuming desire that will not leave a person alone. Strong desire is a legitimate reason to marry; that is part of what marriage is for. Yet marriage will not put the fire out. Some who married quickly to resolve their desires have found that it does not extinguish desire, and adds a second person with her own history, tiredness and struggles; a married man can still look at a woman with lustful intent (Matthew 5:28). Marriage is a God-given place for desire, not a cure for sin.

The Spirit’s fruit of self-control. What, then, is the cure for the heart? Paul’s word for self-control belongs to the same family as the last fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23: not a talent some Christians are born with, but what the Spirit of Christ grows in the people Christ has bought. He bore on the cross the guilt of every lustful look, and he now lives in his people by his Spirit, so the fight against desire is no longer fought alone, or fought to earn his favour. Because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

Already betrothed to Christ. The Lord knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). He does not sneer at desire or demand that it vanish. Every good longing for love was put there by him, a small sign pointing to the love that will at last fill it. He has promised every one of his people a marriage, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9), where no believer will be single and none alone. Whatever fire is burning now burns in someone already betrothed to Christ, and the Bridegroom is coming.

In everyday life. If you are single and struggling, do not fight alone: tell one trusted Christian friend. And if you are married, ask how your church treats its single members (see vv. 34–35).

How strong does desire have to be before I should look to marry? Paul sets no threshold; he gives permission. If the desire for intimacy is a constant pressure, driving you toward pornography, fantasy or compromise in relationships, that is a clear sign to seek marriage prayerfully and actively, and there is nothing unspiritual in it. Talk to mature believers, pray, and take sensible steps to meet godly people. Meanwhile fight the sin now: marriage is not a reward for those who first become pure, but neither is the struggle a reason to marry the first person who is willing. Marry in the Lord (v. 39), and marry someone you can love for a lifetime.

And what if marriage is not open to me? For many it is not: through circumstance, through a lack of anyone godly to marry, through same-sex attraction, or through a spouse with whom this part of life has ended through illness. Such a reader can find this verse almost mocking: the remedy is named and the door is shut. Scripture does not pretend that is easy. But it does say that no one has been promised the fulfilment of every legitimate desire in this life; that the Lord who requires this of some was himself a single man, tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); and that his grace is sufficient precisely where the hardship is not taken away, as with Paul’s own thorn (2 Corinthians 12:9). That is not a tidy answer, but it is better than a demand to feel differently, or a promise God has not made. And to the eunuchs who hold fast his covenant, people the world counted as without a future, God promises a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:4–5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers are not to break up their marriages, but when an unbeliever leaves, the believer is not bound. Paul first gives the Lord’s own command to believing couples: no divorce, and a wife who has left should stay unmarried or be reconciled (vv. 10–11). Then comes his apostolic ruling for marriages to unbelievers: stay if the unbeliever is willing, for the believer makes the marriage and the children holy instead of being defiled by them (vv. 12–14). But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so; God has called you to peace, and you cannot know that you will save your spouse (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” and “I, not the Lord”) shows how an apostle handled the words of Jesus; why it does not make vv. 12–16 less authoritative is set out in the note on vv. 12–13. Verses 12–16 extend the principle of Jesus’ saying to a situation he did not address.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Divorce was common and easy in the Roman world. What to do in a mixed marriage, especially if the unbeliever wanted out, was an urgent question for many in the church. Now: Verse 15 (sometimes called the “Pauline privilege”, the freedom of a deserted believer) is still much debated and much needed, in cases of desertion and of abuse that amounts to it. God has called you to peace is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself forbids believing husbands and wives to break up their marriage; a wife who has left should stay unmarried or be reconciled. Paul gives this not as his own advice but as the Lord’s command.

Not I, but the Lord. Paul is citing the teaching of Jesus that the Gospels record (Mark 10:9–12; Matthew 5:32; 19:6–9); where he has a word from Christ he says so and rests on it. “The married” here are couples where both are believers; mixed marriages come from verse 12.

Should not separate. “Separate” was a common word for divorce; in Greek and Roman practice there was little legal distinction between walking out and divorcing. Paul addresses the wife first: under Roman law at Corinth a woman could initiate divorce, which she ordinarily could not under Jewish law, so he speaks to her directly, as a person who decides for herself and must answer for it. Some Corinthian women may have wanted to leave their husbands for a celibate life (v. 1).

Remain unmarried or be reconciled. A believing wife who leaves without biblical grounds is not free to marry someone else. Paul states the rule and in the same breath deals realistically with its being broken: there will be separations, and the door he leaves open after one is reconciliation.

The husband should not divorce. “Divorce” means send away. Divorce was easy in that world, and among Jews the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any reason. Christ forbids it, so the passage will not support the common assumption that a marriage may be ended because it has failed: because the love has gone, or the two have grown apart, or one of them is unhappy.

The Lord of the beginning. Paul expects the words of a teacher from Galilee to settle the matter in a Greek city twenty years later, because of who spoke them. Asked about divorce, Jesus did not side with one school of rabbis against another; he went behind Moses to creation, restoring his own design: from the beginning it was not so, and what God has joined together, let not man separate (Matthew 19:6–8).

The husband who did not divorce. Behind this charge stands the faithfulness of God himself. He did not divorce his people when they played the harlot; he sent Hosea to buy back an unfaithful wife as a picture of what he would do (Hosea 3:1). He kept covenant with a bride who broke it every day (Malachi 2:14–16). At the cross the Bridegroom paid for his bride’s unfaithfulness in his own body, so that she could be presented to him without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). And every Christian whose marriage has broken, by their own fault or another’s, is held by a Husband who has never yet let go of anyone he took.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul ignores the exception Jesus gave for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9); he is giving the general rule, and he is about to add another exception in verse 15, desertion by an unbelieving spouse. So the historic Protestant position, that Scripture permits divorce on those two grounds and no others, adultery and wilful desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6), is built from the whole of what is written rather than any one text, and it is the reading followed here (on abuse, see below).

If you are divorced. If you are divorced, and particularly if you know your own sin was part of why, this passage tells the church what marriage is; it is not a sentence passed on you. Such were some of you, Paul has said, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (6:11). Divorce is not the one sin left outside forgiveness, and a repentant divorced believer is not on a permanent second tier before God. The command in verse 10 is for a marriage you are in. The mercy in 6:11 is for a life you have already lived.

Is it not cruel to keep someone in an unhappy marriage? Nobody needs a vow for the happy days; it was made for the days when feeling fails. A love that may leave whenever it stops being rewarded is a contract, not a covenant, and leaves the weaker partner, the ill, the ageing, the one who has disappointed, with no security at all. God binds a husband and wife together as he has bound himself to his people, and he did not leave us when we were unlovable (Romans 5:8). The command sends an unhappy couple to repentance, to help and to the church, and an unhappy marriage is often one on the way to being mended. Danger is a different matter.

What about abuse? The charge that a wife should not separate does not require anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated in a Christian home or excused by a church. Leaving to be safe is not the separation Paul forbids, and a church must never send a victim back to an abuser or counsel her to submit to violence, threats or cruelty. Abuse is a crime as well as a sin; it should be reported to the authorities, and the abuser should face the church’s discipline.

Abuse and desertion. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse ends the marriage itself is a harder question. The grounds for divorce remain the two Scripture gives, adultery and desertion. But this commentary holds, with many Reformed pastors and church courts, that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: a spouse who makes the home unsafe and will not repent has deserted the marriage while remaining under the same roof, abandoning every promise he made. That is a judgment about whether desertion has occurred, not a third ground, and it should be made with the elders of the church, never alone and never in a hurry. What is never in doubt is the first step: get safe.

May the innocent party remarry after adultery? The instruction to remain unmarried or be reconciled is for one who has separated without grounds. Where a spouse’s adultery has broken the marriage, Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:9 imply that the innocent partner who divorces and remarries does not commit adultery, and the Protestant confessions conclude that remarriage is then permitted, as if the offending party were dead (Westminster 24.5). Some hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives (appealing to v. 39 and Mark 10:11–12), but Jesus’ exception would mean little if the bond remained intact. Even then divorce is permitted, not commanded; forgiveness and reconciliation after adultery are often possible and always beautiful.

I have already remarried after a divorce that did not fit these grounds. What now? Do not break up the marriage you are in. A second wrong does not undo the first, and the vows you have now made are real vows before God. Repent honestly of any sin in how it began, without excuses and without endless self-punishment; receive Christ’s forgiveness, which is as full for this as for anything else; and keep your present vows faithfully, for life. Ask what you can still do to act justly and kindly toward any children or former spouse affected, and let your pastor help you think it through.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believer married to an unbeliever must not be the one to end the marriage, as long as the unbeliever is willing to stay. Jesus had not addressed the case, so Paul gives his own apostolic ruling.

I, not the Lord. Jesus, teaching within Israel, left no saying about a marriage in which one partner came to Christ and the other stayed a pagan. That does not make Paul’s ruling a private opinion the church may take or leave: he speaks with the authority Christ gave him, and ends the chapter claiming that he too has the Spirit of God (v. 40; 14:37). The distinction concerns the source of the teaching, not its authority, and it is a mark of his honesty.

An unbelieving wife … an unbelieving husband. In a city like Corinth people were converted out of pagan households, and very often one spouse believed and the other did not. Some new believers may have thought they must leave, fearing the union defiled them. Paul says plainly that the believer must not end it, and repeats it word for word for the woman, whose position was harder: a wife was expected to follow her husband’s religion, and one who turned from his household gods to Christ might be seen as disloyal or even subversive.

Ezra reversed. There was an Old Testament precedent, and it went the other way. When the returned exiles were found to have married foreign wives, Ezra had them put away, wives and children both, as an act of covenant faithfulness (Ezra 10:1–3). A Jewish believer at Corinth might have concluded that the holy thing was to end a marriage to a pagan. Paul reverses it: under the new covenant the influence runs the other way (see the note on v. 14).

Sent into the house. The Holy One has come into the world without being defiled by it, and he does not take his people out of it. Hours before his arrest Jesus prayed: I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one; as you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world (John 17:15, 18). The believer married to a pagan is not lifted out of the house but kept in it, and sent there, as Christ was sent among sinners, to be the Lord’s light at that table. The marriage a frightened believer thought an obstacle to following Christ may be the very place to follow him.

What it does not mean. Not that believers may marry unbelievers; Paul forbids that (v. 39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). He is speaking of those already married when one came to faith. Nor does anyone have to remain where he or she is being abused (see on vv. 10–11).

What if my unbelieving spouse opposes my faith, but does not leave? Then stay, and be wise. Opposition is not desertion, and mockery or coldness, painful as they are, do not end a marriage; Paul assumes many believers lived with spouses who disliked the new faith. Keep worshipping and keep loving; do not use your faith as a weapon in arguments, and do not hide it either. Where your spouse forbids something Scripture does not require on a particular day, be flexible; where he or she demands what God forbids, gently and firmly obey God (Acts 5:29). Ask your church to stand with you in prayer and practical help. And if opposition becomes threats, control or violence, that is abuse: seek safety and counsel at once.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer; Paul applies his authority as an apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The believer is not defiled by the unbelieving spouse; instead the believer’s presence sets the marriage and the children apart for God. In such a home holiness, not uncleanness, is the stronger influence.

Made holy because of his wife. This, the reason to stay, is widely misunderstood. It does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved: Paul settles that himself when he wonders whether the believer may yet save the spouse (v. 16). “Made holy” is the ordinary word for sanctified: set apart. The believer was probably worried that sharing bed and table with someone outside the covenant made the marriage unclean, and the children with it. Paul says the influence runs the other way. The marriage is sanctified, acceptable to God, and the unbeliever is set within the sphere of God’s blessing, exposed every day to the gospel and to a godly spouse.

Your children are holy. If the marriage were unclean, the children would be too. But the children of a believing parent are holy: set apart, under the influence of the gospel and a believer’s care, and in that sense distinct from the children of two unbelievers. They are not outsiders.

The direction of transfer. That reversal runs all through the Gospels. Under the old order, touching a leper made you unclean; when Jesus touched one, the leper was made clean (Mark 1:40–42). He ate with sinners and they were forgiven, and on the cross he took the defilement of the world upon himself and gave his own purity in exchange. In the new covenant holiness is not a delicate condition that contamination destroys; it is the stronger force in the room. If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump (Romans 11:16).

The comfort of an anxious believer. That is what the verse is for. If you are the only Christian in your house, your marriage is not a compromise God merely tolerates, and your presence there is not a problem to be managed; it is the reason the place is holy.

What it does not mean. Not that children of believers are automatically saved. They need to be born again and believe, like everyone else. But they are greatly privileged: they hear the gospel from their earliest days, are prayed for by name, and see a Christian life up close.

What about my children if my spouse is not a Christian? This verse was written for exactly that fear. Your children are not disadvantaged before God because only one parent believes; they are set apart, because you are there. Teach them the Scriptures as Timothy’s mother and grandmother did, apparently with a father who was a Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). Pray with them, take them to church where you can, and let them see the faith lived gently rather than argued with their other parent, being honest that you and your spouse see things differently without belittling him or her. And pray for their salvation, and your spouse’s, with real hope.

Where Christians differ: holy children and baptism. Some argue from this verse that the children of believers are in the covenant and should therefore be baptised as infants. This commentary’s view: the verse says the unbelieving spouse is also made holy, yet no one would baptise an unbelieving spouse, so holy here cannot mean qualified for baptism. It means set apart in a special relation to God’s people and blessing. Baptism in the New Testament is for those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38–41; 8:12). This commentary holds this credobaptist reading (baptism for those who profess faith), while recognising with charity that paedobaptist brothers and sisters, who baptise the infants of believers, read the covenant signs differently. The verse was not written to settle that question, and it should not become the thing this chapter is about.
verseByVerse.note: “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing partner.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer may let them go and is no longer bound. God’s call is to peace, not to an endless war to hold on to someone who has gone.

Let it be so. Now Paul deals with the case where staying is not in the believer’s power. “Separates” means divorces, departs. The believer is not to pursue, obstruct or fight to hold a marriage the other has ended; yet this is a permission to let go, not to give up easily, for verses 12–14 assume the believer wants the marriage to continue.

Not enslaved. The word means bound as a slave is bound, a strong word, and Paul says the believer is not bound like that. At the very least the deserted believer is freed from any duty to chase the one who left, or to wait in limbo indefinitely (on remarriage, see below).

God has called you to peace. This clause governs the whole verse. Where the other has gone and will not come back, God does not require you to wage a war to keep hold of something being pulled out of your hands. Paul releases the deserted believer from a clinging that looks like faithfulness and is really a refusal to accept a loss God has permitted. So far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18); when it does not depend on you, peace is still your calling.

The peace of the call. God’s call in this letter is a call into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1:9), and the first peace it brings is peace with God, made by the blood of Christ’s cross (Romans 5:1; Colossians 1:20). So a deserted believer can be called to peace even when the house is in pieces. The one you promised your life to has walked out; the One who called you has bound himself to you, and nothing in all creation can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39).

God does not abandon the abandoned. He says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5), and he says it as the Lord who was himself forsaken. Christ was deserted by every friend he had, and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He went through the darkest desertion there has ever been, so that no one who belongs to him would ever be left by God. He is still in the empty house, and he is not leaving.

The loneliest seat in church. The one who has been left often carries a double burden: the desertion itself, and a persistent sense that a better Christian would have held the marriage together. Paul does not treat the departure as evidence about you. He addresses you as someone something was done to, releases you from fixing what you did not break, and tells you that God has called you to peace, precisely what you have been unable to feel, and precisely what he intends you to have.

What it does not mean. Not that a believer may push an unbelieving spouse to leave, or use this verse as an excuse to end a hard marriage.

In everyday life. If you have been left, let the church carry some of it with you: ask your elders for counsel, accept the meals and the help with the children, and let one or two friends ask how you really are. If someone in your church has been left, do not avoid them because you do not know what to say. Say that you are sorry, and then show up, again and again: sometimes making peace means helping someone carry a loss they did not choose.

What counts as desertion, and what if the one who left calls himself a Christian? Desertion is a settled, wilful abandonment of the marriage: leaving and refusing to return, or refusing to live as husband or wife at all, despite patient efforts at reconciliation. A row, a few weeks apart, or a spouse who is difficult but present is not desertion. If the one who leaves professes faith, the church should call him to return under discipline (Matthew 18:15–17), and if he persists he is to be treated as an unbeliever, and the same freedom follows. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion (see vv. 10–11). The church should never leave the deserted to decide alone.

Where Christians differ: desertion and remarriage. Some say a deserted believer may separate but never remarry while the former spouse lives. This commentary’s view: “not enslaved” means the marriage bond is broken, and the deserted believer is free to remarry, in the Lord. Paul uses similar language of being free to remarry after a spouse’s death (v. 39; Romans 7:2–3). Scripture recognises two grounds for divorce with freedom to remarry: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied by the church or civil authority (the Westminster Confession 24.6). Divorce is always a tragedy, and each case needs care and wise counsel. To call a deserted person not enslaved while holding them to a bond they cannot escape and did not break would be a strange kind of freedom; the Reformers read it this way, and that reading is followed here. Those who read it more narrowly are not to be dismissed, but the deserted should not be left in limbo by a church afraid to say anything.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No believer can know whether he or she will bring a spouse to Christ, so the outcome must be left with God. The question keeps hope alive and lifts an impossible weight at the same time.

Save your husband … save your wife. “Save” means be God’s instrument in bringing them to salvation, as Paul became all things to all people that by all means he might save some (9:22). The verse takes something astonishing for granted: a Christian may be the means by which their own husband or wife comes to Christ. Paul does not say it is likely, but possible, in a way that assumes his readers had seen it happen.

Likewise, as Christ did. When Peter tells wives that unbelieving husbands may be won without a word by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), he begins with “Likewise”, pointing back to Christ: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). The believing spouse wins by becoming a little like the Lord who won them: patient under contempt, gentle without being silent, leaving the outcome to God.

A question, not a promise. “How do you know?” does not guarantee that a faithful wife will win her husband. Some do; some pray for forty years and bury a man who never came. But it also forbids the opposite conclusion, so easy to drift into after years: that he will never change, that there is no point. You do not know that either. Salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9), who opened Lydia’s heart by the riverside and turned a jailer’s house upside down in a night (Acts 16:14, 25–34). Your part is to be in the house, and to ask, and to leave the rest in hands that have never failed to finish what they began.

If my spouse dies without believing, did I fail? No. You were never given the power to save anyone, and this verse is meant to free you from that weight. Grief over a spouse who died without professing Christ is real and deep, and you need not pretend otherwise. But you may leave that person with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and who knows things about the last hours and the hidden heart that you do not. Your faithfulness was not wasted. God saw it, it was a witness, and it was the obedience he asked of you.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s question can be read two ways, both grammatically possible, and commentators have divided over it for centuries. Read hopefully, it is an argument for staying, attached to verses 12–14: who knows, you might win him to Christ, so stay if he is willing (1 Peter 3:1–2). Read soberly, it is a comfort for letting go, attached to verse 15: how can you know that you will save him? You cannot, so do not hold a departing spouse hostage to a hope you cannot guarantee. The second fits verse 15 more closely; the first fits the passage’s encouragement to stay. Paul may well have meant both to be heard, by the two different readers who would need them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your situation is not an obstacle to serving God; it is where he called you, so live for him there. Paul states the principle beneath the whole chapter: lead the life the Lord has assigned (v. 17). Then he tests it on the two great divisions of his world. Jew and Gentile need not change the mark of circumcision, because what counts is keeping God’s commandments (vv. 18–19). Slaves need not be troubled by their status, though they should take freedom if they can, because in Christ the slave is the Lord’s freedman and the free man is Christ’s slave, all bought with the same price (vv. 20–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Puts Social Status in Its Place

Paul’s refrain, remain as you are, is not social conservatism but a matter of what comes first. The gospel puts every earthly status beneath a higher one: in Christ. That does not make social structures indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good); the gospel works from the inside out, changing what every condition means before it changes the condition. This was the seed from which the abolition of slavery grew (see the box “Where Christians differ: did the Bible approve of slavery?” at the end of the note on vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. Paul guards against two errors: treating a change of status as spiritually necessary, and treating it as forbidden. Now: “Remain as you are” answers the anxiety that serving God requires a different job or a different place (see the note on vv. 17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live for God in the situation in which he called you, because what matters is not your outward status but obeying him. This is the principle beneath the whole chapter, and Paul tests it first on the mark that divided Jew from Gentile.

The life the Lord has assigned. Two verbs carry the principle. “Assigned” means apportioned, dealt out: God has given each person their place in life. “Called” points to the moment God called them to faith. Your circumstances are not an accident you must escape before your real Christian life can begin. God dealt them out to you, on purpose. And this is Paul’s “rule in all the churches”, not a special concession to Corinth (4:17).

In the flow. Verses 17–24 seem to wander from marriage into circumcision and slavery, but the chapter turns on them: the married need not leave their marriages (vv. 1–16), the unmarried need not rush into one (vv. 25–40), and here is the principle beneath both. The language of calling takes the reader back to 1:26: what matters is not the position God found you in but the God who called you in it.

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? A shrewd test case, for few marks of identity stirred stronger feelings in Paul’s world. Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to disguise their circumcision, to avoid mockery at the public baths and gymnasiums where men exercised naked (1 Maccabees 1:15). A Jewish believer among Gentile Christians might now find his circumcision embarrassing. A Gentile convert, on the other hand, might feel a second-class member of a faith with Jewish roots, and be tempted to acquire the mark (Galatians 5:2–6). Paul says: neither need become the other. The identity you brought with you is not the problem.

Keeping the commandments of God. A startling statement, since circumcision was itself a commandment. Paul probably means the moral commandments, the law of love, which apply to all: in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), and a new creation (Galatians 6:15). God does not accept anyone because he keeps the commandments; he accepts sinners for Christ’s sake, through faith (Galatians 2:16). But the person he accepts is given a new heart, and a new heart wants to obey (John 14:15).

The assignment the Son accepted. No one was given a harder assignment than Jesus, or served so faithfully in it: some thirty hidden years in a carpenter’s house in Nazareth, a town people mocked (John 1:46), then a short ministry among the poor, then a cross. Yet at the end he could say, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Every Christian tempted to think that real life is somewhere else serves a Lord who did his Father’s will in the place he was put, and whose obedience there is counted to his people.

The obstacle we imagine. If I were married. If I were single. If I had the other job, the other health, the other church: then I could serve God properly. Paul’s answer is that the life you are in is the life you were assigned. There is no arrangement of circumstances in which obedience becomes easy, and none in which it becomes impossible (Philippians 4:11–12).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians can never change their circumstances: Paul is about to tell a slave to take his freedom if he can (v. 21), and he has told the burning single person to marry (v. 9). The principle is contentment, not paralysis.

Does this mean I should not leave a job that is wrong for me, or a sinful one? No. If your work requires you to sin, you must leave it, as tax collectors stopped cheating and soldiers stopped extorting when they repented (Luke 3:12–14). If it is lawful and a good opportunity to move comes, you are free to take it, prayerfully and without guilt. What Paul forbids is the restless conviction that God cannot use you until your situation changes, the habit of making the next change the precondition of obedience. Ask: is this situation sinful? If not, am I free and wise to change it? And meanwhile, serve Christ wholeheartedly where you are.
verseByVerse.note: Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believer’s standing before God does not depend on his station, even slavery; yet freedom is better, and a slave who can gain it should take it.

Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. Paul applies his principle to the hardest case in that society. A bondservant is a slave, and the sentence jars a modern ear; it should not be softened too quickly. Perhaps a third of people in Corinth were slaves, and the church contained many. Roman slavery was not based on race: people became slaves through war, debt or birth; some were educated professionals, doctors, teachers, estate managers; and many in the cities could hope to be freed in time. But slaves had no legal rights and could be beaten, sold and used. Paul can tell them not to let their status trouble them only because of what he says next about who they are: the Lord’s freedmen (v. 22). A slave is fully a Christian, with full dignity before God.

If you can gain your freedom. Manumission, the freeing of slaves, was common in that world, and Paul says: freedom is better, so take it if you can (on the wording, see below).

Two things at once. Paul does not say slavery is good, or that a slave should refuse liberty out of piety. He says two things, and both are needed: your condition does not define you, and if you can be free, be free. Lose the first and nothing can be borne until it is fixed. Lose the second and you get what actually happened in history: this text quoted by slaveholders to tell slaves that Christianity required them to stay put. The words in brackets refute it. It is honest to admit that the New Testament also tells Christian slaves to serve their masters well (Ephesians 6:5–8), and that slaveholders abused those words too; Paul was speaking to people who had no power to change Roman law, not blessing the system.

A Lord who took the slave’s form. The Lord of glory himself took the form of a doulos, a slave (Philippians 2:7). He was sold for thirty pieces of silver, the sum the law of Moses set as compensation for a slave gored to death (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15), and he died by crucifixion, the death Rome used above all for slaves and rebels. No status can put a believer beneath the notice of a Saviour who chose the lowest one. The slave in the back row at Corinth was seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). That is why Paul could say, “Do not be concerned about it”: the slave already had a throne.

What about the circumstances I cannot change? The job you are stuck in, the illness, the family situation, the years not going as planned: Paul’s counsel is neither resignation nor restlessness. Do not let it define you, and if a door opens, walk through it without guilt. Contentment is the freedom to live well in this situation while the door stays shut, praying for the change and taking lawful steps toward it.

Where Christians differ: did the Bible approve of slavery? Some say the New Testament approved of slavery because it did not demand its abolition. This commentary’s view: the New Testament did not call for violent revolution, but it planted principles that undermine slavery: all humans bear God’s image; slave and free are equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11); masters must treat slaves justly, knowing they have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9); slave-trading is condemned (1 Timothy 1:10); and here slaves are encouraged to gain freedom. Christians like William Wilberforce rightly drew on these truths to fight for abolition. The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by the law of Moses itself (Exodus 21:16). The New Testament’s way with this institution was not endorsement but undermining. Paul sends Onesimus, probably a runaway, back to his master with instructions to receive him no longer as a bondservant but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). Those sentences, believed, dissolve the thing from within, and eventually did.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s bracketed sentence is compressed in Greek, literally “but if you are able to become free, rather use”, without saying what is to be used. The ESV notes that it can also be read “make use of your present condition instead”, meaning stay a slave even if offered freedom. The ESV’s main reading is more likely: freedom is better, so take it. Paul goes on at once to say “do not become bondservants of men” (v. 23), which would make little sense if he meant them to refuse liberty.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead.” Slaves could sometimes buy or be granted their freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the slave is the Lord’s free man and the free man is Christ’s slave, for all were bought with the same price; so wherever you are, belong to him and to no one else.

A freedman of the Lord. A Roman freedman, a freed slave, still owed duties to the patron who had freed him, and bore his name; here the patron is the Lord. The slave who becomes a Christian is freed from sin, guilt and death. He owns nothing and may be sold next month, yet in the only sense that finally matters he is free: those the Son sets free are free indeed (John 8:36).

A bondservant of Christ. The free person who becomes a Christian is now Christ’s slave: his word settles what you do with your time, your money and your body, and his approval is the only one you finally need (2 Corinthians 5:15). Both halves turn a man’s standing upside down, in opposite directions, so that neither can rank himself above the other.

You were bought with a price. Paul used the phrase a chapter earlier of the body (6:20); here he uses it of the whole self. Christ’s purchase is like a sale in the slave market, and yet utterly unlike it. The price was not silver but himself: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He bought slaves to free them, and free men to make them his, and the price was so great that no other owner can ever have a claim.

There let him remain with God. The third statement of the principle (vv. 17, 20, 24). “With God”: before him, in his presence. A slave with God is better placed than an emperor without him.

The strangest of owners. The One who paid for us with his own blood then calls us not servants but friends (John 15:15). He has promised that when he returns he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). There is no freedom like belonging to him, and no slavery like belonging to anyone else.

Do not become bondservants of men. Taken literally, it warns against selling yourself into slavery, a common way of escaping debt. More deeply, few readers are legally owned, but many live like slaves to someone’s opinion. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). It is the settled habit of arranging your life around other people’s approval: softening a conviction because of who is listening, taking on more than you should because you cannot bear to disappoint, measuring yourself daily by an audience you did not choose. Paul forbids it, not because you should think more of yourself, but because you are owned: you are not for sale, because you have already been bought. “If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

How do I serve Christ at work if my boss is the one I answer to? Do the work your employer gives you, honestly and well, but for a different Master: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Colossians 3:23–24). That means working when no one is checking, refusing to lie or cut corners even when it is expected, treating colleagues with respect, and accepting unfair treatment without bitterness while pursuing any just remedy available. If your employer requires you to sin, you must refuse, because he did not pay for you. Christ did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the time is short and this world is passing, singleness offers undivided devotion to the Lord, yet whoever marries does not sin. Paul gives counsel, not command, to the unmarried and engaged: in the present distress it is good to stay as you are, but marriage is no sin (vv. 25–28). Hold everything in this world loosely, marriage, grief, joy and possessions, since its present form is passing away (vv. 29–31). The unmarried can give the Lord undivided attention, and Paul says so to spare them anxiety, not to put a noose on anyone (vv. 32–35). An engaged man may marry or refrain, and both do well (vv. 36–38). A widow is free to remarry, only in the Lord, though Paul judges she is happier as she is (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
Nothing in This Age Is Final

Paul’s “as though” clauses (vv. 29–31) are a great relief to a believer under pressure. No good and no loss in this age has the last word. The person who holds them that way is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their final security does not rest on any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress”, the pressures of the short time between Christ’s comings. Now: The time is no less short for us. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, still applies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
