On whether the unmarried should marry Paul has no word from Jesus, so he gives his own trustworthy judgment: in the present distress it is good to stay as you are.

Now concerning the betrothed. “Now concerning” again, and so a new question from their letter. “Betrothed” is literally virgins: unmarried young women, probably those engaged to be married (see weddings and betrothal), and by extension the young unmarried generally. Having spoken to the unmarried in general (vv. 8–9), Paul now applies the rule of verses 17–24 to the never-married, especially engaged couples, with one refrain throughout: whoever marries does not sin (vv. 28, 36).

I have no command from the Lord. Jesus had not spoken directly on this, so Paul gives his considered judgment, as carefully as over mixed marriages (v. 12). A teacher who blurs what God has clearly commanded with his own application of Christian principle, presenting his judgment with the authority of a command, does what Paul refuses to do even when he is confident.

By the Lord’s mercy trustworthy. Paul’s trustworthiness is not a quality he claims for himself but mercy received from the Lord Jesus, who met him on the Damascus road while he was hunting Christians: he had been a blasphemer and persecutor, but he received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13–16). “Trustworthy” is the same Greek word as “faithful” in 4:2, where stewards must be found faithful. The steward is trustworthy because the Master was merciful, and the judgment of a man Christ remade carries weight (v. 40).

The present distress. The word means necessity, pressure. Whatever it was (see below), Paul is not laying down a timeless rule that Christians should not marry. He is giving counsel for a particular time of pressure.

How do I decide something Scripture does not settle? Many of the choices that shape a life, whom to marry, whether to marry, which work, where to live, are not commanded either way. Christians often go looking for a verse or a sign that will remove the responsibility of choosing. Paul’s example is more freeing. He weighs the circumstances, applies the principles, reaches a judgment, states it as a judgment, and leaves the other person free. So: rule out what Scripture forbids; ask what love and wisdom commend; seek counsel from mature believers; consider the circumstances honestly; pray; and then decide, trusting that God guides those who seek him even when no voice speaks (Proverbs 3:5–6; Romans 14:5). Christian maturity is largely made of such wisdom, since most of life is lived in that territory.

Uncertain wording. We do not know what “the present distress” was. It may refer to famine (there is evidence of grain shortages in Corinth around this time), to persecution (hostility toward the young church was real), or to the general trouble of the last days between Christ’s comings (compare v. 29). No one can be sure which, and Paul’s reasoning holds under any of them.
verseByVerse.note: The “present distress” may refer to famine, persecution or the pressures of the last days.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not make a project of changing your state, married or single; yet if you marry you have not sinned, and Paul only wants to spare you the troubles marriage brings.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. If you are married, or engaged, do not try to get out; and if you are free from a wife, do not rush to find one, given the present distress. The principle of verse 17 is applied once more.

You have not sinned. At once, and twice over, once for each party: marriage is not sin. Having commended singleness, Paul will not let his preference become a burden on anyone’s conscience. That instinct is rare: a strong personal conviction, argued for, and then repeatedly protected from becoming a rule for those who decide differently.

Worldly troubles. Literally “trouble in the flesh”, a word used of persecution and hardship: the pressures and anxieties of married and family life, especially in hard times. Paul is more honest than teaching about marriage that stops at the wedding. Marriage doubles the number of people whose suffering you feel as your own, and exposes you to losses you would not otherwise have known. And “I would spare you that” is affection, not a slight on marriage: a pastor who has watched people carry things, wishing they did not have to.

The Bridegroom who chose the trouble. Paul would spare his readers trouble in the flesh, but the gospel tells of a Bridegroom who did not spare himself. The Son of God took our flesh knowing exactly what trouble it would bring, and took to himself a bride whose troubles were her sins. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), bearing her griefs and carrying her sorrows to the cross (Isaiah 53:4). Every married person who finds that loving a spouse means feeling another’s suffering as one’s own has been given a small share in what he chose freely, and without limit.

Honesty is a kindness. For the single, it removes the fantasy that marriage is where difficulty ends, which makes singleness heavier and marriages more disappointing than they need be. For the married in the middle of the trouble, the illness, the strain, the years of difficulty with someone you have promised not to leave, it says you have not discovered a defect in your marriage: Paul told you, in writing, in advance.

In everyday life. If you are thinking of marriage, talk with a married couple a decade or two ahead of you and ask them honestly what was hard, and what carried them. If you are married and in a hard season, say to your spouse this week: this is what Paul said it would be, and I am still here.

Does free from a wife include the divorced? Some read it that way, but the paragraph is about the betrothed and the unmarried (v. 25), so Paul is most likely thinking of those who have not yet married or have been widowed. Remarriage after divorce is settled not by this verse but by verses 10–15 and Matthew 19:9, on the grounds of adultery or desertion (on abuse that amounts to desertion, see vv. 10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the end is near and this world’s present form is passing away, hold everything in it loosely, even marriage, grief and joy. Paul does not tell believers to stop marrying, mourning or buying, but not to live as if any of these were final.

The appointed time has grown very short. “Appointed time” is the decisive season rather than clock time: the season between Christ’s first and second comings. “Grown very short” (synestalmenos) means compressed, drawn together, a verb that could be used of furling sails as a ship nears harbour. Everything on board is worth having and none of it is worth building on, because the port is close.

As though they had none. Five clauses follow in the same startling form; taken with wooden literalness they would be monstrous. Paul cannot mean neglect your wife, for spouses owe each other themselves (v. 3). He means do not let marriage become your ultimate concern, and that is a mercy to marriage itself. A spouse asked to be your saviour will buckle under a weight only God can carry; a spouse loved as a gift, not worshipped as a god, is free to be simply a husband or a wife. Marriage is for this age only: in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30).

Mourning and rejoicing. Grief and joy are real, but not final. Paul cannot mean suppress your grief; he himself writes of sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27). The Christian mourns, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and rejoices without clinging. Grief is included not because it is unimportant but because it too will end. The mourning is right, but it is not the last word about the person you have lost. There will be a morning when the world in which such a loss was possible has passed away.

Buying and dealing with the world. Buy, but hold possessions loosely, as a steward, not an owner. The Greek behind “had no dealings with it” means using something to the full, using it up: use the world, but do not be absorbed by it, for its “present form”, its outward shape, like a scene in a play before the set is changed, is passing away (1 John 2:17). What passes is the shape, not the substance: creation itself will be set free, not discarded (Romans 8:21).

Why the time is short. The season was shortened by something that had already happened. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (15:20), and the new creation has already begun in him (2 Corinthians 5:17). These things are held loosely because they belong to an age whose end was announced on the morning of the resurrection, and whose replacement is already alive in the risen Lord. And the One waiting in the harbour is no stranger, but the Lord who said, “Surely I am coming soon” (Revelation 22:20).

In everyday life. Marry, grieve, celebrate, buy and work, and do not let any of it become the thing you are ultimately living for.

Did Paul think Christ would return in his lifetime? He did not know, and he never set a date. The day would come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2); certain things must happen first, such as the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4); and in other letters he speaks calmly of his own death (2 Corinthians 5:1–8; Philippians 1:23). The time is short because since the resurrection the church has lived in the last days. That is not a mistaken timetable but the posture every generation of Christians is called to: watchful, unhurried, with lamps lit.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul commends singleness to spare them anxiety: the unmarried can give the Lord their whole attention, while the married rightly have a spouse to care for as well.

Free from anxieties. This is Paul’s stated motive for all he says about singleness, and it governs how the rest is heard: he is not recruiting for self-denial but sparing them worry.

The things of the Lord. Here “anxious” is used positively: concerned for, devoted to. The single person can give full attention to the Lord’s work.

How to please his wife. “Worldly things” here are not sinful things but the legitimate, time-consuming business of a shared life in this present world: providing, caring, the household. Marriage is not spiritually inferior, but it takes attention, and attention is finite. The married Christian has two sets of claims, and the second is a person with her own needs, opinions, tiredness and hopes. That is not a defect in marriage. It is marriage.

The verdict comes first. Many Christians hear “how to please the Lord” and feel a knot in the stomach, like a child forever one good deed short of a hard father’s approval. Yet everyone is trying to please someone, a parent, a boss, the crowd online, the judge inside our own head, and whoever we must please ends up running our life. The gospel turns this round. Before Jesus had preached a sermon or worked a miracle, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and the Son lived a life that pleased him at every point: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Joined to Christ, you share that standing; God’s grace has “blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness, that in every other way of life the performance leads to the verdict, but in the gospel the verdict comes first and the performance flows from it. So pleasing the Lord is not earning a smile you lack. It is a loved child running to show his Father a drawing. This week, before a task no one will see, say quietly, “This is for you, Lord,” and do it well. “We make it our aim to please him” (2 Corinthians 5:9).

Attention that is never divided. The Lord who asks for our attention is never short of it for us: he numbers the hairs of every head and the sparrows that fall, he hears the single believer at midnight and the married believer on the school run, and not one of his people is ever at the back of his mind. And hanging on the cross, at the height of an obedience never divided, he saw his mother and gave her into the care of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). Care for family was not a rival to his devotion but part of it.

To each reader. To the single, particularly those who did not choose it: Paul names something you already possess, a freedom of movement and attention genuinely useful to God. It does not remove the loneliness, but your situation is not merely an absence; there is something in your hands. To the married: the attention you give your spouse is not stolen from God; it is the form your obedience takes. What Paul asks is honesty that the cost exists, not years of low-grade guilt that your capacity for other things has narrowed.

Is it wrong to be anxious, then? Jesus told us not to be anxious about our life (Matthew 6:25), and Paul tells us to be anxious about nothing but to pray about everything (Philippians 4:6). Here, though, Paul uses the same word for legitimate concern: the care a man rightly has for his wife and a single believer has for the Lord’s work. The difference is between care carried to God and care that has replaced God. Concern for your family is right; anxiety that forgets your Father knows what you need is not. Bring the concern to him and let him carry the weight.

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of everything Paul has said is not singleness or marriage but undivided devotion to the Lord, and his counsel is a help towards it, never a noose.

His interests are divided. He is pulled in two directions, towards the Lord and towards his wife, and both are legitimate.

The unmarried or betrothed woman. She “is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit”: devoted to God, set apart for his service in her whole person. In a world that defined a woman almost entirely by her household, Paul assumes an unmarried Christian woman has her own devotion to the Lord, her own concerns and her own spiritual vocation. The married woman, likewise, is anxious about how to please her husband, and that too is legitimate.

Not to lay any restraint upon you. This sentence rescues the chapter from every misuse it has suffered. The word behind “restraint” is vivid: brochos, a noose or halter, the loop thrown over an animal to bring it under control. Everything Paul has said about the advantages of singleness is counsel for the reader’s benefit, not a standard by which anyone is to be measured, and certainly not a rule the church may impose.

Undivided devotion to the Lord. Attending on someone without distraction, unlike Martha, who was distracted with much serving (Luke 10:40). This phrase is the goal of the whole chapter. Not singleness. Not marriage. Devotion.

Betrothed to one husband. Devotion to the Lord is devotion to a person. Paul would later write to this church, “I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ”, fearing they might be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2–3). The unmarried woman of this verse is a living picture of what the whole church, married and single, is called to be: a bride waiting for her Bridegroom with an undivided heart.

What undivided devotion looks like. Not a mood, or a count of hours at church, but a heart with one centre. Mary sat at the Lord’s feet while Martha was distracted, and he said that “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42). It shows in turning to him at the start of the day, before the day’s claims begin; in bringing every part of life to him, the marriage or the quiet flat, the work, the money; in noticing what keeps pulling your attention away, household worry or a restless search for someone, and handing it back to him in prayer; and in serving his people with what you have, the married often through a home opened, the single often through time freely given. None of this comes by concentrating harder. It is a heart’s answer to a Lord who was undivided towards us: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and nothing turned him aside until he had finished.

The noose thrown anyway, in both directions. What Paul forbade is what happened, for centuries: the chapter was read as establishing celibacy as the higher path and marriage as the concession for the weak: a two-tier Christianity with the unmarried at the top. Now the same danger runs in the opposite direction. In many churches the noose is thrown over the single: an unmarried adult is treated as a problem to be solved, quietly excluded from a church life assumed to be about families, and made to feel that his or her life has not properly started. That is a restraint Paul forbids just as firmly.

In everyday life. Look at your church through the eyes of its single members this week. Are they invited into homes, trusted with leadership, asked about their work and their walk with God rather than only about whether they are seeing anyone? Fix one thing.

So which is better, marriage or singleness? Paul has refused that question in every way he can find. For one reader undivided devotion will mean a freedom of time and movement to be spent rather than hoarded; for another, loving one person faithfully for a lifetime in a way nobody outside the house will ever see. Both are the same devotion, and the God who assigned them is not comparing.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An engaged man may marry his betrothed, or, if he is settled and free, refrain; both choices are good, and neither is sin.

If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed. If the engagement is straining under strong desire, and “it has to be”, let them marry: “it is no sin.” Once more Paul removes the guilt from the decision before anyone can attach it (on who is meant, see below).

Firmly established in his heart. The conditions are all internal, and all mark a free decision rather than a forced one. Firmly established: settled, not wavering. Under no necessity: not driven by pressure from anyone. Having his desire under control: genuinely able, not merely determined to try. Vows extracted from the young, imposed by an institution, or undertaken as a spiritual achievement meet none of Paul’s conditions.

Good and better. To remain engaged but not marry, in view of the present distress, is also good. “Better” here is not morally better but more advantageous in that situation: both verbs are positive, and the better is the practical advantage he set out in verses 32–35, in the circumstances he named in verse 26. The God of this passage is kind to the undecided: he does not trap young people with impossible choices or punish them for choosing the good instead of the better, but sets two good roads before them and walks down whichever one they take in faith.

The engagement that will end in a wedding. Every Christian engagement sits inside a larger one. God promised his people long ago that he would betroth them to himself for ever, in righteousness and justice, in steadfast love and mercy, in faithfulness (Hosea 2:19–20), and the New Testament shows that promise kept in Christ, who has a betrothed church and is coming for her (Revelation 19:7). He does not behave improperly toward his betrothed or keep her waiting without cause; the delay is patience, so that more may be gathered in (2 Peter 3:9). Human engagements may end in a wedding or in a kind farewell. His will end in a wedding, and the waiting will be forgotten in the joy.

What it does not mean. Not a reason for a modern engaged couple to drift in a long engagement with no end in view. In a world where engagement is not a legal bond, the principle is simply this: decide prayerfully, keep yourselves pure, and do not keep each other waiting without cause.

We are engaged, but one of us is now unsure. What should we do? Take it seriously and slowly, and speak honestly. An engagement is a serious promise, not to be broken on a sudden mood; but it is not yet a marriage, and it is far better to end an engagement than to enter a marriage one of you cannot enter in good faith. Pray together and separately; talk with a pastor or a wise married couple who know you both; ask whether the doubt is about this person, about marriage itself, or about fear. If you end it, end it kindly, take responsibility, and do not leave the other in uncertainty. If you go on, go on gladly, as Paul says: it is no sin.

Uncertain wording. These verses are among the most obscure in the letter, and the ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin”. The older reading takes them to be about a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage; the ESV notes this possibility, and the KJV, which speaks of giving her in marriage (v. 38), leans that way. The other, which the ESV follows, takes them to be about a man and the woman he is engaged to, deciding whether to go ahead with the marriage. The second fits the context (v. 25) and the language of strong passions more naturally, but a reader who meets a different rendering in another Bible is not meeting an error.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin,” and that the passage can also be read of a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage lasts for life, but death ends it, and a widow is free to remarry whom she wishes, provided he belongs to the Lord.

Bound as long as he lives. Marriage is lifelong (Romans 7:2). The verb is a different one from the word used of the deserted believer in verse 15, who is “not enslaved”.

Free to be married. Death ends the marriage bond. Paul says so without qualification or any hint that remarriage is a lesser choice. Widows have often been made to feel that remarrying would betray the person they buried; Scripture attaches no such shame to it. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is honourable, and Paul elsewhere positively counsels younger widows to marry (1 Timothy 5:14).

Only in the Lord. That is, to a fellow believer. The freedom is real and it has one boundary: she may marry whom she wishes, provided he belongs to Christ. A Christian may not marry an unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6:14), and this applies to all believers, not only widows. Here Paul gives a command rather than a judgment, and it stands out against the freedom around it: whom you marry, when, and whether, are all left open; this one boundary is drawn.

Why only in the Lord? Not out of snobbery about outsiders, which would sit oddly in a letter that tells believers to stay married to unbelievers and to accept pagans’ dinner invitations (10:27). The reason is what marriage is: a union of two whole persons, and one in which the deepest thing about one of them is not shared by the other is divided at the root, not without love, but unable to be what marriage is for. Concretely: the person you marry will be the one you cannot pray with about your child’s illness; every Sunday is negotiated; and the thing that matters most to you becomes a subject you learn to leave alone, a habit that does not stay confined to Sundays.

Free to belong to another. Paul uses this same law in Romans to explain the gospel: as a widow is free to marry another, so you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead (Romans 7:2–4). Every believer has passed through a death into a new marriage. And this one can never end as verse 39 says every earthly marriage ends, because the Husband has already died and risen, and death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9).

Two different situations. If you are already married to an unbeliever, Paul’s instruction is to stay, and God’s blessing is on that household (vv. 12–14); here he addresses a decision still to be made. And if you married an unbeliever in disobedience, you are still married: repent of the disobedience, not of the marriage.

In everyday life. If you are single and hoping to marry, tell a friend you will marry only in the Lord, and ask them to hold you to it when your heart is tempted otherwise. If you know a widow or widower, do not assume what they should do; ask how they are, and support whichever path they take in the Lord.

What about dating? Since dating is the road to marriage, a Christian should not begin a romantic relationship with someone Paul’s rule would forbid him or her to marry; a heart once given does not easily turn back. Someone already in such a relationship should be honest that it cannot go where it is heading, and end it kindly. And the rule is not satisfied by a partner who merely calls himself a Christian. “Only in the Lord” means someone whose life shows that he belongs to Christ: who loves the Lord, is part of a church, and wants to grow. Do not marry someone in the hope that he will become a believer afterwards.
verseByVerse.note: “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s last word is his judgment that a widow is more blessed if she stays single, and he reminds them that even his judgment comes with the Spirit of God.

She is happier. Paul gives his opinion one last time, and one last time he labels it as opinion. “Happier” is the word behind the Beatitudes, blessed. Not holier, not more useful, not more pleasing to God: more blessed, given the present distress (v. 26) and the undivided devotion singleness allows (v. 35).

I too have the Spirit of God. A touch of irony, aimed at those in Corinth who made great claims to have the Spirit. But the sentence does real work. Paul has carefully distinguished the Lord’s command from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25, 40), and a reader might conclude that the judgment parts are his private view, take it or leave it. This clause forbids that. Even in what he calls his opinion, he is writing inspired Scripture.

Looking back over the chapter. This chapter has told a church of married, single, widowed, divorced, deserted, enslaved and engaged people that not one of them is in the wrong place, and it rests every word on Christ: the body honoured because he redeemed it, slave and free alike bought with a price (v. 23), the time short because he is risen and coming. No one is left over, and no one is merely put up with. In chapters 8–10 Paul will again refuse to bind consciences where God has not spoken, and will ask the free to give up their rights for others (8:9–13): the same freedom, governed by the same love.

He has never given anyone the wrong life. The circumstances you are in tonight, the marriage that is hard work, the house that is quiet, the person you are still waiting for, the person you have buried, were distributed by someone who has never yet given anybody the wrong life. That is never a reason to stay in danger or to call abuse God’s will for you: cruelty done to you is a sin against you, not your portion from him. The Lord of this chapter had nowhere to lay his head, was deserted by everyone he loved, and died unmarried and childless, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). He took that portion to give us his: the Spirit who guarantees our inheritance, a room in his Father’s house (John 14:2), and a share in the joy of the Bridegroom who will present his whole church to himself in splendour.

Is everything in this chapter binding on me, then? It is all God’s word, but not all of it is command, and Paul has told you which is which. The Lord’s commands, as on divorce (vv. 10–11) and marrying only in the Lord (v. 39), you must obey. His judgment, as on whether to marry or stay single in the present distress, you receive as inspired, wise counsel to weigh seriously, while remaining free to decide either way without sin, because he says so (vv. 28, 36, 38). That is exactly why you may trust both the commands and the freedoms.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.”<sup>2</sup>But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.<sup>3</sup>The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.<sup>4</sup>For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.<sup>5</sup>Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.<sup>6</sup>Now as a concession, not a command, I say this.<sup>7</sup>I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.<sup>8</sup>To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am.<sup>9</sup>But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.<sup>10</sup>To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband<sup>11</sup>(but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.<sup>12</sup>To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her.<sup>13</sup>If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.<sup>14</sup>For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.<sup>15</sup>But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.<sup>16</sup>For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?<sup>17</sup>Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.<sup>18</sup>Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision.<sup>19</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.<sup>20</sup>Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.<sup>21</sup>Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)<sup>22</sup>For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ.<sup>23</sup>You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men.<sup>24</sup>So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.<sup>25</sup>Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.<sup>26</sup>I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.<sup>27</sup>Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.<sup>28</sup>But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.<sup>29</sup>This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none,<sup>30</sup>and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods,<sup>31</sup>and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.<sup>32</sup>I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord.<sup>33</sup>But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,<sup>34</sup>and his interests are divided. keyVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him.
keyVerse.note: Paul calls this his rule in all the churches, and it governs the whole chapter: married or single, widowed, deserted, slave or free, the place you are in is a life the Lord has dealt out to you and the place where God called you. It frees believers both from restlessly chasing a different situation before they can serve God and from fearing that their present one puts them beyond his use. The goal it serves is undivided devotion to the Lord (v. 35).

7.reflection:
Paul refuses to rank marriage and singleness, calling both gifts from God (v. 7). Where have you seen one or the other treated as second-class, in the church or in your own heart, and how does this chapter correct it?

Verses 3–5 describe marriage as two people who have each given themselves away. How does Christ’s self-giving for his bride shape what this means, and what it can never be used to justify?

Verse 17 says the life you are in is the life the Lord assigned you. What circumstance are you tempted to treat as an obstacle to serving God, and what would faithfulness look like in it this month?

Paul’s aim is “undivided devotion to the Lord” (v. 35), and he holds marriage, grief, joy and possessions loosely because “the present form of this world is passing away” (v. 31). What competes most for that devotion in your life, and how could your church help its single, married, widowed and deserted members live it?

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
Where we are. Paul now takes up the second question from the Corinthians’ letter (7:1), food offered to idols, and his answer runs to 11:1. Chapter 8 lays down the principle; chapter 9 gives Paul’s example; chapter 10 forbids idolatry itself.

The message. Being right about God is not enough: knowledge must serve love. The confident Corinthians were right that an idol is nothing and meat is only meat. But a brother whose conscience has not caught up can be ruined by watching them use that freedom, and he is a brother for whom Christ died. So love, not knowledge, decides what a Christian does with his rights.

Why it was said. Most meat in the city had passed through a temple, and guild dinners and family celebrations were held in temple dining rooms (see the introduction and the note on vv. 1–2). Some in the church, proud of their knowledge, ate anywhere, even in the temple itself; others, not long out of idolatry, could not eat such food without feeling that they were worshipping again.

How the chapter makes its case. Knowledge puffs up, love builds up, and what matters is to be known by God (vv. 1–3). He then grants the strong their theology, in one of the highest confessions of Christ in the New Testament: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (vv. 4–6). But not everyone has absorbed this, and food itself gains or loses us nothing with God (vv. 7–8). So the strong must take care: their example in the temple can build a weak brother up to sin, destroy one for whom Christ died, and so sin against Christ himself (vv. 9–12). Paul closes with his own resolve: he would rather never eat meat again (v. 13).

Where it leads. The chapter turns on two sentences about Christ. He is the one Lord through whom all things exist, so no piece of meat belongs to an idol (v. 6); and he is the one who died for the weak brother (v. 11). The Lord who made the world gave himself for the weakest of his people. He was free as no one has ever been free, and he “did not please himself” (Romans 15:3).

For us. Most of us are strong in some matters and weak in others. Ask what your knowledge has built, and whose face you see when you use your freedom: not a principle to defend, but a brother or sister Christ thought worth dying for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Knowledge must serve love, and the strong are right about God. Paul lays down the rule for the whole discussion: knowledge puffs up, love builds up, and what matters most is being known by God (vv. 1–3). Then he grants the strong their theology without reserve: an idol is nothing, and though the world is full of so-called gods and lords (vv. 4–5), Christians confess one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
One God, One Lord: Israel’s Confession and Christ

In vv. 5–6 Paul takes Israel’s confession of the one God (Deuteronomy 6:4) and shares its words between the Father and Jesus Christ, giving both the work of creation, which belongs to God alone (see the note on v. 6). This is not two gods, nor a lesser, created Son; it is that confession (the Shema) opened to include the Son within the one God of Israel, which is what the Council of Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically confident, who knew the idol was nothing. Their knowledge was real, and so was their pride. Now: Those who love the doctrines of grace can make correctness a platform for contempt (see the note on vv. 1–2). Paul’s question still applies: are you known by God? (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing the right answers is not enough: knowledge without love inflates the one who has it, while love builds up others.

Now concerning food offered to idols. Another question from their letter (7:1). The word eidōlothyta, idol-sacrifices, has a sneer built into it; pagans called the same food sacred offering. Paul begins by quoting the confident party, probably one of their slogans: “all of us possess knowledge.” They were not wrong about the facts (vv. 4–6).

Puffs up, builds up. The key principle of chapters 8–10. Physioō is the inflation word Paul has used repeatedly of this church (4:6, 18–19; 5:2): swollen with air, like a balloon, larger than its substance justifies. Oikodomeō is the building word from chapter 3: one course laid on another, like a house, until something stands. Both make a thing bigger. Only one makes it stronger.

Does not yet know as he ought. Being sure you have mastered a matter shows that you have not understood it as you should, because knowing as one ought includes knowing what knowledge is for: love. If I understand all mysteries and all knowledge, but have not love, I am nothing (13:2).

The setting. Trade guild dinners, birthday parties and civic festivals were often held in temple dining rooms (see meals and reclining at table), because trade, family celebration and religion were not separate departments. A Christian who refused every such meal could lose business, friends and standing. So the question was live, and it divided the church.

A knowledge that kneels. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3). Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he rose from supper, took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). He knew that Peter would deny him before Peter knew it, and he washed Peter’s feet too. The knowledge of God he gives is a knowledge that kneels.

What it does not mean. Not that knowledge is bad, or that Christians should not study theology; Paul is about to teach some of the deepest theology in the letter. The problem is never too much truth, but truth held without love.

A warning for readers of theology. Some Christian lives consist almost entirely of acquiring correct positions, on grace, election or baptism, and holding them against people who have not yet arrived. Underneath, the pull is often not love of the truth but love of being right: the old trust in oneself, dressed in doctrine. The Reformed tradition is especially at risk, because its doctrines are genuinely clarifying and the clarity is genuinely enjoyable. Paul’s verdict on the man who uses them to look down on others is not that his doctrine is wrong, but that he does not yet know as he ought.

In everyday life. Take the doctrinal position you most enjoy holding, and ask what it has built: not what it has settled in your mind, but who has been strengthened by your holding it. If nobody comes to mind, it may still be true, but it has been puffing you up. Bring that to the Lord who knew everything and spent it all on building his people; he gives the love that knowledge lacks (Romans 5:5).

So should I stop arguing for what I believe is true? No. Paul argues hard throughout this letter, and truth is worth contending for (Jude 3). The question is why and how you speak. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), aiming at the other person’s good rather than at winning; listen before you correct; distinguish the doctrines on which the gospel stands from those on which faithful Christians differ; and be willing to lose an argument rather than a brother. If you notice that you enjoy someone else being wrong, stop and pray before you say anything more.

Uncertain wording. Greek was written without quotation marks, so translators must judge where Paul is quoting the Corinthians. Most agree that “all of us possess knowledge” (v. 1), “an idol has no real existence” and “there is no God but one” (v. 4) are their slogans, as the ESV marks them, and many think “Food will not commend us to God” (v. 8) is another. Exactly where each quotation ends cannot be settled. The meaning is little affected: Paul agrees with the statements as theology and corrects the way they were being used.
verseByVerse.note: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple; temples also had dining rooms used for banquets and celebrations. The quoted phrases are probably Corinthian slogans.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What matters most is not how much we know about God but that God knows us, and whoever loves him is known by him.

He is known by God. The expected ending would be: if anyone loves God, he knows God. Instead the direction reverses. Paul makes the same turn to the Galatians, correcting himself mid-sentence: now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God (Galatians 4:9). “Known” is the language of relationship and choosing: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). The deepest reality is God’s loving, personal knowledge of us (2 Timothy 2:19; Romans 8:29). And it leaves no room for pride. Knowledge that puffs up is knowledge in which I am the one who knows; once God is the one who knows, there is nothing left to boast of.

I know my own. Jesus claims this knowing, which belongs to God, as his own. I am the good shepherd, he says; I know my own and my own know me, and I lay down my life for the sheep (John 10:14–15). And he speaks its terrible opposite to people rich in religious knowledge and activity, who had prophesied and done mighty works in his name: I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). To be known by God is, concretely, to be known by Christ: one of the sheep whose name he calls (John 10:3), whose sins he carried, for whom he gave his life. Your grip will slip a thousand times. His never has.

I feel I understand so little. Does God know me? This verse was written for you. Some Christians live with a low, persistent anxiety: they read and forget, their theology feels thin next to other people’s, and they suspect that their standing with God depends on how well they have got hold of him. Paul takes the whole question away. Your relationship with God has never rested on the firmness of your grip, but on his. You were known before you knew anything. The one mark Paul looks for is not knowledge at all: if anyone loves God. Do you love him, however feebly? Then he knows you.

And how do I know whether I love God? Not chiefly by the strength of your feelings on a given day. Love for God shows itself in wanting him, coming back when you have strayed, grieving over sin because it offends him, delighting in his word even when you understand little of it, loving his people, and wanting to obey (John 14:15). Peter, after failing badly, could only say, Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:17). That is enough. And even weak love points to something stronger beneath it: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strong are right: an idol is nothing and there is only one God, even though the world is full of so-called gods and lords. Paul grants their theology before he says a word about how to use it.

An idol has no real existence. Verse 4 picks up the question verse 1 left, probably quoting two more of the strong party’s slogans. The wooden thing in the temple is not a god. There is nobody behind the statue, and the meat that passed in front of it has not been altered in any way (Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8).

No God but one; many gods and many lords. The confession of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4), now the church’s. Yet there are so-called gods in heaven, such as Zeus and Apollo, and on earth, emperors declared divine. In one sense they exist: people worship them, and they hold real power over people’s lives. “Lords” was a title for the gods of secret-rite cults such as Serapis, and for the emperor. Zeus had no existence; the worship of Zeus was one of the most powerful forces in that society.

Nothing, or demons? Two chapters later Paul says that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God, and he does not want the Corinthians to be participants with demons (10:20). Both are true, and they answer different questions. In itself the idol is nothing: there is no god behind it, and the food is not contaminated. But idolatry is not therefore harmless, because evil spirits are glad to use the worship offered to a god who is not there. The image is empty; the worship is not. The danger was never in the meat. It was in the worship.

The one true image. Every idol is an attempt to give God a face: something carved, visible and near. The second commandment forbade Israel to make one (Exodus 20:4), not because God cannot be known but because nothing a carpenter carves could show him. And then God gave his own image. Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). What every temple in Corinth was groping after, the Father has given in his Son. The idol is nothing pretending to be God. Jesus is God, come near.

What it does not mean. Not that other religions are harmless paths to the same God. There is one God, and the gods of the nations are not him.

How idolatry works now. Few of us are tempted by a statue. But the things we organise our lives around, money, career, a child’s success, the good opinion of others, a political cause, are not the gods we treat them as, and the devotion given to them does real damage. An idol is usually a good thing asked to do a job only God can do. The money does not steady you. The career does not justify you. The child cannot bear the weight of being your reason for living.

Isaiah’s carpenter. Scripture’s mockery of idols is pastoral. Isaiah’s carpenter burns half a tree to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half, asking it to save him (Isaiah 44:14–17). To turn to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9) is to wake from a dream about firewood into the presence of the One who is real, and who is love.

How can I tell if something has become an idol? Ask what you cannot imagine being content without; what you most fear losing; where you run for comfort when you are low; where your money and spare thoughts go without effort; and what makes you angriest when it is threatened. A good thing has become an idol when losing it would feel like losing your life, or when you would disobey God to keep it. The remedy is usually not to throw it away, but to put it back in its place under God, thank him for it, and find in him what you were asking it to give.

Who are we to call other people’s gods nothing? Not because we are cleverer than the worshippers of Corinth, but because the one true God has made himself known, in his word and finally in his Son, to people who were themselves idolaters until he found them (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Humility is not saying that every claim is equally true; it is receiving the truth as a gift we did not deserve. The verse that denies the idols denies our pride too: the Christian has nothing he did not receive (4:7).

parallels.desc: the LORD our God, the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians confess one God, the Father, the source and goal of all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made and we are made new. In a discussion about meat, Paul places Jesus inside Israel’s own confession of the one God.

Yet for us there is one God, the Father. The force of this verse is lost unless you hear what Paul is echoing: Israel’s daily confession, “The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), known as the Shema. Devout Jews recited it morning and evening and would die rather than compromise it.

From whom are all things and for whom we exist. The Father is the source of all creation, and its goal: from him and through him and to him are all things (Romans 11:36).

And one Lord, Jesus Christ. In the Greek Bible the Shema contains two crucial words: theos, God, and kyrios, Lord, which stands for God’s own personal name (Exodus 3:14–15). Paul applies “God” to the Father and “Lord” to Jesus. He has not added a second deity, having just insisted that there is no God but one; he has put Jesus inside the confession, distributing its words between Father and Son, so naturally that he can say it in passing.

Through whom. The Father is the source and goal; Christ is the one “through whom”: all things were made through him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2), and through him we exist as new creatures, redeemed. In the Old Testament only God creates, and creation is here assigned to Jesus without qualification. The hands that flung the stars into place broke bread in Galilee and were nailed to a Roman cross. The gods of Corinth had made nothing, not one blade of grass.

Why does this belong in an argument about meat? The strong party’s freedom rests on it. If all things are from the Father and through the Son, a piece of meat cannot belong to anybody else. Christ made it, and passing it in front of a carved image does not transfer the title: the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof (Psalm 24:1; 10:26). This is more cheerful than the piety that treats food, pleasure, beauty and the body as suspect, as though holiness consisted in wariness. Paul’s answer is that every good thing came through Christ and belongs to him, and the enemy, who never made anything, cannot own what he did not make.

In everyday life. Take one ordinary good thing today, a meal, a walk, the face of someone you love, and say over it: this came from the Father, through the Son, and it is for him.

How do I explain the Trinity simply to a friend? Say what Scripture says, without pretending to explain everything. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; they are not three gods but one God in three persons, who speak to and love one another (Matthew 3:16–17; 28:19). This verse shows it in miniature: Israel’s one God, confessed as Father and Lord Jesus. Avoid analogies like water, ice and steam, which suggest one person appearing in three forms. It is a mystery, not a contradiction, and it makes the gospel possible: the Father sent the Son, the Son gave himself, and the Spirit brings us to both.

Where Christians differ: the deity of Christ. Groups such as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue that this verse distinguishes Jesus from the one God, making him a lesser being. This commentary’s view: Paul is not separating Jesus from the one God of Israel but including him within it. He divides the words of the Shema between the Father and the Son, and gives the Son the divine work of creation: one of the earliest Christian confessions of the Trinity in seed form. The Father and the Son are distinct persons, but one God, with the Holy Spirit (the Nicene Creed; the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3).
verseByVerse.note: Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus Christ as the one Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Being right about God does not settle how to treat a brother. Some believers’ consciences have not caught up with the truth, and food itself gains or loses us nothing with God (vv. 7–8), so the strong lose nothing by giving it up. If their example leads a weak brother to act against his conscience, they wreck one for whom Christ died and sin against Christ himself (vv. 9–12). Paul closes not with a policy but with his own resolve: he would rather never eat meat again than make his brother fall (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The “weak brother” is someone whose conscience has not yet caught up with the freedom the gospel gives (see the note on vv. 7–8). The strong keep their freedom but must think about its effect on others: Christ, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), is the pattern for laying down a genuine freedom out of love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The question was how the mature should use their freedom without damaging the less free. Now: The applications are many (see the note on vv. 7–8), but the principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not every believer yet feels the freedom the truth gives, and a weak conscience that eats against itself is stained; yet food itself brings no one nearer to God or further away.

Not all possess this knowledge. Not all have absorbed it deeply enough to feel free. “Former association” means habit. These are converts out of paganism, not long out, for whom that meat had been part of a religious act all their lives. Their minds now accept that the idol is nothing; their instincts have not caught up, and instincts formed over a lifetime do not dissolve because a doctrine has been explained. When they eat, something in them registers it as betrayal.

Weak and defiled. Weak means not strong enough to be free; defiled means stained. If they eat against their conscience, they feel guilty, and in fact they sin, because they act against what they believe is God’s will: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

The doctrine of conscience. The conscience is not infallible. It judges our actions by the standard we actually hold, which can be over-scrupulous or simply mistaken, as here, since the food is harmless. Yet a wrong conscience must still not be violated. The man who eats while believing it wrong is defiled, not by the food but because he has trained himself to act against his conviction, and that lesson does not stay confined to meat. A mistaken conscience is to be instructed, slowly, by Scripture, until conviction and truth line up; until then it is to be respected even in its error.

Food will not commend us to God. Probably another slogan of the strong, which Paul accepts (see “Uncertain wording” in the note on vv. 1–2). Eating is spiritually neutral: we are no worse off if we abstain, and no better off if we eat.

What does commend us to God. If food cannot bring anyone nearer to God, something else must. The verb means to present before God, and Paul uses it elsewhere of Christ’s work: he has reconciled you in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless before him (Colossians 1:22). Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), because the barrier between us and God was never on the plate: it was our sin, and he took it away. We have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13), and nothing on any table can add to it.

A bruised reed he will not break. The Lord is gentle with consciences (Isaiah 42:3). He does not drag his weak children forward faster than they can walk; he carries the lambs in his arms and gently leads those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11). And he cleansed his people’s consciences with his own blood, so that they could serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).

Where it applies today. Some Christians cannot do what others do freely, a drink, a film, a Sunday activity, a kind of music, not because Scripture forbids it but because their history makes it impossible. The former alcoholic, the convert from a religion where certain foods were sacred, the believer who came out of the occult and cannot bear certain images: these are today’s weak brothers. The mature response is neither to mock the scruple nor to treat it as a command of God, but to recognise that a real person has been shaped by a real history, and to be gentle with him.

Am I the weak one or the strong one? Most of us are both, in different matters: free about a glass of wine and troubled about Sunday shopping, or the other way round. On any given question, the strong believer rightly understands that Scripture leaves it free; the weak believer’s conscience still forbids what God allows. Neither is a permanent rank (on what each owes the other, see v. 13). Both must grow: the weak in understanding, the strong in love.

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your freedom is real, but if a weaker believer copies your example against his own conscience, your right has become a stone in his path.

This right of yours. “Right” means authority, a genuine entitlement, and Paul concedes it is theirs. Nobody sets out to trip anyone: the strong Corinthian simply exercises a liberty in front of his brother without thinking about the effect.

Eating in an idol’s temple. The strong were attending meals in temple dining rooms; archaeologists have found such rooms at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth. Not the marketplace or a private dinner, both of which Paul will permit (10:25–27), but the most public place there was, and the one most bound up with pagan worship. The strong believer sits there, enjoying his freedom and quite possibly the demonstration of it. And the weak brother walks past and sees him.

Will he not be encouraged? “Encouraged” is literally built up, the word of v. 1, now used with bitter irony. The strong think they are building up the weak by showing them freedom; they are building them up to sin, emboldening them to do what their conscience still condemns. It is a building-up that will bring him down.

The only stumbling block allowed. The gospel has an offence of its own: Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews (1:23). That stumbling block is God’s; no Christian may remove it by softening the cross, and no Christian may add another beside it. Jesus said that whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in him to sin would be better drowned in the sea (Matthew 18:6). He guards the weakest believers fiercely. He was free as no one has ever been free, Lord of the Sabbath and of every food, and he paid a tax he did not owe so as not to give offence (Matthew 17:27). The God who placed the first stone will not have his little ones tripped by a second.

How influence actually works. The damage is not done by argument. The weak brother watched someone he respected, concluded it must be all right, and did it against his own conviction. So every Christian is teaching all the time. The younger believer in your church learns less from what you say about holiness than from what he sees you do with your evenings, your money, your speech when you are annoyed, and your freedom.

What it does not mean. Not that eating in a temple is fine as long as no weak brother sees. In chapter 10 Paul will say that the temple feasts are participation with demons (10:20–21; see the note on vv. 4–5). He answers the strong on their own ground first.

How do I know whether my freedom will trip someone? Not in the abstract, which is why Paul gives no list. The same action is fine in one setting and destructive in another, and the only way to tell is to know the people you are among. Love here requires attention: who is present, what their history is, how young they are in the faith, whether they are likely to copy you against their conscience. When you do not know, ask them gently; when unsure, it is rarely a loss to hold back. The strong Corinthian’s failure was not chiefly theological. He had not looked round the room.

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To lead a weak believer into sin is to wreck someone Christ died for, and so to sin against Christ himself.

This weak person is destroyed. “Destroyed” is the ruin word, used of perishing. Paul means not embarrassment but a man being wrecked, as the habit of overriding conviction spreads to matters where the conviction was right. People are usually destroyed not by one decision but by a series of small permissions.

The brother for whom Christ died. The phrase that ends the argument. On one side, a man’s liberty to eat a particular piece of meat: genuine, defensible, correct. On the other, a person so valuable that the Son of God went to a cross for him, whose whole hope hangs on that cross (1 Peter 2:24), exactly as the strong man’s does. Will you not give up a meal for him? The strong Corinthian was right about the principle. He was not thinking about a person, and the price Christ paid for that person made the principle look very small.

Wounding their conscience. The word means striking, beating. To pressure a weak conscience into acting against itself is to beat it.

You sin against Christ. Christ is so united to his people that sin against them is sin against him (Matthew 25:40, 45); believers are limbs of his body (6:15). The risen Christ said as much to Saul of Tarsus: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The man who wrote this verse had heard those words spoken to himself. The strong man thought he was handling a brother’s scruple; he was handling the holy Lord of the church, whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14).

No private injuries. There is no private injury within the church. The sharp remark, the cold shoulder kept up for two years, the person you have quietly written off: none of it stops with them. Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, a terrifying thought for the offender and an immeasurably comforting one for anyone on the receiving end.

In everyday life. Put the name of the person you find most difficult in your church into this phrase, the brother for whom Christ died, or the sister, and say it aloud. It changes the temperature of everything.

I think I have caused someone to stumble. What should I do? Confess it to God and receive his forgiveness; Christ died for your sin against your brother too. Then, where it is wise, go to the person, own what you did without excuse, and ask their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). Stop what was harming them, at least in their presence. If they have fallen into sin because of your example, help them back gently, and carry them in prayer. Do not drown in guilt: the Lord who warns is the Lord who restores, and he can use even this to teach you love.

Where Christians differ: can a brother for whom Christ died perish? Many sincere Christians, Arminians especially (who hold that Christ died equally for every person and that a true believer can finally fall away), take this verse as proof that Christ died for some who will finally be lost. This commentary’s view: Paul describes the real tendency of the strong person’s action: it would lead the brother to ruin, and the warning is real. But Scripture also teaches that Christ’s death infallibly saves those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; John 10:15, 28). That is definite atonement; and by the perseverance of the saints every true believer will be kept by God to the end. Paul is not inviting speculation about the weak brother’s final destiny. He is telling the strong that their freedom could push someone toward ruin, that this is a sin against Christ (Romans 14:15, 20), and that every brother is precious enough for Christ to die for. God keeps his sheep, and one of the ways he keeps them is through brothers who heed warnings like this one.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul would give up meat for good rather than make a brother fall: love is ready to lose a genuine right for someone else. He concludes not with a policy but with himself.

I will never eat meat. To make a brother “stumble” is to make him fall into sin (vv. 9–11). “Never” is emphatic in the Greek: never, to the end of the age, and not just idol meat but any meat, if it would cause a brother to fall. It is hard to resent a man who has already gone further than he asks you to go. The readiness was costly: meat was a rare pleasure for a working man like Paul, and he would give it up for good, if need be, for a weaker Christian whose name he may not even know. Chapter 9 shows how he has already given up other rights for the gospel.

As I am of Christ. The argument that begins here runs through chapters 9 and 10 and ends with a sentence that shows where it came from: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). Paul gives up meat because his Lord gave up far more; Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3). Writing to Rome on this same question, Paul sets the two side by side: do not let what you eat destroy the one for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15). The strong at Corinth were asked to give up meat for a brother. Christ gave up heaven for his enemies. A meal set against a cross: the comparison settles itself.

In everyday life. Name one freedom you value that you could set aside this week, for one particular person, without any loss to your soul: the drink at a meal with a friend fighting addiction, the film when the young people are watching, the sharp joke in front of someone fragile. Set it aside quietly, without announcing your sacrifice. That is the love of the Lord who did not please himself, and his Spirit grows it in you.

Does this give the most easily offended person a veto? No. Read carelessly, the verse puts whoever is prepared to be upset in control of the church. Paul’s weak brother is not someone who disapproves; he is someone in danger of being led into sin against his own conscience and destroyed by it (vv. 10–11). Being offended is not the same as being made to fall. The man who says, “I disapprove of what you are doing,” is making a criticism; the man about to act against his own convictions because of your example is in danger, and only the second is in view here.

Obligations on both sides. Nor should the weak stay weak. Romans 14, the fullest treatment of the same question, binds both sides: the strong must not despise the weak, and the weak must not pass judgment on the strong (Romans 14:3). Neither is given the whip hand. And where someone insists on a scruple as a rule for the whole church, as the circumcision party did, Paul resists them to the face (Galatians 2:11–14). What remains, when both errors are excluded, is harder than a rule and better: a willingness to lose a genuine right for a particular person, decided case by case, by people who are paying attention to each other.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

keyVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.
keyVerse.note: Every step of the chapter applies this sentence. The strong were right about God, but knowledge used for one’s own freedom only inflates, while love asks what will build up a brother. The love Paul means has a shape: the Christ who died for the weak brother (v. 11) and did not please himself.

8.reflection:
Paul says knowledge “puffs up” but love “builds up” (v. 1). Think of something you know well about the faith. Has it made you more patient with others or less? What would it look like to hold it in a way that builds people up?

Verse 3 turns from our knowing God to God knowing us. How does it comfort a believer who feels he understands very little, and humble one who thinks he understands a great deal?

Verse 6 puts Jesus inside Israel’s confession of the one God, and says all things exist through him. How should that change the way we receive ordinary good things like food, and the way we think about the “idols” our culture offers?

Who are the “weak” believers in your church or circle, people whose history makes certain freedoms dangerous for them? Is there a freedom you could quietly set aside for one of them, and how is that different from letting the easily offended run the church?

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 can look like a digression from food offered to idols, but it is Paul’s own example of the resolve that ended chapter 8: he would give up meat rather than make a brother fall (8:13).

The message. Love gladly lays down its rights for the sake of others and of the gospel. Paul has every right an apostle can claim, and in Corinth he has used none of them. Free from everyone, he has made himself everyone’s servant, so that nothing about him stands between people and Christ. Such a life takes the discipline of a runner bound for a prize that lasts.

Why it was said. The strong in Corinth stood on their right to eat. Some also looked down on Paul: in a city where teachers were measured by their fees and patrons, an apostle who worked with his hands and refused support looked second-rate, and they questioned whether he was an apostle at all (vv. 1–3; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First Paul proves the right (vv. 1–14): common life, the law of Moses, the temple and the Lord Jesus all say that those who serve should be supported. Then comes “Nevertheless”: he has not used it, rather than hinder the gospel (v. 12). Next the reason (vv. 15–23): preaching is a charge laid on him, so his one freely chosen offering is to preach for nothing; and more widely, he has become all things to all people, yet always under the law of Christ, that he might save some. Finally the games held just outside the city (vv. 24–27): athletes deny themselves for a wreath that withers, so run for one that lasts, and let the preacher not be disqualified himself.

Where it leads. Behind every line stands the Lord who had every right there is and laid them all down: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He was free, and took the form of a servant; he became weak to win the weak; he ran his course to the cross for the joy set before him. Paul’s self-denial is only a reflection of that grace.

For us. Ask which of your rights you hold most tightly, and whether anyone is kept from Christ by the way you hold it. Then remember who gave up everything for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The right Paul is about to give up was really his. He is free and an apostle, and the Corinthian church itself is the proof (vv. 1–3). An apostle may be fed by the church, travel with a believing wife and be spared working for a living (vv. 4–6), as every soldier, farmer and shepherd knows (v. 7), as the law of Moses teaches (vv. 8–10), as the temple showed and as the Lord Jesus commanded (vv. 13–14). In the middle comes the surprise: he has not used this right, but endures anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The right of ministers to be supported

Paul argues from the lesser to the greater, from the threshing ox to the people who labour in the gospel (see the note on vv. 8–10), and the Lord Jesus confirmed the principle by command (see vv. 13–14). So the Reformed churches have rightly held that supporting ministers properly is a matter of obedience, not charity.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some Corinthians seem to have thought an apostle who took nothing was not worth much, which is why Paul defends the right even while refusing it. Now: The principle cuts both ways, for congregations and for ministers (see the note on vv. 13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is truly free and truly an apostle, and the Corinthians themselves are the proof, so the rights he is about to give up were really his.

Not a digression. Paul has just resolved never to eat meat if it made his brother stumble (8:13). Now he shows he has done the same on a far larger scale, but first he must prove the right was genuinely his. You cannot admire a man for refusing something he was never entitled to.

Am I not free? He is as free as the strong in Corinth claimed to be (8:9), whose slogan was “All things are lawful for me” (6:12), and more.

Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Some in Corinth questioned Paul’s apostleship. An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord (Acts 1:21–22). Paul saw him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 15:8), and he treats it as an appearance of the risen Christ no less real than those given to the Twelve.

Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? The fourth question strikes home. There would be no church at Corinth to hold an opinion about Paul if Paul had not come. The people judging his credentials are his credentials.

The seal of my apostleship. A seal (sphragis) authenticated a document, like a wax stamp: the mark that proved it was what it claimed to be. Their conversion is God’s seal on Paul’s apostleship.

The Lord behind the seal. Twice in two verses Paul adds “in the Lord”, and the words carry the argument. A seal is pressed by the owner, not by the messenger.
