A congregation of former idolaters is evidence not that Paul was impressive but that Christ is risen, still making new creations out of idolaters, each one a letter in his own handwriting, “written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

In everyday life. Paul is defending himself to people he led to Christ, and the questions have heat in them. If you carry the hurt of ingratitude from someone you served, notice the natural movement: to give less, care less, keep a little back. Paul’s answer to being doubted by his own converts was to go on spending himself on them (2 Corinthians 12:15), and to write them, a few chapters later, the chapter on love the church has treasured ever since.

Are there apostles today? Not in this sense. An apostle as Paul means it had seen the risen Lord and been sent by him in person (Acts 1:21–22), and Paul was the last (15:8). The office belonged to the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and continues only through the apostolic writings in Scripture. Churches that call a missionary or church planter an apostle in a loose sense deserve to be heard charitably; but anyone claiming apostolic authority to add to Scripture or to rule the churches should be refused. We have the apostles: they speak to us in the New Testament.
verseByVerse.note: An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord. A seal authenticated a document.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers those who question him, and his first point is a modest one: an apostle has the right to be fed by the church he serves.

My defense. The words are legal: “defense” (apologia) is the speech for the defence, and “examine” (anakrinō) means cross-examine, the word Paul used at 4:3. Some questioned Paul, perhaps because he refused payment: where a teacher’s worth was measured by his fee and a patron expected to support his teacher, refusing could look second-rate, or like spurning the generosity offered.

Untroubled about himself, not about what was entrusted to him. In chapter 4 their verdict on him mattered very little (4:3–4), because the Lord is his judge; here he mounts a defence. His apostleship is the authority by which the gospel came to them, and if it can be dismissed, so can everything he taught.

Do we not have the right to eat and drink? The case opens at the most basic level: the right to receive food and drink at the church’s expense. “Right” (exousia) is the key word of chapters 8–9, the same word used of the strong Corinthians’ liberty in 8:9, which is exactly the link Paul is building. And the claim is modest: not a stipend or a house, but food and drink. The apostle to the Gentiles establishes, at length, that he would have been entitled to his dinner. In Corinth he chose to go without, knowing hunger and thirst (4:11), rather than claim it.

Silent for himself, plain for the truth. Accused before the high priest, Jesus gave no answer for himself (Isaiah 53:7; Mark 14:60–61); yet asked whether he was the Christ, he answered plainly, “I am” (Mark 14:61–62). He let his reputation be torn to pieces, but not the truth. He to whom the cattle on a thousand hills belong (Psalm 50:10) had nowhere to lay his head, and took no wage for the bread of life he gave away; and he has promised a day when he will dress himself for service and serve his servants at table himself (Luke 12:37). Paul is walking in his Master’s footprints.

When should I defend myself against criticism? First, ask honestly whether the criticism is true; if so, receive it as a gift and change. If it is false and only your pride is hurt, you can usually leave your reputation with God (1 Peter 2:23). But if a falsehood threatens the gospel, the people in your care or a work God has entrusted to you, then speak: calmly, truthfully, without attacking back, and preferably to the person directly. Whatever you do, do not let the hurt shrink your love for the critic.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Barnabas had the same right as the other apostles to take a believing wife along and to be supported by the churches instead of working for a living.

A believing wife. Literally, “a sister, a wife”: a wife who is a fellow believer, travelling with him at the churches’ expense.

As do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? The verse lets slip that Peter (Cephas) was married, and that his wife travelled with him on ministry, supported by the churches. The Gospels agree, for Jesus healed Peter’s mother-in-law (Mark 1:30–31), and Paul treats a travelling wife as the normal arrangement. The brothers of the Lord, a known group with a recognised ministry (Acts 1:14), were James, Joses, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3); James became the leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote a letter in our Bible, and Jude wrote another.

Only Barnabas and I. Paul worked with his hands (Acts 18:3; 20:34), and this verse shows that Barnabas did the same: these two were the exception, supporting themselves by their trades. They have the same right as the rest. It is the one mention of Barnabas in this letter, and it is affectionate. By now the two had parted after a sharp disagreement over John Mark (Acts 15:36–39). Yet Paul names him as a fellow labourer who made the same sacrifice. He does not let the split rewrite the record of what they did together. Later he asks for the very Mark they quarrelled over, as “very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11).

The brothers of the Lord. These men grew up in the same house as Jesus and did not believe in him (John 7:5); his family once set out to seize him, saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). The resurrection changed them: the risen Christ appeared to James (15:7), who later called himself not the Lord’s brother but “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). Kinship with Jesus saved no one. Faith in the risen Lord saved even his own family.

In everyday life. Pray for your pastor’s marriage and family. A minister’s wife and children often carry burdens no one sees; do one practical kindness for them this month.

I have fallen out with a fellow Christian. How should I speak of him now? As Paul speaks of Barnabas: truthfully and honourably. Without pretending the disagreement never happened, refuse to let the quarrel rewrite the good you once did together; speak well of him where you honestly can, refuse to gossip, pray for him, and keep the door open. Paul and Barnabas differed over a judgment, not over the gospel, and both went on serving Christ. Some separations of that kind are not sin; bitterness about them always is. If reconciliation is possible, pursue it.

Where Christians differ: married ministers and the brothers of the Lord. The Roman Catholic Church requires celibacy of most of its priests, and teaches that Mary remained a virgin for life, so that the brothers of the Lord were cousins or children of Joseph by a previous marriage. This commentary’s view: this verse shows that the apostles, including Peter, whom Rome regards as the first pope, had wives. Church leaders may marry (1 Timothy 3:2), and requiring celibacy of ministers has no basis in Scripture. The natural reading is that the brothers of the Lord were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus (Matthew 1:25; 13:55–56). Mary is to be honoured as blessed among women, but nothing in Scripture requires her perpetual virginity. To say it without heat: those who hold the tradition do so out of reverence for the Lord’s mother, which is not a bad motive; but it is not what the words naturally say.
verseByVerse.note: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him. The Lord’s brothers included James and Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone already knows that a worker lives from his work: soldiers are paid, planters eat their grapes, and shepherds drink the milk. Paul begins his case not with Scripture but with common life.

Three trades, one point. Nobody funds his own military service, plants a vineyard and then buys grapes, or tends a flock and buys his milk.

Pictures of the ministry. The three trades are not chosen at random: Scripture uses all three as pictures of gospel work. The soldier: “No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him” (2 Timothy 2:4). The vineyard and the farmer: Israel is God’s vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), and the church is God’s field (3:6–9; 2 Timothy 2:6). The shepherd: the standing image for those who lead God’s people, from Ezekiel 34 to Peter’s charge to shepherd the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2).

The chief Shepherd pays his shepherds. The God of this verse is himself all three to his people: the LORD of hosts who fights for them, the vinedresser who tends his vine, and the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. The flock a pastor tends is not his own: it is the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and when the chief Shepherd appears he will give his under-shepherds the unfading crown of glory (1 Peter 5:4). So the labourer may expect to be fed from the flock, and must never fleece it for his own gain.

I have served for years and see no fruit. Is it wasted? No. The fruit of Christian service is often slow, hidden and later than we would like, and some of it will only be seen on the last day. God measures your work not by visible results but by faithfulness, and he has promised that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (15:58). Keep planting. Ask God for fruit and for grace to wait, and ask a trusted friend whether anything should change in how you serve. But do not mistake slowness for failure. Many you have taught and prayed for will one day tell you what you never knew you did.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law says the same: the ox that threshes may eat from the grain, and the principle behind it is that those who labour should share in the harvest.

The threshing ox. Common sense has made the case; now Paul shows that the Law of Moses says it too. Oxen walked over the threshing floor, or pulled a sledge over it, to separate grain from husk, and the grain was under their feet all day. A tight-fisted farmer might tie the ox’s mouth shut. God’s law forbade it: the animal doing the work eats from the work.

Is it for oxen that God is concerned? This must not be read as if God did not care about animals. This is the God who feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies, who knows when a sparrow falls, who ends the book of Jonah by remarking on Nineveh’s cattle, and whose law commands rest for the working animal (Luke 12:24, 27; Matthew 10:29; Jonah 4:11; Exodus 23:12); “Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast” (Proverbs 12:10). Paul’s question sets the lesser matter aside to reach the greater: is this only about oxen? No; the law carries a principle that reaches much further.

It was written for our sake. Workers should share in the fruit of their labour. If God applies it to a beast at a threshing floor, he certainly applies it to a man in a pulpit. Paul uses the same verse for elders’ pay in 1 Timothy 5:18.

In hope. A man breaking ground in February sees nothing but mud; what keeps him going is a harvest he cannot yet see. Paul has already said that only God gives the growth (3:6–7); here is the comfort that goes with it: the one who works in hope will share in the crop. The Christian teaching a class, visiting the housebound or raising children in the faith is a ploughman working in hope.

Sower and reaper rejoice together. Jesus said that the reaper is already receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together (John 4:35–36). The field is his, the growth is his, and the Lord of the harvest (Matthew 9:38) does not muzzle his workers: he feeds them now, and on the last day brings them into the joy of the harvest home.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? As Paul does here. He treats Deuteronomy not as an archive of obsolete regulations but as written for our sake, addressed ultimately to the church (10:11; Romans 15:4). That does not make every civil or ceremonial law binding on Christians in its original form; the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws belonged to a nation. But every law reveals something of God’s character and wisdom, and usually a principle that still applies. So ask of any command what it shows about God, what principle of love to him or to neighbour lies under it, and how it is fulfilled in Christ. All Scripture is profitable (2 Timothy 3:16–17).
verseByVerse.note: Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor; the law let them eat as they worked.

parallels.desc: you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who bring the gospel may fairly be supported by those they serve, yet Paul has not used this right, because he will put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel. Here the chapter turns.

Spiritual things, material things. The spiritual seed is the gospel; the material harvest is support, and the exchange is wildly unequal: Paul gave them the knowledge of God, the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, and might in return have expected dinner (Romans 15:27; Galatians 6:6). Other teachers in Corinth were already supported, and Paul, their founder, had a stronger claim.

Nevertheless. The surprise. Everything since verse 3 has built the case for his right, and now he says he has not used it at all. That is the lesson for the strong: having a right does not mean you must use it.

We endure anything. “Endure” (stegō) means to cover and so bear up, like a roof under rain; it is the word in “Love bears all things” (13:7). An “obstacle” (enkopē) is a road cut up to stop an advance. In Corinth travelling teachers of rhetoric charged for their lectures: an impressive man arrives, gathers an audience, takes their money, moves on. Had Paul accepted support, he would have been put in that category on the first day. So he made tents, and the message arrived without a price tag.

A message that cannot be sold. The gospel of Christ is that the Son of God laid down every right he had for people who could pay him nothing: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). A preacher who insisted on his rights while announcing that would contradict his sermon with his life. Paul’s tent-making was the gospel made visible: a Saviour who gave, proclaimed by people who give.

A culture fluent in rights. We speak of almost everything as rights, and for good reason: the conviction that the powerful may not trample anyone owes much to the Bible’s teaching that every human being bears God’s image. But the legal scholar Mary Ann Glendon, in Rights Talk, observed that a culture which speaks only in rights tends to make them absolute, and loses the words for responsibility and sacrifice. Paul spends half this chapter establishing his rights, and then holds them in an open hand. The religious man clutches his rights because he thinks he has earned them; the irreligious man because they are all he has. Paul lays his down because Christ did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6). Someone who has received everything by grace need not insist on everything he is owed, and in giving it away he is free in a way the mere holder of rights never is.

What it does not mean. Not that it is wrong for ministers to be paid. Paul defends the right, and accepted gifts from other churches (2 Corinthians 11:8–9; Philippians 4:15–16). He refused it in Corinth for the gospel’s sake.

The principle under the practice. Paul gave up a genuine right not because it was wrong but because of what people in his setting would conclude. So ask whether, in the eyes of the people you are trying to reach, using a right would put an obstacle in their way. It might be the right to be thanked, to win the argument, or to keep your evening when a neighbour needs help.

Should Christians today avoid anything that looks like making money from the gospel? We should avoid anything that makes the gospel look like a product for sale. Churches should be scrupulously honest with money, open in their accounts, modest rather than lavish, and never imply that God’s blessing can be bought (Acts 8:20). Preachers who live in luxury on the gifts of the poor, or promise wealth in return for donations, put exactly the obstacle Paul feared across the road. Fair support of faithful workers is not that; it is obedience. The test is whether money serves the gospel or the gospel serves money.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s priests lived from the altar, and the Lord Jesus himself commanded that those who preach the gospel should live by it. Paul keeps his two strongest arguments for last.

The temple. In Israel the priests and Levites lived from the offerings and tithes (Numbers 18:8–32; Deuteronomy 18:1–5), and those who served at the altar ate portions of the sacrifices (Leviticus 7:6–10). They received no allotment of land; the LORD himself was their portion. It was the system God designed.

The Lord commanded. The highest argument: when he sent out his messengers to stay where they were welcomed, eating what was provided, the Lord Jesus said that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). Later Paul quotes that saying alongside Deuteronomy, apparently under the one heading “the Scripture says” (1 Timothy 5:18): the words of Jesus were received early with the authority of the Old Testament itself.

An altar we eat from. Christians, says Hebrews, “have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10). That altar is Christ’s sacrifice, and believers feed there on Christ himself, by faith. So the minister is not a priest living off sacrifices he offers, but a fellow guest at a table Christ has spread. The LORD who was the Levites’ portion (Numbers 18:20) is now the portion of every believer (Psalm 16:5). The Lord who commanded that his messengers be fed fed five thousand on a hillside and cooked breakfast for his tired disciples after he rose. He does not live on what we bring him; he gives us himself.

A command widely neglected. The one person who cannot comfortably say this is the minister himself. Without meaning unkindness, congregations let a minister’s pay fall behind the cost of living and arrange his housing so that he will retire with nothing, in churches that would be shocked to think they had disobeyed Christ; and the same holds for anyone the church leans on heavily and thanks once a year. Yet Paul establishes the right and then refuses it, so the minister who reads these verses and feels aggrieved has taken in only half the chapter. His freedom is that of a man whose heart does not depend on what the people in the room pay him. Let the church be generous as a matter of obedience, and let the preacher hold his pay loosely enough that it never shapes a sermon.

How much should I give to my church? The New Testament sets no percentage for Christians; it asks for giving that is regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial (16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:3; 9:7). Many believers take the tithe, a tenth, as a sensible starting point and give more as they are able. Give first to the church where you are fed, since this verse makes that a duty, and then beyond it. Give in a planned way rather than only from what is left over. And if your circumstances are very tight, give what you can, gladly; the widow’s two coins were more than all the rest (Mark 12:43–44).

parallels.desc: the priests’ portion

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul preaches for nothing, and serves everyone, because the gospel matters more to him than his rights. Preaching is a charge laid on him, so it gives him nothing to boast of; his one freely chosen offering is to give the gospel away free (vv. 15–18). More widely, free from all, he has made himself the servant of all, taking his place beside Jews, Gentiles and the weak, yet always under the law of Christ, so as to save some (vv. 19–22). He does it all for the gospel, that he too may share its blessings (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology:
Adapting to people without changing the gospel

All things to all people has been badly misused, as a reason to adjust the gospel itself until it gives no offence; what it rightly means is set out in the notes on vv. 19–20 and 21–22. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was one long application of it, rightly understood: learning to speak the language of educated secular professionals, earning a hearing, and then preaching to them the same crucified Christ Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s examples, as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak, match the divisions of his own missionary world. The Damascus road had made him a prisoner of the message; everything else could be negotiated. Now: Every missionary and every church faces the question where fitting in becomes giving in, and it needs constant discernment (on the opposite failure, see vv. 21–22).

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not give up preaching free of charge, because preaching itself is not his choice but a charge laid on him; giving it away is the one thing he can freely offer.

Not a hint. Paul has just spent twelve verses proving he is entitled to support, and he can hear how it will sound: a man angling for payment. So he closes the door: he has refused, and he is not asking them to start paying him now.

I would rather die. So emphatic that the Greek breaks off (see “Uncertain wording” below). His ground for boasting (kauchēma) is not pride in self-denial but being able to preach without charge. That was not commanded; it was the one thing in his ministry he could call his own offering, and he would rather die than lose it. Given no choice about the central thing in his life, he responded not with resentment but by searching out something extra to give, and guarding it fiercely.

Necessity is laid upon me. “Necessity” (anankē) is compulsion laid on a man from outside. Paul was on his way to Damascus with letters to arrest Christians when he was stopped in the road and given a commission he had not applied for (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). So he cannot boast in preaching, any more than a conscript can boast of enlisting. “Woe to me” is the language of the prophets: like Jeremiah, who found the word like a fire shut up in his bones (Jeremiah 20:9), Paul cannot hold it in.

The love that compels. What, in the end, was the necessity? Not a rule but a Person: “the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14). A man pulled from a burning house cannot stay quiet about the fire while his neighbours sleep. “Woe to me” is not the complaint of a reluctant employee but the cry of a man who knows that silence would betray the One who loved him and gave himself for him (Galatians 2:20). Christ did not wait to be sought by the man breathing threats against his church. He came after him, knocked him to the ground, opened his eyes, and laid on him a necessity that became his joy.

In everyday life. The necessities of your own life, the job that pays, the family that needs you, are easy to meet with joyless compliance. You cannot choose the work; you can choose to do it excellently when nobody checks. You cannot choose the illness; you can choose what people find when they visit. The things you have no choice about are the very place where you can give something freely.

Does every Christian have this necessity to share the gospel? Paul’s commission was unique. But every Christian has been entrusted with the gospel in some measure and is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and the church as a whole is under the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20). For most believers that means speaking naturally of Christ to family, friends and colleagues, praying for opportunities, living so that the question is asked, and supporting those sent to preach. You need not feel guilty that you are not Paul; but you should not be silent either.

Uncertain wording. In Greek, verse 15 breaks off mid-sentence, roughly: “I would rather die than… no one shall empty my boast!” Translations, the ESV included, smooth it into one sentence. The broken grammar is a mark of strong feeling, and the sense is not in doubt.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Paul did not volunteer for his task but was entrusted with it, his reward is not wages but the joy of giving the gospel away free.

A stewardship. Paul works out the logic of his position. Had he volunteered to preach, he could expect wages. But the task was laid on him. A steward (oikonomos) was a household manager entrusted with his master’s affairs, often a slave, not paid but obliged (4:1–2). Given a charge he did not seek, he has no claim to wages; he must simply be faithful with what was handed to him. So is Paul with the gospel.

What then is my reward? Paul’s answer is unexpected: his reward is not something he receives but something he gives up. The wage he draws is the privilege of drawing no wage, and he is not gritting his teeth; the gospel has changed what he enjoys. A gift given in secret brings a gladness that receiving the same amount never would, and Paul organised a whole ministry around that discovery.

My food is to do his will. “It is more blessed to give than to receive” is the Lord’s own saying (Acts 20:35). Tired and hungry at a well in Samaria, Jesus gave living water to a woman others seem to have shunned, and told his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). The giving fed him. Paul’s strange wage is a share in the joy of the Son who gave everything and never once wished it back. The Father gave his Son; the Son gave himself; the Spirit is given to all who believe. God loves a cheerful giver because he is one, and he is making us like himself.

In everyday life. Give something away this week in such a way that nobody can return the favour or record the credit, and do not tell anyone (Matthew 6:3–4).

Is it wrong to serve God hoping for a reward? No. Jesus promises reward to those who give, pray and fast in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18), and whoever comes to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is serving for human praise, or imagining that we earn salvation. Scripture’s rewards are gifts of grace from a Father who delights to honour what his own Spirit produced in us, and the greatest of them, as Paul found, is joy in God himself and in giving as he gives. To want that is to want what God wants for you.

Uncertain wording. Verse 17 compresses a whole argument into two conditions. Most take “if I do this of my own will, I have a reward” as a case that does not apply to Paul, since he did not volunteer, and “if not of my own will” as his real situation, a steward under orders; the “reward” of verse 18 is then a deliberate paradox, pay that consists in taking no pay. Some read “of my own will” as the willing heart God rewards. Either way the main point is clear: preaching is a duty laid on him, and preaching free is the offering he chose.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Free from everyone, Paul made himself everyone’s servant, taking on Jewish customs among Jews so as to win as many as possible.

Free, yet a servant. Free (eleutheros): no one owns him. Yet he made himself a slave (douloō) to everyone, and nobody did this to him. Christian freedom is never chiefly freedom from obligation; it is the capacity to take on obligations nobody could have imposed on you. “Win” (kerdainō) is a business word, to make a gain, and it appears five times in verses 19–22.

As a Jew, as one under the law. In Christ Paul no longer relied on being Jewish, or on the law, for his standing with God (Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:19). Yet among Jews he kept Jewish customs out of love: he took a vow (Acts 18:18) and joined in temple purification (Acts 21:23–26). Timothy had a Greek father, and Paul circumcised him because of the Jews of that region (Acts 16:3), to gain a hearing, not for salvation. Keeping Moses’ rules was a courtesy that opened doors, never a price paid for heaven.

Timothy and Titus. Yet when certain men insisted that Titus, a Greek, must be circumcised to be accepted, Paul refused absolutely, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The same operation, opposite answers. When the question was how to get near people, Paul was endlessly flexible; when it was what a man must do to be accepted by God, he would not concede a syllable. The container may be adjusted: language, custom, diet, dress, where a conversation begins. The content may not: the holiness of God, the reality of sin, the necessity of the cross, the call to repentance and faith.

All the way down to where we were. Christ came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). The eternal Word learned a language, a trade and a village’s customs, kept the feasts, and ate with Pharisees and with tax collectors. He came all the way down to where we were, and did not change the truth by one word to make it easier.

Flexibility in both directions. Paul was not simply relaxing his standards to reach the worldly; he also took on restrictions he did not need, in order to sit with the scrupulous. Adapting that only ever gives me more freedom is usually not done for the gospel at all.

So how far should I adapt to reach my friends? As far as love requires and holiness allows. Learn their language and the questions that matter to them; be at home on their ground; give up preferences that put them off without serving the gospel, such as church jargon, your music, even lawful pleasures in their presence if they would stumble. But never join in sin to be accepted, never hide the hard parts of the gospel, and never let fitting in become the goal (see the note on vv. 21–22).

verseByVerse.quote: To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among Gentiles and among the weak Paul likewise took his place beside them, yet always under Christ’s law, aiming not to fit in but to save some.

Outside the law, but under the law of Christ. With Gentiles Paul did not keep Jewish food laws or customs; he ate with them (Galatians 2:12–14). But the safeguard sits inside the text. He was under the law of Christ (ennomos Christou, literally “in-lawed to Christ”): the moral will of God as taught and fulfilled by Christ, summed up in love (Galatians 6:2; John 13:34). Freedom from Moses’ ceremonies is not freedom from God’s moral law. And the law of Christ asks more, not less, because its measure is the cross: a man may eat what he likes and still be under an obligation that reaches to laying down his life.

To the weak. The weak of chapter 8, with tender consciences: Paul does not stand at a distance being patient with them, but stands where they stand. We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, for Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:1–3).

All things to all people. Two things guard the famous phrase from abuse. The first is the stated purpose, repeated through four verses: “that I might win”, “I might save”. A man who adapts endlessly and never gets round to the gospel is using Paul’s words as cover for the opposite. The second is the modest word “some”. It steadies both the evangelist discouraged by a small response and the one who thinks the right presentation would bring everybody. You spend yourself, God gives the growth (3:6), and some are saved.

He became weak to win the weak. The Saviour was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). He did not stand at a distance from our frailty. He was hungry, tired and tempted, wept at a grave and sweated in a garden, so that the weakest believer might know that his High Priest understands.

The opposite failure. A common failure in conservative churches is treating an inherited cultural form, the music, vocabulary and dress, as though it were the gospel. The question is not only whether we will compromise the gospel, but whether we will be inconvenienced for it.

In everyday life. Pray for one person you would love to see saved, and ask what being all things to them would mean this week: an evening on their ground, a question about their life, a willingness to be bored or uncomfortable for them, a plain word about Christ when the moment comes.

Is being all things to all people just people-pleasing? No; the difference lies in the heart. The people-pleaser changes in order to be liked and cannot bear disapproval. Paul changed in order to win people for Christ and could bear any disapproval: the man who ate with Gentiles also opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11), and wrote that if he were still trying to please man he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The test is whether you will say the thing that makes them dislike you, when love requires it. Only someone secure in Christ’s approval is free to adapt without being swallowed.

If God has chosen his people, why does Paul work so hard to save some? Because God’s choosing is the reason evangelism succeeds, not a reason to stop. God ordains the means as well as the end, and the means is the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:14–17). Paul knew the Lord had many people in Corinth (Acts 18:9–10), and that is why he stayed and preached there for eighteen months: election guarantees that his effort will not be in vain. Christians who understand election differently agree this far: we do not know who the elect are, so we offer Christ freely to all, plead with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20), and trust God to open hearts as he opened Lydia’s.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does all this for the gospel’s sake, because he too lives by it and longs to share its blessings alongside those he reaches.

A fellow partaker. “Share” (synkoinōnos) means a fellow partaker. Paul is not outside the gospel handing it to others, but inside it with them, a fellow sinner receiving the same mercy he offers: a beneficiary given the job of telling others where he found it.

The same fountain, with the same empty hands. God had called them into the fellowship of his Son (1:9), and “fellowship” (koinōnia) shares its root with Paul’s word here. The blessing of the gospel is Christ himself: forgiveness in his blood, righteousness in his name, life in his life. Preacher and hearer receive the same Saviour by the same grace, and there is enough in him for every apostle and every slave. The man who had seen the risen Lord still came to the same fountain as the newest convert at Corinth, with the same empty hands, and found it full. His mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23).

The danger of handling holy things. The minister’s Bible becomes raw material for Sunday; the teacher reads only to prepare; the long-standing member hears every sermon as an assessment of the preacher. The warning sign is that you listen and think, “That would help so-and-so,” and the thought “This is about me” no longer comes. “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16).

How do I keep the gospel fresh for myself when I have known it for years? Go back to it as a sinner, not as an expert. Confess specific sins regularly, so that forgiveness stays real. Read Scripture sometimes with no task in view, asking only what God is saying to you. Sing the great hymns about the cross and mean them. Spend time with new believers, whose wonder is contagious. Take the Lord’s Supper as a hungry man, not as a spectator. And pray Paul’s own prayer, to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). The gospel does not grow old; we grow dull, and the Spirit is able to wake us again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Christian life is a race to be won and a fight to be fought, and both need discipline. Athletes at the games deny themselves for a wreath that withers; believers run for a crown that lasts (vv. 24–25). So Paul runs with aim and keeps his own body under control, lest after preaching to others he himself should fail the test (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and effort: the perseverance of the saints

The warning of verse 27 is not a threat to the final security of true believers but one of the means by which God keeps them (see the box “Where Christians differ: could Paul lose his salvation?” at the end of the note on vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived beside the Isthmian Games, and Paul’s comparison would have stung a little: athletes trained more earnestly for a passing prize than many Christians did for an eternal one. Now: Some Christians are wary of any talk of spiritual discipline, fearing that it sounds like earning salvation; why it does not is set out in the note on vv. 24–25.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christian life is a race to be run to win, with an athlete’s discipline, for a prize that will never wither.

The setting. The Isthmian Games, among the great festivals of the Greek world, were held every two years at the Isthmus just outside the city, under its management. Paul’s readers knew the athletes, the races and the prize.

So run. The point of comparison is the manner of running, not the number of winners; Paul does not mean only one Christian is saved. Run like a man who means to win, not like someone jogging round because attendance is expected. He has just said he does everything so that he may share in the gospel’s blessings himself (v. 23), and the race shows this is not automatic. Chapter 10 follows at once with Israel, who all ate the same spiritual food and yet most fell in the wilderness.

Self-control, for a perishable wreath. The word (enkrateuomai) shares its root with the self-control the Spirit grows (Galatians 5:23). Competitors at Olympia swore that they had trained for ten months, under strict diet, saying no to many good things. At the Isthmian Games the winner’s crown was pine, or in some periods dried wild celery: ten months of denial, and the reward was a handful of leaves that browned within a week. Our crown is eternal life and glory (2 Timothy 4:8; James 1:12; 1 Peter 5:4). The rebuke is aimed at us. People discipline themselves ferociously for a marathon, a qualification or a physique, and yet say they cannot find time for prayer and Scripture. The difference is not the time available but how much we want the prize.

Looking to Jesus. Run with endurance the race set before you, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:1–2). He ran the course first: forty days saying no to bread, a lifetime saying no to every shortcut, and a garden where he prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). His self-control was perfect, and it was for us: where our discipline falls short, his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). The Isthmian victor wore celery until it withered; the King of glory wore thorns for a day, so that his people might wear a crown of life for ever. In John’s vision the elders cast their crowns before the throne, because they know whose victory it really was (Revelation 4:10–11).

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by effort. The prize is given by grace, but grace trains us to strive (Philippians 2:12–13; Titus 2:11–12). Nobody supposes an athlete’s training earns him entry to the stadium; he trains because he is in the race, not in order to be admitted to it.

What does spiritual training actually look like? Ordinary, regular, deliberate practices that put you where God has promised to meet you. Daily Scripture reading and prayer. Faithful attendance at the Lord’s Day worship, the preaching and the Lord’s Supper. Memorising Scripture, occasional fasting, generous giving. Honest friendship with a believer who can ask you hard questions. Saying no to things that dull you, often your phone or your screen. None of these earns anything; all of them are means of grace. Start small and keep going: train yourself for godliness, for it holds promise for the present life and for the life to come (1 Timothy 4:7–8).
verseByVerse.note: The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. Winners received a wreath of pine or dried celery.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul runs and fights with aim, and keeps his own body under control, knowing that a man can preach to others and still be found false himself.

Not aimlessly. Two pictures of effort that achieves nothing: the runner with no finish line in view, the boxer swinging at the air. Someone can be busy in a church for thirty years and still be shadow-boxing. Paul’s alternative is not more energy. It is aim.

I discipline my body. “Discipline” (hypōpiazō) literally means to give a black eye; “keep under control” (doulagōgeō) means lead as a slave. Having made himself a servant to all (v. 19), he now makes a servant of his own body. This is not contempt for the body, which he has called a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19). It is an athlete’s relation to his appetites: the body is a magnificent servant and a ruinous master.

Disqualified. “Preaching” (kēryssō) is a herald’s announcement; “disqualified” (adokimos) means failing the test, rejected as counterfeit. The danger is specific: “after preaching to others”. The preacher handles the truth so constantly that it can stop searching his own heart, and he can describe repentance without repenting, competently, for years. God is not impressed by gifts or platform (Matthew 7:22); he looks for a heart that trembles at his word (Isaiah 66:2).

Bought with a price. His body is no longer his own: it was bought with a price, the price of Christ’s own body (6:15, 20). So self-discipline for the Christian is not self-improvement but keeping what Christ bought for the purpose for which he bought it. And the fight is not hopeless, because sin’s ownership was broken when our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). The craving still shouts, but it no longer has the right to be obeyed.

In everyday life. Most of us know which bodily appetite most often wins: food, sleep, lust, the phone, anger that runs through the body before the mind can stop it. The fight is won less by heroic resolutions than by aim, and by the Spirit, through whom we put to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13): knowing the one opponent and landing ordinary blows against it again and again. If you teach or lead, it is a mercy to have a friend who asks about your own holiness, not only your ministry. The man who wrote this finished the race and kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7), because Christ kept him; and the Lord who calls his people to run will not let one of them be lost at the finishing line.

This frightens me. How can I know I will not be disqualified? Look away from yourself to Christ, and then look honestly at your life. Your safety rests on his faithfulness, not on the strength of your discipline: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The very fear that makes you want to take holiness seriously is a sign of life; hypocrites rarely worry about this. Rest in his promises, and answer the warning as Paul did, fighting real sins with real means: confess them, flee temptation, keep company with believers, keep coming to Christ. A sin you both love and hate, and keep fighting, is not proof that you are disqualified; the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17).

Where Christians differ: could Paul lose his salvation? Some take this as proof that even an apostle could fall away and be lost; others say “disqualified” means only losing a reward. Both readings are held by sincere believers who take the warning to heart. This commentary’s view: Paul knows that a person can preach to others and yet prove not to be genuine (Matthew 7:22–23), so he takes his own holiness seriously. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. True believers will not finally be lost: those whom God justifies he also glorifies (Romans 8:30), no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28), and God will sustain the Corinthians to the end (1:8–9). But they persevere by heeding such warnings, not by ignoring them; assurance and diligence go together (2 Peter 1:10). A man who reads this and thinks it could not happen to him has misunderstood it. A man who reads it and disciplines himself is the very man the warning was written to preserve. The fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over.

keyVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them.
keyVerse.note: This sentence gathers up the chapter. Paul proves his freedom and his rights at length, only to show what he does with them: he spends them on others, so that more may be won to Christ. It is the pattern of the Son who, though free and rich beyond measure, took the form of a servant for us.

9.reflection:
Paul proves at length that he had a right to be supported, then says, “Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right” (v. 12). Which of your rights do you hold most tightly, and is there a situation where laying one down would remove an obstacle to someone hearing the gospel?

Verses 13–14 say the Lord commanded that those who preach should live by the gospel. How well does your church care for those who serve it, and how can those who serve hold their pay loosely enough that it never shapes what they say?

Paul became “all things to all people” (v. 22) yet stayed “under the law of Christ” (v. 21). Where is the line between adapting for the gospel and compromising it? Can you think of an example of each?

Paul feared that after preaching to others he might himself be disqualified (v. 27). What helps you keep the gospel personal rather than something you only pass on to others, and what one practice of spiritual training would you like to take up?

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 completes Paul’s answer about food offered to idols (8:1–11:1). Chapter 8 asked those who knew better to give way for the weak; chapter 9 showed Paul giving up his own rights, and ended with the athlete who could still be disqualified (9:27). Now Paul shows that danger in history, and then gives his rulings on the temple, the market and the dinner table.

The message. Belonging to God’s people, sharing its signs and holding the right doctrine will not keep you safe if you play with idolatry. Christ is the host of his people’s table, and he will not share them with demons. So run from idol worship, receive everything else as the Lord’s gift, and spend your freedom on the good of others and the glory of God.

Why it was said. The strong in Corinth felt secure. They were baptised, they shared the Lord’s Supper, and they knew that an idol is nothing, so they saw no harm in a dinner in a temple, where business and family life often required one (see the introduction). Others were anxious about every piece of meat in the market.

How the chapter makes its case. First, a warning from history (vv. 1–13). All Israel was rescued, baptised into Moses and fed and watered by Christ himself, yet most fell in the wilderness through craving, idolatry, immorality, testing Christ and grumbling. It was written for us: let the confident take heed, and let the tempted know that God is faithful and provides the way out. Second, the reason idolatry is impossible for a Christian (vv. 14–22): the Lord’s Supper is a real sharing in Christ, as Israel’s altar meals were a sharing in the altar, and behind the idol stand demons, so no one can drink both cups. Third, freedom rightly used (vv. 23–33, rounded off in 11:1): seek your neighbour’s good, eat market meat and a friend’s dinner with thanks, decline when someone makes the meal a statement of worship, and do everything to the glory of God.

Where it leads. The Rock that followed Israel through the desert was Christ (v. 4). The one they tested and grumbled against is the Son who later stood among their children offering living water, and who, dared to come down from the cross, stayed there. The jealous Lord of the song of Moses is the bridegroom who bought his people with his blood, and the table he spreads gives them himself. The faithful God who limits every temptation kept his own Son through the hardest test of all, and keeps his people by joining them to him. And the one life that did all to the glory of God (v. 31) is counted to everyone who trusts him.

For us. Our idols rarely stand in temples, but the Corinthian reasoning is alive and well: I know it means nothing, so it cannot hurt me. This chapter asks us to stop testing how close we can go, to run to the table where Christ feeds us, and to spend our freedom on other people, until our eating and drinking, and everything else, shows how good he is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Spiritual privileges do not keep safe anyone who is careless with sin, but the faithful God keeps those who watch. All Israel was rescued, baptised into Moses and fed and watered by Christ himself (vv. 1–4), yet most of them died in the wilderness (v. 5). Their craving, idolatry, immorality, testing of Christ and grumbling were written down to warn a church on whom the end of the ages has come (vv. 6–11). So whoever thinks he stands should take care (v. 12), and no one need despair, for God limits every temptation and always provides the way of escape (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ in the wilderness

When Paul says that the rock was Christ (v. 4), he means that the Son of God was already present and at work among his people before he was born of Mary (see the note on vv. 3–4). So the Old Testament is not a story from which Christ is absent: he is there in promise, in pattern and in person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were eating idol food in pagan temples needed to hear that feeling secure is not the same as being safe. Now: A Christian who trusts in baptism and regular communion as automatic guarantees, without faith and watchfulness, is making Israel’s mistake. The Lord’s Supper and baptism are real means of grace, not charms.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Israelite who came out of Egypt shared in God’s rescue and in signs like the church’s own, so religious privilege on its own protects no one.

Do not be unaware. Paul has just described himself as an athlete who could still be disqualified (9:27); now he shows that it has actually happened, to a generation as privileged as any that ever lived. The Corinthians prided themselves on knowledge (8:1); Paul adds what it had left out.

Our fathers. Paul calls the wilderness generation “our fathers” in a letter to a mostly Gentile church. Whoever belongs to Christ is Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), so Israel’s history is the church’s family history. A Corinthian dock worker was being told that the Red Sea was part of his story.

Under the cloud … through the sea. Count the word “all”: five times in four verses. Paul means every last person in the camp, including the many who never reached the land. The pillar of cloud guided them by day and stood between them and Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 13:21; 14:19–20); the sea stood up on both sides, and they walked out on dry ground (Exodus 14:21–22). Cloud above, water on either hand: they were surrounded, and Paul uses the word for baptism to say so.

Baptised into Moses. Not water baptism: Israel did not get wet; the Egyptians did. To be baptised into someone is to be bound to him, so that his deliverance becomes yours, as Christians are baptised into Christ (Romans 6:3). Israel had a mediator in Moses (one who stood between them and God), a rescue, a covenant sign and the visible presence of God. If membership, baptism and the Lord’s table could save anyone, that generation was safe. That is the point Paul is setting up: they were not.

Baptised into a person. The heart of it was never the water but the person: Israel was bound to Moses; believers have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Yet Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, Christ over it as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Moses could lead the people through the sea, but he could not give them new hearts. The greater Moses has passed through deeper waters than the Red Sea, the waters of death itself, and all who are joined to him by faith come up out of them on the other side. A person can have the rite without having Christ; no one can have Christ without faith.

Who this passage is for. The man who was sprinkled as a baby and has the certificate in a drawer, the woman baptised in a river at seventeen, the family that has not missed a Sunday in a decade. Paul does not call these things worthless; he calls them spiritual food and drink. But Israel had the equivalent of every one, in more spectacular form than any church has seen, and it was possible to have the lot and perish anyway. The cloud did not make anyone love God; it only made him impossible to ignore. So thank God for every privilege you have, and then ask the question this passage is about to press: has all this led me to trust and love Christ himself, or only made him familiar?

Does this passage settle how baptism should be done? Not directly. Israel was neither immersed nor sprinkled; they walked through on dry ground. Paul uses the word for union with a mediator, not for a method. This commentary holds to believer’s baptism by immersion on other grounds: the New Testament pattern of baptising those who repent and believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), and the picture of burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the children of believers, read the covenant differently, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Lord. Both sides agree on the point Paul is making: no form of baptism, however it is done, can stand in for faith.

parallels.desc: the pillar of cloud
through the sea on dry ground

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel ate and drank what God supplied in the desert, and the one who supplied it, at every stage of the journey, was Christ himself.

Spiritual food and drink. The food is the manna (Exodus 16); the drink is the water from the rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11): Israel’s equivalent of the Lord’s Supper. “Spiritual” does not mean non-physical; the water from the rock was wet. It means supplied by the Spirit: food no farmer grew, pointing beyond itself to Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35).

The Rock that followed them. A Jewish tradition of roughly this period had a rock literally travelling behind Israel. Paul does not endorse it. Water came from a rock at Rephidim near the start of the journey (Exodus 17:6) and at Meribah nearly forty years later (Numbers 20:11), different rocks in different places. What followed them was the One who gave the water, at both ends of the wilderness and every dry mile between.

The Rock was Christ. The Rock is God’s own name in the song Moses sang over this very generation: the Rock, whose work is perfect; the Rock that bore you, whom you forgot (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18). Paul lays a title reserved for the LORD on Jesus of Nazareth without apology. He is not making a comparison but identifying a person: Christ is God himself. Paul will say the same again: Israel put Christ to the test (v. 9, where the manuscript reading is discussed).

How could Christ be with Israel centuries before he was born? Because the Son did not begin to exist in Bethlehem. He is the eternal Word who was with God and was God in the beginning, through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3). At Bethlehem he took a human nature to himself; he did not come into being. Jesus said that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and that before Abraham was, I am (John 8:56–58). When Israel was led, fed and watered in the desert, the Son was the one doing it. The God of the Old Testament and the Saviour of the New are not two characters but the same Lord.

Before there was a manger, there was a rock in a desert. The Son of God opened a spring for a people who had already decided he was not worth trusting, and gave drink to throats that would soon complain against him. Centuries later, at the Feast of Booths that remembered those years, he cried that anyone who thirsts should come to him and drink (John 7:37): the same voice and the same offer, now standing among them openly. As the rock was struck to give water (Exodus 17:6), he was struck at the cross so that his people might drink.

In everyday life. Read the wilderness stories in Exodus and Numbers looking for him. And when you are in a dry place yourself, remember who stood on the rock. He has not stopped giving water in deserts.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul says the true source of their water was Christ.

parallels.desc: bread from heaven
water from the rock

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet God was displeased with most of that privileged generation, and they died in the wilderness. Their privileges were real, but they protected no one who did not believe.

Nevertheless. All had the privileges; most perished. Of the fighting men who came out of Egypt, two entered the land, Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:29–30), out of more than six hundred thousand (Numbers 1:46). And the phrase is restrained: God “was not pleased”. Paul describes no rage, and yet a generation ends.

Overthrown. Strewn, laid out flat (katestrōthēsan, a verb from Numbers 14:16): bodies spread across a desert floor; on Numbers’ figures, something like forty funerals a day for thirty-eight years. Every one had been under the cloud and through the sea, and Paul answers the Corinthians’ confidence with a graveyard.

They ate the manna and died. “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness,” Jesus told the crowd, “and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die” (John 6:49–50). The manna kept them alive for a day. Nor is the Supper a charm; but Christ himself, received by faith, is a life no wilderness can take away.

The one body on the cross. The God who was not pleased with most of a nation said of one man, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). Everything that generation lacked, he possessed, and the favour that rests on him rests on everyone who is in him. The displeasure that strewed bodies across the wilderness fell, in the end, on the one body on the cross.

What it does not mean. Not that all who died in the wilderness went to hell. Moses died there under God’s displeasure, and Moses is on the mountain of transfiguration (Deuteronomy 34:5; Luke 9:30). His point is that privileges without faith do not protect from God’s judgment, and God’s favour to a group guarantees nothing about any particular person in it.

Were these people ever truly God’s? Some were, and many were not: Israel was a covenant people, but not everyone in it had faith. Hebrews explains what went wrong: the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened, and they could not enter because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19; 4:2). The church today is the same kind of mixture: it is possible to sit among God’s people, sing their songs and share their table, and never have trusted Christ yourself. The answer is not to doubt every Christian around you but to make sure of your own heart, coming to Christ himself and not merely to his people. And if you fear you may be one of those outsiders, the fear itself shows that you want him, and he has promised rest to all who come (Matthew 11:28).

Was God not harsh to let a whole generation die in the desert? It can sound so, until the story is read whole. That generation had watched the plagues, the sea and the manna, and still, as God said, put him to the test ten times and would not obey his voice (Numbers 14:22). Even then the judgment came slowly: thirty-eight years in which the manna still fell six mornings a week, the cloud still led, and their children were raised to enter the land. God is holy, and patient far beyond anything we would be. The real question is not why he judged them but why he bears with any of us, and the answer is that he has not ignored sin but dealt with it, in his Son (Romans 3:25–26).

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shaped Israel’s history into a pattern to warn us, so that we do not crave evil things as they did. Beneath all the sins that follow lies one root: desire set on what God has not given.

Examples for us. Examples are types, patterns (typoi): the impression a die leaves when it stamps a coin. These events really happened, and God shaped them so that the pattern would still be legible centuries later. We are not cleverly finding lessons the Old Testament never intended; it was made this way on purpose.

In the flow. Verses 1–5 told the story; verse 6 says why. Paul now works through four of Israel’s sins, each with its parallel in Corinth, and all bearing on the question of chapters 8–10: may a Christian eat at an idol’s feast? Israel too thought a meal was only a meal.

That we might not desire evil. Paul names what lies underneath the four sins: epithymētas kakōn, cravers of bad things. One of the first collapses in the wilderness was a food riot. They despised the manna and wanted fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic (Numbers 11:5), so badly that they said they had been better off in Egypt. The place was named the Graves of Craving (Numbers 11:4–34). The Corinthians’ craving for temple meals is the same thing in a toga (James 1:14–15).

Not by bread alone. God fed his people with manna that he might make them know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:3). Israel failed that lesson. Centuries later the true Son was hungry in the wilderness, offered bread on the devil’s terms, and answered with that very verse (Matthew 4:4). Where the cravers demanded what God had not given, he went without, learning the manna’s lesson on behalf of a people who never had. The God who rained bread every morning on people who complained about the menu is not stingy, and in Christ he has given the one thing that ends craving at its root: himself, the bread of life (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament stories are merely moral fables; they are history that teaches. Nor is every detail a code to crack, finding meanings Moses would never have recognised. Paul’s typology (reading events as patterns God placed there for his later people) is disciplined and moral: here is a people with advantages, here is what they did, and you are made of the same material. The desert is gone. The craving is not.

In everyday life. Think back over the last week and ask not what you did but what you wanted that you would have been embarrassed to pray for out loud. Then bring that desire to God by name, and ask him for contentment with what he has given.

Is it wrong to want things? No. God made us creatures of desire, and he richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Wanting food, love, rest, children or useful work is not sin. The problem was what the appetite did: it wanted bad things, or good things on its own terms; it despised what God had given in order to demand what he had not; and it valued the gift above the Giver, to the point of preferring Egypt. Can the desire be brought to God in prayer and left with him? One that sulks when God says wait, or would rather have the thing without him than him without the thing, has become craving.

parallels.desc: the graves of craving

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not turn to idols as Israel did at the golden calf, where a feast to the LORD became worship on their own terms. Idolatry is a religious sin, and immorality follows close behind it.

Do not be idolaters. The first of the four wilderness failures is the one everybody knows: the golden calf (Exodus 32), at the very foot of Sinai, weeks after the people had heard God speak the commandments.

To eat and drink. Paul quotes Exodus 32:6 about the meal because the Corinthians are arguing about meals. And Israel did not swap the LORD for a Canaanite deity: Aaron announced a feast to the LORD (Exodus 32:5). They kept the name and changed the terms: a God visible, manageable, in a form they had chosen. That is idolatry, committed in a worship service by the devout. But the LORD is not manageable, and that is our safety: a God small enough to control would be too small to save.

Rose up to play. “Play” is the polite translation of a Hebrew word that covers dancing, revelry, and what happens after the dancing; Exodus notes drily that the people had broken loose (Exodus 32:25). This is what happened at Corinthian temple feasts: eating, drinking and immorality, in that order. Worship on your own terms comes first and sexual sin follows, as Peor, in the next verse, shows again.

The mediator who could not pay. After the calf, Moses asked God to forgive the people, and if not, to blot him out of his book. God refused (Exodus 32:30–33). Moses loved them enough to offer himself, but he was a sinner too and could not stand in their place. The offer that failed on Sinai succeeded on Golgotha: Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Idolaters are not saved by a better resolve but by a better Mediator, the Son who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15): God made visible at last, not in gold but in flesh.

Today’s idols. An idol, as Tim Keller put it, is a good thing that has become an ultimate thing: anything you look to for what only God can give. To find yours, finish this sentence honestly: if I lost this, life would not be worth living. Good things make the strongest idols, a marriage, a child, a ministry, because nobody thinks to suspect them. A plainer test: where the spare money and the free hours go, and what you think about before sleep. A person’s theology is on his lips; his worship is in his diary and his bank statement.

Stop feeding the rival. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to manufacture a stronger devotion to God, but to stop feeding a rival. Nobody has ever loved God more by trying harder to feel it; hearts warm to him when the thing absorbing the heat is set down. That is why Paul’s command a few lines later is “flee from idolatry”, something you can actually do on a Monday, rather than “feel differently”, which no one can do by command (10:14; 1 John 5:21).

Can I worship the true God in a wrong way? Yes; that is the calf’s lesson. Aaron’s people meant the LORD and were still idolaters, because they worshipped him in a form he had forbidden (Exodus 20:4–5). It is possible to believe in the right God and still shrink him: to a God who only comforts and never commands, who agrees with my politics, or who exists to make my plans succeed. The safeguard: let God define himself from his own word, and worship him as he has revealed. Whenever I catch myself thinking, my God would never, I should check whether that comes from Scripture or from me.

parallels.desc: they sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fall into sexual sin as Israel did at Peor, where a dinner invitation led to idol worship and to judgment. Idolatry and immorality came to Israel at the same table, as they did in Corinth.

We must not indulge in sexual immorality. The episode is Baal of Peor (Numbers 25), this chapter’s exact problem in Old Testament dress: the Moabite women invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down (Numbers 25:1–2). It began with a dinner invitation. A Corinthian accepting a temple invitation would have said he was only eating.

Twenty-three thousand. Numbers says twenty-four thousand, but the two texts are not making the same claim. Numbers gives a total for the whole judgment (Numbers 25:9), which included the chiefs executed by sentence (Numbers 25:4–5); Paul says “in a single day”. A day’s toll inside a larger total is no contradiction, and both figures are round, as ancient reporting is. We need not know exactly how Paul reached his figure to hold Scripture true, and the difference shows that no one smoothed the texts into agreement: the mark of real writers handling real records.

The body that belongs to the Lord. Paul has already told this church why Peor matters: your bodies are members of Christ; you are not your own, for you were bought with a price, so glorify God in your body (6:15, 19–20). Sexual sin is never only a private matter between two people. It takes something that belongs to Christ and hands it to another.

In everyday life. Peor began with a dinner invitation. Ask what the dinner invitation is in your life: the friendship that has started to feel secret, the late conversation, the app, the habit of looking. Decline the invitation, and you will rarely face the bed.

Is this verse a sentence on me if I have already fallen into sexual sin? No; it is a warning, and warnings are given so that people can turn back. Paul wrote to a church in which some had been sexually immoral, and only four chapters earlier told them: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (6:11). Justified means declared righteous, the guilty verdict cancelled for Christ’s sake; sanctified there means set apart as God’s own. The judgment at Peor fell on people who went on in their sin; for anyone who turns to Christ, it has already fallen on him. Confess it plainly to God, break off whatever is feeding it, and if others have been wronged, seek to put it right. Then stand up as one who is forgiven, because you are.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul speaks of those who fell in a single day.

parallels.desc: Israel and the Moabite women

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not presume on Christ’s patience, as Israel did when they despised the manna and were struck by serpents.

Put Christ to the test. Ekpeirazō is to test to the limit: to push God to see how far you can go before he acts. As in verse 4, the one Israel provoked in Numbers 21 was the Son of God (on the wording, see the textual note below).

Destroyed by serpents. On the long detour around Edom Israel said, “we loathe this worthless food” (Numbers 21:4–5). The worthless food was the manna: they were complaining about the miracle. Fiery serpents came, and God’s remedy was a bronze serpent on a pole: look at it and live.

What it is to test Christ. Not doubt or hard questions; God is patient with both. Testing treats his patience as an allowance you are entitled to spend. Have you ever done something wrong while quietly counting on being forgiven afterwards, as if the cross were permission? A weak believer falls and is horrified; testing is the sin of the confident, the very people this chapter was written for.

One more sign. Testing has a quieter form: if God would just make this unmistakable, I would obey. Israel had a pillar of fire and asked for evidence. More proof has never yet produced obedience.

He did not come down. Jesus met the demand for proof in his own wilderness, and refused it: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7). Where Israel failed the test, the true Son passed it. The Christ they dared in the desert was dared again at the cross: come down now, and we will believe. He did not come down. Israel spent his patience as if it were theirs, and when the bill came due, he paid it himself. The bronze serpent was his own picture: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). Because he stayed, a rebel poisoned by his own defiance has only to look to him and live.

Is it testing God to ask him for guidance or a sign? Not when it is asked humbly. Asking God for wisdom is commanded, and he gives generously (James 1:5). Gideon’s fleece is often cited, but God had already spoken to Gideon plainly; the fleece was a weak man’s request for reassurance, which God graciously granted, not a method to copy (Judges 6:36–40). The sin is demanding a sign as the price of obeying what God has already made clear. If Scripture has spoken, obey rather than ask for a second opinion. Where Scripture leaves the choice open, pray, seek counsel, use the mind God gave you, and trust him to guide.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord” here, and a few read “God”. It follows the reading with the strongest early support, and the one a scribe was least likely to invent: a copyist puzzled by “Christ” in the wilderness might soften it to “the Lord”, but would hardly sharpen “the Lord” into “Christ”.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.”

parallels.desc: fiery serpents among the people

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not grumble against God as Israel did, for their complaining brought his judgment on them. Grumbling looks small beside idolatry and immorality, but it is a verdict passed against God’s rule.

Nor grumble. Gongyzō is to mutter, to complain under the breath, a word that sounds like what it describes. Yet grumbling killed more of that generation than any other sin: grumbling at the spies’ report shut the door on the whole nation (Numbers 14:1–4, 29). Perhaps the Corinthians were grumbling against Paul.

Why God takes it so seriously. Grumbling is never really about the food. It is a verdict: this arrangement is wrong, and I would have arranged it better. Underneath lies a claim to the throne. It is also the most respectable sin on the list: a man can grumble through forty years of Sundays, about the music, the preacher and the young people, and be thought a pillar.

Grumbling at the true bread. When Jesus said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven,” the Jews grumbled about him (John 6:41), muttering at the true bread as their fathers had at the manna that pointed to him. The same verdict was passed most loudly at the cross, the arrangement that looked like the worst management in history and was God’s wisdom for our salvation (1:23–24).

Not my will, but yours, be done. The Destroyer passed over every house marked with blood, and he passes over still: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (5:7). And the Son, given a cup more bitter than any wilderness hardship, did not mutter. He said, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), and his contentment in the Father’s will is counted to grumblers who trust him.
