What it does not mean. Not that we cannot express sorrow or lament to God. A third of the Psalms are laments, some of them savage: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Psalm 13:1). God put them in the hymn book. The difference is not the pain or the volume but the direction. Lament is spoken to God, and stays in the room with him; grumbling is spoken about God, to everyone except him. Israel in Numbers 11 did not pray; they stood weeping at their tent doors and complaining (Numbers 11:4–10).

The test. When something is wrong, who hears about it first? If it is God, you are a sufferer praying. If anyone else, you are grumbling, and the way out is not to suppress the complaint but to redirect it, which is what the Psalms are for.

Is it grumbling to say my job is hard or my church has problems? Not in itself. Some problems need raising so that they can be fixed. The question is the spirit and the destination. Raising a concern with the person who can address it, for the good, is love; repeating it to everyone else, with a shrug of contempt, for the pleasure of being aggrieved, is grumbling. And a heart that has stopped noticing God’s gifts will find something to complain about in any job and any church on earth.

Uncertain wording. “The Destroyer” is not a title used in the wilderness stories, and Paul does not say which incident he means. The likeliest is the plague after Korah’s rebellion: when the ground had swallowed the rebels (Numbers 16:31–33), the people grumbled the next day, and a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred (Numbers 16:41–49). Some think instead of the spies’ grumbling, after which the men who brought the bad report died by plague (Numbers 14:36–37). The title (olothreutēs) echoes “the destroyer” of the Passover night (Exodus 12:23; Hebrews 11:28), so Paul most likely means God’s destroying angel, the same who passed through Egypt, now walking through Israel’s own camp.

parallels.desc: the destroyer

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s story was written down to warn us, who live in the last days that Christ has begun.

Written down for our instruction. Paul repeats verse 6 so that nobody misses it, and makes two large claims. The first: the Old Testament was written for us. Nouthesia is warning, the correction a father gives. It was written with us in view (Romans 15:4; 2 Timothy 3:16), for a Gentile in a Greek port and for whoever is reading it now.

The end of the ages. The second claim: literally, the ends of the ages have arrived at us. The age to come has already broken in, because Christ is risen and the Spirit has been given (2 Corinthians 5:17), but the present evil age has not yet ended (Galatians 1:4); we live where the two ages overlap. This makes the warnings weightier, not lighter. Israel had a rock in the desert; we have the crucified and risen Son and his Spirit living in us. More light means more privilege, and more to answer for.

Does the end of the ages mean Christ will return very soon? It means the last days have already begun, and they began with Christ’s first coming (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17): the whole period between his ascension and his return is the last days. Nobody knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), but every generation lives at the end of the ages and must be ready. Scripture names things that will come first, such as the final rebellion of 2 Thessalonians 2:3, but not as a timetable to calculate. His return will be one public, visible event, when he comes to raise the dead and judge the world, not a secret coming in stages. Many Christians who expect a secret rapture before the final coming love the Lord’s appearing just as sincerely; this commentary holds to one visible return because passages such as Matthew 24:30–31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 describe the gathering of believers as loud, public and at the end. So the right response is not to calculate but to watch: to live each ordinary week as people who may see him before it ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever feels sure he cannot fall is the one in most danger of falling. The warning keeps the confident from presuming, as the promise that follows (v. 13) keeps the frightened from despair.

Anyone who thinks that he stands. The verse is aimed not at the struggling man who knows he is weak but at the one who assumes he stands and treats it as settled. In Corinth that was the believer with the correct doctrine of idols, sitting down to dinner in a temple. Peter is the classic example: “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29). Within hours he was warming his hands at the enemy’s fire.

The one who prayed for Peter. Just before the boast Jesus said, Simon, Satan has demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). Peter fell, but was not lost, because his standing had rested not on his confidence but on Christ’s prayer. The one who knows he could fall is driven to lean on the Saviour who always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

The quiet kinds of confidence. Overconfidence rarely says, I could never fall. It says that a certain sin is not in my temperament, that this questionable friendship is fine, that a habit which brought down another Christian is manageable for someone with better theology.

What it does not mean. Not that believers should live in fear of losing salvation. Humble watchfulness is the mark of the true believer. A true Christian may fall into grievous sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and suffer for it; but those whom God has truly called he keeps, and they are restored.

In everyday life. Take heed, not by working up anxiety about your standing, but by doing what a person does who knows he could fall: stay near the means of grace (God’s word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the company of his people, Acts 2:42), confess each sin as soon as you see it, tell someone the truth about yourself, and stop telling yourself which sins you are no longer capable of.

The frightened reader. If this verse frightens you, it is already doing its work, and you are not the person it warns. The one in danger reads it, feels nothing, and assumes it is about somebody else. The man most likely to fall down the stairs is the one who says he could walk them in the dark.

Can a true Christian finally be lost? If Christ says no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), why the warning? Because the warning is not an alternative to being kept; it is one of the ways God keeps his people. He does not preserve his own by making them immune to danger while they sleep through it, but by waking them up. Paul writes work out your own salvation with fear and trembling and, in the same breath, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The alarm that gets a family out of a burning house is not evidence that the fire brigade failed; it is how they were saved. This verse is such an alarm, and God has used it to keep people on their feet for two thousand years. Christians in other traditions read such warnings as showing that a believer can finally fall away; they are right that the warning is meant in earnest, and the difference is over what it is for.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every temptation you meet is the common human kind, and the faithful God sets its limit and always provides a way out. Straight after the warning comes the promise: Paul will not leave a frightened Christian without comfort for even one more sentence.

Common to man. Peirasmos covers testing, trial and temptation; here, the pull toward sin. “Common to man” is anthrōpinos: human-sized, the kind all people face. This first mercy answers a private ache: the conviction that my temptation is a freakish thing that would horrify anyone I told. It is not. That loneliness is a lie, and it feeds the sin, because a thing you believe is unique is a thing you will never say out loud.

God is faithful. The ground of the promise is not you. The same phrase closed the letter’s opening thanksgiving: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son (1:9). The faithfulness that limits your temptation is the faithfulness that joined you to his Son.

Not beyond your ability. Not a description of your strength but a limit God sets and enforces, as he set limits on Satan with Job (Job 1:12; 2:6).

The way of escape. Ekbasis is a way out, like a mountain pass that lets an army get clear of a valley. For the Corinthians it was to flee (v. 14). The door is usually earlier than people look for it: the second drink, not the twelfth; the reply typed at eleven at night, not the affair eighteen months later; the decision about what the laptop does after everyone is asleep. Track any fall backwards and you will find the door standing open at a point that felt harmless at the time.

Able to endure it. Sometimes the escape is a road out, and sometimes the strength to stand in the fire without bowing. Both come from the same faithful God (Hebrews 2:18; 2 Peter 2:9).

The Son who would not take the easy way out. In Gethsemane the Son could have appealed to his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and would not, because that way out of suffering would have been a way out of his Father’s will. He is the one man temptation never overcame, and the faithful God keeps his people by joining them to that Son and his victory.

What it does not mean. Not that God never gives us more than we can handle in suffering. That saying is not in the Bible, and Paul flatly denies it about affliction: he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself, so that we might rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). If you read this with a diagnosis in your hand or an empty chair at your table, it is not telling you that your load has been measured to fit your shoulders. The promise is about temptation to sin: God will always enable us to resist, by his grace.

In everyday life. Ask while you are calm: for the temptation I know is coming this week, where is the pass out of the valley, and what would I have to decide today to be standing in it? God has promised the way of escape, and the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you to give the strength to take it (Romans 8:11). He has not promised to carry you through a door you refuse to look for.

If there was always a way out, am I not guiltier? If there was always a door, every time I sinned I could have not sinned. Yes; pretending otherwise would be no kindness. But look at who is standing beside the door. The same sentence that removes the excuse names God as faithful, and a God faithful enough to have built the door is faithful enough to forgive the man who walked past it (1 John 1:9). The verse takes away the alibi and hands over the Father in the same breath.

Does God tempt me, then? No. God tests his people, to prove and strengthen their faith, as he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1); but he never entices anyone to sin. Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God (James 1:13). The same Greek word can mean a test or a temptation, and the same event can be both: God means it for our strengthening while the devil and our own desires mean it for our fall. Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). So in every pull toward sin, God has set its limit, is present in it, and has a purpose of good for you through it.

What if I genuinely cannot see a way out? Then it may be closer and smaller than you expected. Very often it is simply to leave: the room, the conversation, the screen. Often it is to tell someone, today, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Sometimes it is to pray out loud, short and honest: Lord, help me now. And when the escape is not removal but endurance, as with a long-standing desire that does not go away, the way out is to keep saying no, one day at a time, with others alongside you. You do not have to see the whole road. God has promised there is one, and he is faithful.

Where Christians differ: can believers be overcome? Some take this verse to mean believers never actually fall into sin, or that if they do, they were never really tempted beyond ability. This commentary’s view: God always provides a way to resist, so no believer can say, I had no choice. When believers sin, it is because they did not take the way out, not because God failed. The verse does not promise that believers never fall, but that they never have to, and that God’s faithfulness will see them through (the Westminster Confession 17.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A Christian cannot share Christ’s table and an idol’s table, because each meal is real communion with the one honoured there. So flee idolatry, and weigh the reasons (vv. 14–15). The Lord’s Supper is a true sharing in Christ’s blood and body, and the one loaf makes many believers one body (vv. 16–17); Israel’s altar meals show the same thing (v. 18). The idol is nothing, but what pagans sacrifice is offered to demons (vv. 19–20), and no one can drink the Lord’s cup and theirs without provoking a Lord far stronger than we are (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as participation

Paul’s word for the cup and the bread, a participation (koinōnia) in the blood and body of Christ, does not explain how Christ is present, but it insists that he is. Something real happens at the table: believers truly share in Christ and what he has done. (The Reformed view of how he is present is set out in the box “Where Christians differ: what happens in the Lord’s Supper?” at the end of the note on vv. 16–17.)
verseByVerse.examples: Then: For some Corinthians, dinners at a temple were part of the civic and business life their livelihood depended on, so flee idolatry would have cost them something real. Now: Some parts of cultural and civic life still carry a meaning that a Christian cannot share, and they are not always obvious. Paul’s two tables give the test: what am I actually taking part in when I take part in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God is faithful and provides the way out, run from idolatry instead of testing how close you can get to it. Paul commands as a loving father, and gives sensible people his reasons.

Therefore, my beloved. “My beloved”, from a man who has just spent thirteen verses on graves in the desert. He is not a prosecutor but a father; only someone who loves you tells you the graveyard story. God does not drive his people from their idols with contempt; he calls them away with love, because he has something better for them.

Flee from idolatry. This is the way of escape promised a sentence earlier. Paul does not say manage idolatry, test how close you can get, or develop a mature theology of it, as the strong Corinthians had done. He says flee. The verb (pheugō) is in a form that means keep on running, and it is the same verb as in 6:18 about sexual immorality: the only two things in this letter Paul tells the church to run from, and the two that Corinth’s temple culture served up in the same room. For the Corinthians it meant: stop attending temple feasts.

Sensible people. Wise (phronimoi), and the Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom. Having given a flat command, Paul hands them the argument and invites them to check his reasoning: he wants them convinced, not merely obedient.

Running towards someone. In Scripture we never only flee from something; we flee towards someone. John names the one we run to before what we run from: we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:20–21). The One we flee to is the fountain of living waters, and the idols are broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). The Corinthians were called from a dinner with demons to the table of the living Christ who had bought them. Blessed be the God who calls his runaways beloved, and runs to meet them on the road.

Where courage runs. Almost everywhere else Christians are told to stand and fight; here courage looks like running. Joseph did not reason with Potiphar’s wife; he left his garment in her hand and got out of the house (Genesis 39:12). There is no medal for how long you stayed in the room.

What fleeing looks like when the temple is gone. Boring, practical measures people are embarrassed to need: deleting the thing rather than resolving to use it better; taking the other road home; telling one person the truth so that the secret has a witness; handing over the card, the password, the key. It works where resolutions do not, because it removes the opportunity instead of relying on a will that has already proved unreliable.

Is that not avoidance rather than victory? Should a mature Christian not be able to stand in the room? That question repeats the Corinthian error, which treated strength as something to be demonstrated. Scripture never asks anyone to prove he can stand beside an idol. The mature response to a fire is not to practise standing in it. Fleeing is the victory, one that simply gives nobody a story to tell.

Should I get rid of objects connected with my old life? Often, yes. When the Ephesians came to faith, those who had practised magic brought their books and burned them publicly, though they were worth a fortune (Acts 19:19). Objects have no power in themselves, as Paul has said (8:4). But things used in false worship, occult practice or a besetting sin can be a standing invitation back, and getting rid of them is a clear, simple act of turning. There is no need to be superstitious about ordinary things with an odd history; the question is whether this object keeps open a door that Christ has closed.

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the Lord’s Supper believers truly share in Christ, and by sharing the one loaf they are made one body. That is why a meal at an idol’s table can never be merely a meal.

The cup of blessing that we bless. A phrase from the Jewish table: the cup of wine drunk with a prayer of thanksgiving at the end of a meal, especially at Passover. The Lord took it in the upper room, on the night a Passover meal became the first Supper, and made it the cup of the new covenant (11:25). “That we bless” means: over which we give thanks to God.

Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Paul expects the answer yes, and needs it, because his whole argument about temple meals depends on it: eating and drinking at a table can be a real sharing in what the table represents. If the Lord’s Supper is only a memory exercise, then a temple dinner is only a dinner, and the strong Corinthians are right. The word is koinōnia: participation, sharing, communion. Our word fellowship has worn down to coffee after the service; the Greek means real shared ownership, as partners own a firm together. To drink the cup is to share in the benefits of Christ’s shed blood: forgiveness and the new covenant.

The bread that we break. To eat the bread is to share in Christ himself, crucified for us. He did not hand his people a symbol of a distant event and leave them to remember it as best they could. He gives himself.

One bread, one body. One loaf, torn, and everyone eats from it. “Body” shifts its meaning between verse 16 and verse 17: from Christ’s crucified body to the church, his body. Those who share in the body given for them become the body that belongs to him. It is hard to eat from one loaf while insisting “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos” (1:12). The unity of the church is not something we manufacture by agreeing with each other; we receive it by all being fed by the same Lord.

The most common thing on the table. Christ did not hoard what his blood bought, or ration it. He took what cost him his life and made it the most common thing on the table, so that the poorest believer in Corinth could hold it in his hand on the Lord’s Day and know it was his. The Lord of glory spreads a table for sinners and feeds them with himself. And he is a risen Christ, not brought down to be offered again, because the offering was made once for all (Hebrews 10:12).

In everyday life. At the next Lord’s Supper, come expecting to meet Christ. Feed on him by faith, and look around at the one body you belong to. If there is someone in that room you are refusing to be reconciled to, the bread is asking you a question. Begin to put it right before you eat.

If Christ is not physically present, is the Supper only symbolic after all? No: not nothing, and not magic. At the table you are not merely remembering but receiving, by faith, the Christ who died, as certainly as the bread is in your hand; Calvin was content to say he experienced it more surely than he could explain it. Spiritual does not mean imaginary or less real. The Holy Spirit is the most real presence in the world; he is how Christ dwells in his people at all. In the Supper the Spirit truly unites believers to the living Christ, and faith truly receives him, as truly as the mouth receives the bread. The bread is a sign, but not an empty one: God uses it as a means of grace, to nourish faith, deepen assurance and draw us closer to Christ and to each other. So receive it often and with expectation, not as an add-on to the sermon.

Who should come to the table? Those who have trusted Christ and been baptised as believers, who belong to his church, and who come in repentance and faith. This commentary places baptism on profession of faith before the table, following the order of Acts 2:41–42; churches that baptise infants differ on the order, not on the need for faith. It is not for the unbeliever: you cannot share in someone you have refused. But neither is it a prize for the spiritually accomplished. It is food for the hungry: the weak Christian who is fighting sin and trusting Christ should come, because that is exactly who the bread is for. Paul will say more about coming in a worthy manner in 11:27–32.

Where Christians differ: what happens in the Lord’s Supper? Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ’s body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many evangelicals hold a memorial view: the Supper is only a reminder. Those who hold it rightly guard against superstition, and many find great blessing at the table. This commentary’s view: The bread and wine remain bread and wine (11:26–28 still calls it bread). But the Supper is more than a memorial: Paul calls it a real participation in Christ, and a reminder is not a participation. The Reformed view, taught by Calvin, is that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers by faith really feed on him spiritually, receiving him and all the benefits of his death. Christ’s body is in heaven, but the Spirit lifts us up to commune with him (the Westminster Confession 29.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7).
verseByVerse.note: “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk with thanksgiving at a meal, including the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eating from a sacrifice joins the eater to the altar it came from, as Israel’s own sacrificial meals show. That does not make the idol a real god, as Paul at once makes clear.

Consider the people of Israel. Literally, Israel according to the flesh: the nation descended from Abraham. Paul builds his case from three tables, the Lord’s, Israel’s and the demons’, with the same point at each.

Participants in the altar. The practice behind this is the peace offering. Many modern readers assume every sacrifice was burnt whole; it was not. In the peace offering part went up on the fire to God, part went to the priest, and the rest was eaten by the worshipper and his household in a meal on the spot (Leviticus 7:15–16; Deuteronomy 12:17–18). It was a shared dinner with God as host. To eat there was to be counted in, sharing in the worship and in fellowship with the God to whom it was offered.

What do I imply then? Paul steps in front of an objection before it is raised. The clever ones in Corinth will say: you told us an idol has no real existence (8:4), and now you treat idol meat as though it were charged with something. His answer is no retreat. The idol is still not a real god. But what pagans sacrifice, they offer to demons. The Corinthians had drawn a wrong conclusion from a true statement, as a great deal of confident Christian foolishness does.

We have an altar. At Israel’s altar the worshipper ate from a sacrifice and was counted in. At the Lord’s table believers share in the one sacrifice that is never repeated: Christ has made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). We do not eat in order to make peace; we eat because he has made it. And eating with his people has always been God’s heart. On the mountain of the covenant the elders of Israel beheld God, and ate and drank (Exodus 24:11). He fed Israel at the altar, he feeds the nations at the table of his Son, and he will sit down with his redeemed people at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

What about halal or other religiously slaughtered meat today? Meat sold in an ordinary shop or served at a friend’s table, even if a prayer was said at its slaughter, is simply food that belongs to the Lord (vv. 25–27); a Christian may eat it with thanks and need not investigate. What he should not do is take part in a religious act: eat it as part of a festival offered to another god, or in a way that those watching would understand as joining in their worship. And if someone at the table makes a point of its religious meaning, and eating would confuse him or another believer, verse 28 applies: decline quietly, for his sake.
verseByVerse.note: Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idol is nothing, but demons stand behind it, so no Christian can share both the Lord’s table and theirs. Taking part in false worship is unfaithfulness to Christ, as adultery is to a marriage.

They offer to demons. The strong reasoned: the idol is nothing, so the meal is empty. But nothing at the altar is not the same as nobody at the altar. Somebody receives what is offered, and it is not God: demons (daimonia). Paul is quoting the song of Moses again: they sacrificed to demons that were no gods (Deuteronomy 32:17). The Old Testament already held both truths together.

Participants with demons. Koinōnoi means partners, sharers: the same family of words as the participation in Christ in verse 16. The meal makes you a partner of whoever receives the offering.

You cannot. Temple feasts included cups of wine poured out to the god. Paul does not say “may not” but “cannot”: it is an impossibility, the way no one can be faithful to two husbands at once. Trying to have both does not give you both; it loses you the first.

Two tables. Invitations to dine at the couch of the lord Serapis survive on papyrus from Roman Egypt, showing how naturally pagans spoke of a meal hosted by a god. Paul sets beside such a meal “the table of the Lord”, the prophet Malachi’s phrase for the Lord’s altar (Malachi 1:7, 12). Two tables, two hosts, two loyalties. The demons offer their meals in exchange for worship and give nothing back but bondage; the Lord gives his own body and blood and asks only that we come hungry.

The cup that bought you. The Lord’s cup is “the new covenant in my blood” (11:25), the pledge of a covenant sealed with Christ’s own life, and the guest at the Lord’s table has been purchased by the host (6:19–20). To lift the demons’ cup is to offer what Christ has bought to his enemy.

Is any of this still live? The temples are museums now. But the impulse to reach past God for power or knowledge on terms he has not authorised is doing extremely well: the card reading booked as a laugh, the app that gives the daily horoscope, the ancestor shrine kept in the corner because the family expects it, the ceremony entered into on holiday because it seemed rude to decline. In every case the reasoning is the Corinthian reasoning: it is nonsense, so it is harmless. Paul’s answer is that the first clause does not deliver the second.

Where is the line? Being present is not the same as taking part. A Christian may attend a friend’s wedding in a temple, or a family funeral with rites he does not share, as a guest who loves the people there. He may not join in the worship itself: bowing to the image, offering incense, reciting the prayers, or eating what is presented as offered to the god (v. 28). Practices religious in their very content, such as yoga built around chants and devotion to Hindu deities, belong on the same side of the line; simple stretching is not the issue. Under family pressure he can explain gently that he honours them and will be there, but worships Christ alone.

Do thoughtful people still have to believe in demons? Jesus did, and he was not a credulous man. He spoke soberly about Satan and cast out demons as part of his work (Mark 1:34; Luke 11:20). He was not simply speaking the language of his time, for he readily corrected popular beliefs elsewhere (Mark 7:13; John 9:2–3). Scripture does not ask us to see a devil behind every misfortune, and has none of a horror film’s lurid fascination. It simply says that there are created spiritual powers opposed to God, and that false worship is not empty but a service they are glad to receive. For the Christian the main note is not fear but confidence: these powers are real, and they are already under the feet of the risen Christ (Ephesians 1:20–22).

What about Halloween, or Christmas trees with pagan roots? The line in this chapter is participation in worship, not the distant history of a custom. Most customs have tangled origins, and a thing once religious can become simply ordinary, as the market meat did (v. 25). A Christmas tree in a Christian home worships no one. The question to ask of any practice is what it means now, to the people doing it and watching it: is it plain fun, or a celebration of death, the occult or a spiritual power other than Christ? Christians will draw these lines in slightly different places, and Romans 14 asks them not to despise one another for it. But nobody should take part in anything that is, in its present meaning, a rite offered to another power.

parallels.desc: they sacrificed to demons that were not God

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To share in idol worship is to provoke the Lord’s jealous love, and no one is stronger than he is. Paul leaves his two questions unanswered, because they answer themselves.

Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? The words come from the song of Moses: they stirred him to jealousy with strange gods, and provoked him with their idols (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). Israel did it, and was judged. Jealousy sounds like a vice, but there are two jealousies. One is envy, wanting what belongs to somebody else; that is never in God, since everything is already his. The other is the jealousy of a husband for his own wife, and it is not a defect in him but the proof that the marriage is real (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). A man who watched his wife leave with another and felt nothing would have stopped loving her long ago. God has bound himself to a people, and he will not be treated as one option among several.

Are we stronger than he? The second question is flatter and more frightening, and it is aimed at the strong in Corinth. You think you are strong; are you stronger than God? After thirteen verses of corpses in the wilderness, he asks a congregation of the confident whether they have thought about whom they are provoking. There is a way of using Christian freedom that is not really freedom at all but a small experiment in whether God will actually do anything.

The jealous Lord has a name. The Lord whose table it is (v. 21) is the Lord Jesus, and as with the Rock (v. 4) Paul says of Christ what the song of Moses said of the LORD. So the jealousy is a bridegroom’s: “I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

This one comes after his own. Suppose God were not jealous, and watched his people give their affections to whatever caught them, and felt nothing. He would be easier to live with, and worth nothing; nobody has ever been comforted at a graveside by a deity who did not much mind. Is our God strong? Look at the wilderness. Does he care? Look at the jealousy. A god strong and uncaring would be a terror; a god caring and not strong would be a tragedy. The idols are neither strong nor caring. Our God is both. To be loved by someone who will not share you is a fearful thing and a safe thing at once. Cold gods let you drift. This one comes after his own. He is jealous because the cost of getting his people was his own Son, and he does not shrug about what his Son has bled for.

Does God’s jealousy mean he resents the good things I love? No; he gave them to you. God is not jealous of your wife, your children, your garden or your work; he is jealous for your heart, that it should love him first and love all these as his gifts. The things we love are safest when they are not our gods. A child loved as an idol is crushed by the weight of being someone’s whole meaning; a child loved under God can be loved freely. God’s jealousy guards our joys rather than competing with them.

parallels.desc: they have made me jealous with what is no god

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Freedom is given for building others up and for the glory of God, not for display. Paul answers the slogan “All things are lawful” with two tests, whether a thing helps and whether it builds up, and with the rule of seeking the neighbour’s good (vv. 23–24). Market meat and an unbeliever’s dinner may be eaten freely, because the earth is the Lord’s (vv. 25–27); but when someone points out that the food was sacrificed, decline for his sake, though your own conscience stays free (vv. 28–30). Over everything stands one rule: do all to the glory of God, and give no needless offence, so that many may be saved (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology:
To God alone be glory, in ordinary life

The Reformers’ watchword soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory, has one of its roots in verse 31. A meal, a conversation, a day’s work can be an act of worship when it is received from God and done for him. (On all of life lived before God, see the note on v. 31.)
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ask no questions at the market spared the Corinthians needless scruples; take care at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Now: Do all to the glory of God is not a slogan but a habit: asking, in any situation, how this act or this conversation can honour him.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian freedom is real, but the question is not only whether something is allowed but whether it helps and builds up others.

“All things are lawful.” Quoted first at 6:12, the slogan is very probably the Corinthians’ own, the sort of thing a church says when it has learned grace and is enjoying it. Turning from the temple to meat at home and in the market, Paul does not delete it; twice he adds a “but”.

Helpful … build up. Paul’s test is not “Is it permitted?” but two further questions. Is it helpful? And does it build up (oikodomeō, a construction word): does anyone end up stronger because you did it? That is the test of love (8:1). Both questions have someone else in them; the lawfulness question can be answered alone in a room.

The good of his neighbor. This short sentence governs everything from chapter 8 to chapter 11 (Philippians 2:4). The usual version is: enjoy your freedom, but be considerate. Paul puts the neighbour’s good first. And for some Christians freedom itself becomes the idol: being the one who knows better, not bound by the scruples of lesser believers. A liberty that must be shown off to be enjoyed has stopped being a gift and become a badge.

Christ did not please himself. Paul grounds the same rule in Christ: let each of us please his neighbour for his good, to build him up. For Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:2–3). The one who had every right to seek his own good sought ours, all the way to the cross. A Christian who gives up a liberty for a brother is copying, in a very small way, the shape of the life that saved him.

It isn’t hurting anyone. A great deal of Christian liberty is defended on these grounds, and outside the church it has become nearly the whole of our public morality: if it is consensual and harms no one else, it is nobody’s business. In one way that is a real achievement, protecting people from being bullied by other people’s scruples. But it is thin. It can tell you what you may not do to a neighbour; it has nothing to say about what you owe him. A society can keep the rule perfectly and still be full of people nobody needs, lonely in rooms where nothing is forbidden. And the moralist asks the libertine’s question from the other side: how close to the line may I go? Both are about me. Paul’s two questions have a neighbour in them, and they come from a Lord who asked not what he was allowed to keep but what we needed. That is not a smaller freedom. It is the first freedom large enough to have someone else in it.

How do I know whether something builds up? Ask three questions about the people actually involved. Will this help them trust and obey Christ more, or make it harder? Will it draw them toward the church and its fellowship, or push them away? Would I be glad for them to copy me in this? You will not always know, and you are not responsible for every possible reaction. But when you know that a particular brother or sister would be hurt or misled, love lets that knowledge decide. And building up is not only refraining from harm, but looking for the word, the visit or the gift that will strengthen someone.

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meat bought in the market may be eaten freely, without asking where it came from, because everything belongs to the Lord. Paul protects the over-scrupulous as much as the over-confident.

The meat market. The makellon was the covered meat market at the centre of the city; excavators at Corinth have found an inscription naming one. Much of the meat had come from temples, whose sacrifices produced more carcasses than could be eaten.

Without raising any question. Paul’s ruling is not “ask, and then decide” but “do not ask”. Once the meat has left the temple, it is just food. There is pastoral kindness in that: a conscience kept permanently on duty does not become holier, only more exhausted. Sometimes the godly course is to close the question rather than research it.

The earth is the Lord’s. The reason is Psalm 24:1, a verse later Jewish teachers cited as the reason to give thanks before eating. A priest can mutter over a carcass all afternoon and it remains God’s property. Every field of wheat, every herd on every hill, every loaf on every table belongs to him, and no idol has ever stolen a crumb of it. And the owner is named in this letter: one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (8:6; Colossians 1:16–17). The believer is not eating in enemy territory but at the table of his own Lord, who made the meat, rules the market and redeemed the man who buys it.

What it does not mean. This does not contradict verses 14–22. Buying a chop that once passed an altar is different from taking a seat at the altar. The first is a question about property, and God owns everything. The second is a question about allegiance, and no one may hold two. The line falls exactly where participation begins.

Does this mean Christians may eat any food at all, including what the Old Testament forbade? Yes. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and God taught Peter the same lesson in a vision (Acts 10:13–15). The food laws marked out Israel under the old covenant and pointed to a holiness Christ has now brought. So a Christian may eat pork, shellfish or anything else with thanks. What remains is the law of love: if your eating would harm a brother, you may choose not to (Romans 14:20–21). And what remains is the call to self-control; freedom to eat anything is not a licence to be ruled by the stomach.

parallels.desc: the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accept an unbeliever’s invitation and eat what you are given, but if someone points out that the food was sacrificed, decline for his sake. Nothing about the meat changes; what changes is what eating it would say.

If one of the unbelievers invites you. Paul assumes that Christians will be invited to unbelievers’ homes, and may accept. Fleeing idolatry is not avoiding idolaters; for that you would need to go out of the world (5:10). “If … you are disposed to go” (thelō) leaves the decision open, and some invitations are not wise for a given believer. But the default is yes.

Whatever is set before you. Do not interrogate your host; eat what is set before you (Luke 10:8). A guest who cross-examines his host about the origin of the lamb is not being holy, only a poor guest.

If someone says. The one situation that changes everything. The word is hierothyton, sacred offering, the polite pagan word rather than the Jewish and Christian word for idol food; it sounds like something said at the table, perhaps half as a test of the Christian.

Then do not eat it. Nothing about the meat has changed; the information has. Once someone has said it, the meal has become a statement, and it will be read as approval of idol worship. The speaker may be a young believer watching to see what freedom looks like, or a curious pagan. Either way, a person has told you that this matters to him, and Paul says let it matter: your liberty is no longer the only fact in the room.

How to decline. Quietly: a Christian who declines and then explains at length why he is entitled to eat has given up the meat but still made a show of his freedom. And without shaming the host, since a refusal that sounds like a judgment on the household does the very harm it was meant to prevent.

The Lord who accepted invitations. Jesus went to dinner with Levi and his tax-collector friends, with Zacchaeus, and with Pharisees who were watching him (Luke 5:29; 19:5; 14:1). He was called a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and did not stop going, because he had come to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). A Christian at an unbeliever’s table is walking where his Lord walked.

What is the modern equivalent? The clearest one is alcohol. A Christian is free to drink wine in moderation; Scripture calls it a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and drunkenness, not drinking, is the sin. But at a meal with a friend fighting alcoholism, or a young believer just out of a drinking life who says so, your glass is no longer only a glass. Leave it empty that evening, without fuss or explanation, and enjoy his company. You have lost nothing, and he may have gained a great deal.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, repeat at the end of verse 28 the line “the earth is the Lord’s”; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Giving way for someone else’s conscience does not bind your own: you remain free before God, and for love you choose not to use that freedom there. Paul protects both the weak brother and the thankful believer.

I do not mean your conscience, but his. Paul has just said “do not eat it”, and now asks why anybody else’s conscience should govern him. This clause resolves the apparent contradiction: your own conscience is clear; you abstain for the other person’s sake.

Why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? In principle my freedom is not ruled by others’ scruples; I am still free before God (on whose voice this is, see below). What Paul surrenders in verse 28 is the use of his freedom on that occasion, not the freedom itself or the verdict on it. He does not walk away from that dinner thinking he was nearly defiled, or that the meat was unclean after all. He walks away free, having chosen not to spend his freedom in front of someone it would injure.

With thankfulness … denounced. Denounced (blasphēmeō) is spoken against, slandered. Paul gives way so that his good thing is not spoken of as evil (Romans 14:16). And there is a small warmth in “with thankfulness”. Paul’s instinct at a table is to give thanks, which is what a man does who believes verse 26: that the food, the evening and the world belong to God. He is not defending a right to indulge but a right to be grateful without apologising for it (Romans 14:22; 1 Timothy 4:4–5).

Two opposite disasters. Lose the distinction between having a freedom and using it, and you get one of two disasters. One is the Christian who bulldozes: my liberty is real, and if that ruins you, learn some theology. The other is a church governed by whoever is most easily upset, where the narrowest conscience in the room rules everyone. Love limits what I do with my freedom. It does not hand my conscience over to a committee.

The free Son who paid the tax. Asked about the temple tax, Jesus said that kings do not tax their own sons, so the sons are free. Yet, so as not to give offence, he sent Peter to find a coin in a fish’s mouth (Matthew 17:24–27). The Son of the house owed nothing, said so plainly, and paid anyway. And the brother for whose sake a Christian yields is never a mere obstacle: he is the brother for whom Christ died (8:11).

A rule the anxious can live by. Giving something up for another Christian is not conceding that he was right, or adding a rule to your own life; you need not feel guilty about the thing next Tuesday when he is not there. A conscience that takes on every restriction anybody around it holds ends unable to enjoy anything, serving other people’s opinions rather than God. Know that you are free, and then choose, in this room, for this person, not to use it.

Who is the weaker brother I should give way to? Not simply anyone who disapproves of me. In Paul’s argument the weak brother is someone who might be drawn by my example into doing what his own conscience still condemns, and so be damaged in his faith (8:10–11). That is very different from the person who has turned his own preferences into rules for everybody and is merely annoyed by my freedom. Jesus did not yield to the Pharisees over hand-washing or healing on the Sabbath (Mark 7:1–13; 3:1–6); when people try to bind consciences with man-made rules as if they were God’s law, love may require standing firm (Galatians 2:3–5). The question is always: would my action wound a fragile believer, or only offend a critic?

Uncertain wording. Verses 29b–30 are compressed, and it is not certain whose voice they carry. Paul may be speaking for himself, explaining why giving way at that table does not surrender his freedom; or he may be voicing the strong believer’s objection, as he quotes the Corinthians’ sayings elsewhere (6:12; 10:23), and answering it in verse 31. On either reading he agrees that the believer remains free before God, and gives way out of love, not because another’s conscience binds his.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in life, down to eating and drinking, is to be done so as to show how great and good God is.

Whether you eat or drink. Three chapters about butchers, dinner parties, weak brothers and demons come down to one sentence broad enough to cover a life, and it begins not with prayer or preaching but with chewing and swallowing. If eating qualifies, nothing is excluded: work, rest, speech, spending, sleep. No part of an ordinary Tuesday lies outside it.

Do all to the glory of God. To glorify God (doxa is glory) is to show his worth, to make him look as great as he is. A man eating his dinner glorifies God not because the dinner is impressive, but because the God who made the wheat and the fire and the mouth is recognised as his gifts are used, by a creature who might have eaten in silence and thought he had provided it all himself. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: man’s chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him for ever (Q. 1). The Reformers stressed that the milkmaid and the minister serve the same Lord.

What has to be true of a plate of food for it to glorify God? The phrase can be repeated for years without meaning anything, so spell it out. That it is received rather than seized: taken as a gift from a hand, not a right that was owed. That it is eaten with thanks, spoken and meant, since everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). That it is enjoyed and not worshipped; there is a way of eating that is really an attempt to be comforted by something that cannot comfort. That it is not taken at someone else’s expense, which is the whole burden of this chapter. And that the one eating is content for God to be looking, a test that can be run on any activity in about four seconds.

The one whose food was his Father’s will. The God worthy of all this glory shared our table: in Christ he ate and drank among us, gave thanks for bread, and broke it. And only one life has fully kept this verse. At the end Jesus could say to the Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). But the life that perfectly glorified God is counted to those who belong to him: God treats the believer as having his Son’s obedience, because he is joined to him by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). We do not glorify God in order to be accepted; we glorify him because in Christ we already are.

What it does not mean. Not that we must be consciously thinking about God every second. A surgeon glorifies God by concentrating on the operation, not by thinking about theology during it. It means the whole of life is offered to him and done in a way that honours him.

In everyday life. Take the last hour of yesterday and ask what would have had to change for it to have been offered to God. Very often the answer is nothing about the activity and everything about the aim.

How do I glorify God in a dull job or a long day of chores? By doing it well, honestly and for him. Paul told slaves, who had the dullest and hardest work in the ancient world, to work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, because it is the Lord Christ they were serving (Colossians 3:23–24). The spreadsheet, the nappy, the shelf-stacking and the commute are not interruptions to the Christian life; they are where most of it happens. Do the work with integrity, treat the people around you with kindness, give thanks for the strength to do it, and rest when the day is done, trusting God with what is left undone. Nobody sees most of it. God does, and he is glorified by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put no needless obstacle in anyone’s way, but give up your own advantage, as Paul did, so that many may be saved.

Give no offense. Aproskopoi: causing no stumbling, putting no unnecessary obstacle in anyone’s way. Paul names three groups and so covers the whole world: Jews, Greeks and the church of God. He circumcised Timothy for the sake of the first (Acts 16:3), lived as one outside the law among the second (9:21), and would give up meat for ever for the sake of the third (8:13).

I try to please everyone. Paul also wrote that if he were still trying to please man, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The two do not contradict, because the motives are opposite. In Galatians, pleasing people meant changing the message to escape persecution (Galatians 6:12). Here it means giving way to people for their good (9:19–22): Paul gave way when it brought others nearer to Christ, and was beaten for the gospel he would not bend (2 Corinthians 11:24–25).

Not seeking my own advantage. He yields his preferences, diet, rights and dignity to remove every obstacle between a person and Christ, and will not yield one syllable of the gospel to remove an obstacle between himself and trouble.

As I am of Christ. Paul’s next sentence says where he learned this: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). Though he was in the form of God, Christ made himself nothing, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–8), and every Christian’s given-up rights are a small copy of that great descent. He did not seek his own advantage. He sought the good of many, that they might be saved, and he won them.

What it does not mean. Not avoiding the offence of the cross (1:23). The gospel itself offends; we must not add needless offence of our own.

In everyday life. The next time you soften something, delay something, or leave something unsaid, ask whom the accommodation is actually for: whether the other person is nearer to being saved, or you nearer to being comfortable. The two look identical from outside and are opposites inside.

How far can I adapt to win people? As far as you like in everything that is truly indifferent, and not an inch in what God has commanded or forbidden. Paul changed his diet, customs, manner and timetable for others; he would not change the gospel, join in sin, or hide the cross. So learn the culture of the people you love, eat their food, speak their language, enjoy their company, and drop the habits of your own background that are mere preferences. But never pretend to agree with what Scripture calls sin, and never soften the message so that Christ sounds less necessary. Adaptation is for the sake of the message, never at its expense.

For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.<sup>5</sup>Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.<sup>6</sup>Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.<sup>7</sup>Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”<sup>8</sup>We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.<sup>9</sup>We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,<sup>10</sup>nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.<sup>11</sup>Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.<sup>12</sup>Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.<sup>13</sup>No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. keyVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
keyVerse.note: Three chapters of argument about idol food end in this sentence, and it reaches far beyond them. The warning from Israel, the two tables and the rulings on the market all serve one aim: that God, not my appetite or my freedom, is honoured in what I do. Only Christ has lived it perfectly, and those joined to him begin to live it in the most ordinary things.

10.reflection:
Israel had the cloud, the sea, the manna and the water from the rock, and still most of them fell (vv. 1–5). Which spiritual privileges in your own life are you most tempted to rely on instead of Christ himself?

The strong in Corinth reasoned that because an idol is nothing, a meal in its temple was harmless (vv. 19–20). Where do Christians today use the same reasoning, and what would fleeing look like in practice (v. 14)?

Verse 13 promises that God is faithful and always provides the way of escape. Think of a temptation you know is coming: where is the way out, and who could help you take it?

Verses 23–33 ask not only whether something is allowed but whether it builds others up and glorifies God. What is one freedom you enjoy that you might use differently this month for someone else’s good?

11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Where we are. Verse 1 closes the argument about food and freedom begun at 8:1; then chapters 11–14 turn to the church’s gatherings for worship.

The message. When the church gathers, it gathers before God, and the way it gathers should show the gospel. Men and women worship side by side as equals who are not the same, honouring the order God built into creation; rich and poor eat at the Lord’s table as one body, because the meal proclaims a death that put them all on the same level. Worship that displays our own glory, or the world’s ranking of people, contradicts what it declares.

Why it was said. Some wives were praying and prophesying uncovered, in a city where a respectable married woman covered her head in public; perhaps they reasoned that in Christ such distinctions no longer mattered. And at the shared meal of which the Supper was part, the well off ate the best food early while latecomers, often slaves, arrived to little or nothing (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul sets out an order of headship in which even Christ has a head (vv. 2–3), and argues for the man uncovered and the wife covered from shame, creation, nature and the churches’ practice (vv. 4–10, 13–16), with the balance at the centre: in the Lord man and woman depend on each other (vv. 11–12). Then the praise stops: at the Lord’s meal one goes hungry and another gets drunk (vv. 17–22). Paul answers by retelling what Jesus did on the night he was betrayed (vv. 23–25), for the Supper proclaims his death until he comes (v. 26). To eat with contempt sins against the Lord, who has been disciplining them as a Father (vv. 27–32); so examine yourselves, and wait for one another (vv. 33–34).

Where it leads. Two portraits of Christ hold the chapter. One is the Son who gladly submits to his Father (v. 3), whose headship looks like a towel, a basin and a cross. The other is the Lord who, on the night his friends betrayed and deserted him, gave thanks, broke bread and said, “This is my body, which is for you” (v. 24). No one comes to his table by right; he puts himself into the hands of the undeserving first.

For us. Ask what your church’s gathering says without words about men and women, rich and poor, and who matters. Then come to the table, not because you are worthy, but because his body was given for you, and look around at those who come with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men and women honour God in worship by gladly keeping the difference he made between them, without either claiming to be worth more. After praising the church (vv. 1–2), Paul sets out an order of headship in which even Christ has a head (v. 3), and argues that a man should pray uncovered and a wife covered, as Corinth would read those signs (vv. 4–6). The order rests on creation (vv. 7–10), yet in the Lord man and woman depend on each other, and all things come from God (vv. 11–12). Nature agrees (vv. 13–15), and the matter must not become a quarrel (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, order and the Trinity

Paul models the relationship of husband and wife on the relationship of the Father and the Son (v. 3), and this is one of the most debated texts in the doctrine of the Trinity. (The question is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: does the Son submit to the Father eternally?” at the end of the note on v. 3.) Paul takes the order within God’s own life as the pattern for an order between equals in the church’s worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Corinth a married woman praying with her head uncovered could be read as immodest, or as rejecting the order of marriage, and that would harm the church’s witness. Now: In most Western settings a head covering no longer carries that meaning. The principle remains: worship should honour God with fitting dignity, and the difference between male and female is a gift to be honoured, not erased.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Copy Paul, because Paul is copying Christ. The verse closes the argument begun at 8:1: give up your rights for others, as Paul has, and as Christ did first.

Be imitators of me. Imitators (mimētai), the word from which we get “mimic”. On its own it sounds arrogant. But Paul has just described a man who gave up his right to be paid (9:12), to marry (9:5), to eat what he liked (8:13), and to be understood, so that others might be saved (9:19–23; 10:33). He is not saying “admire me”, but “watch what I gave up, and do that”.

As I am of Christ. The second half of the sentence controls the first. Paul is a copy, and careful to say so. The pattern is the Son of God, who did not please himself (Romans 15:3), who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). And Christ does not merely set the example and leave us to it. By his Spirit he is forming himself in his people, so that the copies, faint as they are, grow slowly more like the original until the day we see him and are made like him.

How the Christian life is learned. Nobody learns to be a Christian from a definition. People learn it the way they learn a trade or an accent: by being near someone who does it, long enough to catch it (Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). And both problems that follow, head coverings and a supper where the rich humiliated the poor, are questions about whether a congregation will lay down its rights for others in the room.

Is it not dangerous to tell people to follow a man? It is a good objection. Church history is littered with the wreckage of ministries built on a personality, and this very congregation had split into fan clubs, “I follow Paul”, “I follow Apollos” (1:12), which Paul had spent four chapters demolishing. The safeguard is in the second half of the sentence, and anyone can apply it: follow a Christian only as far as he is following Christ, which means you must know Christ well enough to see where the line falls. That is the difference between a disciple and a fan. A fan goes wherever his man goes; a disciple keeps checking his man against the Master, ready to stop the moment the two diverge.

Whom should I learn from? Not the most gifted person available, nor the most confident, but the one whose life shows the marks Paul has just described: rights not used, comfort spent on other people, a willingness to be thought less of. Gifts can be counterfeited; that pattern cannot. If you cannot think of anyone near you, ask God to bring someone into your life, spend time with the older members of your church whom nobody notices, and read the lives of faithful Christians from the past. Very often the person you need is already sitting a few rows away, and has simply never been asked.

In everyday life. Live so that someone younger can learn from you. If a new believer copied your week exactly, what would he learn about Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul praises the Corinthians for holding on to the teaching he handed them, before he corrects them. What he passed on came from the Lord, and keeping it is the mark of a church that can still be taught.

I commend you. Praise first, in a letter that has not been generous with it. Perhaps their own letter claimed that they remembered his teaching, and Paul accepts the claim before correcting them. A church that has stopped listening cannot be corrected, only left; the most dangerous position is not being wrong but reaching the point where nobody is permitted to say so.

The traditions. The word makes some Christians uneasy, because it has been used to smuggle in doctrines the Bible does not teach, but Paul uses it without embarrassment. Paradosis is a parcel passed from hand to hand; “delivered” (paradidōmi) is the regular word for passing on authoritative teaching, used again of the Supper (v. 23) and of the gospel (15:3). What is handed on here came from Christ through the apostles, and is now preserved in the New Testament. A tradition is trustworthy when you can trace the parcel back to a hand that had the right to fill it.

The Lord who was handed over. Paul’s verb for handing on the teaching is the verb he uses in verse 23 for what happened to Jesus: “on the night when he was betrayed”, literally “handed over”. The Father handed over his Son (Romans 8:32); the Son handed himself over for us (Galatians 2:20). At the heart of the tradition is Christ himself, delivered for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). And he is the first hand in the chain, holding every hand after it: empires have fallen and Bibles have been burned, yet the gospel Paul handed to Corinth has reached us whole, because the Lord who gave it has kept it.

When tradition and the Bible pull apart. Paul’s test is whether the parcel came from the Lord (v. 23). Where a practice can be traced to that source it is binding, however inconvenient; where it cannot, it may be valuable, but it can never be made a test of obedience. Many church quarrels would end quickly if the parties sorted their practices into those two boxes first.

A chain of hands. Nobody has worked out the gospel from first principles; it reached each of us through somebody: a mother, a preacher, a friend who would not let the subject drop, a translator who died for the privilege. A healthy tradition is not a dead weight but a chain of hands, and the question is whether you intend to be one of them. Think of the people who handed the gospel on to you, and thank God for them by name. If any are still living, tell them.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has ordered human life under heads, on the pattern of the Father and the Son, in whom order and perfect equality stand together. If God is the head of Christ, headship can never mean that the one who leads is worth more.

The head of every man. In English “head” has shrunk to one meaning: the boss. In Greek (kephalē) it could mean the source of something, as we speak of the head of a river; the one who leads or represents; and the part of a body without which the rest cannot live. Here it means one with authority and responsibility, as in Ephesians 1:22 and 5:23. Some argue it means only source; both ideas may be present, since verses 8–9 speak of origin, but in Paul’s usage headship includes leadership.

The head of a wife is her husband. The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife”, “man” and “husband”, and the focus on the married woman’s head covering suggests husband and wife. Headship in Scripture is a marriage relationship (Ephesians 5:23–25), not a rule that every woman is under every man, though Paul applies it in the church’s worship, where the order of creation shapes how all men and women take part.

The head of Christ is God. The Son, as incarnate Mediator, submits to the Father (15:28; John 5:19, 30; 14:28). A mediator stands between two parties to bring them together (1 Timothy 2:5); incarnate means that he took a real human nature, body and soul, without ceasing to be God. In that role, sent by the Father to save us, the Son obeys, yet he is fully equal with the Father (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6).

Headship and equality. This is the key to the passage. A head cannot be superior in worth to what it heads, or the third clause would make Christ inferior to God, which the New Testament will not allow: the Son is the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3), in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). Paul has picked the one relationship in the universe where perfect equality and willing order are both beyond dispute, and made it the model. Christ is not less than the Father because he submits to him; a wife is not less than her husband because she submits to him. Order is not the enemy of equality; it is the shape love takes when two equals are doing something together.

A towel and a basin and a cross. The Son has never resented having a head. He came gladly to do his Father’s will: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). His submission was not the loss of his dignity but the display of it. And Christ, the head of every man, exercises his headship by laying down his life. What a God, whose authority looks like a towel and a basin and a cross.

What it does not mean. Headship gives no cover to harshness or abuse (see the note on vv. 8–9).

Does headship mean the husband always gets the final say? In the rare case where a decision must be made, the two cannot agree, and nothing sinful is involved, yes: someone must bear the responsibility, and God has laid it on the husband. But a marriage that keeps reaching for the final say has already gone wrong. Headship is first a responsibility, not a casting vote: to pray for his wife, lead in loving, apologising and serving, protect and provide, and care for her soul. A wise husband listens long, seeks his wife’s counsel as God’s gift, and often defers to her judgment gladly. And no husband may ever ask his wife to sin; her first obedience is to Christ (Acts 5:29).

Where Christians differ: headship. Egalitarians (those who hold that no role in home or church is limited by sex) argue that head means only source, and that Christ’s coming abolished all role distinctions between men and women. Many hold this from a sincere concern for the dignity of women and a careful reading of texts such as Galatians 3:28, and serve Christ faithfully. This commentary’s view: Paul grounds this order in creation (vv. 8–9), not in culture or the fall, and compares it with the relation of the Father and the Son. Men and women are equal in worth, dignity and salvation (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7), but God has given husbands the responsibility to lead their families, and qualified men the responsibility to lead and teach in the church (1 Timothy 2:12–13). This is the complementarian view: equal in being, distinct in role. Husbands must lead as Christ leads: by sacrificial love, not domination.

Where Christians differ: does the Son submit to the Father eternally? Most Reformed theologians have been careful here: the Son’s submission is real, and it belongs to his mission (the sending, the incarnation, the obedience unto death) rather than being a subordination of nature within the Godhead, since the Father and the Son share one undivided divine essence. Others have argued for an eternal ordering of persons in authority and submission. It is a discussion worth conducting with great care and very little heat. This commentary’s view: of those two views, the first is the more likely. Scripture plainly shows the Son submitting to the Father in his mission (15:28; John 5:19), but never makes him anything less than fully God (Philippians 2:6). His submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook, and is no subordination of his being.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife.”

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In worship a man should pray with his head uncovered and a wife with hers covered, because in Corinth those signs showed whom each one honoured.

His head covered. The likeliest background is the Roman custom in which a man leading pagan worship drew his toga over his head; a Christian man doing the same would look like a priest of the idols. His head is Christ (v. 3), and he needs no priest’s gesture, because he has a great high priest through whom he may draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:14–16; 10:19–22). Whether a man wears a hat in church today is a matter of courtesy, not of this text.

Her head uncovered. In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and her honour as a wife; to remove it in public could suggest she was unattached or immoral. She shamed both herself and her husband, who is her head (v. 3). To pray uncovered, Paul adds, is the same as if her head were shaven, and a shaved head was a sign of disgrace for a woman, perhaps associated with punishment for adultery or with certain pagan practices.

Who prays or prophesies. One thing here is easily missed, because it is assumed rather than argued. Women are praying and prophesying in the Corinthian assembly, out loud, and Paul does not object; he objects to how they are dressed while doing it. That is striking in a letter often thought to silence women, and it needs to be held onto.

Garments speak. Every culture has clothing that speaks, which is why nobody wears a swimming costume to a funeral. The covering is never really about cloth, but about whose worship this is.

How can chapter 11 assume women speak, and chapter 14 tell them to be silent? The hardest question in the chapter is better answered here than left to ambush the reader later. Whatever Paul meant, he did not think he was contradicting himself. Chapter 14 sits inside a paragraph about prophecy being weighed by the congregation (“let the others weigh what is said”, 14:29), and ends by telling the women to ask their questions at home (14:35). It regulates one activity: the public sifting and questioning of prophecies, which is a way of ruling on what the congregation is taught. That differs from praying and prophesying, which chapter 11 takes for granted that women do. The seeming contradiction comes from reading “silent” as absolute when Paul has already shown, in this verse, that he does not mean it so (see the note on 14:34).

So what may a woman do in church today? A great deal, and churches that hold this view should say so as loudly as the limits. She may pray aloud in the gathering, read Scripture, share what God has taught her, lead in song, give testimony, and use every gift of mercy, administration, hospitality and wisdom. She may teach women and children, as Titus 2:3–5 commands the older women to do, and like Priscilla with her husband she may explain the way of God privately to a man who needs it (Acts 18:26). What she does not do is hold the office of elder or bring the church’s authoritative preaching. That is no judgment on her gifts, many of which may exceed those of the men in the room; it is the shape God has given his household.

Where Christians differ: women praying and prophesying. How does this fit with 14:34 (women should keep silent in the churches) and 1 Timothy 2:12? This commentary’s view: Women may pray and contribute in the church’s life, and in New Testament times some prophesied (Acts 21:9). What is reserved for qualified men is the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church (14:29, 34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds, with many Reformed churches, that prophecy as new revelation belonged to the church’s apostolic foundation (Ephesians 2:20) and ceased when the canon of Scripture was complete; many faithful brothers and sisters believe it continues, and they deserve a respectful hearing. On that view the question today concerns praying, sharing and teaching: women serve in many ways, but the office of elder and the authoritative preaching of the church belong to qualified men.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and married status. Christians differ on how the principle applies today.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife who throws off the covering might as well cut off her hair, so let her cover her head; a man should not, for he is the image and glory of God, and the woman is the glory of man.

Cut her hair short. Paul pushes their practice to its end: if she will abandon the sign, she may as well take the shears to her hair, and everyone in Corinth knew what a cropped head on a woman meant. It is like saying that if you leave the wedding ring at home, you may as well announce that you do not want to be known as married.

The image and glory of God. The theological reason comes from Genesis 1:26–27: man was made in God’s image and reflects his glory, as a king’s statue stood for him in a distant province.

But woman is the glory of man. Paul does not say that the woman is not the image of God: “God created man in his own image … male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27).
