The difference lies in the word “glory”, meaning that which honours and displays another. She was made from man and for him (vv. 8–9), and she brings him honour, as an excellent wife is the crown of her husband (Proverbs 12:4).

A glory veiled before a greater one. When the church gathers, God is the one being honoured, so nothing should visibly compete. The woman, in that culture, reflected her husband’s honour, and Paul asks that this be covered while God is worshipped: not because it is shameful, but because it is glorious, and this is not its hour. The covering is no badge of inferiority but the veiling of a real glory before a greater one, as the seraphim cover their faces in Isaiah’s temple (Isaiah 6:2).

The image who came. Sin defaced God’s likeness in men and women alike. Then the New Testament names the one who bears it perfectly: Christ, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15; 2 Corinthians 4:4). The King whom Isaiah saw high and lifted up was, John tells us, Jesus (John 12:41), the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3). That glory took flesh, walked into rooms like the one in Corinth, and shines now into ordinary hearts in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). God chose believers beforehand “to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29): every man and woman in that Corinthian room was being remade to look like him.

Is it wrong for a woman to have short hair today? Not in itself. Paul’s argument depended on what a cropped head meant in Corinth: disgrace, or a public rejection of being a wife, which in most cultures today a short haircut says nothing of. What remains is that men and women should not try to erase the God-given difference between them, or use their appearance to protest against the order God has made. A woman with short hair who is glad to be a woman and honours her husband is not breaking this verse; someone who styles himself or herself deliberately to blur the line between the sexes is going against its grain, whatever the length of their hair.

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The difference between man and woman goes back to creation, not to custom: the woman was made from the man and for him. The order of verse 3 is rooted in how God made us, before any culture had opinions about it.

Woman from man. The woman was taken from the man, built by God out of Adam’s side (Genesis 2:21–23). “From” does not mean lesser: Adam’s response was not to assert rank but to break into what is often called the first poetry in the Bible: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23).

Woman for man. She was made for him, in answer to the first thing in the creation account that God calls not good: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18). Then God built the woman and brought her to him, the first wedding, with God himself giving the bride away. “For” does not mean a tool for his use. Helper (ʿēzer) is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself helping his people (Psalm 33:20; 121:2): one who comes to the aid of somebody who cannot manage alone. It describes a role, not inferiority.

What Paul is establishing. Because headship is grounded in creation, the difference between men and women is no human custom that a modern-minded congregation may drop. Nor is it a difference in worth, as Paul soon makes plain (v. 11).

A mystery hidden in the garden. Paul quotes the same chapter elsewhere, “a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife”, and says it refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The first marriage was drawn as a picture of the last: Christ the husband who came for his bride, the church made for him and loved by him (Ephesians 5:25, 30). The “from” and the “for” are lines in a portrait of the Son and his people.

How this text has been misused. This must be said, or a wounded reader is left unhelped. Verses like these have been quoted by men to treat their wives as inferiors, to shut down every disagreement, and in the worst cases to demand submission to cruelty. That is not a misapplication at the edges but the exact reverse of what the passage teaches, and it is wickedness. The measure of headship in the New Testament is never the authority a man may claim but the death a man must die: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), a standard that ruins domineering before it starts. Christ’s headship consisted of washing feet, absorbing insult, and being executed for people who had contributed nothing. Any man who quotes 1 Corinthians 11 to get his own way has picked up a verse about the Trinity and used it as a stick, and he will answer for it. Order in the Bible always runs downhill in service, never in privilege.

What if my husband is harsh or abusive? Then hear this clearly: nothing in this passage requires you to endure abuse, and no faithful church will ask you to. Headship is a calling to self-giving love, and a man who threatens, hits, controls or terrorises his wife has abandoned it. Your safety, and your children’s, comes first. It is right to leave a dangerous home, to call the police where a crime has been committed, and to tell your pastor or elders, who should protect you and confront him, not counsel you to go back and submit harder. Abuse is a grievous sin against God and against you. Whether a marriage broken this way may end in divorce is a further question, to be worked through with your elders in the light of Scripture’s teaching on adultery and desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6). This commentary holds that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, and the elders should help judge each case; but separation for safety is never disobedience to this text.

In everyday life. Husbands, measure your headship by Ephesians 5:25 this week: what would it cost to love your wife as Christ loved the church in one specific thing? Do it, by his Spirit, and when you fall short, rest in the Husband who never has. And if you know a home where this passage is being used as a weapon, do not stay silent; speak to someone who can help.

parallels.desc: a helper fit for him; she shall be called Woman

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So a wife should wear on her head the sign of authority, because the church worships in the sight of heaven.

A symbol of authority. The older reading takes the covering as a sign of her husband’s authority over her. But the words can as naturally mean that the covering is her authority, giving her standing to pray and prophesy in the assembly within the order of verse 3. On that reading the veil is not a leash but a licence, which fits the flow, since Paul has assumed since verse 5 that she prays and prophesies (see the box at the end of this note).

Because of the angels. However the detail is read, the plain point is that a congregation at worship is not alone in the room. The singing is overheard, and the company is far larger and older than the one you can see (Hebrews 12:22).

What the angels are watching. Through the church the manifold wisdom of God is now made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10); these are “things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). The angels were never redeemed. When sinners bought by Christ’s blood gather in his name, heaven’s servants are watching the one thing they could never experience and never tire of studying: grace.

Should I pray to angels, or try to sense them? No. Angels are fellow servants, not objects of worship or prayer; when John fell at an angel’s feet, he was told at once to worship God (Revelation 22:8–9). Scripture never invites us to seek contact with them, and an interest in angels that crowds out Christ leads away from him (Colossians 2:18). What it gives is a comfort and a dignity. They are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14); and ordinary Sunday worship, in a small hall with a weak organ, is watched by heaven.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases here are among the hardest in Paul’s letters. The Greek says simply that she ought to have authority on her head; “symbol of” is the translators’ addition, and whether the authority is her husband’s or her own is uncertain. “Because of the angels” has four main readings. A widely held one today takes the angels as guardians of the created order who observe God’s order in the church (4:9; Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12), so that to overturn it deliberately in worship would affront the very servants charged with upholding it. A second, with a long history, sees them as fellow worshippers in the heavenly assembly the church joins (Psalm 138:1 in the Greek reads, “before the angels I will sing your praise”; compare Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4 and 5). A third, the oldest, appeals to Genesis 6 and Jewish traditions in which angels fell through desire for women, so that the covering was protective; but it needs a speculative account of angels the text does not supply. A fourth notes that the law was given through angels (Galatians 3:19), so their presence would call for the order the law required. The first two are the likeliest, and both mean that the church worships in the sight of heaven.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present at worship and to guard God’s order.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in the Lord neither man nor woman stands alone: each depends on the other, and both come from God. Paul adds the safeguard himself, so that nobody can use verses 8–9 to set men above women.

Not independent. What was said about the garden stands, but it entitles nobody to independence or superiority. Neither sex on its own shows all that God made humanity to be.

Born of woman. Then a piece of homely wit. The first woman came out of a man, and every man since has come out of a woman. If anyone wants to argue about origins, the score was level again as soon as the first child was born.

All things are from God. The arrangement traces back past both to the one who made the pair, so neither may boast.

In the Lord. To be in the Lord is to be joined to Christ by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of you. A believing husband and wife stand before God on exactly the same ground: both dead in sin, both bought with the same blood, both clothed in the same righteousness, heirs together of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7). Christ did not die for men a little more than for women. The order of creation is not cancelled in him, but lived by two people who know they were rescued together. Sin turned difference into domination, as God’s words of judgment after the fall foretold (Genesis 3:16). In Christ the difference remains and the domination has no place.

Fed by a mother in Bethlehem. The difference between men and women is not a problem to solve, nor a weapon for either side. It is God’s workmanship, made deliberately and called very good. And when the Son came to redeem them both, he was born of a woman (Galatians 4:4): the eternal Word, carried, delivered and fed by a mother in Bethlehem.

Keep all four verses. Some teaching quotes verses 8 and 9 loudly and lets verses 11 and 12 fall silent. Paul wrote all four, seconds apart, and the church is not free to keep only the half that suits it (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 5:21). Working dependence looks like a husband who does not know what he thinks until he has heard his wife, and says so in company, and like men who would notice within a fortnight if the women stopped serving. It shows in who gets consulted before a decision.

What does this mean for single people? All this applies to you as fully as to the married. You are not half a person waiting to be completed. You belong to a church where men and women depend on one another as brothers and sisters, mothers and fathers in the faith, and you have gifts the rest of the body cannot do without. A single woman is not under the headship of every man in the congregation; she is under Christ and the shepherding of her elders, as the men are. And single people can often show this mutual dependence most freely, in friendships, hospitality and service across the whole family of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the ordinary sense of what is fitting says a woman should pray with her head covered, for nature has already given her long hair as a covering. As at 10:15, Paul leaves it to their own judgment: having given the theology, he appeals to their sense of what is fitting (prepō).

Nature itself. Hair grows on everyone, and many cultures have thought long hair splendid on a man, but Paul is not making a biological claim. Physis here is the settled instinct of a people about what is fitting, and in his world long, dressed hair on a man was widely associated with effeminacy. It supports the argument; the foundation was laid in verses 3 and 8–12.

Whose handwriting nature is. Paul appeals to Christ, creation, the angels, and now the ordinary human sense of what is seemly, treating the shared instincts of decent people as a real witness: never one that may overrule Scripture, but not nothing (Romans 2:14–15). Nature has an author: all things were made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16–17). So Paul is not borrowing a pagan argument but reading the handwriting of the same Lord who wrote Scripture, faint where Scripture is clear, but his.

Is long hair on a man therefore a sin? Scripture sets no hair length for men; the Nazirite let his hair grow long as a mark of devotion (Numbers 6:5). Paul’s concern is what a hairstyle signalled in Corinth: a man presenting himself as a woman. Where a style carries no such meaning, it is a matter of conscience and taste, and no Christian should judge another by the length of his hair.

What about dress more generally? The principle reaches further than hair. The law of Moses forbade a man to wear a woman’s garment or a woman a man’s (Deuteronomy 22:5), and the concern was not a particular cut of cloth but the blurring of the line God drew between the sexes. What counts as masculine or feminine dress varies between cultures and centuries; in many countries today trousers on a woman are simply women’s clothes. The question is whether, here, it says “I am glad to be the man or woman God made me”, or says the opposite. And modesty applies to both sexes: dress for worship and for life in a way that does not draw attention away from God to yourself.

In everyday life. If you have felt pressure, from the world or your own heart, to resent the body God gave you, bring that to him honestly; he made you on purpose, and makes no mistakes. And be slow to judge other Christians over dress and hair where Scripture has left room.

Where Christians differ: must women wear head coverings today? Some churches require head coverings in worship today; most do not. This commentary’s view: The principle is permanent: the distinction between men and women, and the husband’s headship, rooted in creation, should be honoured in worship. The head covering was the cultural expression of that principle in first-century Corinth, where an uncovered married woman sent a message of shame or rebellion. Where coverings carry no such meaning, the principle should be expressed in other ways: modest dress, and clear distinctions between men and women. Christians who wear coverings out of conviction should be respected (see the note on v. 16).

Uncertain wording. Exactly what covering Paul means is not certain. In verse 4 the Greek says literally that a man prays “having down the head”, most likely a garment drawn over it, and in verse 15 “for a covering” could also be rendered “instead of a covering”. So some conclude that the hair is the covering and no cloth was ever in view. That reads oddly against verse 6, where cutting the hair short is the alternative to covering the head. The better sense is that nature has already given a woman a covering in her hair, and the cloth covering follows that lead.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes the subject by refusing to let it become a quarrel: the churches of God have no such practice. Corinth must not go its own way.

If anyone is inclined to be contentious. The last word is not another argument but a door closing. Contentious (philoneikos) means fond of quarrelling, loving to win, and Paul expects some to argue.

The Lord who did not need to win. Christ had every argument on his side, and “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). He came not to win a debate with his people but to lay down his life for them, and he calls us to the same mind: “in humility count others more significant than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3–7). A contentious Christian is defending his own rights; his Lord gave his up. And over all the quarrels of his people stands the Prince of Peace, who made peace by the blood of his cross, and whose church, for all its contentions, will be presented to him at last without a single division left.

Are Christian women meant to cover their heads in church today? It deserves an answer, not an admiring description of how difficult it is. Begin with what does not change. The theology of verses 3 and 8–12 is rooted in the Trinity and in creation, neither of them a first-century custom. That men and women are equally God’s image, genuinely different, mutually dependent and ordered in relation to one another is not up for revision, and a congregation that quietly erases the difference has departed from Paul, whatever it is wearing.

What does change. The visible sign is a different matter, as Paul’s way of arguing suggests: from what is disgraceful, what nature suggests, what the churches do, things people read at a glance in a particular place and time. A sign works only if people can read it. In Corinth an uncovered head in worship said something everyone heard; in most Western congregations today a hat says nothing whatever, and a woman who wore one to make Paul’s point would find that nobody received the message.

So, practically. Where the covering is still meaningful, as in some cultures and congregations it plainly is, wear it, and let nobody sneer at those who do; they are obeying Scripture in a way their neighbours can read. Where it is not, the principle must find a form people can see: a church where men and women are equally welcome to pray and not embarrassed to be different; where the distinction is treated as a gift, not an awkwardness to be managed; where dress and manner in worship are chosen to honour God rather than display the wearer. Either way verse 16 governs: whatever a Christian concludes, he may not become contentious about it, for the apostle who spent fifteen verses on the matter refuses to let it become a battlefield.

What if my conviction differs from my church’s practice? Then follow your conscience quietly, and do not make it a cause. A woman who believes she should cover her head may do so where few do, and should be welcomed gladly; one who does not believe it required should not be pressed by the opinions of others. Neither may treat the other as less faithful or turn the question into a campaign; that is the contentiousness this verse shuts out. If the difference becomes a constant source of strife, talk humbly to your elders, and remember that the unity of the church weighs more than this sign.

Uncertain wording. “No such practice” may mean the practice of contentiousness (we do not fight about this) or the practice of women praying uncovered (no church does what you propose). Either way the appeal is to the shared life of the churches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church meal that shames the poor is not the Lord’s Supper at all. Paul withholds his praise, because their gatherings are doing harm (v. 17). They are divided, and God is using even the divisions to show who is genuine (vv. 18–19). At the meal each eats his own food first, so that one goes hungry and another gets drunk (vv. 20–21), and that despises the church of God and humiliates those who have nothing (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper and the equality of the gospel

Paul’s answer comes from the cross. The Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26), the death of the Son of God who became poor for our sake and gave one body for all his people. A Supper that ranks people by wealth is not merely unkind; it contradicts what the meal itself declares. (On discerning the body, see v. 29.)
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Roman society guests at a meal were served according to their rank, and the Corinthians had brought that arrangement straight into the church. Now: The Lord’s Supper is still a place where the gospel’s welcome is either shown or denied. A church where wealth, race or education decides who is welcomed and who is overlooked has made the Corinthian mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has no praise for gatherings that leave the church worse off, divided at the very meal that proclaims its unity. Yet God is at work even in the divisions, showing who is genuine.

I do not commend you. In verse 2 Paul wrote, “I commend you”; now he deliberately takes it back. Whatever they had held on to, they had lost the thing that mattered most.

For the worse. Not that the meetings were dull, but that these people would have been better off at home. There is such a thing as a church service that leaves people further from God than it found them.

Divisions. The word of 1:10 (schismata), but here the divisions are social: rich and poor.

And I believe it in part. A model of pastoral care. Paul has heard something, perhaps from Chloe’s household (1:11), and refuses both to pretend it is nothing and to convict them of everything alleged.

There must be factions. A hard sentence. Factions (haireseis, from which comes heresies) are parties or sects, and this is not approval: Paul has attacked them since chapter 1. He speaks with irony and realism about how God works even through what he hates. In a church of forgiven sinners in a fallen world, factions will come, and God rules over them for his own ends, as Jesus said that temptations must come, yet woe to the one by whom they come (Matthew 18:7). Trouble sorts people. When a congregation splits along the lines of money or personality or taste, it becomes visible who was there for Christ and who was there for the circle. Genuine (dokimoi) was used of coins and metal tested and approved. Nobody discovers what an alloy is made of while it sits on a shelf; it is found out in the fire, and a divided church is a furnace (1 John 2:19). There is comfort in it too: a church going through an ugly season is not outside God’s hands.

Divided at his table. They were dividing at the one place built to proclaim that Christ had made them one. He died to break down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14–15), and in him there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28). To split the church into the comfortable and the overlooked, at a meal that announces his death, is to contradict with the seating what the bread says with its breaking.

Should I leave a church that is divided? Usually not at the first sign of trouble, never simply to escape discomfort. Do not conclude that God has abandoned the place; verse 19 says he is at work in what feels like collapse. Do not join a party, for the sifting is between those who are for Christ and those who are for a camp. And ask the question this verse presses: when the fire came, what did it show I was made of? There are times when leaving is right: when the gospel itself is denied, when abuse is covered up, or when the leaders will not be corrected by Scripture. But most church troubles are a call to stay, pray, speak truthfully and seek peace.

In everyday life. The next time you hear a report about another member, do what Paul did: believe it in part, refuse to repeat it, and if it matters, go to the person.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A meal where some feast while others go hungry is not the Lord’s Supper at all, but contempt for his church.

Not the Lord’s supper. A devastating sentence. They gathered as a church, took bread and a cup, said the words, and the apostle tells them it was not the Lord’s Supper. It had become a private party, and lost the right to its own name.

The setting. The Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal, the love feast (Jude 12), in the homes of wealthier believers. A dining room, the triclinium, held perhaps nine or a dozen reclining guests; everyone else was in the courtyard. Roman writers describe hosts serving the best food to high-status friends and lesser fare to lesser guests. The slaves and labourers came when their work let them, which was late, to find the meal eaten, the good wine gone, and their brothers in the inner room flushed and full.

Each one goes ahead with his own meal. Goes ahead (prolambanō) means takes beforehand, or devours: “One goes hungry, another gets drunk.”

Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Then the anger breaks out, and Paul does not tidy it: a cry of disbelief, “What!”, then four questions, none of them gentle. If you want a private feast, have it at home.

Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? The sharpest word falls not on the drunkenness, bad as that is, but on what was done to “those who have nothing”. A man who arrives late and hungry and watches the meal end without him has been told something about his worth, at the table where Christ’s death for him is celebrated. That is what Paul cannot bear: snobbery at the Lord’s table shames the poor, and that is contempt for God’s church. The Corinthians thought they were having a slightly untidy dinner. They were preaching, in actions, the opposite of the gospel they said with their mouths. Shall Paul commend them? No.

Whose supper it is. It is the Lord’s supper: his table, his rules of hospitality. And the Lord at his last supper rose, tied a towel round his waist and washed his disciples’ feet, the work of the lowest slave, and said, “I have given you an example” (John 13:4–5, 15). The host took the place the Corinthians gave to their late, hungry slaves. He has never once humiliated those who have nothing; he has filled the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53). At his table the slave and the master eat the same bread, because both are beggars who have been fed by the King.

The world’s seating plan. The sin is not really greed but the effortless importing of the world’s seating plan into the church. Nobody in that house had to decide to humiliate the poor; they only had to do what everyone in Corinth did and let the ordinary arrangements stand. Congregations rarely resolve to grade people by money or accent or schooling; they simply fail to notice that the surrounding culture has already done it for them (James 2:1–4). Beneath it lies an old idol of the heart, the need to be seen as someone who matters, which Corinth fed with couches and good wine. The gospel meets it another way: the only verdict that finally counts has already been given at the cross, to rich and poor on exactly the same terms (Romans 3:22–24).

Where does this happen today? Rarely at the communion table itself, and often all around it: at the coffee after the service, when the same circles form every week and the visitor stands alone with a cup; when the leaders all come from one profession or class; when the poorer members are served but never invited home; when young families and the elderly never speak; when people from another country or race are welcomed politely and never befriended. None of it is deliberate; all of it says, as Corinth did, that some here matter more than others. The remedy is not guilt but attention: look for who is on the edge, and go and stand there.

What if I am the one left out? Then the apostle is on your side, and so is the Lord whose table it is; Paul’s anger here is on behalf of people like you. Your place at Christ’s table does not depend on whether anyone made room for you at the coffee urn; it was bought with his blood, and he does not grade his guests. It is still right to speak gently and honestly to an elder about how the church welcomes people, and often worth taking the first step yourself towards one other person. But do not let other people’s neglect persuade you that you do not belong. You belong to Christ, and therefore to his body.
verseByVerse.note: The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal. The wealthy, free to arrive early, ate and drank before poorer members — often slaves — could come after work.

parallels.desc: your love feasts

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Supper proclaims the Lord’s death, so it must be eaten in a way that fits that death. Paul hands on what he received from the Lord: Jesus’ words over the bread and the cup on the night he was betrayed (vv. 23–25). Every celebration announces his death until he comes (v. 26). To eat with contempt for his body is to answer for it (vv. 27–29), and the Lord has been disciplining the Corinthians as a Father, to save them from condemnation (vv. 30–32). So each must examine himself and come, and all must wait for one another (vv. 28, 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology:
The real presence: the Reformed understanding of the Supper

Calvin, working closely with this passage, taught that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the Supper. The views are weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: This is my body” at the end of the note on vv. 23–24.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Anyone who understands that Christ died for the rich and the poor alike cannot eat well while his brothers go hungry at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper is one of the church’s plainest proclamations of the gospel, which is why abusing it is so serious, and why a church gathered as equals around the cross is a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Supper comes from the Lord himself, who on the night he was betrayed gave thanks, broke bread and gave it as his body “for you”. Paul answers the Corinthians’ abuse of the meal not with new rules but by retelling what Jesus did.

Received from the Lord. Paul stops arguing and recites, in the words for handing on tradition (v. 2; 15:3): the teaching originates with Jesus himself, passed on through the apostles. This is probably the oldest written account of that night, from about AD 54, before any of the Gospels and within about twenty-five years of the event, its wording already shaped by regular use in the churches.

The night when he was betrayed. On the night he was handed over to death, he handed this meal to his church. A man who had eaten with him for three years had already taken money (Matthew 26:14–16), and none of the others would stand by him either. The Supper was given on the worst night in the history of friendship, which is precisely why an unfaithful Christian may still come to it.

When he had given thanks. The verb (eucharisteō) gives the old name Eucharist. In Scripture thanks is more than manners: it confesses that what you have is a gift, and that there is a Giver. Its opposite is the root of human rebellion: “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (Romans 1:21), the quiet assumption that life is owed to us. Jesus did not give thanks because things were going well; that night they were about to go as badly as anything has ever gone. He gave thanks knowing what the bread meant and what the next day held, because he trusted his Father’s goodness in the dark.

Which is for you. For you: two small words (hyper hymōn) carrying the whole gospel, on your behalf, in your place. And he said it to a room that, on Luke’s account, still held the man who had sold him (Luke 22:21), as well as the man who would deny him.

In remembrance of me. Remembrance (anamnēsis) is more than recalling a fact. It is remembering a past event as your own, as at Passover a father told his children the feast was kept “because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt” (Exodus 13:8), though he himself had never been there. The Christian at the table takes hold of the cross as his own.

He put his body into their hands first. He knew the kiss that was coming, the whip, the nails and the forsaking, and he lifted bread to his Father and gave thanks. He did not wait for his friends to prove faithful: he put his body into their hands first, in bread, then gave it on the cross for the same men who ran. Every time his table is spread, the Lord of glory serves himself, gladly, to guests who have deserved nothing. So his people hold the one thing no circumstance can take away: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15).

This is my body. The body Jesus spoke of was there at the table, handing them the bread, and he regularly spoke in such pictures (see the box at the end of this note). Yet “represents” is far too weak a word for what the previous chapter called “a participation in the body of Christ” (10:16). The believer who takes the bread receives Christ, truly, by faith, through the Spirit, and the receiving is as real as the crumbs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a re-sacrifice of Christ. He was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28).

What should I actually do in my mind while I eat? Look back to the cross: this body was given for me, in my place. Look in, with honest faith: I have nothing to bring, and I receive him gladly. Look around at your brothers and sisters, who eat the same bread and are one body with you. And look forward to the day he will eat it new with you in his kingdom. You need not feel anything dramatic, only take what is given, trusting the giver. The Lord’s Supper is not a test of your concentration; it is his gift to your faith.

In everyday life. Grace turns thankfulness from a mood into a habit. At your next meal, or at the Lord’s table, name one thing in your day, even a hard one, and hand it back to God with thanks (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Where Christians differ: This is my body. Roman Catholics take is literally: the bread becomes Christ’s body (transubstantiation), while continuing to look and taste like bread. Lutherans say Christ’s body is present in, with and under the bread. Zwinglians say it is purely a symbol, a vivid memorial of something now absent. This commentary’s view: Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said it; the disciples could not have understood him to mean the bread had become his body. Jesus often spoke in metaphors: I am the door, I am the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). The bread signifies his body. But it is not an empty sign: through it, by the Spirit and through faith, believers truly receive and feed on Christ (10:16; the Westminster Confession 29.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7). Christ is spiritually and really present to faith.
verseByVerse.note: This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup is the new covenant, sealed in Jesus’ own blood: God’s promise of forgiveness and a new heart, made sure by his death.

After supper. The Passover moved through a sequence of cups, and the one after the main course came to be called the cup of blessing, Paul’s phrase at 10:16. On this night Jesus, the host, took the cup from Israel’s meal of rescue and gave it a new meaning: his own death.

The new covenant. A covenant is a binding relationship with promises, sealed by an oath or a sacrifice: more than a contract, because it binds persons, as marriage does. God’s covenants are his gracious commitments to his people: “I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” The covenant at Sinai depended on Israel’s keeping it, and Israel broke it. Jeremiah had promised a new covenant, not like that one: the law written on hearts, everyone knowing the LORD, sin remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus tells them, holding a cup, that it arrives with his death.

In my blood. He would be dead by the next afternoon, in the city where the Passover lambs had just been killed; he knew it, held the cup steady, and called it “the new covenant in my blood”. Moses sprinkled the people with the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8); this covenant is sealed with the blood of Christ himself. He shed it to pay for our unfaithfulness, so the covenant is sure from our side as well as from God’s (Hebrews 9:15–22): he has kept its terms for us, and his blood has paid for every breach. When you drink the cup, God is renewing his pledge to you that all this is yours in his Son.

As often as you drink it. No rule about frequency, only the assumption that it will be often: the Lord knew his people would need feeding regularly.

What should the cup contain? Jesus used the Passover fruit of the vine (Matthew 26:29), which in his day was wine, and wine is the fitting element. But the New Testament gives no rule about the vessel, and a church that uses grape juice for the sake of a recovering alcoholic or a troubled conscience has not broken the Supper. Nor does the Supper need to be a full meal: Paul tells the Corinthians to eat at home if they are hungry (v. 34), separating the ordinary meal from the Lord’s table.

In everyday life. You belong to the new covenant: your sins are forgiven and remembered no more. When an old sin rises in your memory to accuse you, answer it with the cup: God has promised to remember it no more, and he sealed that promise in blood.

Where Christians differ: how often? Some churches hold the Supper weekly, believing that was apostolic practice (Acts 20:7); others less often, to preserve its solemnity. This commentary’s view: Scripture does not command a frequency. The early church seems to have celebrated it each Lord’s Day, and Calvin wished for weekly communion. Frequent celebration is a great blessing, as long as it is done with understanding and self-examination, not mechanically.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every time the church eats this bread and drinks this cup, it announces Christ’s death, and it will go on announcing it until he comes again.

You proclaim. Paul’s own comment, still calling it “bread” after Jesus’ words have been spoken over it, points the Supper in two directions, backwards first. Katangellō is announcing, preaching. The Supper is a public announcement made with hands and mouths: Augustine called the sacraments visible words. A congregation eating together tells everyone watching that a man died, that his death is their whole hope, and that they are not ashamed of it: a sermon even the illiterate can preach and no one can misquote.

Until he comes. Then forwards. The Supper is a meal for the road, and will one day be overtaken by the thing it points to: Christ will drink the fruit of the vine new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29; Revelation 19:9). He gives himself to faith at every Supper, but he is not yet here in the body, and every celebration is a prayer: “Our Lord, come!” (16:22).

A man who is not dead. The death we announce belongs to one who died and is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). Every loaf broken for two thousand years has been his pledge that he is coming. And the Host who broke bread on the night he was betrayed will wait on his people at the wedding supper of the Lamb.

A meal of joy and of hunger. It gives real food and leaves you wanting a fuller one. Anyone who has taken the bread in grief knows how well it fits: this worship, built around a death and a waiting, does not require you to pretend all is well. A foretaste is meant to make you hungry, and that ache at the table is not a failure of devotion but the sacrament working.

Every culture has its sacraments. Many modern people find ritual faintly embarrassing, yet all week we are shaped by rituals we never call by that name. The philosopher James K. A. Smith has described the shopping centre as a kind of temple, with its own pilgrimage, pictures of the good life and promise that the next purchase will make us whole. The last scroll through the phone before sleep, the anthem before the match, the early start at the gym: each, repeated, teaches the heart what to love. That is part of why Jesus left his people not only a doctrine to remember but a meal to repeat. Bread in the hand and wine on the tongue train the heart the other way, from taking towards receiving. Every other liturgy tells us we are what we acquire. This one tells us we are what we have been given, and it goes on telling us until he comes.

What if I feel nothing at communion? Then you are in good company, and you have lost nothing. The Supper does not work by the strength of your feelings but by the faithfulness of Christ, who gives himself to faith whether faith feels warm or cold. A starving man is nourished by bread even when he is too tired to taste it. Come, take, and believe the promise attached to it. Over time many find that the quiet, repeated meal does its work below the surface, steadying faith as no single moment could. And sometimes dryness is a call to come with more expectation: prepare during the week, read the passages beforehand, and pray for eyes to see him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To take the Supper in a way that treats it, or the people at it, with contempt is to sin against the Lord himself.

In an unworthy manner. This verse has probably kept more Christians away from the table than any other, usually by being read backwards. Paul does not write “whoever is unworthy” but whoever eats “in an unworthy manner”; the King James Version’s “unworthily” is the same word, describing how one eats, not who one is. That is the difference between a table and a locked door.

What is an unworthy manner? Paul has spent six verses describing it: coming to the table while treating the people at it with contempt, despising the poor and treating the meal carelessly; eating well in front of the hungry; taking the sign of a death that put everybody on the same level, and using it to show that you stand above them.

Guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord. Guilty means liable, answerable (enochos): to treat the Supper with contempt is to sin not merely against a ritual but against the Lord whose body and blood it sets forth. Israel learned at the ark what careless hands mean near the holy God (2 Samuel 6:6–7), and the God of the ark is the God of this table.

Guarded by holiness, opened by mercy. The Lord is too holy to be treated with contempt, and too merciful to turn away a single sinner who comes hungry. Nobody has ever been worthy of the body and blood of the Son of God; that is why the body was broken. A Supper for the worthy would be a Supper for nobody, and Christ handed it to a table of deserters.

Who should hesitate. Not the one who feels unworthy, but the one who despises a brother and means to go on doing so, or clings to a sin he has decided not to give up, and reaches for the bread as though that did not matter.

If you have stayed in your seat. If you have stayed in your seat because you knew yourself too sinful to come, hear this plainly: you have understood your own heart correctly and this verse wrongly. The table is not a reward for the clean. It is food for the starving, and a sense of your own unworthiness is very close to the qualification. Christ came to call not the righteous but sinners, and he invites the hungry to come and eat without money and without price (Matthew 9:12–13; Isaiah 55:1).

What if there is a sin I keep falling into? Then come, provided you are fighting it and not keeping it. The believer who hates his besetting sin, confesses it again and again and keeps asking Christ for help is exactly who the Supper is for; it is given to strengthen weak faith in the fight. The person who has made peace with a sin and intends to go on in it should not come until he has repented. If you are unsure which you are, asking with a troubled heart is usually a sign of the first. Speak to a pastor if it helps, confess the sin to God before you eat, and receive the bread as the pledge that Christ’s body was given for this sin too.
verseByVerse.note: “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating — despising the poor — not to whether the individual was worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before eating, each believer should test his own heart, and then come and eat. Self-examination is the way to the table, not a reason to stay away from it.

Examine himself. Examine (dokimazō) means test, prove, the root of the “genuine” of verse 19: metal tried in the fire. And the sentence ends “and so eat”: Paul assumes the person who has examined himself will be at the table, not in the car park. A whole tradition of self-examination ends in abstaining, leaving sincere Christians with their hands in their laps for years, thinking that staying away shows how seriously they take it. It is a misreading, and it deprives the very people the meal was made for.

What am I actually looking for? Not a morbid inventory of every failure since the last Supper; that is introspection, which ends with the self at the centre and Christ somewhere in the background. Paul’s examination is short, and faces outwards. Do I trust Christ, and not myself, for my standing before God? If the answer is yes, however shakily, the door is open. Am I repenting of known sin? Is there anyone in this room I am refusing to be reconciled to? That is the one Corinth failed; if there is, deal with it, as the Lord said to leave the gift at the altar and go and settle it first (Matthew 5:23–24). Am I coming to honour Christ and his body, to receive rather than to perform? That last one catches the respectable.

Ten looks at Christ. Robert Murray M’Cheyne advised taking ten looks at Christ for every look at yourself, and the test here ends in eating. You look in long enough to see that you have nothing, then look up at the Lamb who was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and whose perfect obedience is counted as yours. The examination does not ask whether you are good enough, but whether you are resting on the one who is. And the God who bids us examine ourselves has already searched us and knows the worst, and still set the table.

A fence around a fire. The table belongs to the Lord. To say openly and warmly who it is for, with the warning attached, does not shut people out; it is a fence around a fire, built because something is precious and dangerous.

In everyday life. Examine yourself a day or two before the next Supper, rather than in the thirty seconds while the plate approaches. Confess what needs confessing, forgive whoever needs forgiving, send the message that needs sending. Then come gladly.

What about children who profess faith? In a church that holds believer’s baptism, as this commentary does, the order is baptism first, then the table. When a child gives a credible profession of faith, understands simply what the gospel and the Supper mean, and shows the beginnings of a changed life, the elders and parents may well judge it right to baptise him and welcome him to the table. The age differs from child to child, and no church should rush or refuse it for the sake of a rule. Our paedobaptist brothers usually admit children to the Supper after a public profession of faith, reaching a similar place by a different road. Both agree that the Supper is for those who can examine themselves and discern the body.

Where Christians differ: who may come to the table? Some churches practise open communion, inviting anyone; others closed communion, inviting only members of that church or denomination. This commentary’s view: The table is for baptised believers who trust Christ, are not under church discipline, and examine themselves. Churches should explain this clearly and invite all such believers, whatever their congregation. Unbelievers and those living in unrepentant sin should be lovingly warned not to partake (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 173). This is called fencing the table.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever eats without recognising the body of Christ, and above all his people gathered at his table, brings the Lord’s judgment on himself.

Discerning the body. It may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as Christ’s body, which the Corinthians were despising (v. 22; 10:17); perhaps Paul means both. The Corinthians’ failure was not a wrong theory about the bread and wine but that they could not see the church. To fail to discern the body is to look around a congregation and not see Christ’s own people there.

Judgment on himself. Judgment (krima) is not final condemnation, though the King James Version rendered it “damnation”; for that Paul uses “condemned” (katakrinō) in verse 32. It is a verdict, here God’s discipline: a Father’s correction, so that we may not be condemned along with the world (v. 32).

Look up. Before the plate reaches you, look along the rows and ask whether there is anyone you are quietly writing off: the tedious one, the one who was rude to you, the one whose politics you find intolerable, the one with less money whom you have never invited home. Those people are the body of Christ. When we look around the table and see one another, we are seeing what his death has made: a family that no human power could have built and no division can finally destroy.

The modern danger. Our danger is less despising the member across the aisle than forgetting he is there, treating communion as a private matter between me and God, eyes shut. Paul assumes a meal around one loaf that makes one body (10:17). Discerning the body is not only refusing to despise; it is bothering to notice.

Do I need to understand the theology of the Supper perfectly to discern the body? No. You need to know what it is about and whom it is for: that the bread and cup set forth Christ’s body and blood given for sinners, that he gives himself to faith through them, and that everyone who eats with you is one body with you in him. A child or a new believer can grasp that. What the verse warns against is not limited understanding but careless contempt: eating as though the meal were ordinary, and as though the people around you did not matter. So a believer of long standing whose mind is failing through dementia should not be turned away; the verse forbids contempt, not frailty.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the Lord’s body”; the earliest have simply “the body”.
verseByVerse.note: “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as his body.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord had been disciplining the Corinthians for their contempt at his table, with sickness and even death, but as a Father, so that they would not be condemned with the world.

Weak and ill. Paul links their behaviour at the table with sickness and deaths among them; “died” is literally “fallen asleep”, the Christian word for believers’ death (15:18, 20). He does not soften it, but the wrong lesson drawn from this verse has caused enormous and needless pain.

What it does not mean. Not that every illness is a punishment for sin, nor that anyone may look at a sick Christian, or a sick child, and go hunting for the hidden fault. Jesus demolished that assumption. Asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, he answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:2–3). Told of Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen crushed by a falling tower, he asked whether the victims were worse sinners than everyone else, and answered his own question: no (Luke 13:1–5). The whole book of Job exists to destroy the theory that suffering reliably shows guilt. What the verse does mean is that God sometimes disciplines his people through physical affliction.

A specific diagnosis, not a general theory. Paul speaks as an inspired apostle about a particular congregation’s particular sin. Nobody today has that information about anyone else’s illness, and to imitate the diagnosis without the revelation is cruelty with a Bible verse attached. If you are reading this from a hospital bed, or after a funeral, this text is not an accusation aimed at you. If God has something to say to you, he does not do it in code.

If we judged ourselves truly. Verse 31 gives the simple way to avoid such discipline. Judged (diakrinō) shares its root with “discerning” in verse 29: if we judge our own sin and turn from it, God does not need to correct us for it.

Disciplined. Verse 32 makes the passage comforting. Disciplined (paideuō) means trained, as a father trains a child (Hebrews 12:5–11). Two things are named here that must never be confused: discipline belongs to sons; condemnation belongs to the world. God does not punish his children for sin in the sense of making them pay for it, because that punishment fell on Christ, once, at the cross. What he does with his children is train them, and training hurts.

So that we may not be condemned. God let believers in Corinth become ill and some die, so that they should not be condemned with the world. Even the severest thing in the passage is a rescue. The hand that struck was holding on (Revelation 3:19). And the God who disciplines is the God who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). He does not bruise his children from a safe distance. He took the condemnation himself.

Does God still discipline believers with sickness today? He may, but you can almost never know that a particular illness is discipline, and you should never conclude it about someone else. Most sickness in a Christian’s life is simply part of living in a fallen world, and God uses it to draw us nearer rather than to correct a specific sin. The right response to any illness is not a frantic search for hidden guilt but the healthy practice of verse 31: ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, confess what he brings to mind, and rest in his fatherly care. Pray for healing, use the doctors he has provided, and trust that whatever he allows, he means for your good (Romans 8:28).

Is it not cruel for God to discipline with sickness and death? From a stranger settling scores it would be. But a father who pulls his child roughly back from a cliff edge is not cruel, even if the child is bruised. Sin at the Lord’s table was carrying the Corinthians towards ruin, and God loved them too much to let them go quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when you gather to eat, wait for one another, and satisfy your hunger at home, so that your meeting brings blessing and not judgment. After the warnings, the remedy is one small act of love.

Wait for one another. The verb (ekdechomai) means wait for, and some scholars argue that here it also carries the sense receive, welcome. Notice the smallness of it. Paul has taken them to the upper room, to the return of Christ and to graves in their own congregation, and he asks them to sit still until the slaves get off work. Repentance usually looks like that: not a programme, but a small, slightly inconvenient change next time. And those asked to wait are not the poor, who were already waiting, but the comfortable, who could arrive early. The cost falls on those with something to give up, which is the direction love always travels in this letter (8:13; 9:19; 10:24).

Eat at home. There is nothing wrong with a good dinner; there is something badly wrong with treating the Lord’s table as one.

When I come. Some things Paul would not settle at a distance, but face to face. Not everything was written down, but everything necessary was (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Welcomed, so welcoming. The comfortable should wait because Christ waited for them: “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you” (Romans 15:7). No one on those couches had arrived at Christ’s table early, with something to offer. Each came in late and empty from the courtyard of the world, and found the Son of God had kept a place for him. Picture a wealthy Corinthian on his couch, hearing footsteps in the courtyard, putting the bread down until the man with the calloused hands has sat beside him: the death of the Son of God preached in that room by two men starting to eat at the same moment. And behind it stands a vast patience: the Lord is not slow, as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The Host is still waiting for his last guests.

What does waiting for one another look like in a church today? A hundred small courtesies that say: you matter here. Holding the service until the bus from the care home arrives. Keeping a seat for the latecomer with three small children. Making sure the food at the church lunch reaches the back table before seconds are offered at the front. Not starting the meeting before the person who works shifts can get there. Choosing, at the Supper itself, to receive the bread together rather than as isolated individuals. None is dramatic; all preach the sermon a Corinthian host preached when he put his bread down and waited.

In the flow. The body that Corinth failed to discern at the table is the body chapter 12 will describe: one body with many members, where the weaker parts are indispensable (12:22).

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.<sup>2</sup>Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.<sup>3</sup>But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.<sup>4</sup>Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,<sup>5</sup>but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.<sup>6</sup>For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head.<sup>7</sup>For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.<sup>8</sup>For man was not made from woman, but woman from man.<sup>9</sup>Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.<sup>10</sup>That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.<sup>11</sup>Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman;<sup>12</sup>for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.<sup>13</sup>Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered?<sup>14</sup>Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him,<sup>15</sup>but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.<sup>16</sup>If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.<sup>17</sup>But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.<sup>18</sup>For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part,<sup>19</sup>for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.<sup>20</sup>When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.<sup>21</sup>For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.<sup>22</sup>What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.<sup>23</sup>For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread,<sup>24</sup>and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”<sup>25</sup>In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”<sup>26</sup>For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.<sup>27</sup>Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.<sup>28</sup>Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.<sup>29</sup>For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.<sup>30</sup>That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.<sup>31</sup>But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged.<sup>32</sup>But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.<sup>33</sup>So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—<sup>34</sup>if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

keyVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
keyVerse.note: This verse tells the church what it is doing whenever it gathers at the table: preaching Christ’s death to all who watch, and looking for his return. That is why the Corinthian meal was so wrong, for a supper that shamed the poor preached the opposite of a death that gave one body for them all. Every faithful celebration says again that our whole hope is a crucified Lord who is coming back.

11.reflection:
Paul says, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (v. 1). Who has shown you what following Christ looks like in ordinary life, and who might be learning it by watching you?

Verse 3 makes the Father and the Son the pattern for order between equals, and verses 11–12 insist that in the Lord man and woman depend on each other. Why do people often assume that order and equal worth cannot go together? How does Christ’s glad obedience to his Father help?

The Corinthians brought the world’s seating plan into the Lord’s Supper (vv. 20–22). Where might your church, without meaning to, show that some people matter more than others, and what one change would help?

Paul tells us to examine ourselves “and so eat” (v. 28). How should a believer who feels unworthy come to the Lord’s table, and what would it look like for you to prepare for the next Supper by looking more at Christ than at yourself?

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Where we are. Paul takes up another question from the Corinthians’ letter, spiritual gifts, in an answer that runs to the end of chapter 14, with love at its centre.

The message. The Holy Spirit is known by what he says about Jesus, not by how overwhelming he feels, and his gifts are given not to rank Christians but to bind them together. Every believer has been joined by the one Spirit to Christ’s body and given some gift for the good of others, and no member can say “I do not belong” or “I have no need of you”.

Why it was said. The Corinthians prized the dramatic gifts, tongues above all, as badges of superior spirituality (see the introduction). Their pagan past had taught them that: Greek religion, from the trance at Delphi to the frenzy of Dionysus, took being carried away as the sign of a god. So some felt superior, and others felt they did not belong.

How the chapter makes its case. First the test: the Spirit’s mark is the confession “Jesus is Lord”, not ecstasy (vv. 1–3). Then the source: one Spirit, one Lord and one God give many gifts, to each believer, for the common good (vv. 4–11). Then the picture: one body, baptised in one Spirit (vv. 12–13). The image was common in ancient politics, and Corinth knew a local version: at the temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, worshippers left clay models of the body parts they wanted healed, many since dug up. Paul’s body is no heap of separate parts but one living whole. He answers the member who feels he does not belong (vv. 14–20) and the one who needs no one (v. 21), and shows God honouring the weaker parts, so that all suffer and rejoice together (vv. 22–26). You are Christ’s body, and no gift is given to all (vv. 27–30); and there is a better way still (v. 31).

Where it leads. “So it is with Christ” (v. 12): the church is so joined to him that he counts what is done to it as done to himself. Its Head knelt to wash feet, bore the curse alone, and was raised from the place of no honour to the name above every name; and the more excellent way of chapter 13 is his life.

For us. No Christian is giftless and none is self-sufficient. Stop measuring yourself or others by one gift; offer what you have been given, and go looking for the members your church has overlooked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit is known by the Christ he confesses, and he gives every believer some gift for the good of others. Paul first sets out the test: the Spirit never curses Jesus and always leads people to call him Lord, however quiet or dramatic the experience (vv. 1–3). Then he traces every gift to one source, the Spirit, the Lord and God (vv. 4–6), gives each believer a share for the common good (v. 7), and names nine examples, from wisdom to the interpretation of tongues (vv. 8–10), all handed out as the Spirit wills (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

In verses 4–6 Paul assumes the Trinity in passing. Reformed teaching has grounded the gifts here: they are not the Spirit’s work apart from Christ, but the common work of Father, Son and Spirit. That guards against two opposite mistakes, making much of the Spirit and little of Christ, and neglecting the Spirit’s present work.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were competing for the most impressive gifts and using them to gain social standing. Grounding every gift in the one God removes the competition at its root. Now: The same rivalry can run in different directions: some churches prize dramatic gifts over quiet ones, others prize intellectual gifts such as teaching over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both rankings.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians thought they understood spiritual things, but their pagan past had taught them to judge the divine by how overwhelming it felt, and Paul begins by correcting that. As pagans they had been swept along by gods that could say nothing.

Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers. “Now concerning” (7:1; 8:1) signals another question from the Corinthians’ letter. The word here, pneumatika, may be their own; at v. 4 Paul changes it to charismata, grace-gifts, shifting the focus from spirituality to grace. They thought they knew about spiritual things; Paul says they need teaching.

Mute idols. Of all he could have said about their old gods, Paul chooses one detail: they could not speak. “They have mouths, but do not speak” (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18), and on Carmel Elijah watched four hundred and fifty men shout all day at a silence (1 Kings 18:26–29). Picture the temple: incense, drums, a crowd, and a painted statue that has never said a word. Because the god never speaks, nobody can test what its worshippers say in their frenzy.

However you were led. Led (agō) means carried off, swept along. Pagan worship in Corinth involved real frenzy, trance and ecstatic utterance, as in the cults of Dionysus, and the Corinthians had come into the church believing that the more overwhelming an experience, the more divine it must be. But the Holy Spirit does not work by mindless compulsion: “the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (14:32).

He opened not his mouth. The idols were mute because there was nothing in them. The Son of God was silent because he chose to be: “like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7), so that people who had spent their lives before gods that never answered might hear a God who calls them by name. The Word made flesh went quiet at the cross, and because he did, he will never be silent towards his people again.

How can people of other religions have powerful spiritual experiences? Because human beings are made for God, and because there are real spiritual powers in the world besides the Holy Spirit (10:20). Ecstasy, visions, healings and trances are reported in many religions; Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ signs (Exodus 7:11, 22). So an experience settles nothing by itself. Be neither impressed nor frightened, but ask Paul’s question: what does this say about Jesus Christ?

Are emotions in worship wrong, then? Not at all. The Psalms shout, weep, dance and clap, and a Christian moved to tears by the love of Christ is responding rightly. Paul objects to using feeling as the measure of God’s presence. Healthy worship engages mind and heart together (14:15): it understands what it sings and feels its weight and wonder. Strong emotion that rises from the truth about Christ is a gift; strong emotion pursued for its own sake is the temple of Dionysus with Christian words.

In everyday life. Think of the most powerful spiritual experience you have had, and ask what it left you believing about Christ, and how it changed the way you live. That is the measure of it.

Uncertain wording. Pneumatika can mean either “spiritual things” or “spiritual people”, and the context does not finally decide. Many think it was the Corinthians’ own word, for the gifts they prized or for those who had them; since the chapter is about gifts, “spiritual gifts” is the likely sense.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit is recognised not by how an experience feels but by what it says about Jesus: he never curses him, and no one truly calls him Lord except by the Spirit. So every believer who confesses Jesus as Lord has the Spirit.

The curse. Accursed is anathema. Whether anyone in Corinth actually shouted it is debated. Perhaps someone in an ecstatic state had said it and shaken the church. Perhaps unbelievers in the synagogues were cursing Jesus and pressing Christians to do the same, as Paul himself once did (Acts 26:11). Perhaps Paul names the worst thing imaginable to set the principle at its extreme. Either way the rule holds at both ends: the Spirit never speaks against Christ, and no one comes to confess Christ without him.

Jesus is Lord. One of the earliest Christian confessions (Romans 10:9; Philippians 2:11). Anyone can pronounce the syllables; Paul means handing the running of your life to a crucified Jew from Nazareth and owning him as God and master. That cannot be produced by good arguments, a strong upbringing or an emotional evening. It is the fingerprint of God on a human heart. By nature the mind is blind to the glory of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4–6): a person may admire Jesus and even defend him, but he will not bow to him until the Spirit gives him new birth (John 3:3–5).

What does Lord mean here? More than master or sir. Kyrios is the word the Greek Old Testament used for the name of God himself, the LORD, so to call Jesus Lord was to give him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). It was also costly: the Roman world said “Caesar is Lord”, and Christians who refused to say it, or said Jesus instead, were sometimes killed. So the confession means three things at once: Jesus is God, Jesus has the right to rule me, and Jesus outranks every other power that claims my loyalty.

The accursed one is the Lord. Put the two cries side by side and the gospel stands between them. To the synagogue a crucified man was under God’s curse, for the law said “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and many think that is where the cry “Jesus is accursed” came from. The gospel does not deny the curse; it explains it. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He hung where the curse falls so that those who trust him would never bear it. So the Spirit does not teach a believer to say that Jesus was never under the curse. He teaches him to look at the one who bore it, and call him Lord.

The practical use of the test. Corinth needed a way to tell the Spirit’s work from spiritual theatre, and Paul’s needs no special insight: listen to what is said about Jesus. The Spirit’s whole business is to glorify Christ (John 16:14). He is like a floodlight trained on a building at night, doing all the work, unlooked at, content that what people see is the building. So a movement, teacher or book that makes much of the Spirit and little of Christ has failed the only test the New Testament gives, however remarkable the things that happen in it; and a quiet congregation where Christ is honoured and trusted has passed it (1 John 4:2–3).

How do I know I was not simply talked into this? If Christ is genuinely your Lord, not merely your preference or your heritage, then according to this verse somebody did that in you, and that somebody was the Holy Spirit. The most ordinary Christian confession in the world is a supernatural event.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gifts are many and different, but they all come from the one God, Spirit, Lord and Father, so none of them can be grounds for rivalry. The church’s variety is no threat to its unity, because the unity lies in the Giver.

Varieties of gifts. Three sentences of the same shape, variety on one side and sameness on the other, show where the unity comes from. Varieties (diaireseis) means distributions, allotments. Gifts is charismata, from the word for grace: God’s undeserved kindness given a definite shape in a particular person, the ability to explain a passage clearly, to open a home to strangers, to sit with the dying. Peter calls those who use them “stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10).

Varieties of service. Diakoniai, from which we get “deacon”: a gift is not an ornament but a job.

Varieties of activities. Energēmata, from which we get “energy”: workings, effects. It is God actually doing something through a person, not a talent the person owns and operates.

The Trinity. The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, laid out in passing in a paragraph about church squabbles. The doctrine is sometimes called a late invention of the bishops at Nicaea in AD 325. The careful vocabulary came later, but the pattern is here, some twenty-odd years after the crucifixion. Unity in diversity in the church reflects unity in diversity in God, within whose life there has never been a moment of competition. The Father is not diminished by the Son’s glory; the Spirit does not resent being the one nobody looks at. Out of that life, unthreatened and entirely at peace, came a world, and a cross, and a church full of quarrelling people in a Greek port, each handed a gift of grace and set to work.

The same Lord, who came to serve. Every diakonia in the church is rendered to Jesus, who turned service from a slave’s job into a glory. To disciples arguing about rank, as the Corinthians were, he said, “I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27), and then he washed their feet and gave his life. A gift used to climb above other people is offered to that Lord in a spirit he never once showed.

Why the competition collapses. Put the three nouns together. If a gift is grace, nobody earned it. If it is service, it was never given for display. And if it is God working, boasting about it is as odd as a chisel congratulating itself on the furniture.

Should I pray to the Holy Spirit? You may: the Spirit is fully God, and the church has addressed him for centuries in hymns such as Come, Holy Ghost.
