The ordinary New Testament pattern is to pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). And Paul’s three sentences settle the worry behind the question, that attention paid to one person is withheld from another: the gift in your hands was given by the Spirit, is a service rendered to the Lord, and is God at work in you. One act, three persons, no seams.
verseByVerse.note: Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer, without exception, has been given some showing of the Spirit’s work, and it was given for the good of others. This purpose is the key to chapters 12–14.

To each is given. “To each”: not to the impressive, the ordained or the articulate. In a church of slaves, dockworkers and people not wise, not powerful, not of noble birth (1:26), every believer had received a manifestation of the Spirit. There are no giftless Christians; not every Christian has a prominent gift, but every Christian has one. And “is given”: received, not earned.

The manifestation of the Spirit. Manifestation (phanerōsis) means display, showing. When a member of your church comforts the grieving well, keeps the accounts honestly or makes a passage clear, you are watching the invisible Spirit become visible. Every Christian is a place where God has chosen to show himself.

For the common good. The word (sympherō) means what benefits, what helps. A gift is not a spiritual souvenir or evidence of standing, but the congregation’s property held in one person’s hands for a while, and that purpose ruins gift competition for good.

Anointed for others. The pattern was set in Christ. When the Spirit came upon Jesus at his baptism, the first thing the Gospels record is a refusal to serve himself: hungry in the wilderness, he would not turn stones into bread (Matthew 4:3–4). In Nazareth he read out what the Spirit was for: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). The gifts in a church are that same anointing shared out among his members, pointing the same way: outward.

How do I find out what mine is? Not mainly by introspection. The New Testament tells a Christian to examine himself about his standing before God and his conduct at the Lord’s table (11:28; 2 Corinthians 13:5), never about which gift he has. Gifts are discovered in use. Start serving something the church actually needs, and notice what happens. Watch for what leaves others strengthened rather than merely impressed (on gift and talent, see vv. 8–9). Ask two or three Christians who know you well and will tell you the truth, because gifts are easier to see from outside. And notice what you keep being asked to do. Whether you enjoy the work, and whether you are naturally good at it, are useful signs but not decisive: this is a manifestation of the Spirit, not a personality test, and the Spirit has worked through people who found the work difficult all their lives.

What if I am too old, ill or worn out to do anything? Then your gift has not been taken away; it may have changed shape. Some of the most fruitful members of any church can no longer leave the house: they pray through the church list every morning, write to the grieving, telephone the lonely, and receive visitors with such faith that the visitors go home strengthened. Suffering borne with trust in Christ is itself a ministry (2 Corinthians 1:3–6). The common good does not require energy, only a member who still offers what God has given.

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit gives different gifts to different people, some spoken, some practical, some plainly supernatural, but every one of them comes from the same Spirit.

The utterance of wisdom. Paul offers no definitions (see “Uncertain wording” below). A word of wisdom (logos sophias) is something said, not merely possessed, and wisdom in this letter is not cleverness: the wisdom of God is Christ crucified (1:23–24; 2:6–7). So this is probably the ability to speak God’s wisdom into the situation in front of you: the believer, not especially learned, who in a crisis says the one sentence that helps.

The utterance of knowledge. A word of knowledge (logos gnōseōs) is probably the ability to grasp the truths of the faith and explain them clearly, close to teaching. The Corinthians loved knowledge (8:1); even knowledge, Paul reminds them, is a gift, not an achievement.

Faith. Every Christian has saving faith, so Paul means a particular God-given confidence for a particular thing: the believer who is certain God will provide for a work while everyone else is doing sums, and is proved right. It is the faith that moves mountains (13:2; Matthew 17:20).

Gifts of healing. Both nouns are plural in Greek: not a standing power a man carries around, but gifts of healings, given occasion by occasion, as the apostles healed in particular cases (Acts 3:6–8; 5:15–16; 28:8).

Jesus Christ heals you. So Peter said to Aeneas, paralysed for eight years (Acts 9:34). The apostles never claimed the power as theirs; it was the name of Jesus, by faith in his name, that made the lame man strong (Acts 3:16). Matthew roots Jesus’ own healings in the cross: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases” (Matthew 8:17; Isaiah 53:4). Every healing of his people is a fruit of the cross.

What it does not mean. Not that this is a complete list, or that each person has only one gift. Paul’s lists all differ (Romans 12; Ephesians 4; 1 Peter 4).

Does God still heal? Yes, and Christians should pray for the sick expectantly and without embarrassment, as James tells them to (James 5:14–15). That is different from a gift by which a person could heal at will, as the apostles did (Acts 5:15–16; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Such a sign gift marked out a messenger as truly sent by God, as the signs given to Moses did (Exodus 4:1–5), so the Lord bore witness to the apostles’ word by signs and wonders done by their hands (Acts 14:3). It belonged to the apostolic foundation and has ceased with it (see the box “Where Christians differ” at the end of the note on vv. 10–11); and the eagerness of continuationist brothers and sisters to pray for the sick is a rebuke to cold hearts. So pray for the sick with confidence in God, and treat claims to a healing ministry with caution, testing them by Scripture and by what actually happens.

And does he always? Plainly not, and the New Testament is candid about it. Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Epaphroditus nearly died, and Paul calls his recovery a mercy, not an entitlement (Philippians 2:27). Timothy got advice about wine for his stomach, not a healing (1 Timothy 5:23). And Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was told no: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). If the apostle who raised a young man from the dead at Troas (Acts 20:9–12) could not heal his friend or himself, then unhealed sickness in a Christian is not evidence of a lack of faith but of a will wiser than ours. No one who has prayed and not been healed should be told the failure was theirs.

What is the difference between a spiritual gift and a natural talent? God gives natural abilities to believers and unbelievers alike: a good mind, a fine voice, a head for figures. A spiritual gift is an ability the Spirit gives, or takes up, in a believer to build up Christ’s body: often a talent turned to new ends, sometimes something never there before. The real difference is in the fruit: a talent impresses, a gift strengthens. When people go away from your service closer to Christ, rather than merely admiring you, the Spirit is at work.

In everyday life. Pray for the sick in your church this week, by name, expecting God to hear; and tell someone who explains the faith clearly how their words helped you.

Uncertain wording. Paul names the “utterance of wisdom” and the “utterance of knowledge” without defining them, and they appear as named gifts only here, so the exact difference between them is not known. The explanations above are the likely sense, inferred from how Paul uses “wisdom” and “knowledge” elsewhere in the letter. The modern use of “word of knowledge” for supernatural insight into a person’s situation comes from later practice, not from the verse.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends with the gifts Corinth prized most, and Paul’s last word on all of them is that the Spirit hands them out as he chooses, so no one may demand a gift or boast in having one.

Miracles. Five more gifts, three of them treated at length in chapter 14. The working of miracles is literally “workings of powers” (energēmata dynameōn): acts of power beyond healing, such as Paul striking Elymas blind (Acts 13:11) or raising Eutychus (Acts 20:9–12).

To another prophecy. Not mainly prediction, but speaking a message revealed by God for the church’s strengthening, encouragement and comfort (14:3), which could lay bare the secrets of a heart (14:24–25). Paul assumes it must be tested, “let the others weigh what is said” (14:29), which no one would say about Scripture. So prophecy in Corinth stood under the apostolic word, never beside it, and never added a line to the Bible.

Distinguishing between spirits. Its presence in the list is telling: Paul assumes that not everything claiming to be from God is from God, and that some believers were given a nose for the difference between the Spirit and false spirits (1 John 4:1). The public test is the confession that Jesus is Lord (v. 3); this gift is the ability to apply it well.

Tongues. Speaking by the Spirit in languages one has not learned, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:4–11), with interpretation the ability to explain what was spoken so the church could understand (14:13, 27–28). These were the gifts Corinth prized most and understood least. Paul includes them without scorn, and speaks in tongues more than any of them (14:18). Yet they come last, here and in verse 28, perhaps deliberately, since the Corinthians ranked them first.

As he wills. The closing sentence governs the whole chapter. The Spirit wills (bouletai): he is a person, not a force to be switched on. That comforts anyone who has begged for a gift, not received it, and been told the fault lies in his faith. The distribution is the Spirit’s free act, and gives nobody grounds for despising a Christian who lacks something.

Every gift with one subject. One name runs through all five gifts. The miracles of Acts were done in the name of Jesus. “The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” (Revelation 19:10). Spirits are discerned by whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (1 John 4:2). And at Pentecost the crowd heard the mighty works of God in their own languages (Acts 2:11), and Peter said the risen Jesus had poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). The Spirit hands out the gifts as he wills, but he has only ever had one message, and his greatest work, in the humblest believer, is still the one he never stops doing: taking dead hearts and making them alive to Christ.

What about Christians today who say they speak in tongues? Treat them as brothers and sisters, not suspects; many love Christ deeply and are sincere. A cessationist will believe it is not the New Testament gift of real languages given as a sign, but a form of prayerful speech; a continuationist will see it differently. Both can agree on what Paul requires in chapter 14: nothing unintelligible in church without interpretation, everything done decently and in order, and no gift made the badge of the Spirit’s presence (12:30). Where those rules are kept, the disagreement need not divide fellowship in the gospel.

What if someone says God told me? Listen humbly, and test it. God does guide his people, by his word, wise counsel, the circumstances he arranges, and the Spirit’s inward work in the conscience. But an impression is not a revelation, and never carries the authority of Scripture. If it contradicts Scripture, it is not from God; if it agrees, its authority comes from Scripture, not from the impression. And no one may bind your conscience with a word they say God gave them about your life. The canon is closed, and in it God has given us everything we need for life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Where Christians differ: do the miraculous gifts continue? Continuationists hold that all these gifts are available today, and they have real reasons: Paul gives them for the common good (v. 7), tells the church to desire them and not to forbid them (14:1, 39), and says they will pass away when the perfect comes (13:10), which many take to be Christ’s return. This commentary’s view: the gifts of miracles, healings, prophecy and tongues served as signs confirming the apostolic message while Scripture was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation of apostles and prophets laid and the canon (the complete collection of Scripture) closed, these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased as ordinary gifts in the church. God still heals in answer to prayer and does wonders as he pleases, and the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, faith, discernment, teaching, serving and mercy continue. This cessationist view is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters, with whom we share the gospel. Whichever way a reader lands, verse 11 forbids looking down on another Christian over it: the Spirit apportions as he wills, and that clause has never yet been amended by a committee on either side.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every believer belongs and every believer is needed, because the one Spirit has joined them all to Christ as one body. Paul states the picture and its ground: Jew and Greek, slave and free have all been baptised in one Spirit into one body (vv. 12–13). He then answers the member who feels he does not belong, since God himself placed every part (vv. 14–20), and the member who thinks he needs no one (v. 21). God has given greater honour to the weaker parts (vv. 22–24), so that the members care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Church and Salvation Joined

The church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised every believer into union with the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real, which is why the suffering of one member is felt by the whole (see the note on vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The competition over gifts had produced both contempt (those with prized gifts dismissing the rest) and despair (the rest feeling shut out). Paul answers both: the despairing are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church has members who look impressive and members who look marginal by the world’s standards. Both were placed by the same God, and the body needs both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is one body made of many members, because every believer, whatever his background, has been joined by the one Spirit to Christ. Its unity is not something the members achieve but something they have been given.

One body, many members. The body was a familiar political picture of a united society. In the fable Livy tells of Menenius Agrippa, the limbs that went on strike against the belly were told to go back to feeding it: the common people should return to their duty and support the ruling class. Paul turns the picture round: in Christ’s body the weaker and less honoured members are indispensable and receive the greater honour (vv. 22–24).

So it is with Christ. The natural ending would be “so it is with the church”; Paul writes “so it is with Christ”. The church is not merely like a body; it is his body (v. 27; Ephesians 1:22–23), so united to him that it bears his name. The risen Lord said it to a man on the Damascus road who had never laid a finger on him personally: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Saul had been arresting Christians; Christ counted it as an assault on himself. The man who heard that sentence is the man writing this one.

Baptised into one body. In one Spirit, or by one Spirit. The words “all” and “one” answer a troubling question: is there a second experience after conversion, a baptism in the Spirit, which some believers have and others lack? Paul writes to a church whose spiritual life was a shambles, with factions, immorality, lawsuits and drunkenness at the Lord’s table. If any congregation was second-class in the Spirit, it was this one, and he says all of them have had it. Baptism in the Spirit, here, is what happened to every Christian when he became one: the entrance, not the upgrade. It is the Spirit’s work of uniting us to Christ, of which water baptism is the sign, so that his death counts as our death to sin and his risen life flows into us (Romans 6:5; Galatians 2:20).

Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. The deepest divisions of that world, ethnic and religious, social and economic. The Spirit does not abolish the differences; a slave still went back to his master. He puts them in one body, so that the differences remain but stop being walls (Galatians 3:27–28; Ephesians 2:14–16). So a church split into the parties of Paul, Apollos and Cephas (1:12) is told what it already is: one body, because Christ is not divided (1:13).

Made to drink. The Spirit is like water poured out and drunk, as the prophets and Jesus himself said (Isaiah 44:3; John 7:37–39): not sprinkled on the surface but taken in. The Corinthian docker and the reader of this page have drunk from the same river.

The hunger behind the question. Those who speak of a later baptism in the Spirit are usually reaching for something real. Scripture plainly teaches fresh fillings of the Spirit after conversion (Acts 4:31, of believers already filled in Acts 2), and Christians are commanded to go on being filled (Ephesians 5:18). So the hunger should not be shamed. A Christian may and should ask for more of God; what he need not ask for is admission to a body he has already been baptised into.

In everyday life. Look at the Christian you find most different from yourself, in background, race, class or politics: the Spirit has put you in one body with him. Treat him like it.

Then what is water baptism for? It is the outward sign the Lord commanded for those the Spirit has joined to Christ (Matthew 28:19), picturing washing, burial and rising with him (Romans 6:3–4): the believer’s public confession of faith, his entrance into the visible church, and a means God uses to strengthen faith and assure his people that they belong to him. So this commentary holds, following the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to those who have professed faith in Christ. Paedobaptists (those who baptise infants) see it as the sign of God’s covenant promise to believers and their children, as circumcision was in Israel; this commentary holds that the New Testament joins the sign to repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41), yet gladly owns them as brothers and members of the one body this verse describes. Baptism does not make anyone a Christian. It is how the Lord marks out those who are.

Where Christians differ: baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals often teach that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: Paul says all believers, including the immature Corinthians, were baptised in the one Spirit into the one body. Spirit baptism happens at conversion; it is the Spirit’s work of joining us to Christ and his body, not a second blessing for some. Believers may and should seek to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), which is different from the once-for-all baptism in the Spirit.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “made to drink” (potizō) can also mean “water”, as a gardener waters a plant (3:6, “Apollos watered”). So Paul may mean that we drank the Spirit in, or that he was poured out over us. Some see a reference to the Lord’s Supper or to baptism, but most take it, with the first half of the verse, as another picture of conversion. Either way, every believer has received the one Spirit, and deeply.

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believer who feels he does not measure up does not stop belonging to Christ’s body; feelings do not decide membership. Paul speaks to the discouraged first; the proud come at verse 21.

The foot’s complaint. Diversity is essential to a body, and Paul now gives the body a voice. The first thing it says is a complaint about itself. The foot has admired what the hand can do, found it cannot do any of it, and concluded: “therefore I am not really part of this”. That feels like humility. It is in fact a verdict on God’s arrangement by a body part that has decided it knows better. And the foot did not compare itself to a foot but to a hand, which makes the comparison useless and painful at once. Discouragement measures you against a gift you were never given and treats the shortfall as a personal failing.

No less a part. Feelings of not belonging do not detach anybody from Christ’s body, any more than a man’s low view of his own left foot detaches it from his leg.

Whose body it is. The foot talks as if the body were a club with membership depending on qualifications. But the body is Christ’s (v. 27), so who belongs is his to answer, and he has answered: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). He does not rank his members by usefulness. He bought every one with the same blood, and he knows the foot and the hand by name. The discouraged member argues from his gifts: “I cannot do what the hand does, so I cannot be his.” The gospel argues from Christ: he called you, he joined you to himself, and he does not disown what he has joined.

The quiet withdrawal. The foot does not merely feel bad; it withdraws. People who conclude they do not belong stop offering, then stop coming, and because they leave slowly and apologetically, nobody chases them. If that has been your drift, the answer is not a compliment but a fact: leaving would not make you any less a part of the body, and it would leave the body without a foot. And since the discouraged rarely announce themselves, asking a quiet member what he is finding hard, and meaning it, is body maintenance.

What if my church really does not seem to want me? Sometimes the problem is the body’s neglect, not the foot’s feelings. If you have offered to serve and been passed over, or made to feel unwelcome, the church must answer for it, and verses 21–26 are written to it. But the answer is rarely to withdraw. Speak to an elder honestly and without bitterness; ask where help is needed; befriend others on the edges. If after real effort a church persistently refuses to receive you, it may be right to seek another, but go to belong somewhere, not nowhere. You need a local expression of Christ’s body, as it needs you.
verseByVerse.note: The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united community.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A body made of one kind of part would not be a better body but a helpless one, and a church needs every gift because each does what the others cannot.

If the whole body were an eye. Paul argues from absurdity, and we should feel it. Picture a body that is one enormous eye: a helpless monster, unable to hear a shout or smell smoke. That is what Corinth was trying to become. If tongues were the true mark of the Spirit, the ideal congregation would be one where everybody speaks in tongues and nothing else happens. A church where every member has the same gift is not a super-church. It has lost the ability to do everything that gift does not do.

The opposite error. The argument works as well against sober congregations. A church of teachers talks and never visits; a church of activists never thinks. A church that has quietly decided which sort of Christian it approves of, and every church has one, is growing a second eye where an ear should be. God did not scatter gifts around a congregation to make it interesting, but because the work requires all of them.

Senses the eye does not have. Hearing and smell are not other ways of seeing; they know what the eye cannot know. A church with a narrow range of gifts is less aware. The pastoral instinct that notices a family in trouble and the discernment that notices a teacher beginning to drift are different senses, which is why the members a church finds least congenial are so often the ones it most needs. The person whose questions are awkward may be the congregation’s sense of smell, and a body that silences him will not notice the smoke.

The measure of Christ’s fullness. There is a deeper reason one gift will not do. The body is built up “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13), and its Head is not a one-gift Lord. In Jesus the teacher and the healer, the one who wept and the one who rebuked, the one who noticed a widow’s two coins and the one who overturned the tables, lived in a single life. A church that is all eye can only ever show one feature of his face; it takes the whole body, every gift working, to grow up into him.

Is it wrong for a church to be made up mostly of one kind of person? Not wrong to reflect its place; a village church will look like its village. But it is wrong to be content with it, or to arrange things so that others feel they do not fit. The gospel creates a people from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 7:9), and the local church is meant to be a foretaste of that. A church that has become all one age, class or background should ask, without despair, whom it has been failing to reach or keep.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each member’s place in the church is God’s own decision, made on purpose, and the many members are already one body. Here is the answer to the discouraged foot: not a kind word but a truth about God.

God arranged the members. The verb (tithēmi) means deliberate placement, and it is personal: each one of them, not individuals falling where they may. The gift you have was chosen for you, the gift you lack was withheld on purpose, and the congregation you are in is where you were set down. “As he chose” echoes the Spirit who gives as he wills (v. 11), and it cuts both ways. A man proud of his gift has forgotten it was a present. A man who wishes he were somebody else is complaining about the placement, and the one who placed him knew exactly what he was doing.

Many parts, yet one body. A single member is not a body. And Paul does not say many parts that ought to become one, but many parts that already are. Unity is not something the church achieves; it is where the church starts, and all Paul asks is that the Corinthians stop contradicting what is already true of them (Ephesians 4:3–4).

The Son who took the place appointed for him. No one has ever accepted an arrangement as Christ did. The eternal Son took the place his Father appointed: a manger in Bethlehem, a workshop in Nazareth, and some thirty years of which the Gospels record almost nothing. His neighbours knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6), and at the end he could say to the Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Whoever resents the smallness of his place serves a Lord who spent most of his earthly life in a smaller one, and called it obedience.

A smaller life than you would have chosen. If you feel assigned a quieter role and abilities that will never be remarked on, that is not a mistake in the distribution. The body has parts nobody has ever photographed, and it dies without them.

What it does not mean. Not that you cannot grow in your gifts or seek new ways to serve. Nor is “God arranged” a licence to refuse anything you have not been specially equipped for. Much of what a church needs is simply obedience, required of everyone: to give, to pray, to show hospitality, to speak the truth in love, to bear with difficult people, to tell others about Christ, whether or not any of it comes easily. Gifts describe how you will serve most fruitfully, never the limits of what you will do. A hand that declines to help because carrying is the shoulder’s work has misread the whole chapter.

Should I move churches if my gifts are not being used? Rarely for that reason alone. God placed you, and the first question is whether you have offered what you have where you are. Gifts often go unused because nobody knows about them: speak to your elders and serve where help is needed, even in ways that are not your strongest; some of the best gifts grow out of years of doing whatever needed doing. There can be good reasons to move: a family move, a church that has left the gospel, a real call elsewhere. But a restless search for the congregation that “will appreciate me” is usually the foot talking again, and the place God has set you down deserves more patience than that.

In everyday life. Name one need in your church that is not a gift of yours but simply a duty, and do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
No member, however gifted, can do without the others; to say “I have no need of you” is not only unkind but false.

I have no need of you. First the discouraged member spoke about himself; now the impressive member speaks about somebody else. The eye and the head, the noble parts everybody looks at, dismiss the hand that does the work and the feet that do the walking. It is a precise little satire on Corinth, where the members with visible gifts had concluded that the rest were not really needed.

Cannot. Paul does not say the eye should not say it, but that it cannot, because the statement is false. An eye that announces it has no need of hands will be needing them within the hour.

The Head who knelt at the feet. The head here belongs to the physical picture, not to Christ; but the church has a true Head, and he answered the eye’s boast before Corinth ever spoke it. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rose from supper, tied a towel round his waist, and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). The one man with every right to say “I have no need of you” knelt at the lowest part of the body and did a slave’s work, and said, “I have given you an example” (John 13:15). A church whose Head did that has no room for an eye that looks down on a hand. He who needs nothing has chosen to need his people: to speak through their mouths, to serve with their hands, to walk on their feet into every street of the world.

How contempt works in a church. It is seldom spoken. It works by omission: who gets consulted, who gets invited, who is treated as background, the conversation that stops when a certain person joins it. And the temptation belongs almost entirely to the gifted, the busy and the capable, who can generally manage without help and so come to believe that they do.

What does repentance look like here? Not a warmer feeling about people you find tedious; feelings cannot be produced by deciding to, and manufactured ones turn into condescension, which is worse. Ask a member you have overlooked for advice about something that matters to you, and take it. Sit somewhere else. Find out what a person you had filed as marginal actually does with his week. Contempt is broken by discovering that “I have no need of you” was false, and the only way to discover it is to need the person and see what happens. The eye cannot argue itself into valuing the hand. It has to try picking something up.

In everyday life. Whose absence next Sunday would make the least difference to you? Ask what would actually stop if that person stopped; if you do not know, that is itself the answer, so go and find out. None of us has valued every member as the Head has. He did it perfectly, and for us: his obedience is counted as ours, and he washes clean even the eye that looked down on others.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has deliberately built the church so that its weakest and least regarded members are indispensable and receive the greater honour. This is not sentiment about the underdog; it is how the body is made.

The weaker parts. Paul upends the world’s ranking with an observation anybody can check. The strong parts are on show: arms, shoulders, face. The parts you cannot survive without are soft, hidden and defenceless: heart, lungs, brain, tucked behind bone because they could not take a blow. In the church those who seem weakest may be the most vital: those who pray, the faithful elderly, the quietly serving.

Less honourable parts. “Bestow the greater honor” is literally “put honour around”, the verb used of putting a robe on someone (Matthew 27:28), so Paul very probably means clothing. We take more care covering what is unpresentable than displaying what is presentable: a man will leave his face bare in all weathers and would not dream of leaving the rest of himself so.

God has so composed the body. Composed (synkerannymi) means blended, as a painter mixes colours. God arranged the body so that members with no natural standing are given an honour they did not earn, as he chose what is low and despised in the world (1:27–28). A congregation that honours its unimpressive members is not being nice. It is being accurate.

Honour given to the one who lacked it. This is how God has always worked, and the cross is where he did it most. His Son took the place of no honour at all: stripped, mocked and hung up outside the city (Hebrews 12:2). He humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:8–9). “Greater honor to the part that lacked it” describes what God did for his Son before it describes the church, and a congregation that honours its overlooked members is copying what God did with Jesus.

Who are they? Be concrete. The housebound woman who has not been in the building for three years and has prayed for half the congregation by name. The man with a learning disability whose questions slow the Bible study down. The elderly member whose memory has gone, and who is still, by this verse, a part the body cannot do without. The person who cleans up afterwards. The one who is simply hard work.

What does greater honour look like in practice? The overlooked given the best, not the leftovers. Visiting the housebound as faithfully as the leaders are consulted. Asking the elderly to pray for specific things, then telling them how God answered. Making the building accessible before making it impressive. Thanking in public, by name, those who clean, count and set up. Seating the person with a disability where he can take part. Listening to the slow question as though it might be the most important one asked, because it may be. Honour is not a feeling; it is attention, time and place given on purpose.

The fear of becoming a burden. Ask people what they dread about growing old, and many will name neither pain nor even death, but this: I don’t want to be a burden. Our culture insists on equal worth but quietly measures it by independence and output, so the moment we need help we feel we cost more than we are worth. In Oregon’s official reports on assisted dying, the fear of being a burden on family and carers is among the reasons most often given. Paul’s body has no such scale. The parts that seem weaker “are indispensable”, and a church that needs its housebound and its forgetful is telling the truth about how God values people. The gospel goes further. Every Christian is someone who was a burden: we brought nothing, and Christ carried us, sins and all, and did not hold the cost against us. The God who says “to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4) is not keeping accounts.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God arranged the body so that its members would not divide but care for one another, sharing each other’s sufferings and joys as a real body does.

That there may be no division in the body. Here is God’s aim. Division (schisma) is the word of 1:10 and 11:18: the unity of a church is not a project the members dreamt up but what God was after when he handed out the gifts. Positively, the members are to have the same care for one another: care (merimnaō) is the word for anxious concern, each concerned for the others, equally.

If one member suffers, all suffer together. Paul does not say they ought to; he says they do, because that is how bodies work. Stub a toe in the dark and the whole body reacts: the breath catches, the eyes water, the hands reach. Nobody has to persuade the shoulder to care about the foot, because the foot is not somebody else. When one believer suffers, the whole church should feel it (Romans 12:15; Hebrews 13:3).

All rejoice together. It is often easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice. Sympathy costs time; gladness at another’s success means you must stop comparing yourself with him. When someone else gets the thing you have prayed for and not received, the child, the recovery, the post, what happens in you at that moment measures the body’s health more accurately than any funeral.

The Head feels it first. The body suffers together because its Head does. “In all their affliction he was afflicted” (Isaiah 63:9), and in Christ that sympathy took flesh: a High Priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), who wept at the grave of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). He shares his people’s joy as well: “he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). A congregation learns to feel with its members because it is joined to a Lord who already does.

How does a body come to feel what its members feel? Not by resolving to. Nerves are built out of information: knowing people’s names and what is happening in their lives, and asking again the following week. Much suffering stays unshared because nobody asked a second question. The sharing runs both ways. A member who tells nobody anything has, with the best intentions, cut his own nerve; in a body, privacy is how a limb goes numb. Letting people know you are struggling is not weakness, and this verse quietly requires it, because a body cannot suffer together with a member determined to suffer alone. That need not mean telling everyone; one or two trusted brothers or sisters, or an elder, is where most of us begin.

How can I rejoice when I am envious? Honestly, by bringing the envy to God rather than pretending: “Lord, I wanted that, and she has it, and it hurts.” Remember that when another member is honoured, you are honoured in him. Thank God for the specific good he has given that brother or sister, and do something kind for them; gladness often follows the act rather than preceding it. And bring your own unanswered longing back to the Father who sees it; his love for you has not been reduced by his kindness to someone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This congregation is Christ’s body, and no gift is given to all, so the way forward is not to grasp at the impressive gifts but to seek what builds others up, and above all love. Paul applies the picture (v. 27), ranks the gifts with the ministries of the word first and tongues last (v. 28), and with seven questions that expect the answer no shows that no gift is the badge of the Spirit (vv. 29–30). Then he points to a still more excellent way (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The numbered list in verses 28–30 shows that Paul does rank the gifts, not because some are better in themselves but because some build up the whole church more directly. Apostles and prophets laid the foundation; teachers explain it. The more excellent way of chapter 13 is not one more gift above tongues and prophecy. It is the love that makes the use of any gift excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth had turned the order upside down, treating tongues, which without interpretation builds up only the speaker, as the most prestigious gift. Paul puts it last, not dismissing tongues but reordering their values. Now: A gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up has missed what gifts are for. The more excellent way is open to every Christian who puts his gift under love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This very congregation, with all its faults, is Christ’s body, and in it God has set the gifts in order, with the ministry of his word first.

You are the body of Christ. The verb to watch is “you are”: not “you should be”, or “you will be once you sort yourselves out”. To this congregation, factional, arrogant, drunk at communion, tolerating scandal, the apostle says it. The identity comes first and the instructions afterwards. Then “individually members of it”: not the body on your own, nor swallowed by it. A hand in a body is more itself, not less.

What it means to be his body. A body is how a person is present and acts. So: You belong to him, as a hand belongs to a man, and his life flows into you by his Spirit (Ephesians 4:15–16). He acts through you: the Lord who promised to be with his people to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20) goes on doing his work through them. And he remains distinct from you and over you: the church does not replace Christ or become him; he is the Head, and the body takes its orders from him (Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18).

First, second, third. Appointed is the verb of verse 18, and this list, unlike the first, is numbered. The first three all concern the word of God: apostles, the foundational witnesses of Christ who received and delivered it (Ephesians 2:20); prophets, who spoke revelation in the early church; and teachers, who explain it. They come first because everything else in a church is built on what God has said. Take the word out and the rest is mere activity.

Helping and administrating. Helping (antilēmpseis) means practical aid to those in need, set in the same list as miracles. Administrating (kybernēseis) is a nautical word for what a ship’s pilot does: steering, guidance. So the person who keeps the accounts straight, arranges the rota and makes sure the widow gets visited is exercising a gift of the Holy Spirit, named alongside the spectacular ones.

What it does not mean. Not that those with lower-ranked gifts are less valuable as persons. The ranking concerns how much each gift builds up the church (14:5).

If God appointed first apostles, are there apostles today? Not in the sense Paul means here. An apostle had seen the risen Lord (9:1) and was commissioned directly by him, and the apostles are the church’s foundation, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). A foundation is laid once; a building with a permanent foundation-laying department has a serious problem. The word also has a broader use, a messenger of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23), and that work never stopped: church planters and missionaries doing what Paul did at Corinth. Those who use the title today usually mean this, and the disagreement is often smaller than the vocabulary suggests. What verse 28 settles is the order: the word that founds the church comes first, and every later gift is measured by it.

And prophets? The prophets named here stand with the apostles as part of the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5), bringing God’s revealed word before the New Testament was complete, and that revelatory office has ceased with the closing of the canon. Continuationist brothers often distinguish these prophets from a humbler, ongoing gift of prophecy that must always be weighed (14:29); this commentary does not think the New Testament draws that line clearly enough to build on, but recognises that careful and godly readers hold it. What continues is the ministry of the word: preachers and teachers who explain and apply what God has given once for all. When a sermon pierces your heart and you feel God has spoken to you, he has, through his written word, not beside it. That is why this commentary reads the third item on the list, teachers, as the living heir of the first two.

Uncertain wording. “Helping” and “administrating” translate two Greek words found nowhere else in the New Testament. Elsewhere the first is used of help or assistance and the second of steering a ship, so the general sense is clear; exactly what tasks they covered in Corinth, and how far they match the later work of deacons and elders, is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No gift is given to every Christian, so no gift can be the badge of the Spirit or the measure of a believer.

Are all apostles? Seven questions, and in Greek each is framed to expect the answer no. Paul is not wondering aloud; he is closing a door.

Do all speak with tongues? The sixth question is the one Corinth cared about, and the answer is no: not every Christian speaks in tongues. That single syllable dismantles the system the church had built, in which one gift was the badge of the Spirit’s presence and those without it were second-class. If the Spirit had meant tongues as the mark of genuine Christianity, he would have given it to everyone. He has not, and that is itself the argument.

The one work never shared out. When it came to bearing the sin of the world, no apostle stood beside him, no prophet spoke for him and no healer eased him; all the disciples left him and fled (Mark 14:50). The redemption that could not be divided he finished by himself, and then he rose, sent his Spirit, and divided everything else among fishermen and slaves and housewives and tentmakers, so that none of them could manage without the others, and none could manage without him. Glory to the Head who did alone what only he could do, and does the rest through his body.

The Corinthian error in other clothes. Any church that makes one gift the test of spiritual seriousness has fallen into the Corinthian error: tongues for some, and for others doctrinal precision, evangelistic boldness, expressive worship, or a particular pattern of daily devotions. The same question answers them all. “Do all?” No.

A release for the discouraged. Turned round, the questions that rebuke the proud release everyone who has spent years feeling second-rate in church. You were never meant to be able to do all of it. The Spirit gave the whole list to nobody, and the apostle writing the sentence does not make himself the standard.

In everyday life. If you have been measuring your Christian life by a gift you do not have, put the measuring stick down. Measure it instead by verse 3 and by chapter 13: do you confess Jesus as Lord, and are you growing in love?

Where Christians differ: tongues as the evidence of the Spirit. Some Pentecostal groups teach that speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of being baptised in the Spirit, often because in Acts tongues accompanied the Spirit’s coming (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6), and many who hold it have known real blessing. This commentary’s view: Paul’s question expects the answer no: not all speak in tongues. Yet all were baptised in the Spirit (v. 13). So tongues cannot be the required evidence of Spirit baptism. The evidence of the Spirit is confessing Jesus as Lord (v. 3) and the fruit of the Spirit, above all love (Galatians 5:22–23; 1 Corinthians 13).

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells the church to want the gifts that most build others up, and then points beyond every gift to the way all of them must be used.

But earnestly desire the higher gifts. After thirty verses on the Spirit apportioning as he wills, this looks like a contradiction. But the two sit together, as always in Scripture. God decides who is saved, and we still pray for the lost; he provides our daily bread, and we still ask for it. That God decides makes asking safe, because we ask a Father who will not give a stone to a child who asks for bread (Matthew 7:9). Earnestly desire (zēloō) means be zealous for, and it is plural: Paul is telling a congregation what to want for itself.

What “higher” means. After everything said about eyes and feet, not more impressive but more useful to others: the gifts that build up the church most, such as prophecy and teaching (14:5). A gift ranks higher in proportion to the good it does the person sitting next to you, and by that measure the faithful visitor of the sick outranks a great deal that gets applauded.

A still more excellent way. More excellent (kath’ hyperbolēn) means beyond comparison. Everything is set for Paul to name the top gift, and he does not. He steps off the ladder, because the more excellent way is not a gift for some but the way all gifts must be used: love, required of everybody, open to everybody, and without which the whole list is worth nothing. They wanted to know which gift was best; Paul is about to tell them the question was wrong, and that a man may exercise every gift with power and be nothing whatever.

The way has a face. Paul’s verb is “I will show you”. He is about to put something in front of them and let them look, which is why chapter 13 reads less like an argument than a portrait. And the portrait is recognisable. There has been exactly one life that was patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not irritable, bearing all things and enduring all things to the end. The more excellent way has been walked, once, from Bethlehem to Golgotha, by Jesus Christ.

So should I pray for spiritual gifts? Yes, in the way Paul means. Pray, with your church, for the gifts that build others up, wisdom to counsel, clarity to teach, compassion to visit, faith to persevere, and for faithful preachers and leaders: tools, not trophies. And pray above all for love, because without it every gift is noise. The Father delights to give good gifts to those who ask him, and the best gift of all, the Holy Spirit, he has already given (Luke 11:13).

Uncertain wording. In Greek “earnestly desire” has the same form whether it is a command or a statement, so some read it as a description of the Corinthians’ ambition (“you are eagerly seeking the so-called higher gifts”), which Paul then redirects. Most translations, like the ESV, take it as a command, matching 14:1, “earnestly desire the spiritual gifts”. Either way, the next clause turns them from ranking gifts to love.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.<sup>2</sup>You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.<sup>3</sup>Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.<sup>4</sup>Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;<sup>5</sup>and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord;<sup>6</sup>and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.<sup>7</sup>To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.<sup>8</sup>For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit,<sup>9</sup>to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,<sup>10</sup>to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.<sup>11</sup>All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.<sup>12</sup>For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.<sup>13</sup>For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.<sup>14</sup>For the body does not consist of one member but of many.<sup>15</sup>If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>16</sup>And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>17</sup>If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?<sup>18</sup>But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.<sup>19</sup>If all were a single member, where would the body be?<sup>20</sup>As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.<sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”<sup>22</sup>On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,<sup>23</sup>and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,<sup>24</sup>which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,<sup>25</sup>that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another.<sup>26</sup>If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.<sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.<sup>28</sup>And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.<sup>29</sup>Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?<sup>30</sup>Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?<sup>31</sup>But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

keyVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter flows into this sentence. Paul does not tell a quarrelling church that it should become Christ’s body but that it already is, so every member belongs and every member is needed. Because the body is Christ’s and not ours, no gift can be boasted of and no member despised.

12.reflection:
Paul’s test of the Spirit’s work is what is said about Jesus, not how powerful an experience feels (vv. 1–3). Why are we so easily impressed by the dramatic? How would this test change the way you judge a church, a book or your own spiritual life?

Every believer has been given a gift for the common good (v. 7). What gifts have you seen in others in this group, and how could you encourage them? Where might you start serving in order to discover your own?

Verses 14–21 answer the member who says “I do not belong” and the one who says “I have no need of you”. Which voice is closer to your own heart, and what does Paul’s answer say to you?

God gives greater honour to the parts that seem weaker, so that the members suffer and rejoice together (vv. 22–26). Who are the overlooked members of our church, and what would it look like to honour them, and to share their sorrows and joys, this month?

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 stands at the centre of Paul’s answer about spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14). He has just shown that the church is one body with many members, each gift given by the Spirit for the common good, and has promised “a still more excellent way” (12:31). Chapter 14 then applies it to tongues and prophecy in the gathered church.

The message. Love is the way every gift must be used, and the one thing that lasts. Without it the greatest gifts and sacrifices are worth nothing; with it ordinary believers begin to look like Christ; and when the gifts the Corinthians fought over have done their work, love will still be there, because God is love.

Why it was said. Though it is often read at weddings, the chapter was written to rebuke a quarrelsome, proud church that ranked its members by spectacular gifts, especially tongues, and was puffed up with its knowledge (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. In three steps. Without love, tongues, prophecy, knowledge, wonder-working faith, even giving everything away and dying as a martyr, gain nothing (vv. 1–3). Love is then described in action, in a string of verbs, most saying what love does not do and nearly each naming a Corinthian failing (vv. 4–7). Finally, love outlasts the gifts: prophecy, tongues and knowledge are partial, like a child’s speech or the image in a dim bronze mirror, and will give way when the perfect comes and we see face to face; faith, hope and love abide, and love is the greatest (vv. 8–13).

Where it leads. Read verses 4–7 with Jesus’ name in place of love, and they describe him exactly: patient with slow disciples, kind to the despised, seeking not his own way but ours, bearing our sins all the way to the cross for people who had not earned it. And the chapter ends with the hope of seeing him face to face, fully known and still loved.

For us. Read the chapter with your own name in place of love and it shows how far you fall short, even on your best day. That is meant not to crush you but to send you to the One who loved you first, so that his love can begin to love through you. Then ask which gifts you prize, and whether love is the reason you use yours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without love, even the greatest gifts and the costliest sacrifices are worth nothing. Paul tests the gifts the Corinthians prized most, tongues of men and of angels, then prophecy, all knowledge and mountain-moving faith, and finds that without love the gift is noise and the gifted person is nothing (vv. 1–2). Then he tests the most extreme deeds anyone could do, giving away everything and going to the flames, and finds that without love they gain nothing (v. 3). He writes “I”, not “you”: the test falls first on himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Aquinas, following Augustine, called love (caritas) the form of all virtues: the quality without which no virtue is truly virtuous. Paul’s three sentences make the same point: gifts without love are not merely incomplete but cancelled. Reformed teaching has grounded this in the two great commandments, to love God and to love our neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40), so that the whole Christian life, gifts included, finds its goal and measure in love. A gift not used in love has been cut off from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian who spoke in tongues in a public meeting, leaving the congregation untaught and only himself built up, was the noisy gong in practice: the gift was real, the love was absent, and the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than his hearers, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he argues with, the worship leader who loves the experience he creates more than the people he leads: all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without love, even speech like the angels’, complete knowledge and mountain-moving faith leave a person nothing before God. Paul measures every gift by one test, and by writing “I” puts himself under it first.

Tongues of men and of angels. Paul starts at the top, with the gift the Corinthians prized most, and grants more than they were claiming: not merely every human language, but the speech of angels. Then he demolishes it.

But have not love. Love in this chapter is not mainly a feeling but a self-giving commitment to another’s good, defined by God’s love in Christ: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9–10). At its simplest it is choosing another person’s good and paying for it yourself. It is measured not by what it feels but by what it gives, and its measure is a cross.

A noisy gong. Instruments like these sounded in the pagan cults the Corinthians had come out of, especially those of Cybele and Dionysus: bronze, loud, resonant, and carrying no words. Paul tells the man proud of his tongue that his gift, used without love, makes the same sound. A gong is not silent. It is the loudest thing in the room, and that is the trouble with it: everyone turns round, and afterwards nobody can say what it said.

Prophetic powers … all faith. Paul moves up to prophecy, which chapter 14 will rank above tongues (14:1, 5). To “understand all mysteries and all knowledge” would be to know not a great deal of theology but the whole of it, without gaps. All faith is not saving faith but the gift of faith that works wonders (12:9); faith that moves mountains is the Lord’s own picture of the largest faith imaginable (Matthew 17:20).

I am nothing. Not that the gift is nothing, but that I am. A gifted person without love is spiritually zero. God can use a man powerfully as his instrument when that man is not a Christian at all, and the gifts will not tell him which he is.

The gifts are no evidence about the man. It is possible to preach well, pray in public with feeling, know your Bible thoroughly, give your time generously, be thanked for it all, and be nothing. The gifts are given as the Spirit wills (12:11), so they say more about the Giver than about the man holding them. Judas was sent out with the Twelve with authority to heal (Matthew 10:1–4), and nobody at the Last Supper suspected him even as he left (John 13:27–30). Our Lord warned that many will claim on that day to have prophesied and cast out demons in his name, and he will say he never knew them (Matthew 7:22–23). Yet the people in that warning are untroubled and sure of themselves. A believer who reads this verse and fears for his own heart is showing the very tenderness they lacked, and the remedy for that fear is not more gifts but Christ, who loves the loveless into love.

Not one word he said was noise. There was once a man with every gift in this list and more. He spoke as no man ever spoke, he knew what was in every heart, and the mountains were his own, because he had made them. And not one word he said was noise, because every word was love. He used his gifts not to be admired but to heal lepers, feed crowds and raise a widow’s son, and then he laid them all down and went to a cross. The more excellent way is not a technique. It is the way he walked, all the way to Golgotha, for people who had nothing to offer him but their need.

What it does not mean. Not that gifts do not matter. Paul has just urged them to desire the higher gifts (12:31), and will say it again (14:1); the church needs them. But gifts without love have no value before God and none to the man who has them.

How can I tell whether my service is done in love? Ask who it is for. Love serves the person in front of it; pride serves its own reputation. Would I still do this if no one ever thanked me or knew it was me? Am I glad or deflated when someone else does it better? Do I notice the people I serve, their names and burdens, or only how it went? When the work is criticised, do I care first whether people were helped, or whether I was hurt? No one passes these perfectly, and that is no reason to stop serving (see the note on v. 3); bring the mixed motives to Christ and ask him to make love the reason.

Uncertain wording. Whether Paul thought angels had a language of their own is not known; some at Corinth may have believed their ecstatic speech was exactly that. He is plainly reaching for the most extreme case he can imagine, as with “all mysteries” and mountain-moving faith. When angels speak in Scripture, people understand them (Luke 1:13; 2:10), so the verse gives no ground for an unintelligible heavenly tongue. Some continuationist believers take the phrase as a hint that a tongue need not be a human language; that is possible, but it is a great deal to build on a sentence that begins with “if”. The likely meaning: if even the speech of angels would be worthless without love, so is everything less.
verseByVerse.note: Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even giving away everything you own and dying for the faith gains nothing if it is done without love. Paul moves from the gifts to the deeds, and to the two no one has ever been able to top.

If I give away all I have. The verb (psōmizō) means to dole out in morsels: parcelling out everything you own to feed the poor until nothing is left.

To be burned. The second deed is martyrdom: a man walks into the fire rather than deny his Lord. These are the summit of Christian devotion, and Paul says even these can be worth nothing.

I gain nothing. The most extreme thing a human being can do may be done for the wrong reason. A man may give away his fortune because he cannot bear to be thought ordinary, or go to the stake because his own consistency has become what he worships, or because he cannot face climbing down in front of people who are watching. Sacrifice proves that something mattered more than comfort. It does not prove what. This is religion used as self-salvation, the sacrifice offered as a payment so that God or the onlookers will owe the giver something. The irreligious man keeps his life for himself; the religious man may give his life away and still be keeping it for himself. In verse 2 it was “I am nothing”; here it is “I gain nothing”: a life poured out and admired may yield its owner nothing at the end, because on the last day love is the only thing that will count.

He loved us and gave himself up. Paul’s own words for the cross join exactly what this verse pulls apart: “walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). Here a man hands over his body with no love in it, and the result is nothing. At Golgotha a Man handed over his body and there was nothing in it but love. If any self-giving ever deserved to gain something, it was his, and what he gained was us. Every human sacrifice is weighed against that one, and it is the love in it, not the size of it, that God regards.

In everyday life. Look at your giving, of money and of time. Is any of it arranged so that it will be noticed? Give something this week in a way that leaves no trace of your name, and thank God that he sees in secret.

But if love is the one thing that counts, and I find little of it in me, what do I do? Not try harder to feel it; the chapter never suggests that. Love is received before it is returned: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). So the road to more love runs through more knowledge of his love: the cross, what he forgave you, how fully he knows you and loves you anyway (v. 12). Ask him for it plainly, for it is the fruit of his Spirit (Galatians 5:22). Then do the loving thing while the feeling lags; affection very often follows obedience rather than going before it.

Should I stop giving until my motives are pure? No. Our motives this side of glory are always mixed, and if we waited for pure ones we would never give a penny or lift a finger. Keep giving and serving, and ask God to purify your heart as you go. The warning is not against giving but against trusting the giving, as though the size of the sacrifice could stand in for love or earn us something before God.

Textual note. The ESV, like the KJV, reads “to be burned”, and notes that some manuscripts read deliver up my body that I may boast. Two Greek words differing by a letter or two lie behind the phrase; several of the oldest manuscripts read boast, and the NIV and NRSV follow them. Burned fits martyrdom; boast fits the Corinthian pride, and is almost bleakly apt: a sacrifice offered so that one has something to say about it. Either way the meaning is the ultimate sacrifice of self.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body [to death] that I may boast.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love is known by what it does, and Paul’s portrait of it is both a portrait of Christ and a mirror held up to Corinth. Love waits long and does good, and has no room for envy, boasting or the puffed-up pride Corinth was known for (v. 4). It does not shame others, push its own way, flare up or keep an account of wrongs (v. 5). It takes no pleasure in another’s fall but is glad with the truth (v. 6). And it covers, trusts, hopes and stays under every load (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Portrait of Christ

Put Jesus Christ in place of love in verses 4–7 and the sentences remain true (see the notes on v. 4 and v. 7). Love is not only a command to be obeyed but a Person to be united with, and as Christ is formed in us (Galatians 4:19), his character becomes ours.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth, to be used as a diagnosis, not only as an aspiration. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? Now: One of the strongest witnesses a church can give is not an argument but a fellowship that actually loves like this, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring. The watching world knows what love looks like, and it is waiting to see whether the church shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love shows itself in how it treats people: it waits long, does good, and has no room for envy, boasting or pride. In Greek every item is a verb: love acts patiently, behaves kindly, refuses to envy. This describes not a feeling but conduct, which means it can be checked.

Patient. The word (makrothymeō) joins “long” and “anger”: love has a long fuse. It is not the patience of waiting for a bus but of putting up with people who wrong you, the word family the New Testament uses of God bearing with sinners for centuries (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9). Its measure is not how you behave the first time someone irritates you but the fortieth.

And kind. The word (chrēsteuomai) means actively doing good to others. Patience is love holding back when it is wronged; kindness is love going on to do good in return. It is possible to endure someone indefinitely while giving them nothing at all, and some marriages and churches are held together on exactly those terms. Patience alone is endurance. Patience with kindness is love.

Love does not envy or boast. Envy (zēloō) is what happens when the other person has the good thing; boasting is what happens when you have it. They look like opposites, but they are one illness in two positions: the habit of measuring yourself against other people. The Corinthians envied one another’s gifts (3:3) and boasted in their gifts and leaders. The rare word behind boast (perpereuomai) suggests a windbag, who cannot let a story pass without improving his own part in it. Love rejoices in others’ blessings and has no need to advertise its own.

It is not arrogant. Puffed up, inflated with air (physioō): Paul’s signature word for Corinth, used of their factions (4:6) and their knowledge (8:1). Love is humble because its attention is on the other person, not on itself.

A portrait of Christ. Every quality in this list was perfectly shown by Jesus, and only by him. Put his name in place of love and the sentences remain true: Jesus is patient and kind; Jesus does not envy or boast; he is not arrogant. He was patient with disciples who argued about who was greatest and kind to a woman everyone else despised. Put your own name in, and you see how far you fall short, even on your best day. Yet his perfect love was lived in your place, and by his obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19), so the mirror does not condemn you.

What it does not mean. Not that love tolerates everything, or that patience never addresses a wrong. Love says hard things too, but with patience, kindness and humility.

In everyday life. Picture the person you find hardest in your congregation or family, and read the items again with that name after each verb. Am I long-tempered with him? Do I actively do him good? Am I glad when he does well? Love in this chapter always has a name attached. God has borne with you far longer, and his Spirit is at work in you: be patient and kind to that person today, in one specific act.

Am I meant to read my own name into this list? Yes, but as a mirror, not a ladder. The list is not a set of rungs by which to climb into God’s favour; Christ has done that for you. It describes what his love looks like as it grows in his people. So read it with your name in, honestly, and let it drive you to him. Then read it with his name in, and rest. The Christian who does both is neither crushed by the standard nor careless about it.

parallels.desc: love covers all offences

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love does not shame people, push its own way, flare up at them, or keep a record of their wrongs. Four more items, each a photograph of the Corinthian church.

Or rude. The word (aschēmoneō) means to behave disgracefully, in a way that shames, as the Corinthians were doing at the Lord’s Supper (11:21–22). Manners in a list of Christian virtues should give pause to the believer who prides himself on being blunt. Rudeness is not a personality type in the New Testament; it is a failure of love. No gift, calling or strength of conviction entitles a Christian to make another person feel small in front of others.

It does not insist on its own way. Literally, love does not seek its own things, as at 10:24 and 10:33 (compare Philippians 2:4). It sums up chapters 8 to 10 in a phrase, and it is the hardest item on the list, because insisting on one’s own way rarely feels like selfishness from the inside. It feels like being right. The strong at Corinth were right that an idol is nothing, insisted on their right to eat, and were destroying weaker believers by it.

It is not irritable. The word (paroxynomai) gives us paroxysm: provoked to a flash, touchy. Everyone knows the person whose mood a whole household checks before speaking. Irritability is usually excused as temperament, but Paul lists it as a failure of love.

Or resentful. Literally, love does not count up the wrong (logizetai to kakon), an accountant’s phrase: love does not enter the wrong in a ledger. That is what resentment is: not the memory of an injury, which is involuntary, but the keeping of it where it can be produced later. When a quarrel starts, does a list arrive, with the dates and wording of things said years ago? Nobody has that at his fingertips by accident. It is there because it was filed.

The ledger and the gospel. Behind the image lies the gospel. Logizomai is the very word used for righteousness credited to believers, and for God not counting our trespasses against us (Romans 4:8; 2 Corinthians 5:19). The Christian is a person whose own ledger has been cancelled, not reduced, not suspended, cancelled, and who is therefore in no position to keep one on anybody else. God will never produce your sins against you, not on the last day and not on a bad Tuesday, because Christ has paid for every one of them (Romans 8:1, 33–34). Forgiveness is the closing of an account you were entitled to keep open.

What it does not mean. Not that love ignores serious sin or abuse. Love confronts sin for the person’s good (Galatians 6:1), and may need to remember facts for the sake of protection or justice (see v. 7). Keeping no record of wrongs is not pretending nothing happened. But love does not nurse grudges, rehearse injuries, or hold them in reserve as weapons.

If I forgive, do I have to trust him again straight away? No. Forgiveness releases the debt: you give up the right to punish or repay, and it can be given at once, because Christ has forgiven you. Trust is rebuilt over time by changed behaviour, and wisdom may require boundaries meanwhile, especially where someone has been harmed or is at risk. A wife can forgive a husband’s betrayal and still need time, honesty and counsel before trust returns. Forgiveness says: I will not hold this against you. It does not say: nothing has consequences.
