What if the memory keeps coming back? Remembering is not resenting. You cannot command your memory, but you can decide what to do when it arrives: not rehearse it, add to it, or imagine the speech you would make, but hand it back to God (Lord, I gave you this; I give it again) and pray for the person, even briefly. Many Christians have to forgive the same wrong many times before the feeling follows the decision, and that is not failure; it is what forgiving looks like in real life.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love takes no pleasure in anyone’s wrongdoing or downfall, and stands gladly on the side of the truth. Love and truth are allies, not rivals.

It does not rejoice at wrongdoing. Paul means not only approving of sin but the small, private pleasure that rises when something bad turns out to be true about somebody else: the flicker of satisfaction when a colleague’s promotion falls through, a critic’s marriage is in difficulty, a preacher you found insufferable is found out. Nobody chooses that flicker, but because it arrives uninvited it is an accurate reading of the heart. At Corinth it had a public form: the church was arrogant about gross immorality in its membership instead of mourning (5:2), and the factions probably cheered when a rival came off badly. But the private form is the commoner one.

But rejoices with the truth. We would expect the opposite to be grieving at wrongdoing. Instead Paul pictures love and the truth standing side by side, glad about the same things. That settles a question that comes up constantly: whether being loving means going quiet about what is true. Love does not celebrate a wrong even when it is convenient, and does not suppress a truth even when it is awkward. A love that requires lies is not love, and a truth-telling that enjoys the damage is not truth-telling either (Ephesians 4:15).

Not rivals but one face. God has never once been glad at our fall. He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). When the son came home, the father did not rehearse the waste; he ran. And the Son of God is the Truth in person (John 14:6), in whom love and truth are one face. He told the woman at the well the whole truth about her life, and she went back into the town to tell everyone about him, because the one who knew it all had not rejoiced over her sin but come to take it away.

Gossip. Nobody says, I am glad this happened to him. People say they only mention it so that you can pray. Here is a test: would you be disappointed to discover the report was false? If the correction would come as a relief, the interest was love. If it would come as a small disappointment, the interest was that flicker of pleasure at another’s fall.

In everyday life. When you hear of someone’s sin this week, refuse to enjoy it or repeat it, and pray for him instead.

So when may I speak about someone else’s sin? When speaking serves the person or protects others, and you are speaking to someone who needs to know. Go to the person first where you can (Matthew 18:15). Speak to elders when the matter concerns the church’s care, and to the proper authorities when someone is in danger or a crime has been committed; love never hides abuse. Ask a wise friend for counsel without dressing the story up. What love does not do is pass the story to people who can do nothing about it, add colour to it, or enjoy the telling. Before you speak, ask: is this person part of the problem or part of the solution?

How is the flicker killed? Not by scolding yourself for having it, which only drives it out of sight. It dies when the other person stops being a competitor, and he stops being one when you genuinely believe that God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose (12:18). A man certain that his own place was given him has nothing to gain by another man losing his.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never gives up on people: it covers their failings, thinks the best of them, keeps hoping for them and stays under the load. Four verbs, each with “all things”, and the effect is of a wall that will not come down.

Love bears all things. Bears (stegō) is related to the word for a roof (see the uncertain wording below). Love puts a roof over the person it loves, refusing to broadcast his failures, though not pretending they are not there. “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12): it does not repeat the story, and carries burdens instead.

Believes all things. Not gullibility, but a readiness to think the best and give the benefit of the doubt where doubt genuinely exists, assuming the better explanation until it cannot.

Hopes all things. When the evidence has run out, love goes on expecting God to do something with a person. It is the parent still praying for a son twenty years after the last conversation.

Endures all things. The word (hypomenō) means to remain under a weight rather than get out from under it. Love does not leave when loving becomes expensive.

He put the roof over us. There is one love that covered sin not by hiding it but by bearing it. “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24), so of everyone who trusts him it can be said, blessed are those whose sins are covered (Romans 4:7). He put the roof over us at the cost of standing under the storm himself. He went on believing the Father in the dark, when the Father’s face was hidden; he hoped when there was nothing visible to hope on, for the joy that was set before him; he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2), and stayed under the weight until it was finished. And the love that held then holds still: he will bear with his people all the way home.

A guard on these four verbs. These words have been used to do great harm. Bears all things has been quoted at a woman to keep her silent about what is being done to her at home; believes all things, to persuade a congregation that a credible allegation must be a misunderstanding; endures all things, to send people back into danger. Paul’s own letter proves that is not his meaning. Eight chapters earlier he told this church to put a man out of the fellowship for his sexual conduct and not even to eat with him (5:11–13). He named Alexander the coppersmith and warned Timothy about him (2 Timothy 4:14–15). He rebuked Peter to his face, publicly (Galatians 2:11), and did not think he was contradicting verse 7.

What love does with wrongs. The four verbs describe what love does with the wrongs it suffers, not with the wrongs it discovers. Love will absorb an insult without publishing it; it will not absorb an assault and call it patience. Believing all things means refusing to assume the worst about a person’s motives; it has never meant refusing to believe a victim, and using this verse to silence one turns it on its head. Where someone is being hurt, love’s roof goes over the person being hurt, and the wrongdoer is brought into the light, which is itself the most loving thing that can happen to him. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered, and a person in danger should seek safety and help at once, from the church’s leaders and, where a crime has been done, from the police. Leaving danger is not a failure of love.

Does hoping all things mean I must believe a person will change? It means you never write anyone off as beyond God’s reach, and you keep praying for them. It does not mean pretending change has happened before it has, or putting yourself back in harm’s way on the strength of a promise. Hope rests on God, not on the other person’s words. You can hope for a man’s repentance with all your heart and still wait to see its fruit before you trust him again (Matthew 3:8).

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of bears (stegō) is uncertain. Related to the Greek for a roof, it can mean to cover, as a roof keeps off the weather, or to bear up under, as a roof holds a weight; Paul uses it in the second sense at 9:12, “we endure anything”. Since the verse ends with endures all things, many think covers is meant here, to avoid saying the same thing twice. The ESV’s bears keeps both open, and both fit: love shelters another’s failings from view and takes their weight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love lasts for ever, while the gifts the Corinthians prized belong to this passing age. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge will be put out of use (v. 8), because they are partial and will give way when the perfect comes at Christ’s return (vv. 9–10). Paul gives two pictures of the difference: a child growing into a man (v. 11), and a dim bronze mirror giving way to sight face to face (v. 12). Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest of these is love (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gifts Pass, Love Remains

Whether the perfect means the completed New Testament or the return of Christ has long been debated (see the note on vv. 9–10 and its box “Where Christians differ: what is the perfect?”).

What the passage does settle is the order of things: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who prized tongues above all else were investing in something that would not survive into the coming age, while neglecting the one thing that would. Now: A church rich in programmes, gifts and activity but thin in love has the Corinthian problem in modern dress. Every tradition can produce churches that are impressively gifted and loveless, and Paul’s word to all of them is the same: love never ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love will never fail, but the gifts the Corinthians prized will one day be put out of use. The portrait stops and the argument resumes, and the hinge is the word never.

Love never ends. The verb (piptō) means to fall, the way a leaf or a building falls. Everything else in the chapter has a collapse in its future; love does not. It continues into eternity, because God is love (1 John 4:8).

Prophecies … tongues … knowledge. Precisely the three the Corinthians had been ranking. Prophecy and knowledge will pass away (katargeō): be rendered inoperative, put out of use. All three have an expiry date, a hard thing to say to a church that had built its status system on them. The gifts they were fighting over were, on the apostle’s own account, temporary equipment.

Why the gifts pass away. Not because they are inferior. They came from the Spirit for the common good, and Paul will tell this church to desire them earnestly and not to forbid them (14:1, 39). They pass away because they are the equipment of a journey, and journeys end. Nobody consults a map after arriving. Paul raised the subject not to settle a timetable but to tell a church obsessed with the temporary that it was neglecting the one thing that will still be standing when the sun burns out.

Why is love the exception? Not because love is more useful. The other three are things we do in a world where God is not yet seen, while love is what God is (1 John 4:8). Prophecy exists because we cannot see him; knowledge, because we do not yet know him as we will; tongues, because we are still on the road. Love existed before there was a road, in the giving between Father, Son and Spirit, and it will still be there when the road has been rolled up. Before the mountains were brought forth, love was. Creation was the overflow of it, redemption the cost of it, and the new creation will be its home for ever. On earth it was seen in the Son, who, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end (John 13:1).

The last sermon. The most gifted preacher who ever lived will one day preach his last sermon, and there will never be need of another. Every commentary will be as obsolete as a candle at noon. And the smallest act of love done by the least-noticed believer will still be there, because it belongs to what is coming rather than to what is passing (1 Peter 1:24–25).

What it does not mean. Not that knowledge itself ends in heaven; we will know more, not less (v. 12), as starlight gives way to the sun.

Does the different verb for tongues mean they stopped first? Paul uses one verb of prophecy and knowledge, they will be rendered inoperative, and another of tongues: they will cease, in a form that can suggest ceasing of themselves. Some have built on that the claim that tongues were to stop of their own accord before the other two. It is a slender foundation; Greek writers use that form loosely, and the three clauses are plainly parallel. A doctrine should not be hung on a verb ending. The case for the cessation of these gifts, which this commentary holds, rests on other ground: the once-for-all foundation of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20) and the signs that confirmed their message (Hebrews 2:3–4).

Is love just chemistry? On a strictly materialist account, love is a set of hormones and instincts that served our ancestors’ genes, a late and local accident in the universe that will end with the brains that produce it. Yet nobody can live as if that were true. No one tells a dying friend that their bond was useful while it lasted. We grieve as though love had been pointing at something real, and Paul agrees: love is not younger than the universe but older. The clearest proof is a love no theory of self-interest can explain: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Genes look after their own. A love that dies for its enemies is a glimpse of what lies underneath everything.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All we know and prophesy now is partial, and it will be set aside when the perfect comes at Christ’s return. Paul includes himself: the apostle who received revelations knew in part.

But when the perfect comes. The perfect (to teleion) is the complete, the goal reached, the end for which a thing exists. When it arrives the partial is no longer needed. The candle is not despised when the sun comes up; it is simply no longer lit.

Why the perfect is Christ’s return. Paul defines his terms two verses later: then we shall see face to face (v. 12). No Christian began to see God face to face when the book of Revelation was finished, and nobody alive knows God as fully as God knows him. The then of this passage is the day we see him. So this passage does not, by itself, prove that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles, though some careful teachers have concluded so.

The case on other ground. The case for their ceasing rests on the grounds noted at v. 8. It adds that a church expecting fresh revelation is exposed to every confident voice, and observes that much of what is called prophecy or tongues today bears little resemblance to Acts, where tongues were known languages (Acts 2:6–11). B. B. Warfield argued it a century ago, and it deserves a serious answer rather than a sneer.

The other side, fairly stated. Paul told this church plainly, do not forbid speaking in tongues (14:39), and told another, do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, but test everything (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Those are commands, and continuationist brothers point out that no verse announces their repeal. Today’s claimed gifts often look unlike the New Testament’s, they argue, which calls for testing them, not abolishing the category; and in Corinth, unlike at Pentecost, no one understood a tongue without interpretation (14:2). Cessationists answer that commands to churches with living apostles and prophets assume conditions that no longer hold, as the instructions about apostolic visits do. Godly men such as Martyn Lloyd-Jones have been open to the continuationist view.

So where should an ordinary believer land? The cessationist case, made on that other ground, is the stronger (see the box below). But three things can be said with confidence, and they are enough to live by. First, this passage forbids looking down on a brother who reached the other conclusion; the chapter is about love, and a man who wins this argument uncharitably has lost the chapter. Second, no gift is the mark of the Spirit’s presence; the mark is the confession that Jesus is Lord (12:3). Third, and this is Paul’s actual point, all of it is partial. Both sides are arguing about equipment for a journey that is nearly over.

What it does not mean. Not that Scripture is partial or imperfect; it is complete and sufficient for this age (2 Timothy 3:16–17). But our knowledge, even with Scripture, is partial compared with seeing Christ. The map is perfect; our reading of it is still the reading of travellers.

If the gifts have ceased, does God still heal and guide today? Yes. Cessationism means not that God has stopped working, but that the gifts by which the apostles and prophets received new revelation and confirmed it with signs were for the foundation period. God still answers prayer and still heals the sick, sometimes in ways no doctor can explain; James tells us to call the elders and pray (James 5:14–15). He still guides his people through his word, wise counsel, providence, and the Spirit’s illumination of Scripture. What he does not do is add new revelation to the Bible. A strong impression in prayer may be used by God, but it must be weighed by Scripture, never given Scripture’s authority.

What should I do if my church, or a friend, believes the gifts continue? Love them, and keep the main thing the main thing. Many continuationists are sound on the gospel, love the Bible, and put cessationists to shame in prayer and evangelism. Be clear about what you believe and why, but do not make it a test of fellowship among those who confess Christ crucified. Watch for two things in any setting: whether claimed words from God are tested by Scripture and kept below it, and whether Christ and the gospel stay at the centre. Where those hold, there is real unity to enjoy.

Where Christians differ: what is the perfect? Some cessationists (who hold that the revelatory and sign gifts have ceased) argue that the perfect is the completed New Testament canon (the finished collection of Scripture’s books), so that tongues and prophecy ceased when Scripture was finished. Continuationists (who hold that all the gifts continue) argue that since the perfect is Christ’s return, the gifts must continue until then. This commentary’s view: The perfect is best understood as the return of Christ and the age to come, when we will see face to face and know fully. This verse says that these gifts will certainly end by then; it does not say whether some of them might end sooner. The case for the cessation of the revelatory and sign gifts rests on other texts: the foundational and unrepeatable role of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), the confirmation of the apostolic message by signs (Hebrews 2:3–4), and the closing of the canon (Jude 3).
verseByVerse.note: “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things when Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our present knowledge of God is like a child’s: true, but small, and one day we will grow out of it into something far fuller. Paul is explaining what he means by partial.

When I was a child. This is often read as a rebuke, as though Paul were telling the Corinthians to stop being childish. He does that elsewhere (3:1; 14:20), but not mainly here. There is nothing wrong with a child’s speech. A three-year-old’s thinking is real thinking, and on its own scale it works. It is simply small: he is not mistaken about the world; he has less of it.

Childish ways. Gave up is the same word as pass away in verses 8 and 10 (katargeō). The present gifts are like childhood speech compared with the maturity of the age to come. There may also be a gentle rebuke in the background: the Corinthians, proud of tongues, were acting like children.

True knowledge on a child’s scale. That is Paul’s verdict on our present knowledge of God, and it rules out two errors. One is the confidence that imagines our systems and creeds have God mapped, with nothing left to astonish us. The other is the fashionable humility that says nothing can really be known. The child does know his mother. He simply does not yet know what she gave up for him, what she fears at three in the morning, or what she was like at twenty. What comes next is not a correction of his knowledge but a growing up into it, and growing up is not something a child achieves by concentrating. It happens to him. So does this: when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). One day the child will see his Father’s face and understand what the Father gave up for him, and then, at last, he will know how to thank him.

Firm and light. So hold convictions firmly and carry them lightly: on the harder questions you are, at present, three feet tall. A church divided over prophecy and tongues is a nursery of children shouting about a subject on which every one of them speaks like a child. That is an argument not for indifference but for the patience this chapter describes.

How do I know which convictions to hold firmly and which lightly? Hold most firmly what Scripture states most clearly and the church has confessed together through the ages: the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by faith alone, the authority of Scripture, his return. Hold more lightly conclusions that depend on harder texts and on which faithful Bible-believing Christians have long differed, such as the details of the gifts, church government, or the order of end-time events. Believe and teach them, but do not treat the brother who differs as an enemy of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we know God truly but indirectly, as in a dim mirror; then we will see him face to face and know him as fully as he already knows us. Here is the great hope of the Christian, and the ground of the whole chapter.

In a mirror dimly. Corinth was famous for its bronze, and mirrors were polished metal, giving back a darkened, slightly warped face: recognisably you, and never quite you. Dimly (en ainigmati) is literally in a riddle, from which we get enigma. Our present sight of God is not blindness: we see him truly, through his word and works. But we see him indirectly, as a face in dark metal, or a riddle that is genuinely about him.

But then face to face. The hope of the whole Bible in three words. God spoke to Moses mouth to mouth, clearly and not in riddles (Numbers 12:8), and Paul’s word for dimly echoes that verse. Yet when Moses asked for one thing more, “Please show me your glory,” he was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live”; he was put in a cleft of the rock, covered with a hand, and allowed to see the back of God going past (Exodus 33:18–23). The barrier was not distance but holiness: sinful man cannot stand before the unveiled purity of God (Isaiah 6:5).

They will see his face. The last page of the Bible says of ordinary redeemed people, without ceremony: “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). What Moses was not given, the least believer is promised, because something will have happened to him first: he will have been made holy, washed in the blood of the Lamb, so that the sight which would have undone him becomes his joy (Hebrews 12:14; Revelation 7:14). The church has called this the beatific vision, the sight of God that makes us blessed, our full and final happiness (Psalm 16:11; 17:15).

Whose face will we see? The face of God in Christ. The glory of God has already shone in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and on that day we will see the Son, risen and glorified, with the marks of the nails still on him (John 20:27; Revelation 5:6), and in him the Father (John 14:9). We will not see the divine essence with bodily eyes, for God is spirit and infinite, but we will know him directly, without veil or riddle, as fully as creatures can.

Then I shall know fully. Not infinitely, as God knows, but without the distortions and gaps of the present.

Even as I have been fully known. God already knows us completely (8:3; Galatians 4:9). In merely human love you are either loved by people who do not fully know you, who love a version of you assembled from your better hours, or known by someone who has seen the worst and whose affection you can feel adjusting. Underneath runs one fear: if they knew everything, they would not stay. Paul writes of God, “I have been fully known”, in the past tense: already accomplished. There is no file not yet opened, nothing that will emerge in the last hour and change the verdict. The one who knows the whole of it, the thing you have never told anyone, the thing you would not put in a prayer, is the one who set his love on you before you had done anything at all.

The ground of the whole chapter. A person who is fully known and fully loved has nothing left to protect, and a person with nothing to protect can afford to be patient, kind, unenvious, and to keep no record of wrongs. Love like this is not squeezed out of the loveless by effort. It leaks out of people who have stopped being afraid of being found out.

He looked at the whole record. The Son of God knew exactly what he was buying. He looked at the whole record, not the edited version, and went to the cross for it anyway, so that on some morning still ahead he could stand before the people he died for with nothing hidden on either side, and be looked at. That is what he wanted: not servants at a distance, but a face to face. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

In everyday life. Think of the thing you most fear being known about you. Bring it to God by name: he knew it before you told him and loves you no less. Then, in one relationship this week, stop protecting yourself a little: admit a fault, ask forgiveness, let yourself be seen. People who are fully known by God can afford it.

Will we recognise one another? Scripture gives good reason to think so. If our knowledge then is fuller, we will not know less than we do now. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Matthew 17:3–4); the risen Jesus was known by those who loved him; Paul expects to glory over the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). The relationships of grace are not erased but perfected, and every face we know will be turned the same way, toward his.

What happens to believers who die before that day? They are with the Lord at once, consciously and gladly: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). They do not sleep in unconsciousness, and there is no purgatory between. Yet the fullest face to face waits for the resurrection, when Christ returns and body and soul are reunited in glory (15:51–54).
verseByVerse.note: Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect reflection; Corinth was famous for its bronze work. The ESV notes that “dimly” is literally “in a riddle.”

parallels.desc: with him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles

verseByVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith, hope and love are what last, and the greatest of them is love. The chapter that began by pricing the gifts ends by naming what will outlive them.

Faith, hope, and love abide. Abide (menō) means to remain, to last. The three appear together all over Paul’s letters (1 Thessalonians 1:3; Colossians 1:4–5), and between them they cover a believer’s whole life: faith takes hold of what God has done, hope leans forward to what he will do, and love is how he lives now.

But the greatest of these is love. Why? Faith saves; love does not. Faith is how a sinner is justified, declared righteous by God for Christ’s sake, and Paul of all people will not demote it. The answer is in the word abide. Faith is trusting a God you cannot see, and when Christ returns you will see him, so faith will have become sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Hope waits for what has not yet arrived, and then it will have arrived, so hope will have become possession (Romans 8:24). Neither is lost; each is swallowed by its own fulfilment. Some careful readers think faith and hope remain in glory in a changed form, as endless trust and glad expectation; even so, love is greatest, for God himself is love (1 John 4:8, 16).

Why love alone remains. Faith and hope are things creatures do: God does not trust, because he knows, and does not hope, because he holds. Love alone arrives unchanged, because there is nothing better for it to turn into. It is the only thing in the Christian life that will be doing in eternity exactly what it does now, which is why practising it is the one activity of this life that is not preparation for something else.

What hope is. In ordinary speech hope is a shrug: I hope it stays dry, I hope the scan is clear. Biblical hope is the confident expectation of a good God has promised and not yet handed over, as sure as his word but not yet here. Everyone lives on some hope: the next job, the right person, the children doing well, a comfortable retirement. Whatever it is quietly rules our moods, for when it wobbles, we wobble, and every such hope can be taken away. Christian hope cannot, because it is not finally a thing but a Person. God “has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). It is living because he is. The tomb that should have ended it is empty, so the future is not a gamble but an appointment, and Paul can simply call him “Christ Jesus our hope” (1 Timothy 1:1). See also Hope in the Theological Dictionary.

Three ways of holding on to Christ. Faith, hope and love are not free-standing virtues; all three are fixed “in our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Faith rests on what Christ has done; hope waits for him to appear; love is his own love, poured into his people and flowing out through them. So the three that abide are three ways of holding on to one Person, and the chapter ends by pointing past every gift to him.

In the flow. This verse opens the next chapter, which tells the church to pursue love and desire the gifts (14:1), and the letter ends with one instruction for everything: “Let all that you do be done in love” (16:14). Corinth’s troubles, from factions to lawsuits to the Lord’s Supper, were at bottom failures of love, and this is the cure.

In everyday life. When something you were counting on falls through this week, say plainly: that was something I hoped for, but it was never my hope; and lift your eyes to the One who is coming. At the end of today, ask not only, did I believe? did I hope? but, did I love? Thank God for one person you loved well; confess one you did not, and plan one concrete act of love for that person tomorrow. Then go to sleep resting in his love, not yours: only he has ever loved perfectly, and he did it for you.

If love is greater, does it save us? No. We are justified by faith alone, not by our love. Faith is not the greatest virtue, but it is the empty hand that receives Christ, whose righteousness is what saves (Romans 3:28; 5:1). Love is the fruit, not the root. A faith that produces no love is dead (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17), but even the believer’s best love is imperfect, and if we had to stand on it we would fall. We stand on Christ’s love for us, received by faith, and that love then begins to love through us.

If love is what matters most, why do Christians make so much of doctrine? Because love needs to know what is true in order to do good. A friend who warmly waves you onto a bridge he knows is down has not loved you, however kindly he smiles. The love of this chapter rejoices with the truth (v. 6), and it is defined by a historical event, God sending his Son to die for sinners (1 John 4:9–10); take away the truth about Christ and love shrinks to a warm feeling that cannot save anyone. The opposite mistake is just as real: correct doctrine without love is the noisy gong of verse 1. The aim is not truth or love but both: truth spoken in love (Ephesians 4:15).

13.text: <sup>1</sup>If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.<sup>2</sup>And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.<sup>3</sup>If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.<sup>4</sup>Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant<sup>5</sup>or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;<sup>6</sup>it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.<sup>7</sup>Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.<sup>8</sup>Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.<sup>9</sup>For we know in part and we prophesy in part,<sup>10</sup>but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.<sup>11</sup>When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.<sup>12</sup>For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

keyVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s argument comes to rest here. The gifts the Corinthians prized belong to this passing age, but faith, hope and love remain, and love is the greatest because it alone will be doing in eternity exactly what it does now, for God is love. This one verdict puts every gift, every debate and every ambition in its place.

13.reflection:
Paul says that tongues, prophecy, great faith and even costly sacrifice are worth nothing without love (vv. 1–3). How is it possible to be highly gifted and yet loveless? Which of your own gifts or kinds of service is most in danger of becoming mere noise?

Read verses 4–7 aloud with Jesus’ name in place of love, and then with your own. What does each reading show you? Which phrase was hardest to say with your own name, and how does the first reading help with the second?

Love “is not irritable or resentful” and “bears all things”, yet Paul himself confronted sin and named those who did harm. How can we keep no record of wrongs without covering up wrongdoing or abuse?

Paul looks forward to knowing fully, “even as I have been fully known” (v. 12). How does being fully known and still loved by God free us to love others? How should the hope of seeing Christ face to face shape the way a church handles its disagreements, including those about spiritual gifts?

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 completes Paul’s answer about spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14). Chapter 12 showed that every gift comes from one Spirit for the good of one body; chapter 13 that love is the way every gift must be used. Now Paul applies that love to what actually happened when the Corinthians met.

The message. Love wants the people around it built up, and only what is understood can build them up. So in the gathered church the test of every gift is not how spiritual it looks or feels, but whether the person in the next seat, and the stranger at the back, is helped to know God. The God who is “not a God of confusion but of peace” (v. 33) is honoured by worship that is clear, ordered and full of his word.

Why it was said. Spiritual gifts in Corinth, especially tongues, had become marks of status (see the introduction). The meetings had grown noisy and confused: many spoke in tongues at once, with no one interpreting, prophets talked over one another, and a visitor could make nothing of it. Underneath lay a church acting as though its worship was its own to invent (v. 36).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul first ranks the gifts by love: prophecy, spoken in words people understand, builds up the church, while an uninterpreted tongue reaches God alone (vv. 1–5). He presses the point with pictures, a tuneless flute, an unclear bugle, a foreign language, and with his own example: pray and sing with the mind as well as the spirit, so that others can say Amen; five words that teach outweigh ten thousand in a tongue (vv. 6–19). From Isaiah he shows that speech no one understands is a sign of judgment that leaves unbelievers outside, while plain prophecy can lay bare a stranger’s heart and bring him to worship (vv. 20–25). Then come practical rules: everything for building up; tongues and prophecy in turn and few in number; tongues only with interpretation; prophecy always weighed, and women not taking part in that weighing; all because God is a God of peace, and because this is the Lord’s command, shared by all the churches (vv. 26–38). Paul ends by holding eager desire and good order together (vv. 39–40).

Where it leads. The God who wants to be understood has spoken his clearest word in his Son, the Word made flesh, who taught so that a child could follow him and spoke peace to a storm. Plain words about Christ are what lay a stranger’s heart bare, and his presence is what the stranger finally confesses: “God is really among you” (v. 25). The gifts will fall silent, but the Lamb who was slain will be praised for ever by a multitude in which every voice is distinct and all are one.

For us. Few churches today struggle with a room full of tongues, but many have their own ways of leaving people outside: jargon, performance, worship that suits only the few who lead it. Ask of everything done in church who is built up by it, and come ready to give as well as to receive, so that a visitor might go home saying that God is truly here.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love chooses the gift that helps others most, and in the gathered church that is prophecy. Paul keeps love as the aim and the gifts as its tools (v. 1), then sets two gifts side by side: an uninterpreted tongue speaks mysteries to God that no one else understands, while prophecy speaks to people to build them up, encourage and console them (vv. 2–3). So the one builds up the speaker and the other the church, and only interpretation can make a tongue as useful as prophecy (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Understanding Comes Before Building Up

The God who speaks is a God who makes himself known, so worship that puts his word out of the people’s reach works against him (see the note on v. 6, which also traces the Reformers’ insistence on worship in the people’s own language).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the factions. Paul’s preference for prophecy puts the good of all above the spectacular. Now: The same test reaches beyond tongues (see vv. 4–5). Does the person who attends understand what is happening, and is he being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep love as your aim, and within it set your heart on the gifts, above all on prophecy, because a tongue speaks only to God while prophecy speaks to the people in the room.

Pursue love. After a chapter saying that gifts without love are worth nothing, the obvious inference would be to stop caring about gifts. Paul heads that off at once: love is not an alternative to gifts but the way they are to be used. Pursue (diōkō) is a hunter’s word: chase it down.

Especially that you may prophesy. “Earnestly desire” is the verb behind our word zeal: be zealous for both, love first and gifts within it. And among the gifts, prophecy, because the people in the room can understand it and so be built up. “Love builds up” (8:1) will now test everything in worship.

Not to men but to God. Without interpretation a tongue is prayer or praise addressed to God, not teaching for the congregation (vv. 14–16).

Mysteries in the Spirit. “Understands” is literally “hears”: people hear the sounds, but no one grasps the meaning. Mysteries here are not riddles but the things of God, spoken in a form the listeners cannot open.

What tongues were. A tongue (glōssa) is simply a language. In Corinth no one present knew it, so a separate gift of interpretation was needed. Three things are certain: it was genuine speech given by the Spirit, it was addressed to God, and hearers could not understand it unless it was interpreted. Whether these were real languages is weighed in the box below.

Not the mark of the Spirit. Tongues are not the sign of a Spirit-filled Christian; that was settled at 12:3 and 12:30. The Spirit gave different gifts to different people, Corinth had turned the difference into a ranking, and this chapter patiently takes the ranking apart.

Love first, because love is his. Why must love come before the gifts? Because the love of chapter 13 is not an ideal Paul invented but a portrait of Christ, and it is how the Son of God used every power he had. He could have turned stones into bread and would not do it for himself (Matthew 4:3–4); he had all authority and spent it washing feet and carrying a cross. So the order of this verse is the shape of his life: gifts are tools, and love is the likeness of the Son that God is making in his people (Romans 8:29).

Is the private prayer language some Christians speak of today the same thing? This commentary holds that it is not. New Testament tongues were real languages, a sign gift, whose chief purpose was to mark the apostles’ message as God’s own, as signs and wonders did (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). It belonged to the apostolic foundation, the once-for-all laying of the church’s base by the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20): a foundation is laid once, and then the house is built on it. Scripture gives no warrant for a private prayer language for later believers. Many sincere Christians who practise something they call tongues love Christ deeply, and should be treated as brothers and sisters, not mocked. They point to verses 4 and 28, where the speaker builds himself up and speaks to himself and to God; Paul did allow such speech, but he was describing a gift of his own day, not promising it to every later believer.

Free to pray. No Christian needs such an experience to pray fully and freely. The Spirit helps every believer in his weakness and intercedes for him (Romans 8:26), and you may pour out your heart to your Father in your own words.

Where Christians differ: what were tongues? Some think the Corinthian tongues were ecstatic, non-human speech, pointing to 14:2, where no one understands the speaker, and to the tongues of angels (13:1); others that they were real human languages, as at Pentecost. This commentary’s view: at Pentecost tongues were known human languages, understood by foreigners (Acts 2:6–11); Paul’s own analogy here is foreign languages (vv. 10–11), and interpretation means translation. So tongues were most naturally real languages the speaker had not learned. The tongues of angels (13:1) are a hypothetical extreme, not a description of the gift.

Uncertain wording. “In the Spirit” translates one word (pneumati), which can mean the Holy Spirit or the speaker’s own spirit (the ESV notes “or in his spirit”); “my spirit” in verse 14 slightly favours the second. The sense is much the same either way: words given by the Spirit, spoken from the depths of the person rather than from his understanding.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophecy speaks to people in words they understand, and its mark is what it does to them: it builds them up, strengthens them and comforts them.

For their upbuilding. Paul defines prophecy not by its source, its feel, or whether it predicts anything, but by its effect: a usable test, for the church can see what happened to the people who heard it. Upbuilding (oikodomē) is the builder’s word and the key word of the chapter (vv. 3, 4, 5, 12, 17, 26): the congregation is a structure going up, and this kind of speech adds another row of stones.

And encouragement and consolation. Encouragement (paraklēsis), from a verb for calling someone to your side, means putting strength into a person, by urging or by comfort. Consolation (paramythia) is the plain word for what you say to the grieving. Prophecy as most people imagine it is dramatic, predictive and slightly alarming; as Paul describes it, it leaves a congregation stronger, braver and comforted. A word that leaves people frightened, confused or impressed with the speaker has failed this test, whatever it claimed about its source.

Another Helper. Jesus used the same family of words. In the upper room he promised another Helper, the Paraklētos, the one called alongside (John 14:16). “Another”, because they already had one: Jesus had walked beside them, putting strength into the weak and comfort into the grieving (1 John 2:1), and the Spirit would bring to their remembrance all that he had said (John 14:26). So words that build up and console are at their truest Christ’s words, carried by his Spirit into a room that needs them.

What it does not mean. Not that prophecy was only encouragement and never correction; it could expose sin (vv. 24–25). Nor that it is the same as preaching, though they share these purposes. Preaching expounds a text already given; prophecy here was something said into a particular room on a particular day, which then had to be weighed (see vv. 29–31).

If prophecy has ceased, what does this verse ask of me? A great deal. These three effects are what preaching should aim at, and what any Christian’s conversation after the service may aim at, whether or not the gift continues. Somebody in the room this Sunday needs building up, somebody needs courage, somebody needs consoling, and the words that do it, drawn from Scripture, are the nearest thing to this verse most of us will ever handle (1 Thessalonians 5:11; Hebrews 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tongue builds up the one who speaks, but prophecy builds up the whole church, so in the meeting prophecy is the greater gift unless the tongue is interpreted.

Builds up himself. Not a sneer but a fact: the speaker might be edified by praising God even without understanding the words. But gifts are for the common good (12:7), and Corinth had made something that built up the individual the centrepiece of the gathering.

Even more to prophesy. “I want you all to speak in tongues” is a wish, not an expectation that all will (12:30), like his wish that all were single as he was (7:7). Paul is not removing anything but reordering it, which is the harder and better kind of correction.

Unless someone interprets. Greater means more useful to the church, and the qualifier shows why: interpreted tongues do what prophecy does, because the room understands and is built up. The greatness Paul measures is not in the gift itself but in how many people benefit.

So that the church may be built up. The test for everything, and it reaches far beyond tongues: the sermon full of allusions the congregation cannot catch, the prayer meeting a newcomer could not join, the music pitched where only the musicians can sing it. The activity may be excellent; the question is whether anyone else is being built by it, or only the one doing it.

Christ did not please himself. Paul uses the same building word in Romans and grounds it in a Person: let each of us please his neighbour for his good, to build him up, for Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:2–3). That is the deepest reason why a gift that edifies only its owner cannot be the centrepiece of worship. The Son of God had every right to please himself, and chose the road that saved his people. A church that measures its gatherings by whether others are built up is being shaped like its Lord.

Is it wrong to go to church for what I get out of it? Not wrong, but incomplete. Come hungry to be fed by the word and to meet God, who delights to feed you; but come for the others too. Every believer comes as a member of a body, with something to give as well as to receive (12:7). The two are not rivals: the Christian who comes to serve is very often the one who goes home most fed, and the one who comes only to consume is often the first to complain that he got nothing.

parallels.desc: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Speech that no one understands helps no one, so worship must reach the mind as well as the spirit. Paul imagines himself arriving with tongues and nothing else (v. 6), then presses the point with pictures: a flute that never becomes a tune, a bugle no soldier can make out, a foreign language that turns neighbours into strangers (vv. 7–11). So the Corinthians should turn their eagerness for the Spirit to building up the church (v. 12): pray to interpret, and pray and sing with the mind as well as the spirit, so that others can say Amen (vv. 13–17). Paul, who speaks in tongues more than any of them, would still rather speak five words that teach (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship as the Act of a Body

Paul’s insistence on understanding rests on what a Christian gathering is: not a private experience shared by many individuals at once, but one body built up together. That requires understanding: no one can say Amen to what he cannot follow, and a congregation’s Amen is the sign that the body is truly worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The enthusiasts for tongues were bringing a private practice into the meeting without asking whether the rest could take part. Paul’s five words against ten thousand are a principle: ask whether what is done can be received and answered by the whole church. Now: The principle applies to any part of worship that puts the experience of some above the building up of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even an apostle speaking in tongues would do the church no good unless he brought it something it could understand. Paul courteously puts himself in the frame.

How will I benefit you. The same question, whose advantage is served, governed the argument about idol meat (10:23, 33). Paul does not ask whether an activity is spiritual, permitted or sincere, but whether anyone is better off.

Revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching. Not four synonyms. Revelation is a message God discloses, and prophecy that message spoken into this room now; knowledge is a grasp of the truth, and teaching the patient explanation that makes it stick. All four have this in common: the hearer understands.

All four in one Person. Behind the argument lies the character of God. Unlike the mute idols of 12:2, he speaks, and when he came in person he came as the Word. All four meet in Jesus Christ: he is the revelation of the Father (Matthew 11:27); in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3); he is the Prophet Moses promised, to whom the people must listen (Acts 3:22). The eternal Word became flesh and told stories about seeds and coins and lost sheep, so that a child could follow him and a scholar never exhaust him. Everything about him leans toward being understood, so worship that puts God’s truth out of the people’s reach runs against the grain of who he is.

The Reformation and the ploughboy. That conviction is why the Reformers fought for services in the people’s language, and why William Tyndale vowed that a boy driving the plough would one day know more of the Scriptures than the learned cleric he was arguing with. A Latin service in an English village failed this verse as an uninterpreted tongue failed it in Corinth: true and beautiful words, and the man in the back row went home with nothing.

Things that are nobody’s fault. A preacher who quotes Greek untranslated, or a hymn whose language was ordinary in 1780 and is now a puzzle, leaves somebody outside with no bad intent at all. And Paul asks about benefit, not interest: a congregation can find a sermon interesting and go home with nobody stronger by the end.

In everyday life. When you explain your faith to a friend this week, drop the church words and say it in the language you would use about anything else that mattered to you.

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sound without clear meaning is useless, and when it is meant to call people to action it is dangerous.

The flute or the harp. Notes that never resolve into a tune. An orchestra tuning up is a wonderful noise, and nobody hums it on the way home: no single sound is wrong, but the shape that makes sound into music is missing. That is what uninterpreted tongues do to a service.

If the bugle gives an indistinct sound. The second picture has consequences. A bugle in a camp was command: different calls meant advance, retreat, gather, stand to. A bugler who blows something ambiguous does not produce a slightly confused response; he produces a camp of men looking at each other while the enemy comes over the ridge.

From taste to survival. The flute shows that unclear sound is unpleasant; the bugle, that it is dangerous, for a congregation that cannot make out what is said cannot obey it. So for anyone who speaks to God’s people clarity is a duty, not a style preference, and a sermon admired but not understood has failed as the bugle failed. The Levites in Nehemiah’s day read from the Law clearly and gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8). Israel in the wilderness gathered and set out by trumpet calls whose meaning never changed (Numbers 10:1–7), and God’s people still depend on a clear signal. Muddled teaching hurts most those with least background: the new believer, the visitor, the man who came in troubled and needed one clear sentence and was given a beautiful fog.

The one clear note. What note must every Christian voice sound distinctly? Paul told this church: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (2:2), and he names the tune at 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. A church may be uncertain about many secondary things and survive, but not about him: a man who does not know whether his sins are forgiven cannot get ready for any battle, least of all the last. Christ himself never sounded an uncertain note: the crowds were astonished, because he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes (Matthew 7:29). And one trumpet will give no uncertain sound: “the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). On that day no one will mistake the call.

What if I am not a gifted speaker? Clarity is not eloquence; it is saying one true thing in a way the listener can take home. Before you speak about Christ, ask what one thing you want this person to understand; say that, in ordinary words, and stop. Some of the clearest witnesses in the church would never call themselves speakers at all.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet sounded signals to soldiers in battle.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speech nobody understands reaches nobody, and it turns the people in the room into foreigners to one another.

Speaking into the air. Intelligible (eusēmos) means clear, distinct. “You will be speaking into the air” sums up the chapter, and it is more desolate than it sounds. Such words are wasted, like the blows of a boxer beating the air (9:26): not nonsense, not wicked, but real words that reach nobody, sound going out into an empty room and dispersing.

None is without meaning. A generous concession: languages (phōnai, literally voices, sounds) all carry meaning. Paul is not saying tongues were gibberish; the problem is the gap between speaker and hearer.

A foreigner. The word (barbaros) began as Greek snobbery, probably imitating how foreign speech sounded: bar-bar-bar. A foreigner was a barbarian, a person who made noises. Anyone who has stood in a hospital in a foreign country knows the feeling: surrounded by meaning, cut out of all of it. The comparison also supports the view that tongues were real languages.

Strangers in God’s house. The gift Corinth prized most was producing, in the person three feet away, the loneliness of a stranger abroad, in the one place on earth where nobody is supposed to be a foreigner. Christ died to end exactly that: those once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:13, 19). The cross tore down a wall, and Corinth was rebuilding it out of syllables. At Babel God confused the languages and the nations were scattered; at Pentecost he spoke the one gospel in many languages and the nations began to be gathered. Christ has made foreigners into family.

Any church can manufacture barbarians. A congregation that would never make the Corinthian error can do it with unexplained jargon, in-jokes, a way of praying outsiders cannot join, and the assumption that everyone knows where the book is kept. None of it is malicious; all of it tells the person at the back: you are not from here.

How can our church help a newcomer not feel like a foreigner? Small things do most of the work. Say who is speaking and what comes next. Give page numbers and Bible references, and explain a word like justification or communion the first time it is used. Make sure someone sits with a visitor, shows him the reading, talks with him afterwards about something other than the weather, and asks him to lunch. Each says what Paul wants said: you are welcome here, and this is meant for you too.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you are eager for the Spirit’s gifts, put that eagerness to work building up the church.

Eager for manifestations of the Spirit. Literally, “you are zealots for spirits”. A model of correcting without crushing: Paul takes their eagerness as given and turns it round. You want the Spirit’s manifestations, so excel at what they are for.

Strive to excel in building up the church. Excel (perisseuō) means to abound. Paul does not abolish the Corinthian instinct to outdo one another; he gives it a new field. If you must compete, compete at doing the most good to the people in this room. In this league table the member who has quietly rebuilt the confidence of a struggling family is winning, and does not know there is a competition.

The test. For any activity in a church, ask not “was it spiritual?” or “did I feel God in it?” but “who is stronger because of it?” And the test exposes a quiet idol. Corinth’s appetite for spiritual display was at bottom a hunger to be somebody. The gospel ends that hunger by giving us a standing we could never win, for in Christ we are already loved, chosen and made holy (1:2, 30), and people who no longer need to be impressive are free to be useful.

Zeal for his house. There was once zeal pointed exactly where Paul points the Corinthians’. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, his disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9). His zeal was not for experiences but for the house of God, and it took him to the cross. That house is now the church (3:16): spend your zeal where he spent his.

A word for the flat. Some Christians are eager for nothing: they have never longed for more of God or asked him for anything they could not arrange themselves, and they mistake their flatness for maturity. Paul’s command assumes the eagerness is there. This is not a word against the grieving or the depressed, whose flatness is suffering, not choice; the Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), and he does not ask them to manufacture feelings.

How do I find out what I can do to build up my church? Ask your elders where there is need, and offer to fill it. Notice what others thank you for, and what you care about unasked. Pray for the people around you, one face at a time, and you will soon see what they need. Most building up is ordinary: a meal taken round, a child taught, a hand held at a funeral, a verse given at the right moment. Faithfulness in small things is how gifts are discovered.

In everyday life. Somewhere in your church this week is a family having a hard time that nobody has noticed. Eagerness for God, pointed the right way, looks like a meal on their doorstep or a message asking how they really are.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship must engage the mind as well as the spirit, so the one who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret it.

Pray that he may interpret. If you have the one gift, ask God for the other, so that the tongue can benefit others.

My mind is unfruitful. “My spirit” is the inner person moved by the Spirit; mind (nous) is the understanding. Unfruitful (akarpos) does not mean the speaker is in a trance and not responsible, for Paul’s next sentence says “I will” four times, a man deciding what to do. It means his mind is producing nothing anyone can pick up.

With my mind also. Not one or the other, but both. Paul refuses the two great mistakes about worship. The first wants the spirit without the mind: worship as pure experience, where thinking is felt to interrupt the feeling and doctrine is an obstacle to it. The second wants the mind without the spirit: worship as instruction only, correct and cold, where a congregation could sing about the blood of Christ with the expressions of people reading a timetable, and any warmth is suspected of being manipulation. Each cuts off half of the worshipper, and each is usually a reaction against the other.

Singing with the mind. The rule covers singing, where most Christians meet it: singing words we understand and mean, letting the word of Christ dwell in us richly (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19). Anyone who has reached the end of a hymn with no memory of the middle verse knows how possible it is to sing with neither.

The whole man at prayer. Jesus prayed exactly so. In Gethsemane he offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and no prayer was ever more deeply felt; yet it was entirely clear: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). That night, after the Supper, he sang a hymn with his disciples, very likely the psalms that end the Passover (Matthew 26:30), and meant every word. Spirit and mind were never at war in him. The one true worshipper the world has seen worshipped with all of himself, and that is the pattern Paul is restoring to Corinth.

I often feel nothing when I sing. Is my worship worthless? No. Feelings rise and fall with tiredness, health and grief, and God does not measure worship by them. He asks that you mean what you sing, mind engaged and will offered to him; sometimes that is all a weary believer can give, and it is a true offering. Very often warmth returns as the mind is filled with what God has done, and on the days it does not, the Spirit still carries your praise to the Father.

In everyday life. Before the service, read the words of what you are about to sing. During the prayers, mean the Amen. Afterwards, ask what was said. That is praying with the mind, and it costs a Christian not one degree of warmth.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prayer others cannot understand shuts them out, because no one can say Amen to words he cannot follow.

Say “Amen”. Amen is Hebrew, taken over from the synagogue untranslated, and means firm, sure: so be it. It was the congregation’s response to prayers (Nehemiah 8:6; Psalm 106:48). When one person prays aloud and the congregation says Amen, they are not being polite; they are signing the prayer, and it becomes theirs.

The position of an outsider. The outsider (idiōtēs) is an ordinary, uninstructed person: the enquirer, the newcomer, the person who came because a friend asked him. Since you cannot say Amen to what you do not understand, he has not merely missed a nice moment. He has been shut out of the congregation’s prayer, present at it and unable to join it: the one guest who most needed including, quietly left out by the thing everyone else found most exciting.

Sincerity is not the test. Paul concedes that the thanksgiving is real (“you may be giving thanks well enough”), and God has heard it; but it fails in its public purpose. Something can be entirely genuine and God-directed and still wrong in a service, because of who else was in the room. Paul’s test in these chapters is never sincerity but what it does for the person next to you.

The Yes beneath every Amen. A congregation can say Amen firmly because all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). Jesus Christ is himself the Amen, the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14). A Christian’s Amen is not a hopeful guess that God might do what was asked, but a signature under promises Christ has already secured by his death and resurrection. And the outsider most needs to hear those promises in words he can follow, so that one day he too may say Amen through Christ.

Should I say Amen out loud in church? Yes, if your church’s practice allows it, and most do. It is a biblical way of joining the prayer and encouraging the one who led it; where the custom is quieter, a silent Amen from the heart is still yours to give. What matters is that you have followed the prayer and mean it. You need not sign a prayer you cannot agree with, but an honest Amen is one of the simplest ways to share in worship.

Uncertain wording. “Anyone in the position of an outsider” is literally “the one who fills the place of the idiōtēs”. A few take “place” literally, as a recognised seat for enquirers; most take it to mean anyone in that condition. Whether the idiōtēs is an uninstructed believer or a visitor outside the faith is also unclear (in vv. 23–24 he stands beside the unbeliever but is named separately). Either way, whoever cannot follow cannot join.
verseByVerse.note: “Amen” (“so be it”) was the congregation’s response to prayer and thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prized tongues more than any of them, yet in the gathered church a few words that teach outweigh any number that do not.

More than all of you. Paul is not criticising tongues out of jealousy or lack: he had the gift abundantly, more than the congregation most famous for it, and his attitude is not tolerance but gratitude. Every rule in this chapter comes from someone who prized what he was regulating.

In church. In the gathered congregation: the same activity can be excellent in one setting and out of place in another. Instruct (katēcheō, from which we get catechise) means to teach, and its measure is not length but transfer: whether something that was in one head is now in another.

Ten thousand words. Ten thousand (myrioi) is the largest Greek number word, and the ratio, two thousand to one, is a deliberate absurdity. In the assembly, speech understood and speech not understood are not on the same scale: five intelligible words that teach somebody outweigh an entire evening of the other.

Five words. In English, “Christ died for our sins” (15:3) is exactly five, and it is fitting that the sentence which best suits Paul’s number is about Christ, because the instruction that builds a church is always, in the end, about him. There is freedom here for anyone who feels he has nothing to offer: five plain words that instruct one person are, on the apostle’s scale, worth more than the most impressive thing that happened in Corinth that year.

Where did Paul speak in tongues, then? Having spent seventeen verses saying the gift does not belong in the assembly without interpretation, he must have used it chiefly elsewhere: perhaps in his own prayers, perhaps in mission among people of other languages, where tongues could work as at Pentecost. The text does not say. It does show the apostle who travelled constantly, was beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and carried the anxiety of all the churches, giving thanks for every gift God had given him and using each for its purpose.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mature thinking asks what worship does to the outsider who walks in. Paul calls the Corinthians to grow up in their thinking (v. 20) and turns to Isaiah, where foreign speech no one could follow was God’s judgment on people who had mocked his plain word (v. 21). Uninterpreted tongues work the same way: they leave the unbeliever outside, convinced the church is mad (vv. 22–23). Plain prophecy, by contrast, can search his heart, bring him to his knees and make him confess that God is really among you (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who walks into the meeting shows that the church’s worship is not only for the converted. A congregation that worships so that the outsider is addressed, convicted and drawn to worship is doing something a meeting full of tongues cannot do. That does not make evangelism the main purpose of the gathering, which is the glory of God, but it does mean that worship of the living God, when it is understood, reaches outward.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s use of Isaiah turns their pride upside down: uninterpreted tongues are a sign linked with God’s judgment, not his favour. Now: A church whose worship is closed to the outsider (see vv. 9–11) is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be what disturbs him, not the confusion of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grow up in your thinking: Scripture shows that speech people cannot understand is a sign of judgment on unbelief, while prophecy is the sign of God speaking to his own people.

Not children in your thinking. Corinth thought itself advanced; Paul says it is behaving like a toddler, drawn to whatever is loudest and shiniest (13:11).

Infants in evil. The one respect in which he does want them childish: as innocent as a baby about evil, the sort of person who has to have wickedness explained to him, but grown up in understanding (Romans 16:19; Matthew 10:16). And a mature mind, as Paul now shows, cares what each gift does to the outsider who walks in.

In the Law it is written. The Law here means the Scriptures, for the quotation is from Isaiah, and its setting matters. The drunken leaders of Israel mock Isaiah: his plain speech sounds to them like baby talk, a string of nonsense syllables (Isaiah 28:9–10). Very well, says God: if my clear word through a prophet is only babble to you, you shall have a message you genuinely cannot understand. He means the Assyrian army, whose foreign speech would soon be heard in their streets (Isaiah 28:11–12). Unintelligible language was the judgment: the sound of God no longer speaking to them in words they could follow.

A sign for unbelievers. Paul does not mean tongues are a good way to reach unbelievers, but that they work as in Isaiah: the mark of people outside, hearing sounds that carry nothing to them, a sign of judgment, not of welcome. At Pentecost tongues also signalled that the gospel was going to the nations, and many see in them a warning that judgment was coming on the generation that refused its Messiah (Acts 2:40).

A sign for believers. Prophecy is a sign the opposite way: the mark of a God present with his people, showing his favour and speaking in words they understand, and, as verses 24–25 show, bringing unbelievers to faith. So verse 23, where outsiders conclude that a room full of tongues is mad, does not contradict verse 22 but demonstrates it: the sign leaves the outsider outside, just as Isaiah said.

A famine of hearing. One of God’s most fearful judgments is not fire but unintelligibility: a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), a pulpit full of noise, a religion that has stopped saying anything. It can happen to a congregation without anybody deciding it, and those inside are usually the last to notice.

The stone in the same chapter. A few verses later, to the same scoffers, God says that he has laid as a foundation in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, and whoever believes will not be in haste (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament knows who that stone is, and applies it to Christ (Romans 9:32–33; 1 Peter 2:6). So the strange tongues of judgment and the cornerstone of mercy stand in one chapter of Isaiah. Those who mocked God’s plain word were left with babble; those who trust the stone he has laid will not be put to shame. The clearest word God ever spoke is a Person.

What does it look like to be mature in thinking? Weighing things by Scripture, not by how impressive they are. A child is drawn to noise and novelty; a mature believer asks what is true, what builds up and what honours Christ, holds a disputed question patiently, tells the central from the secondary, and is not swept along by whatever is exciting this year. And it goes with innocence about evil: the mature Christian is not the one who knows the most about sin, but the one who knows the most about Christ.

In everyday life. Since you have been washed and made holy in Christ (6:11), guard your innocence: turn away this week from one thing you watch or read that teaches you more about evil than you need to know.

Uncertain wording. Verse 22 is among the hardest sentences in the letter, for at first sight it seems to contradict verses 23–25. “Sign” clearly takes its meaning from the Isaiah quotation; less clear is whether it also carries the Pentecost sense of the gospel going to the nations. The reading above fits both the quotation and verses 23–25 best.
verseByVerse.note: “The Law” here means the Scriptures. In Isaiah, foreign speech (that of the Assyrian invaders) was a sign of judgment on those who refused to listen.

parallels.desc: by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A meeting full of tongues makes an outsider think the church is mad, but a meeting where God’s word is spoken plainly can search his heart and convict him.

If the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues. Paul asks them to picture their meeting, perhaps all the house churches gathered in one place, through the eyes of someone at the door: a neighbour, perhaps, or a husband who finally agreed to come once. He steps in, and everyone is speaking words he cannot understand, all at the same time.

Will they not say that you are out of your minds? Out of your minds (mainomai) means raving, like the frenzy of the pagan cults he knew. He does not conclude that the doctrine is false; he has not heard any. He decides these people are unhinged, goes home, and does not come back. And here is the sting: he was never given the chance to reject Christ. He rejected a room. Paul assumes unbelievers may walk into a Christian gathering, and that worship should be understandable to them when they do.

The offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles. The world finds the gospel foolish anyway, it may be objected, and so it does (1:23). But the offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles are different, and a church may not confuse the two. If people are put off, let it be by Christ crucified, and not because nobody explained anything.

But if all prophesy. Not one gifted speaker doing the work: if all speak God’s word intelligibly, one by one (v. 31), the whole congregation is speaking words that build up, encourage and console.

He is convicted by all, he is called to account by all. Convicted (elenchō) is a courtroom word: exposed, shown his sin. Called to account (anakrinō) is another: examined, searched. Nobody has singled him out; the congregation is talking about God, and the truth spoken plainly does its own work on a man who came only to keep somebody company.
