He came to observe and finds himself on trial, as happens whenever God’s word is intelligible in a room (Hebrews 4:12–13).

Face to face with Jesus. Convict is the word Jesus used for the Spirit’s work: he will convict the world concerning sin, because they do not believe in him (John 16:8–9). So the conviction is never finally about the church’s opinions: the Spirit brings the visitor face to face with Jesus and his own refusal of him, and no one needs secret knowledge about him for that. The same voice that called Lazarus out of the tomb calls dead men to life through the plain speech of ordinary believers. That is a comfort to anyone who feels evangelism requires a technique he lacks. The best thing a congregation can do for the friend it has finally persuaded to come is not to arrange something special, but to be, that Sunday, a people who mean what they say and say it in words he can follow.

Should our services be changed to suit visitors? Not their substance, but their clarity. Watering down the gospel, dropping the hard parts of Scripture or turning worship into entertainment would remove the very word that converts them. But everything should be done so that a visitor can follow it (see vv. 9–11): the clearest worship serves believer and stranger alike.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s word is spoken plainly, a stranger can find his heart laid bare, fall down in worship and confess that God is truly present.

The secrets of his heart are disclosed. More than most of us expect on a Sunday. The unbeliever feels: this is about me; God knows me. The word of God walks into a man’s private rooms and turns on the lights, and he stops hearing about people in general and starts hearing about himself.

Falling on his face. Not a nod of agreement but the posture of awe and surrender, like Ezekiel by the river and John on Patmos, brought down not by the atmosphere of the room but by the holiness of God pressing close, the God before whom Isaiah cried that he was lost, because his eyes had seen the King, the LORD of hosts (Isaiah 6:5).

God is really among you. The sentence Paul wants said about a congregation: not “these people are warm”, or “that was a fine argument”, or “they made me feel welcome”, good as those are, but that God was in the building, through his word convicting hearts.

The nations coming in. The visitor’s words are not new. “Surely God is in you, and there is no other” is what Isaiah promised outsiders would one day say about Israel, foreigners bowing down and confessing that God was there and nowhere else (Isaiah 45:14; compare Zechariah 8:23). Paul lays those promises on a house church in a Greek port: the gathering of the nations has begun, in an ordinary room, one man at a time.

Immanuel in a front room. A visitor can truthfully say God is among a roomful of Corinthians because God has come among us in a Person. Immanuel, God with us, was the name given to the child (Matthew 1:23). The Lord promised that where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is among them (Matthew 18:20), and since Pentecost his Spirit makes the gathered church God’s temple (3:16). So the outsider’s cry is the literal truth about a congregation that meets in Jesus’ name. And Christ is the one before whom every secret will be disclosed, and the one who has borne every secret sin of his people: to be found out by him is to be found by him.

Say something true, and let God be extraordinary. What converts a visitor is not the excellence of the arrangements, the music or the welcome, though none should be neglected, but a congregation talking plainly about a God who is actually there. Corinth thought the way to impress an outsider was to show him something extraordinary. Paul says the way is to say something true, and let God be extraordinary.

What it does not mean. Not that prophecy is the only way unbelievers are converted. The preaching of the gospel does the same today, and the Spirit uses the plain word of Scripture in every age to lay hearts bare and bring sinners to their knees.

Does God want me to feel exposed in church? He wants you to be known, so that you can be healed. A sermon that names the sin you hoped was hidden can hurt, but its purpose is never to shame you, only to bring you to the One who already knows and has come to forgive. The visitor here is not crushed and sent away; he worships. Conviction is the doorway, and on the other side is mercy. When the word finds you out, do not run; confess, and come to Christ.

Is this not just emotional manipulation? A fair question, for churches have sometimes worked up feelings with music, lighting and pressure and called it conviction. But nothing here is staged: only ordinary people speaking God’s truth plainly, one at a time. Manipulation goes around the mind; this goes through it. The man understands what is said, and it is true about him, so the result is not a passing thrill but worship. The word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12), and it needs no help from technique.

parallels.desc: God is with you only
we have heard that God is with you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything in the gathering must build up the church, and the God of peace wants it done in order. Each member may bring something, but all of it serves that one rule (v. 26). So tongues are limited in number, taken in turn and always interpreted (vv. 27–28); prophecy too is limited, taken in turn and weighed by the church (vv. 29–31); and no one may plead that the Spirit made him lose control, for God is not a God of confusion but of peace (vv. 32–33). Women are not to take part in the public judging of prophecy (vv. 34–35). Paul then calls Corinth back under the Lord’s command, which all the churches share (vv. 36–38), and ends by holding eager desire and good order together (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

Orderly worship rests on the doctrine of God: he is not a God of confusion but of peace (see the note on vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s rules (two or three, in turn, with weighing) are not red tape but pastoral wisdom about how a church can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the setting in which his gifts can be received and used by the whole church.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever each member brings to the gathering, everything must be done to build up the church.

Each one has. One of the New Testament’s rare glimpses of a church meeting. Many took part: one brought a hymn (psalmos, perhaps a psalm or a new song), another a lesson (didachē, teaching), a revelation (a prophecy), a tongue, or its interpretation. It was a room of contributors, not an audience, and for all their disorder Paul does not stop it; he regulates it, in a single clause.

Let all things be done for building up. The rule for everything: not “sincerely”, or “reverently”, or “with excellence”, but “for building up” (oikodomē), measured by the effect on other people. Paul binds the church to this criterion, not to an order of service. And the New Testament plainly places teaching at the centre, listing teachers before most other gifts (12:28) and telling Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13).

The word of Christ dwelling richly. What were these hymns and lessons about? Paul answers elsewhere: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16). Some of those songs may survive in the New Testament itself (Philippians 2:6–11). A Roman governor, Pliny, reported around AD 112 that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god. Building up the church means building it on him, until Christ is formed in his people (Galatians 4:19).

A rebuke to passivity. Whatever the Sunday structure, “What am I bringing?” is a fair question on the way in: a conversation prepared for someone struggling, a burden carried into the prayers, a heart ready to sing. That instinct survives every difference of tradition.

What is the regulative principle? It is the conviction that God alone decides how he is to be worshipped. In ordinary life we may do whatever Scripture does not forbid; in public worship we offer what Scripture appoints, because worship is God’s, not ours to invent: Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire and died (Leviticus 10:1–2), and Jesus condemned worship built on human traditions (Mark 7:7). Time, order, tunes and building are matters of wisdom; the elements themselves (listed in the box below) are what God has given, and they are enough.

Where Christians differ: how should worship be ordered? Some take this verse as the model for open worship in which anyone contributes; Brethren assemblies and many charismatic churches hold this out of a real concern that every member take part, and that instinct is good. Others hold to the regulative principle: worship should include only what God commands, led by qualified men. This commentary’s view: the apostolic church had more open participation, partly because of the revelatory gifts then active. With the canon closed and those gifts ceased, the core elements of worship are those God has appointed: reading and preaching the Scriptures, prayer, singing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, the sacraments, and giving (the Westminster Confession 21.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.5). Worship should be ordered, led by those God has called, and above all edifying. Within that, the congregation takes full part in singing, prayer and Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tongues in the meeting must be few, one at a time and always interpreted; without an interpreter the speaker keeps silent and speaks to God alone.

Two or at most three, and each in turn. Strikingly specific rules, designed not to reduce the gift to nothing but to make it useful. A maximum of three implies Corinth had been running many more; “each in turn” implies they had been speaking over one another.

No interpreter, no tongue. Without an interpreter, the speaker keeps silent in church. And if a person can be told to wait his turn, he is able to wait it, as Paul says outright at verse 32 (see the note there).

To himself and to God. Quietly, in his own heart. He is not told his gift is bogus, but where it belongs; it may not take up the congregation’s time producing nothing for anybody.

Is this the room? Here is a model for handling many things good in themselves and unsuited to the assembly: a favourite doctrine or emphasis, a particular burden, the experience that changed a life. None need be denied to be given its proper place. The question is never only “is this real?” but also “is this the room?”

The love of restraint. Two or three and no more, even of a good thing the Spirit gave, though somebody with something real to offer will go home without offering it. Such restraint is a form of love, and its pattern is Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:4–7). The One who had the most right to the floor gave it up for us. Holding back a good word for another’s sake is a small likeness of him.

What should a church do today if someone stands up and speaks in a tongue? The elders should act gently and by Paul’s own rules. A church that holds, as this commentary does, that the gift has ceased will not make room for it in its services, and will explain why kindly and privately. Even a church that allows it is bound by this chapter’s limits. Whatever is said must be weighed by Scripture, and the person concerned should be treated as a brother or sister, not shamed in front of others.

In everyday life. Self-control is a fruit the Spirit grows in you, not a feat of willpower. In your next church meeting or Bible study, let someone else speak first, and leave one good thing unsaid if the time is better given to another.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophecy too must be limited and orderly, and everything said must be weighed by the church, so that all may learn and be encouraged.

Let two or three prophets speak. The same limit as tongues, and then something tongues did not get.

Let the others weigh what is said. Weigh (diakrinō) means to sift, evaluate, discern. Congregational prophecy was not automatically accepted but tested against apostolic teaching (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1), and that one instruction settles more about the gift than any definition could.

Nobody weighs Scripture. Nobody sifted Isaiah to see how much of him to keep. A prophecy tested by its hearers was not on the same footing as the written word of God, which is not weighed but obeyed. “Thus says the Lord”, said in a manner that forbids questioning, is precisely what this verse rules out.

How is it weighed? Four questions do most of the work. Does it agree with Scripture? If not, it is finished at once, whatever accompanied it. Does it exalt Christ, or the speaker? Does it build up, encourage and console (v. 3)? And does the speaker’s life commend what he says? The Bible never asks anyone to accept a spiritual claim unexamined; the Bereans are commended for checking an apostle against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11).

Let the first be silent. One speaker at a time: if something is given to a person sitting down, the one on his feet stops. No one has the floor by right, and the mark of a man truly hearing from God is that he does not mind sitting down.

So that all may learn and all be encouraged. Both halves matter. Learning without encouragement makes a congregation informed and flat; encouragement without learning, cheerful and hollow. Paul asks for both from the same activity, a high standard and the right one.

The spirit of prophecy. Christ is what prophecy was always about. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, the angel told John (Revelation 19:10). Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, the risen Lord interpreted to his disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and he said the Spirit would glorify him, taking what is his and declaring it (John 16:14). So weighing a word is finally asking whether it leads to him. And there is one Prophet whose words no congregation weighs. On the mountain the Father said of him: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Mark 9:7).

Is there prophecy today? The gift of prophecy, like tongues, belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture it has ceased. Continuationists read this very verse the other way: because congregational prophecy had to be weighed, it never stood level with Scripture, and so can continue without threatening a closed Bible. That is a serious argument; this commentary answers that these prophets still spoke revelation (v. 30), which the apostolic foundation supplied once for all. The passage still serves. When someone says the Lord told him something, the church weighs it by the questions above. An impression may be sincere and even wise, but it never binds anyone’s conscience; only the voice of God in Scripture does.

What should I do when a Christian friend says God told him something about me? Listen graciously, thank him for caring, and weigh it: does it agree with Scripture, and is it wise? Talk it over with your elders or a mature believer if it matters. If it is a call to repent of something Scripture forbids, take it seriously, because it may be God’s word to you through Scripture whatever your friend calls it. If it is a claim about whom to marry, where to move or what will happen, you are not bound by it. Your guide is the Bible, and you need not fear disobeying God by setting aside a word Scripture does not give.

parallels.desc: test everything

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit never takes away a speaker’s self-control, because God is not a God of confusion but of peace, and orderly worship shows what he is like.

The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. This answers the defence offered ever since: “I could not help it; the Spirit came on me.” The prophet is in charge of his own mouth, or Paul’s rules would be unenforceable.

The Spirit’s signature. The priestess at Delphi was thought to be seized by her god, and her loss of control was taken as proof of his presence. The Holy Spirit does not do that. He never overrides a person; he restores him to himself. Self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23), and an experience that removes it is evidence not of more of the Spirit but of something else. The man from whom Jesus cast the legion was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (Luke 8:35). That is the Holy Spirit’s signature.

Not a God of confusion. Confusion (akatastasia) is the word used of riots and upheaval. Paul settles order not by taste or custom but by the character of God, who from the Bible’s first page has brought order out of chaos: the Spirit hovering over the deep, light separated from darkness, the waters given their bounds. Worship preaches before the sermon starts, for the way a church behaves when it meets tells onlookers what its God is like. A room where everyone shouts at once says that God is restless and careless of others; a room where people listen, wait and make room for one another says that he is the God of peace (Romans 15:33).

Peace with a face. The God of peace is not an abstraction. He came in Christ, who stood up in a boat in a storm and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39), who told frightened disciples that he was leaving them his peace (John 14:27), and who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). A well-ordered gathering is a small echo of that peace: people reconciled to God can wait their turn and listen without fear, because the deepest confusion of all, war with God, is over.

Is the spontaneous always more real? Many of us assume a written prayer is less sincere than an unplanned one. The literary critic Lionel Trilling traced how the older ideal of sincerity, meaning what you say, gave way in modern culture to authenticity, being true to an inner self against every outward form. Corinth’s version was: the less control, the more Spirit. Paul disagrees, and not because he prefers tidiness. The most authentic human being who ever lived said, “I do nothing on my own authority” (John 8:28). Jesus was never more himself than when he was most surrendered to his Father, and the Spirit he sends does the same in us: he does not dissolve the self, he gives it back. Uncontrolled display can be its own kind of performance. Order in worship is not the enemy of the heart; it is what a heart looks like when it no longer needs to prove anything.

Peace is not the same as quiet. This verse has been used to smother things it was never aimed at. A church can be so orderly that no one would weep, or stay behind, or say anything not on the sheet; that congregation has not obeyed this verse, only avoided the problem it addresses. Paul is regulating a fire, not a filing cabinet, and he ends the chapter by forbidding them to put the fire out (v. 39).

But what about people in the Bible who were overwhelmed by God? With awe, yes: Isaiah cried woe is me, and John fell at Christ’s feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). But they were never turned into puppets: Isaiah answered here I am, send me; John was raised up and told to write, and wrote clearly. Being deeply moved by God is right, and tears in worship are no disorder. What Paul rules out is the claim that the Spirit makes a person act against his own control and the order of the church. The Spirit humbles us, but he never dehumanises us.

Uncertain wording. “As in all the churches of the saints” may end the sentence about God’s peace or begin the next one about women, as the ESV takes it; the Greek was written without punctuation. Either way, Corinth is reminded that it is not the only congregation in the world, and that its practice is not its own invention.

verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the gathered church, women are not to take part in the public judging of prophecy and the questioning that went with it, for that weighing carried teaching authority over the congregation.

The women should keep silent in the churches. Few passages are harder, and the difficulty is not the culture but Paul himself. Three chapters ago he regulated how women should be dressed when they pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5), without objecting to their doing it. A man does not regulate how women pray aloud in church and then forbid them to open their mouths, so this cannot be total silence; any reading that makes this the flat opposite of 11:5 has gone wrong somewhere.

Look where these verses sit. The context is the weighing of prophecies (v. 29), a public, judicial act in which the assembly sat in judgment on a claim to speak for God.

As the Law also says. No verse is quoted. Most likely Paul means the order of creation in Genesis 2, part of the Law in the sense of the five books of Moses, which he cites elsewhere for the same principle (11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13). The principle is headship, not culture alone. Headship means the responsibility God gives a man to lead, protect and serve in love, as Christ leads his church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:23–25): a calling to responsibility, not a claim to greater worth.

Ask their husbands at home. Verse 35 regulates not praying or prophesying but the cross-examination that went with the weighing. Wives publicly challenging prophets, perhaps their own husbands, would undermine order and headship, so Paul directs their questions to the home, assuming that women should learn. The setting fits the ancient room, where most women had far less schooling than the men. So when Paul adds that it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, “speak” carries the sense of the public judging and questioning just described.

Four readings. The first, a universal ban, founders on 11:5, and those who hold it do not apply it: their women sing, confess the creed and answer Amen. The second, that Paul did not write the verses, is ruled out because every manuscript contains them somewhere (see the textual note below). The third takes them as a Corinthian slogan that Paul demolishes in verse 36; it is ingenious, but nothing signals a quotation, and verse 37 calls what he writes the Lord’s command. The fourth, which fits best, reads the verses in their own context, the weighing of prophecy.

Read that way, the two passages agree. A woman may pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5) but not exercise the congregation’s governing judgment over its teaching, and 11:5, 14:29 and 1 Timothy 2:12 all stand as written. Egalitarian brothers and sisters deserve to be heard with respect, and the two sides share far more than divides them: the same Saviour, the same Bible, and the same concern that no woman be silenced by cruelty.

Mary has chosen the good portion. The Lord Jesus let Mary of Bethany sit at his feet and listen to his teaching, and when her sister complained he would not send her back to the serving: she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:39–42). He opened the deepest truths about worship to a Samaritan woman at a well (John 4:21–24), and on the morning of his resurrection he sent Mary Magdalene to tell his brothers that he was alive (John 20:17–18). The Lord who orders his church cherishes every daughter in it as an heir with her brothers of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).

What does this mean for a church today? The restriction concerns the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church, which Paul elsewhere reserves to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). It does not forbid women to pray aloud, read Scripture, sing, give testimony, teach other women and children (Titus 2:3–5), or speak in a members’ meeting. And since prophecy has ceased, the part women once played in praying and prophesying (11:5) is now their full share in the church’s prayer and praise.

And women with no husband to ask? Paul’s point is an orderly meeting, not women kept from learning. A single woman, a widow or a wife whose husband does not believe should be taught by the elders and other mature believers, like every member; questions after the service or in classes fit Paul’s concern exactly.

What it does not mean. Not that women are less intelligent or spiritual, or that their questions are unwelcome; Paul wants them to learn. The same apostle wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28), greeted Junia as well known to the apostles (Romans 16:7), and honoured Priscilla, Phoebe, Euodia and Syntyche for their labour alongside him (Romans 16:1–4; Philippians 4:2–3). Equal in worth and in Christ; different in calling within the church and the home.

A misuse to refuse. This passage has been used to shame women into silence far beyond anything Paul wrote, doing real damage. A congregation where women are afraid to speak at all has not obeyed this text; it has ignored chapter 11. And headship in Scripture is never a licence for control; it is the self-giving love of Christ for his church (Ephesians 5:25). A husband who uses this verse to belittle or dominate his wife has turned it upside down, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered in the name of submission.

Why would God give men and women different roles if they are equal? Because difference is not inequality, as the Trinity shows: the Son is fully equal with the Father, yet in the work of salvation gladly does the Father’s will (11:3; John 6:38). Ordered roles among equals are part of creation’s beauty, not a scar on it. God made man and woman both in his image (Genesis 1:27) and gave them to each other as partners with different callings, so that the home and the church might picture Christ and his bride. The man is called to lead by laying down his life, the woman to honour that leadership freely, and both to serve. Where this is lived in love, it is not a cage but a dance.

In everyday life. Husbands, ask your wife what she took from Sunday’s sermon, and listen. Sisters, ask your questions, and do not let anyone tell you that your understanding of God does not matter; it matters to him.

Where Christians differ: women’s silence. Some take this as an absolute ban on women speaking at all in church. Others say it was a cultural rule for disruptive Corinthian women and no longer applies, or even that Paul did not write it. Many who hold these views are egalitarians (Christians who hold that every ministry in the church is open to men and women alike), out of love for Scripture and a sincere wish to honour the women God has gifted, like those who prayed, prophesied and laboured beside Paul. This commentary’s view: since Paul allows women to pray and prophesy (11:5), this is not a ban on all speech, but on women taking the role of authoritatively judging prophecy and teaching in the gathered church, which belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:11–12). This is the complementarian position. Women may sing, pray, testify, and serve in countless ways. The principle is grounded in creation, not merely culture.

Textual note. The verses are in all the manuscripts, though a few move them after verse 40.
verseByVerse.note: Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Interpreters differ on what speaking is forbidden here; many take it as the public judging of prophecies just mentioned (v. 29).

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians did not originate the word of God and are not its only recipients, so they may not set their own practice against that of all the churches.

Or was it from you that the word of God came? Two ironic questions, the sting in the tail of the chapter, expose Corinth’s real problem: not tongues but independence. Behind every fault in this letter lies a congregation that thought itself the centre of things, its practices its own to invent and its founder’s instructions only suggestions.

Or are you the only ones it has reached? Did the gospel start here? Is this the only place it has got to? Both answers are humiliating and obvious. The word came to Corinth from elsewhere, brought by a man who had received it himself, and had reached many other cities whose churches did not do what Corinth was doing: one church among many, receiving the same word, bound to the same practice. The link with verse 33 is exact: “as in all the churches of the saints”. Whatever they had concluded about worship, they had concluded alone, and that alone was a warning sign.

The word has a source. The answer to Paul’s first question is that the word of God came from Christ. The risen Lord told his apostles that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47), and Paul insists that what he delivered to Corinth he had first received (15:3), not from any man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12). A church that treats the apostolic word as its own to revise puts itself in the place of the Lord who spoke it. It is free as one who receives the word, not as one who writes it.

There is no self-made believer. The word was carried to Corinth, a city with a bad reputation and no interest in it (Acts 18:8). Nobody there had generated a word of it, and no Christian since has either. Every one of us stands somewhere downstream of an empty tomb, reached by a word that was running toward us before we were born, sent by the Father, bought by the Son and carried by the Spirit. We did not invent it. We received it, and that is grace.

Novelty is worth examining. Truth is not decided by counting congregations; at the Reformation a few were right and the many wrong. But a church doing something no other Christians have thought necessary should at least ask whether the Spirit really has told it alone. There is humility in this for individuals too: the believer convinced that he has seen something in Scripture the whole church has missed is occasionally right, and usually a man who has been reading alone for too long.

How do I tell faithful conviction from mere novelty? Ask three questions. Does Scripture plainly teach it, read in context, or am I building on one verse? Have faithful Christians in other times and places seen it too (the creeds and confessions help here)? Would my elders and wise believers in my church recognise it, or am I hiding it from them? A conviction that cannot be found plainly in Scripture, has no friends in church history and must be kept from the church’s leaders deserves deep suspicion.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
True spiritual insight shows itself by recognising Paul’s instructions as the Lord’s command, and whoever refuses to recognise them is not to be recognised.

If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual. The most spiritually confident would be the ones to object, so Paul sets a trap openly: if you are a prophet, or spiritual, you will recognise that what I write is the Lord’s command. Any spirituality that reaches a different conclusion from apostolic instruction has failed at the only point where it could be tested.

A command of the Lord. Not Paul’s best judgment, but the Lord’s command. That is the apostolic authority the New Testament rests on: not that these men were wise, but that they were sent, and what they wrote carries the weight of the one who sent them. The Lord here is Jesus, who told his apostles that whoever receives the one he sends receives him (John 13:20), so to refuse Paul’s instructions on worship is to refuse Christ’s. A sceptic may hear a bid for power, but the man who writes this had been beaten, imprisoned and left hungry for this word (2 Corinthians 11:23–27), and he puts himself under it as fully as he puts Corinth: if even he, or an angel from heaven, preached a different gospel, he says, let him be accursed (Galatians 1:8). Paul is not claiming that the word belongs to him; he is insisting that he belongs to the word. Peter already counted Paul’s letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15–16).

He is not recognised. Short and cold: not recognised by God, or by the church as a true prophet. He wanted to be acknowledged as a prophet, and he is not acknowledged at all.

A self-refuting claim. This answers the commonest form of spiritual manipulation, the claim to an authority, insight or experience that places a man above correction from Scripture. A genuine work of the Spirit will always submit to the word the Spirit gave; the test is not whether a man sounds spiritual, but what he does when the Bible contradicts him. The Lord has not left his church to the competing claims of the confident. He has put his own voice into a book that every believer can open, and he rules his people by it with the gentleness of a shepherd.

How do I run this test on myself? Everyone has a place where Scripture cuts across something he wants: a grudge, a habit, a plan, an opinion held for thirty years. A man who reaches for a reason why the passage does not quite apply to him has just learned the real source of his convictions. Yet there is mercy in Paul’s verb: acknowledge, come to see, as one recognises a face. He does not say at once or without a struggle; recognition can take a while. Bring your struggle to God honestly, and keep reading until you bow.

In everyday life. Name one place where the Bible is currently cutting across your will, and pray today for the grace to yield. None of us bows perfectly, but Christ bowed perfectly in your place (Romans 5:19), and his Spirit works in you to will and to work (Philippians 2:13).

Textual note. The manuscripts vary slightly here between he is not recognised and let him not be recognised (the KJV’s let him be ignorant follows the second). Either way the man is outside the circle he was claiming to lead.

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sums up: be eager for the gift that builds the church, do not forbid what God has given, and let everything be done fittingly and in order.

Earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid. After a chapter of regulation Paul wants not a subdued church but one hungry for the gift that builds people up. And “do not forbid” is a command, placed exactly where a lesser writer would have put a ban. Tongues rightly used were a genuine gift then, and having restricted the practice, Paul forbids the church to forbid it. He knows what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, and the next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment.

Decently and in order. One expression from the drawing room, one from the parade ground. Decently (euschēmonōs) is fittingly, beautifully, with dignity; in order (kata taxin) is in proper order, like soldiers in ranks. The phrase is often quoted by people who want a quiet church, but verse 39, with its commands to desire and not to forbid, stands in front of it.

The fire and the grate. The balance the whole chapter has held: a church neither chaotic nor cold, where the Spirit’s work is wanted and not feared, a stranger at the back can understand, and everything is measured by whether anybody was built up. Corinth had the fire and no grate. Many congregations since have had a beautiful grate and no fire.

In the flow. These two lines close the answer about spiritual gifts begun at 12:1, and clear the ground for the next chapter, where Paul turns from how the church speaks to what it must always say, the gospel of first importance: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised (15:3–4). Orderly, understandable worship exists so that this message can be heard.

Order around a miracle. Fire and order were never at odds in the Lord himself. When five thousand hungry people were on a hillside and he was about to feed them from five loaves, he first had them sit down in groups on the green grass, by hundreds and by fifties (Mark 6:39–40). Then all ate and were satisfied: power and order in the same afternoon, both from the same Lord, who still feeds his people through his word.

Perfect order and perfect love. Underneath it all is the God of verse 33, whose own life is perfect order and perfect love at once, and who has never had to choose between liveliness and dignity. When Christ ascended on high he gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8–13), so that a room full of ordinary people might be built up into something that will last after every tongue has fallen silent. And on the last day the whole redeemed creation will worship him in perfect order and unbounded joy, ten thousand times ten thousand, every voice distinct and every voice one, crying that the Lamb who was slain is worthy (Revelation 5:11–12).

How does a church that believes tongues have ceased obey this command? By recognising that Paul was protecting a gift then active, and holding its conclusion that the gift has ceased with humility, not scorn. The instinct to shut down anything that cannot be controlled is not a Christian virtue, and it is not what this apostle did with a church that had abused almost every gift it had: he regulated, and then he protected. In practice, elders should test any claim to tongues by Paul’s own rules (see the note on vv. 27–28). And “earnestly desire to prophesy” is obeyed today by longing for the clear, Spirit-given proclamation of the word that builds the church up.

How can a cessationist church keep from becoming cold? By remembering that cessationism concerns certain gifts, not the Spirit himself, who is as present and powerful today as at Pentecost: he convicts, regenerates, comforts, sanctifies and makes the word come alive. A church that believes the Spirit speaks fully and sufficiently in Scripture has every reason to be warm. Pray for his blessing on the preaching, expect conversions, sing with heart and mind, and love one another fervently. The great revivals under Whitefield and Edwards, and the preaching of Spurgeon, came through men who looked for no new revelation, and they were not cold.

In everyday life. Pray for this Sunday’s gathering: for a clear preacher, true singing, visitors who understand. Then come with your own heart prepared, as part of the answer to that prayer.

Where Christians differ: does “do not forbid” apply to tongues today? Continuationists argue that churches today must not forbid tongues, since the command stands in Scripture with no stated end, and they take it as seriously as any other. This commentary’s view: Paul’s command applied when the gift was active. If the revelatory and sign gifts have ceased with the apostolic age, as this commentary holds because they confirmed the apostles’ once-for-all foundation (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4), the question is whether present-day phenomena are the same gift, and cessationists believe they are not. Churches should neither mock nor exclude continuationist believers, and all should agree on the principles here: everything must be understood, edifying, tested by Scripture, orderly, and done in love.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.<sup>6</sup>Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?<sup>7</sup>If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played?<sup>8</sup>And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?<sup>9</sup>So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.<sup>10</sup>There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning,<sup>11</sup>but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.<sup>12</sup>So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.<sup>14</sup>For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.<sup>16</sup>Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?<sup>17</sup>For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.<sup>18</sup>I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.<sup>20</sup>Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.<sup>21</sup>In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”<sup>22</sup>Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.<sup>23</sup>If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?<sup>24</sup>But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,<sup>25</sup>the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.<sup>26</sup>What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.<sup>27</sup>If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret.<sup>28</sup>But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.<sup>29</sup>Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.<sup>30</sup>If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent.<sup>31</sup>For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,<sup>32</sup>and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.<sup>33</sup>For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,<sup>34</sup>the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says.<sup>35</sup>If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.<sup>36</sup>Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?<sup>37</sup>If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord.<sup>38</sup>If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.<sup>39</sup>So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.<sup>40</sup>But all things should be done decently and in order.

keyVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on “building up”, which returns again and again (vv. 3–5, 12, 17, 26). This verse takes the Corinthians’ eagerness for the Spirit and points it where the Spirit’s gifts are meant to go: not to display, but to the good of others. It is the love of chapter 13 put to work in the gathered church.

14.reflection:
Paul’s test for everything in the gathering is whether others are built up (vv. 3–5, 12, 26). What in our worship and church life would look different if we asked that question honestly, and what might you bring on a Sunday if you came to give as well as to receive?

Paul says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also” (v. 15). Which do you find easier to neglect in worship, the mind or the heart? How does Jesus, who prayed in Gethsemane with loud cries and perfect clarity, help you hold them together?

Verses 23–25 picture an outsider walking into the meeting. What might make a visitor to our church feel like a foreigner (v. 11), and what would help him hear plain words about Christ and conclude that “God is really among you”?

Paul grounds order in the character of God: “not a God of confusion but of peace” (v. 33). How can a church be both orderly and warm, neither chaotic nor cold, and what part can you play in that?

15.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 is the letter’s last great subject and its summit. After fourteen chapters on divisions, sexual sin, idols, worship and gifts, Paul answers the error that undermines all the rest, before closing with the collection and greetings of chapter 16.

The message. Christ has truly been raised from the dead, and because he has, all who belong to him will be raised too, in bodies made imperishable and glorious like his. Death is a defeated enemy, so nothing done for the Lord is wasted.

Why it was said. Some in Corinth were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead (v. 12), which fitted Greek thinking well. Many Greeks thought of the body as the soul’s prison (see the note on vv. 12–14): salvation meant the soul escaping, not the corpse rising, and at Athens some mocked Paul for speaking of resurrection (Acts 17:32). In a tragedy of Aeschylus the god Apollo says that once the dust has soaked up a dead man’s blood, there is no rising again. The Corinthians probably still believed in Christ’s resurrection and some spiritual life after death, but not in the raising of their own bodies.

How the chapter makes its case. In four stages. The facts: the gospel they received, Christ’s death, burial and rising, and the witnesses who saw him (vv. 1–11). The cost of denial: if the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised, faith is futile, sins are unforgiven and the Christian dead are lost (vv. 12–19). God’s plan: Christ the firstfruits, reigning until death is destroyed and God is all in all, with Christian living and risk as further evidence (vv. 20–34). The resurrection body: sown like a seed, raised imperishable in the image of the man of heaven, changed in an instant at the last trumpet (vv. 35–58).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter rests on one Man: the firstfruits whose harvest is sure, the last Adam who gives the life the first could only receive, the King who must reign until his last enemy falls. Death swallowed him and could not keep him down, and so death itself will be swallowed up in victory (v. 54). The chapter ends in a shout: “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 57).

For us. Our age, like Corinth, prefers a soul that drifts on to a body that rises. This chapter promises more: sins forgiven, real bodies made new, faces we know, death undone. It lets the grieving hate death and gives them reason to hope, and it sends every believer back to ordinary work, steadfast and immovable, “knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (v. 58).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The resurrection of Jesus is not a theory but the heart of the gospel that saved the Corinthians, and it rests on God’s promise and on named witnesses. Paul reminds them of the message they received and stand in (vv. 1–2), recites the early creed of Christ’s death for our sins, his burial and his rising on the third day, all as the Scriptures foretold (vv. 3–4), and lists those who saw him alive: Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and last of all himself (vv. 5–8). He is the least of them, a forgiven persecutor, what he is by the grace of God; and whoever preached, this is the one message they all believed (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

The creed Paul hands on is among the earliest Christian statements we have (see vv. 3–4). Both the death and the rising are in accordance with the Scriptures, with Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53 and Hosea 6:2 the likeliest passages in view. The two belong together. The resurrection is not an isolated miracle but God’s vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection we would have no word from God that the death had worked; without the death, the resurrection would be a wonder that saves no one. Together they are the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Paul spoke of the resurrection at Athens, some mocked and some wanted to hear more (Acts 17:32), the usual Greek reaction. Now: Today the objection is usually put in scientific terms: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same as then, the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this body, on this morning, was raised by the God who made bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel that saved you is the ground you stand on, and you go on standing only by keeping hold of it. Before answering the deniers, Paul walks the Corinthians back to the message that made them Christians.

I would remind you. Remind (gnōrizō) is to make known again. Taught by Paul for eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and by Apollos after him, the Corinthians were not short of information; they needed someone to walk them back to the first thing. What steadies a believer in a hard year is rarely new: it is the old thing, remembered at the right moment, by someone who troubled to say it again.

Which you received, in which you stand. Four verbs make a small map of the Christian life. The gospel was preached: it came from outside, as news; nobody worked it out, and it found us before we found it. It was received: taken by faith, as a gift is taken. It is the ground they stand in, a pointed word for a congregation that had been standing on its gifts, its wisdom and its teachers. And by it they “are being saved”: God accepted them the day they believed, and that is settled for ever (Romans 5:1); he is still rescuing them from sin’s grip day by day, and one day will rescue their bodies from death (Romans 8:23).

If you hold fast. Hold fast (katechō) is to keep a firm grip; in vain (eikē) is without cause or result. The clause can badly frighten a Christian troubled about his perseverance, so read it carefully. Paul does not say you will lose what you have if you slip. He raises the possibility that some of them believed in vain: a profession that never had anything living in it. If they let go of this gospel, they would show that their faith was empty. That is a different thing from a believer falling out of God’s hand, which this apostle elsewhere says is impossible (Romans 8:38–39).

Holding fast is evidence, not cause. In the New Testament holding fast is not the cause of being kept but the evidence of it: God keeps his people by making them keep going. So this clause is not a threat held over a frightened Christian but a question put to a comfortable one: not “Do you remember believing?” but “Are you still holding on?” (Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14).

The setting. Some at Corinth denied the future resurrection (see the note on vv. 12–14); some may have thought they had already been raised spiritually (4:8; 2 Timothy 2:18). After fourteen chapters of correction Paul turns to what all of it rests on, and his tone changes. It is the chapter Christians have read at gravesides for two thousand years, and it ends not with a sigh but with a shout of thanks.

The gospel is a person. What the Corinthians received was not first a set of ideas but Christ himself: “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (Colossians 2:6). The ground they stand on is not their grasp of a doctrine but his finished work (vv. 3–4), as solid as an empty tomb. And the One by whom they are being saved is alive to finish it: “he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Every tense of salvation here has the same subject: he saved, he holds, he will complete.

I am afraid I might not hold on. The fear itself is a good sign: people who have truly let go of Christ are rarely troubled about it. Holding on is not gritting your teeth but looking at Christ, who holds you far more firmly than you hold him; no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). So when you feel your grip weakening, do not stare at your grip. Go back to the gospel of verses 3 and 4, read it, pray it, and take the Lord’s Supper with his people. Faith is strengthened by being fed, and its food is Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the body; most Greeks thought the body was left behind at death.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the centre of the gospel stand events God has done in history: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, just as the Scriptures had promised. Paul is reciting what he was given, and he calls it “of first importance”.

Delivered and received. The standard vocabulary for handing on a fixed tradition word for word, the same pair Paul used of the Lord’s Supper at 11:23.

How early is this creed? Paul is writing a little over twenty years after the crucifixion, around AD 54. But he received this formula, so it was already fixed when he was taught it, most likely in his first years as a Christian, perhaps during the two weeks he spent with Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18), within a very few years of the event. This is not a legend that grew over generations. It is a summary recited while many who had seen these things were still alive.

Christ died for our sins. The little word “for” (hyper, on behalf of) means on our account, and with Isaiah 53 standing behind the whole creed it carries substitution: in our place. Sin’s just sentence is death (Romans 6:23), and God does not pretend it away; so the Son took the sentence himself, and the punishment that brought us peace fell on him (Isaiah 53:5). Without that word “for”, his death is only a tragedy; with it, it is an exchange: he took our place, and we go free.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The phrase comes twice, for the death and for the rising: this was not an emergency. Isaiah had described a servant pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, a lamb led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:5, 7). The plan is older than the crime.

He was buried. It settles that he was really dead: there was a body, men carried it, and it was heavy. And the resurrection was bodily: the body placed in the tomb was the body raised. A burial means a tomb, a tomb has an address, and Jerusalem is a small city. The claim was placed where it could be checked.

Raised on the third day. The form of the verb (egēgertai) says two things: God raised him, and he remains raised. The resurrection is the Father’s verdict on the cross. On the third day is a historical date, counted the ancient way, where any part of a day was a day: Friday afternoon to early Sunday. The “three days and three nights” of Matthew 12:40 is the same span in a Jewish idiom, not a stopwatch.

In accordance with the Scriptures, again. The rising too was foretold. God would not let his Holy One see corruption (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27), and Isaiah’s servant, after his death, would see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10).

Why is the gospel news rather than advice? Because it tells what God has done, not what you must do to reach him. Advice says: try harder, and you may get there. News says: it has been done; believe it. The gospel is a report of three events, a death, a burial and a resurrection, and an announcement of what they mean: your sins can be forgiven, because Christ has borne them. The commands follow the news: you do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because in Christ you have been.

In everyday life. Learn these two verses by heart this week, so that you can say the gospel to anyone in a breath, and then say it to one person who needs to hear it.

Where Christians differ: the meaning of Christ’s death. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of love, or as a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore the punishment for sins. This commentary’s view: Scripture presents his death as many things, including example and victory, but at its heart it is penal substitution: he stood in our place, bearing the penalty of God’s just wrath against our sins, so that we might be forgiven and declared righteous (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). This is of first importance.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–5 are an early summary of the faith that Paul had received — within a few years of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ was seen alive by named witnesses, beginning with Peter and the Twelve. The first name on the list is a scandal.

And that he appeared to Cephas. Cephas is Peter, and the last thing the reader knows about Peter is that he swore three times by a courtyard fire that he had never met the man. Yet he is first on the list. Luke preserves it: “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34). Nobody records what was said in that meeting, which is a mercy.

Then to the twelve. At that point there were not twelve: Judas was dead, and Thomas was absent from the first appearance (John 20:19–29). The Twelve had become a title rather than a headcount, as a regiment keeps its number after a bad year (John 20:24). A man polishing a story would not leave a countable discrepancy in the second line of his creed; the rough edge marks a formula used by people who were there.

Tell his disciples and Peter. The angel at the tomb had already signalled it (Mark 16:7), and those two extra words are the gospel in miniature. Peter’s name was spoken separately, in case he assumed the message was for the others and not for him. On the shore of Galilee the restoration was completed: three questions for three denials, and a commission, feed my sheep (John 21:15–17).

He went back to his friends. Not to the Sanhedrin, or to Pilate, or to the crowd, but to his friends, and the first name on the list is the one who had let him down worst. He begins with the man who has to be told twice that he is still wanted, and if you have failed him, he still comes to you. Such is the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, and such is the love that rose from the dead.

Could the disciples have been mistaken or deceived? Hallucinations are private; they do not happen to groups, eat fish or invite touch. A stolen body would not explain why the men who knew where it was went to their deaths saying he was alive. Legend takes generations to grow, and this creed was fixed within a few years. And the disciples were not expecting a resurrection; they were hiding behind locked doors. Something turned frightened men into bold witnesses within weeks, in the city where he was buried and where anyone could have produced a body. The simplest explanation is the one they gave: he appeared to them.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. “The twelve” was the title of the group even when only eleven were present.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ was seen by more than five hundred people at once, most of them still alive to be asked, and by his own once-unbelieving brother. The list is an invitation to check.

More than five hundred. Perhaps the meeting on the mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–17), though Scripture does not say. It is recorded nowhere else: Paul knows more than the Gospels chose to write down.

Most of whom are still alive. Not a devotional remark but an invitation: twenty years on, many could still be questioned, and the letter was going to a port city with constant traffic to Palestine. Several hundred people saw this at once, Paul is saying; go and ask them. A man inventing a story would locate his miracle somewhere quieter.

Fallen asleep. The Christian word for believers’ death: the body lies down for a while, and there will be a waking at the resurrection.

Then he appeared to James. This is James the brother of the Lord, who came to lead the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21; Galatians 2:9) and, by early accounts, was stoned to death around AD 62. The Gospels record what he thought before: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5), and his family once went out to seize Jesus, saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Nobody is harder to convince that a man is the Son of God than the brother who grew up with him. James went from that to leading the mother church and dying rather than take it back, and this verse is the explanation. The brother who once thought him mad would open his letter by calling himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1).

Then to all the apostles. Perhaps at the ascension (Acts 1:3–9), including a wider group beyond the Twelve.

He showed himself. None of these witnesses went looking for the risen Christ; in every case he came to them: he presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs (Acts 1:3). The evidence for the resurrection is, at bottom, the risen Jesus deciding to be seen.

In everyday life. When someone asks why you believe, start where Paul starts: with the people who saw him. And pray for the sceptic in your own family; the risen Christ still changes the hardest hearts by showing himself alive.

Why are the women not on the list? All four Gospels say the women found the tomb empty, and Matthew and John record that they were the first to see him (Matthew 28:9; John 20:14–18). Paul is assembling something like a legal brief, and in that world a woman’s testimony carried little weight in court, which is precisely why the Gospels’ keeping the women in is such powerful evidence of honesty. Nobody building a case puts his least admissible witnesses first; they did it because it happened. And the Lord himself chose a weeping woman, Mary Magdalene, to be the first to see him and to carry the news to the apostles.

Where are my Christian loved ones now? With Christ, consciously and gladly. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with the Lord, which Paul calls far better (Philippians 1:23). There is no waiting room of unconsciousness and no purgatory; Christ’s blood has cleansed them fully. Their bodies, meanwhile, rest in the grave, still united to Christ, waiting for the resurrection. So you grieve the parting, but you do not grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). They are more alive now than they ever were with you.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some take fallen asleep to mean that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. This commentary’s view: Sleep describes the appearance of the body in death and the certainty of waking. But Scripture teaches that the souls of believers go immediately into the presence of Christ, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 6:9–11; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).
verseByVerse.note: Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote. James is the Lord’s brother, who had not believed during Jesus’ ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was the last to see the risen Christ, and he never forgot that Christ came to him as he was persecuting the church. He is an apostle only by undeserved mercy.

Last of all, as to one untimely born. The resurrection appearances ended with Paul. The word (ektrōma) is blunt: an abnormal birth, a miscarriage, one that came violently and out of season. It may have been his opponents’ name for him, the runt, picked up because it fits. The Twelve had some three years beside Jesus; Paul was on a road with warrants in his bag when the risen Christ intercepted him (Acts 9:3–6), outside the normal time of the appearances. He was not raised into apostleship; he was seized into it.

The least of the apostles. True humility, with no performance in it: later he calls himself less than the least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8) and, later still, the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The longer he walked with Christ, the smaller his estimate of himself; self-made religion runs the other way.

Humble, but not self-cancelling. Yet he never says he is not an apostle: the commission was given, not his to resign. A Christian can hold two things at once: an honest low estimate of himself, and a settled certainty about what God has said about him. Losing either produces a distortion, arrogance on one side, false humility on the other.

I persecuted the church of God. He had hunted, imprisoned and helped kill believers (Acts 22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13): the witnesses laid their garments at his feet while Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58), and he dragged off men and women to prison (Acts 8:3). There were widows in Jerusalem who knew his name. And Jesus had said to him, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:5): a blow struck at the least of his people lands on him, which is why Paul calls it the church of God, and why the forgiveness is so staggering.

He called him by name. Grace is not a general kindliness; it walked out onto a road and stopped a man on his way to arrest more of the family. The risen Lord could have struck him dead. He called him by name instead, and the man who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning wrote nearly half the books of the New Testament.

A hard fact for the sceptic. A trained, well-connected opponent, with everything to gain by continuing, changes sides, loses his standing, and spends thirty years being beaten and imprisoned for the thing he was suppressing. Something happened on that road. He says he knows what it was.

Can someone who has done terrible things really be forgiven? Yes, and Paul is the proof; so do not write anyone off as too far gone, either. Christ not only forgave a man complicit in murder but made him an apostle, precisely so that he might be an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so dark that Christ’s blood cannot wash it, for those who turn to him. Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence or make the past unimportant, but it removes the guilt before God entirely. If you are carrying a past you cannot bear to look at, bring it to the One who met Saul on the road.
verseByVerse.note: “Untimely born” describes an abnormal birth — Paul’s sudden, late calling.

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything Paul is and does is the gift of God’s grace, and that grace made him work harder than anyone; whoever the preacher, the message is the same. Paul holds together what people are forever pulling apart: grace and effort.

By the grace of God I am what I am. Apostle, Christian, forgiven sinner: all of it an unearned kindness that intercepted him going the other way. That is grace: not a reward for the deserving, nor help for those doing their best, but God’s favour given to people who deserve the opposite (Romans 5:8).

Not in vain. In vain (kenē) is empty. Grace is never inert; where it truly lands, it does something.

I worked harder … not I, but the grace of God. It sounds like the boast he has just disowned, until the last clause gives the credit to grace without denying the work. Even his hard work was grace at work in him, and Paul refuses to resolve the tension by choosing a side. Grace is not an alternative to effort; it is what produces the effort, the same pattern as “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

The grace that is with me. Grace in Paul is never a substance or a force; it is the Lord himself, present and at work: “struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me” (Colossians 1:29). “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); “my grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul was never working alone, and neither is any servant of Christ. Every good thing in any Christian, every prayer, every kindness, every hour of faithful work, is the grace of God that is with him.

Two mistakes about grace. The first hears grace and concludes that effort is unspiritual, that a Christian should wait to be moved. Paul worked himself to exhaustion, through many a sleepless night (2 Corinthians 11:27), and did not think so. The second hears work and quietly begins keeping score, measuring itself against other Christians and pleased with its own diligence. Paul really had worked harder than the others, and in the same breath he gave the credit to grace.

Whether then it was I or they. The Corinthians had been dividing over exactly this, Paul, Apollos, Cephas (1:12), and here is the man himself waving the question away. The messenger is not the point; what was preached is, and it was the same from all of them. These verses establish what nobody in Corinth disputed; from verse 12 Paul argues from that common ground.

How do I work hard without trusting my work? Work as a son, not as a hired hand. A hired hand works to earn wages; a son works because he already belongs and loves his father. Begin each task remembering that you are already accepted in Christ, so nothing rides on it for your standing with God; then pour yourself into it, asking for his strength. When it goes well, thank him; it was his grace. When it fails, confess any sin and rest; your acceptance never depended on it. That is how a Christian can be both tireless and at peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised, and without a risen Christ the whole faith collapses. Paul follows the Corinthian denial to its end. It cuts the ground from under Christ’s own resurrection (vv. 12–13), which empties the preaching and the faith built on it (v. 14), makes the apostles false witnesses about God (v. 15), and leaves believers still in their sins (vv. 16–17). Then he carries the argument to the graveside: the Christian dead have perished, and those who hoped in Christ for this life only are the most pitiable people alive (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Verse 17 ties the resurrection to the atonement: the resurrection is the Father’s yes to the Son’s sacrifice (see the note on vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s answer to the Corinthian denial is that salvation redeems the whole person, body and soul, as it did for Christ, whose body was raised, not merely his spirit. Now: A milder form of the same position appears whenever Christians treat the soul going to heaven as the whole story (see vv. 35–49).

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You cannot believe that Christ was raised and also deny that the dead are raised, for his resurrection and ours stand or fall together. Paul now names the actual problem in Corinth.

How can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? Some in Corinth seem to have accepted Jesus’ resurrection while denying that the rest of us will be raised bodily.

Why it felt reasonable to them. Educated Greeks had a low view of the body: the soul was the real self, the body its container and, for many, its prison, in a well-worn play on words, sōma sēma: the body is a tomb. Death was not the enemy but the release. Immortality of the soul, gladly; but for God to put you back into a body would be, to them, not salvation but being sent back to prison.

The reasoning is exact. What they wanted to keep cannot survive what they wanted to drop: Christ’s resurrection is one case of a dead man being raised.

Not even Christ. Jesus had staked his own claims on this event: he told his disciples plainly that he must be killed and after three days rise again (Mark 8:31), and he said of his body, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). If the tomb is still occupied, he was wrong about the one thing he most insisted on, and cannot be the Lord. If it is empty, he is everything he said he was.

Preaching and faith in vain. Empty: not mistaken in a detail, but containing nothing at all. Faith is only as good as what it rests on; if that is not there, the sincerity of the resting changes nothing.

Why not simply say his spirit lives on? Most modern people are nearer to the Corinthians than to Paul: at funerals we hear that the one we loved lives on in our hearts or is watching over us; hardly anyone says her body will be raised, which sounds crude. But the historian N. T. Wright, in The Resurrection of the Son of God, has argued that this is exactly the move the first Christians could have made and did not. In their world, Jewish and pagan alike, resurrection never meant a soul’s survival but a body alive again after death, and no Jew expected one man to be raised ahead of everyone else in the middle of history. Had the disciples only meant that Jesus’ cause lived on, or that he was with God, they had ready words for it. They chose the one word that meant an empty tomb, because nothing less fitted what they had seen. And that is good news, not an embarrassment. A soul floating free would mean losing the faces, hands and embraces we love. The risen Christ said, “Touch me, and see” (Luke 24:39). God does not plan to rescue us out of his creation but to give it back to us whole.

The easier letter Paul did not write. Paul does not offer the doubters a Christianity that keeps the ethics, the community and the comfort and quietly drops the miracle. A faith adjusted to whatever a generation finds credible cannot contradict that generation, and so has nothing to offer it. Christianity stakes everything on an event and offers to be checked. Our hope is not a theory about the soul but a man who was dead and is alive forevermore (Revelation 1:18). God did not ask us to believe a comfortable idea; he did a thing in history, in a garden outside a city wall, and he has never undone it.

In everyday life. When a doubt comes, do not ask first how you feel; ask what happened in Jerusalem on the third day.

Is it wrong to have doubts about the resurrection? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to him and showed him his hands (John 20:27). Bring your questions into the light: read the Gospels and a careful book on the evidence, talk to your pastor, and pray, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Paul invites inquiry rather than forbidding it, and many careful sceptics over two thousand years have found the evidence stronger than they expected. What would be wrong is to settle into doubt as a comfortable place, or to treat the resurrection as optional. It is the centre.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Christ was not raised, the apostles are lying about God and every believer is still guilty before him. There is no middle ground, and forgiveness itself hangs on it.

Misrepresenting God. Literally, we are found to be false witnesses of God. If there was no resurrection, the apostles have been telling the Mediterranean that God did something he did not do: liars, and liars about God. Paul never says the gospel is worth believing even if it never happened. And people do not usually die for what they know to be a lie; the apostles suffered for this testimony, many of them, by early accounts, to the point of death.
