Still in your sins. Futile (mataia) is useless, without result. Then the worst consequence. If the death pays for sin, why does the rising matter? Because a death, by itself, tells you nothing about whether it worked. Two men crucified beside him paid for nobody. The cross needed a verdict, a public act by which the Father declared the sacrifice received and the debt cleared, and the resurrection is that verdict. Jesus “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). Justification is the courtroom word: God acquits the guilty, not because they have improved, but because the righteousness of his risen Son is reckoned to them (2 Corinthians 5:21).

The receipt. Until the paper comes back stamped, a man cannot know his payment went through. The empty tomb is the stamp. On Friday the price was paid; on Sunday the Father put it in writing, in a form that could be walked into.

No accuser can reopen the case. The Father’s verdict over the cross cannot be reversed: “It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” (Romans 8:33–34). No accuser can reopen a case the Judge himself has closed. Glory to the risen Saviour, whose life is the proof of our pardon.

A verse about assurance. This verse points the troubled Christian away from his feelings to a garden outside Jerusalem. “You are still in your sins” is about where we stand before God, not how we feel, and that works the other way too: since Christ has been raised, forgiveness is a fact whatever we feel. The believer who feels nothing on a grey Tuesday is no less forgiven: the tomb did not become less empty overnight.

What if I still feel guilty after I have confessed? Guilt can linger long after God has forgiven, through habit, a tender conscience, the accuser’s whispers, or consequences that remain. Measure your forgiveness not by your feelings but by Christ: he was raised, so the payment was accepted. If there is something still to put right with another person, put it right. Then tell your conscience what God has said: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Faithful, because he promised; just, because Christ has paid. The feelings will often follow the truth in time.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without the resurrection, Christians who have died are simply gone, and a faith that offers only this life makes believers the most pitiable people alive. Paul takes the denial to the graveside.

Perished. There were graves in Corinth with Christians in them, whose families were in the room when this letter was read out. Without a resurrection they are not asleep but finished, and every Christian funeral is a lie. A doctrine can be discussed in a room of healthy people; take it to a graveside and you find out what it is.

Fallen asleep in Christ. The word sleep for a believer’s death goes back to Jesus himself: “The child is not dead but sleeping” (Mark 5:39); “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him” (John 11:11). He could call death sleep because he could end it with a word, and “in Christ” says why it is still sleep: the believer’s union with him is not broken by the grave (Romans 8:38–39; 1 Thessalonians 4:14). Christ has gone through death and come out on the far side, and he has left the door open behind him.

Most to be pitied. If this life is all there is, the Christian has made the worst bargain of anyone alive. Paul had given up his standing, his safety and his comfort (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). Without a resurrection that is not nobility but a man throwing his one life away on a rumour. The verse also quietly indicts a Christianity valued for what it does now, steadying a family and providing friends and a moral framework. That is real, but this faith is not primarily a way to live. It is a claim that a dead man is alive, and everything else follows from that or falls with it.

In everyday life. This week, do one thing that would be foolish if the tomb were still full: give away something you would rather keep, forgive a debt, or speak of Christ where it will cost you.

Does this mean the Christian life is miserable now? No. Paul wrote elsewhere of joy, peace and contentment in all circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13). He means that its sacrifices only make sense if Christ is raised; much of its joy is the joy of hope, of people who know where they are going. Take the destination away and the road becomes foolish; keep it, and even suffering can be borne with joy, because it is preparing for us “an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ has in fact been raised, and his rising is the beginning of God’s great harvest, which will end with death destroyed and God all in all. Paul steps out of the nightmare of verses 12–19: Christ is the firstfruits, the pledge that those who sleep in him will follow (v. 20), the head of a new humanity as Adam was of the old (vv. 21–22). The rising comes in order, Christ first and then his people at his coming, and then the end (vv. 23–24). Meanwhile he reigns until every enemy is under his feet, death last of all (vv. 25–27), and at the end the Son presents the finished kingdom to the Father (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Adam and Christ, and the Scope of Redemption

The comparison of Adam and Christ (as in Romans 5:12–21) is central to Paul’s teaching on both sin and salvation (see the note on vv. 20–22, and on the reach of “all” the box “Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved?” at the end of it). And the life Christ brings is at least as real as the death Adam brought.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had buried members of their church needed to know that those deaths were sleep awaiting a harvest, not permanent loss, and the firstfruits gave them an image they knew from Israel’s worship. Now: A Christian stands at a believer’s graveside with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared, and the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who gave the pledge.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ really has been raised, as the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees ours: as all who belong to Adam die, so all who belong to Christ will be made alive. Paul steps out of the nightmare of verses 12–19 into what is true.

But in fact. Two words in Greek (nyni de, but now), and they turn the whole chapter. After eight verses picturing a world without a risen Christ, Paul steps out of it without argument. Not “if”, but “in fact”.

The firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The picture comes from the farm and from Israel’s worship at once. On the day after the Sabbath following Passover, a single sheaf of the new barley was cut, brought to the priest and waved before the LORD (Leviticus 23:10–14; see firstfruits). One sheaf, in a field still standing: not the harvest but its promise, given to God first, the proof that the field would be reaped. On the most likely reckoning, that ceremony fell on the very morning Christ rose.

The first of a series. So the resurrection is not a stand-alone wonder; nobody waves a sheaf over an empty field. It is God’s public statement that the harvest of the dead has begun, and it says something about every Christian grave that has ever been dug: ours will follow. Not one ear of grain will be lost.

By a man. Death came through Adam’s sin (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12). Christ had to be truly human to undo what a human did.

In Adam, in Christ. Paul sees the human race under two representatives, and what each did counts for everyone belonging to him. Adam sinned, and death entered and spread to all who are in him, which is everybody, by birth. Christ obeyed, died and rose, and life comes to all who are in him, united to him by faith, by new birth. The first man brought death into the world, and the second walked into death and broke it open from inside.

Whichever man you are joined to. His outcome is yours. You did not choose to be in Adam, and the evidence is that you will die. But the principle that ruins you also saves you, for being in Christ works the same way: not by achievement, but by belonging (Romans 5:17–19).

In everyday life. Next time you pass a churchyard, remember the sheaf. The harvest has begun. And if you have a Christian grave to visit, go and stand by it this week and say: firstfruits.

How do I know I am in Christ and not only in Adam? You come to be in Christ by faith: by turning from your sin and trusting him as your Saviour and Lord. The Spirit unites you to him, and his death, righteousness and resurrection life become yours. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you are in him; faith is the hand, and Christ the treasure it holds. Look for the fruit too: a new love for him, a new hatred of sin, a desire for his people and his word. These do not make you his; they show that you are. If you are not sure, come to him now; he has never turned anyone away.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Universalists read “all” in both halves of verse 22 the same way. This commentary’s view: the two alls are defined by “in Adam” and “in Christ”; those who belong to him (v. 23) will be made alive to glory, and Scripture is clear that some will rise to judgment (John 5:28–29).
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come — at the time of the Passover festival.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection comes in God’s set order: Christ first, then his people when he comes, and then the end, when he hands the kingdom to the Father with every hostile power destroyed. The future has a shape, and the shape has stages.

But each in his own order. Order (tagma) is a military word: a rank, a division, a company of soldiers moving in sequence.

Those who belong to Christ. The first stage, Christ’s rising, is behind us; the second is still to come. At his coming (parousia, arrival, the word for a king’s visit to a city), all believers will be raised. Not those who achieved or understood something, or belonged to the right party in Corinth: the only qualification is that he owns them.

Then comes the end. The end (to telos) is the goal, the consummation of history. The whole campaign, from the incarnation to the resurrection of the dead, ends with the Son, the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), handing the finished work to his Father, like a commander reporting to the one who sent him. What is handed over is no ruin salvaged from a fire but a kingdom, every enemy dealt with and every subject alive.

Every rule and every authority and power. Every power opposed to God: human rebellion, death itself, and the spiritual forces behind the visible ones, the powers the Christian actually wrestles with (Ephesians 6:12). Not reformed or accommodated, but abolished. That steadies anyone reading the news: the powers that look permanent are on a list with a completion date, and nothing on it will survive the arrival of the King or require a second campaign (Colossians 2:15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule ends. He hands the kingdom over in the sense that his work as Mediator, bringing sinners to God and subduing every enemy, is complete; but he reigns forever with the Father: “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15).

In everyday life. When the news frightens you this week, name the thing that frightens you and add three words: until he comes.

If Christ is reigning now, why is the world still so evil? Because his reign is a campaign still under way. He has won the decisive battle at the cross and the empty tomb, and now rules from the Father’s right hand, gathering his people from every nation by the gospel and restraining evil. But the enemies are not yet all under his feet, and his people still suffer, as he did. He reigns, and we wait. The evil you see is real, but it is on borrowed time, and its end is set. Meanwhile his kingdom grows like a mustard seed, quietly, in every place where sinners bow the knee to him.

Where Christians differ: the millennium. Premillennialists see a gap between his coming (v. 23) and the end (v. 24), filled by a thousand-year earthly reign of Christ. Many of them careful students of Scripture, they read “then” as leaving room for an interval, pointing to Revelation 20:4–6, where the saints reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Amillennial Christians answer that Christ must reign until the last enemy, death, is destroyed (vv. 25–26), and death is defeated at the resurrection itself (vv. 54–55), so there is no room after his coming for a further age in which death still reigns. This commentary’s view: The most natural reading is that the end follows Christ’s coming directly. Christ is reigning now (v. 25), from heaven, and will reign until his return, when the dead are raised and death is destroyed. This is the amillennial view: the millennium of Revelation 20 describes Christ’s present reign during the church age. There is one return of Christ, visible and public, not a secret rapture followed by a later coming. Christians who expect a thousand-year reign love his appearing as truly as anyone; the difference is about the order of events, not about whether he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is reigning now, and he will go on reigning until every enemy is beaten; the last to fall will be death itself. Death is an enemy, and its end is fixed.

He must reign. From Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament echoes more often than any other: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.” Christ is reigning now (Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 10:12–13), and must (dei) means it is God’s plan. He is putting his enemies under his feet one by one, working his way toward the grave.

The last enemy. Destroyed (katargeitai) means abolished, rendered powerless. Death is not called a doorway or a friend at the end of a long day, but an enemy, the last one standing. Christ has already defeated it by his resurrection, going into death’s own house and taking the keys; at his return it will be abolished entirely (Revelation 20:14; 21:4). To deny the resurrection is to leave death undefeated: a gospel with no resurrection has a King who never wins his last battle.

Permission to hate death. That word enemy is worth more to a grieving Christian than much that is said at funerals. Religious talk often tries to make peace with death; the Bible gives the mourner permission to hate it, as the Lord himself did. On his way to the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he would call him out alive that same day, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), and the word John uses of him a moment earlier suggests something closer to indignation than sorrow (John 11:33). He was not weeping about the outcome; he was standing in front of the enemy itself, doing to a family he loved what it does to everybody.

What death does. It takes a person who was in the room and makes the room empty. It takes a hand that has been held for fifty years and makes it cold in an hour. It leaves a chair, a coat, a voice on an old recording that is now unbearable to play. The Christian is not asked to pretend, but to believe that the enemy is on a schedule: not tamed, not made bearable, but destroyed, and last, because everything else goes first.

Until the last grave is empty. There will come a day on which no one will ever again have to be told that someone has died. Glory to the King who must reign, and who will not lay down his sceptre until the last grave is empty.

In everyday life. If you are grieving, tell God that you hate what death has done, and then tell him that you believe it is on a schedule. If someone near you is grieving, do not hurry them toward serenity; sit with them, and remind them, when the time is right, that death is the last enemy, and it will be destroyed.

Is it a lack of faith to be afraid of dying? No. Death is an enemy, and it is natural to shrink from it; our Lord himself was in agony in Gethsemane. Faith does not remove every fear but shows what lies beyond it: death has lost its sting (v. 55), cannot separate you from Christ, and will not keep you. Many fear the process of dying more than death itself; bring that fear honestly to God. He has promised to be with you in the valley (Psalm 23:4). Very often those who have feared most find, when the hour comes, that grace is given for it.

parallels.desc: until I make your enemies your footstool

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everything has been put under Christ, the Son will present his finished work to the Father and gladly take his place under him, so that God may be all in all. This is where all history is heading.

All things in subjection under his feet. Psalm 8:6 is, in the first place, about human beings: “what is man that you are mindful of him?” (Psalm 8:4). It describes the task God gave the human race, to rule the earth under him: given in the garden and abandoned there. Paul applies it to Christ, the last Adam, the true human being, doing at last what humanity was made for (Hebrews 2:6–9). Psalm 8 has not been wrenched out of context; it has finally found a man it fits.

He is excepted. Paul states the obvious because it needs stating: the Father is not among the things subdued.

The Son himself will also be subjected. This has troubled readers for centuries, because it seems to make the Son permanently lesser. It does not. It describes not the Son’s nature but the completion of his mission. He was sent, obeyed, died, rose, reigns and subdues; and when the work is finished he presents it all to the Father and, as the one sent, gladly places himself under the Father who sent him. The Son who is “the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3) does not become less divine by handing over a completed kingdom. It is the same Son who said in a garden, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

That God may be all in all. The goal of history: God’s rule complete and unchallenged, filling everything (Ephesians 1:23; Colossians 3:11). The Son will lay all things at his Father’s feet, not because he must but because he delights to, and the Father will be glorified in the Son, and the Spirit will fill all things. Every place where a believer has felt God to be distant will have been abolished, along with distance itself.

Back down to Corinth. From this summit Paul comes straight back down to Corinth in verse 29: a hope this large must show in ordinary choices.

Will we still see and worship Jesus when God is all in all? Yes, forever. The Son does not disappear into the Father at the end. He remains the God-man, with his risen body, and the Lamb is on the throne in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:1, 3). God is all in all precisely in and through Christ: “the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). The whole of creation will ring with the praise of Father, Son and Spirit, and we will worship the Lamb who was slain for all eternity.

Where Christians differ: is the Son inferior to the Father? Arians, ancient and modern (followers of Arius, a fourth-century teacher who held that the Son was created), use this verse to argue that the Son is a lesser being. This commentary’s view: The subjection here is of the Son as incarnate Mediator, in his role of redemption, not of the Son in his divine nature. In his divine nature the Son is equal with the Father, of the same substance (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). In his role as Mediator, he submits to the Father’s will (John 6:38). This is the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, as summarised in the Nicene Creed and in the Westminster and 1689 Confessions (Westminster Confession 2.3, 8.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3, 8.2).

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How people live shows what they believe about the dead, and both Christian practice and Christian sacrifice make sense only if the dead are raised. Paul turns from argument to life. The practice of baptism on behalf of the dead assumes the dead have a future (v. 29). His own daily danger, his dying every day and his fight with beasts at Ephesus would be a waste if they do not (vv. 30–32a). Without the resurrection the party-goer’s creed would be the only sensible one: eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (v. 32b). So he warns them against the company that is leading them astray, and calls them to wake up and stop sinning, because the denial springs from not knowing God (vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Ground of Christian Living

If there is no resurrection, a life of self-denial, risk and suffering for others makes no sense, and the man who says let us eat and drink is simply being consistent. Paul’s own life is an argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes sense on no other footing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus may be literal or a picture of violent opponents; either way it was real mortal danger, and Paul asks what it was for if the dead are not raised. Now: The missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who will not trim his convictions, the church member who gives up promotion for the sake of integrity: each life of this kind makes sense only if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the Corinthians’ own practices, and the apostles’ daily risks, make sense only if the dead will rise. Paul adds a second kind of argument, from practice.

If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Whatever the practice was (see the box below), how Paul uses it is certain, and that is what matters. He is not teaching it. He speaks not of “you” or “we” but of other people, holding the practice at arm’s length, and simply points out that it makes no sense unless the dead have a future: the Corinthians’ own behaviour contradicts their theology. That is a fair method. People are often better than their opinions, and one honest answer to a bad idea is to show that no one lives as though it were true. Nobody grieves as if the dead were nothing. Nobody attends a funeral and behaves like a man who thinks a machine has stopped.

Why are we in danger every hour? Paul turns to his own life, an argument that runs to the end of verse 32: why would the apostles risk death constantly if there were nothing after this?

Buried with him in baptism. Christian baptism itself only makes sense if the dead are raised, because it pictures Christ’s death and rising: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). A church that baptised and denied the resurrection acted out the gospel with its hands and denied it with its mouth.

Can I do anything for a loved one who died without Christ? Nothing can change a person’s state after death; Scripture gives no second chance and no way for the living to alter it (Hebrews 9:27). That is hard, and it is right to grieve it honestly. But remember two things. You do not know what passed between that person and God in their last hours, and the thief on the cross shows how late grace can come. And the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Leave them with him. What you can do is pray for the living, and speak of Christ to those who are still within reach of the gospel.

Where Christians differ: baptism for the dead. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, based on this verse. This commentary’s view: Paul mentions the practice without endorsing it, and notice he says people, not we. Nowhere else does Scripture teach it. The New Testament is clear that each person must believe for themselves, and that after death comes judgment, with no second chance (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:26). Baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. (Christians who baptise the infants of believers agree that no one can be baptised on behalf of the dead.)

Uncertain wording. Baptism “on behalf of the dead” is probably the most puzzling phrase in the letter; more than forty interpretations are said to have been suggested, and it is better to admit that than to pretend to a certainty nobody has. Three readings are worth knowing. The plainest sense of the Greek is that some people at Corinth were being baptised as proxies for relatives or friends who had died unbaptised, hoping it would do the dead some good; early writers such as John Chrysostom knew of such practices among heretical groups and condemned them. A second takes “on behalf of” to mean “because of”: converts baptised because of the dead, moved by a believer whose hope had held to the end, or longing to be reunited with believing loved ones. A third takes it as baptism with one’s own coming death and resurrection in view. The first is the most likely. It is possible to hold a passage loosely without holding the Bible loosely: the resurrection does not rest on verse 29, and a doctrine built on one difficult sentence, against the plain sense of the rest of Scripture, stands on a very narrow footing.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; most likely some Corinthians were being baptized as proxies for the dead. Paul mentions the practice without approving it, only to show that it assumes a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul faces death every day for the gospel, and that makes sense only if the dead are raised; if they are not, the party-goers have understood life better than the martyrs.

I die every day! Not first a saying about self-denial but a description of his working conditions (2 Corinthians 4:10–11), and a man in that position needs a reason. He swears to it, oddly, by “my pride in you”: even mid-argument he tells this difficult congregation he is proud of them.

What do I gain? Paul had been in a place where he did not expect to come out alive (on the beasts, see the box below). “Humanly speaking” (kata anthrōpon) probably means with merely human hopes, as a man with nothing to look for beyond this life. The honest answer, if the dead are not raised, is nothing, and Paul says so without flinching.

Let us eat and drink. The quotation is from Isaiah 22:13: a city under siege that ought to have been repenting threw a party instead. It is the philosophy of the ancient world and of ours: if this is all there is, get what you can before the lights go out. Paul does not sneer at it. If death is the end, the person eating and drinking has understood the situation better than the martyr.

To die is gain. Paul’s letters give the other half of the answer: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). If the tomb is full, he gains nothing; if it is empty, he gains the Lord himself. Paul did not risk the beasts for a cause but for a Person, and because that Person is risen, every danger faced for him was an investment, not a loss.

Tomorrow he would die for us. The Lord Jesus did not eat and drink because tomorrow he would die; he took bread and a cup and gave them away, because tomorrow he would die for us. He laid down his life and took it up again, so every life laid down for him is kept. Because he is risen, self-denial is wisdom and martyrdom is victory.

Why are we always in a hurry? The eat and drink of Isaiah’s city has a modern form, and it is not only the party. It is the bucket list, the fear of missing out, every weekend made the most of. The German sociologist Hartmut Rosa has argued that the speed of modern life is partly an answer to death: if this life is all we get, the only way to have more is to cram more in. No wonder time always feels short. The resurrection takes the pressure off. If Christ is raised, this life is not your one chance at joy but the first chapter of a life that will not end, with the One of whom it is said, “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11). So you are free to miss things. You can spend an evening with someone dull and lonely, turn down the promotion, sit with a dying friend, and lose nothing. The person who believes in the resurrection is the one person who has time.

But many people with no hope of resurrection live generous lives. Does that prove Paul wrong? No. Many unbelievers are kind, and some put Christians to shame; but their kindness has no ground in their creed. If death ends everything, self-giving love is a beautiful habit with nothing underneath it, and those who practise it live better than their beliefs, as the Corinthians did in verse 29. The Christian can give his life away for a reason: the One who gave his life away first was raised, and nothing given for him is lost (v. 58).

Is it selfish to serve God for the sake of heaven? Not if heaven is God himself. The Bible’s reward is not a payment unrelated to the work, like money for a chore, but the natural end of loving God: being with him and enjoying him forever. A man who marries for love is not mercenary for looking forward to the wedding. Jesus himself endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). To want Christ, at the cost of everything else, is not selfishness but the very thing we were made for.

Uncertain wording. What “I fought with beasts at Ephesus” refers to is not known. It is probably a picture of fierce human opposition, since a Roman citizen was unlikely to be thrown to animals, and Paul does not mention it in his list of sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Some link it with the riot of Acts 19:23–41, though the letter was probably written before it; more likely it refers to the “many adversaries” Paul mentions at Ephesus (16:9), opponents who acted like wild animals. Either way the sense is the same: he had been in mortal danger.
verseByVerse.note: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition; a Roman citizen could not normally be sent to the arena.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let the people who deny the resurrection lead you astray: wake up and stop sinning, for their error comes from not knowing God. In Corinth wrong belief and wrong living were already feeding each other.

Do not be deceived. The proverb is a line from the Greek poet Menander, probably a common saying by Paul’s day. Paul is willing to quote a pagan poet, as he did at Athens (Acts 17:28), because truth is truth wherever it turns up. A sentence about company in an argument about the resurrection shows what Paul assumes: people rarely reason their way into a false belief; they drift into it, in company, over time.

How faith is usually lost. Many who abandon the faith do not do it in a library, but through friendship, through the desire to be thought reasonable by people they admired, through a slow adjustment of what could comfortably be said aloud. Paul is not commanding a retreat from the world (5:10), but telling the church to stop finding the confident deniers inside it impressive. If you recognise some of that drift in yourself, the fact that it troubles you is a sign of life: Paul’s word is “wake up”, not “give up”.

Wake up. Wake up (eknēphō) is what you say to a man sleeping it off: sober up, come round. To a congregation that thought itself the most spiritually advanced in Greece, he says not that they are mistaken but that they are not properly conscious.

No knowledge of God. No knowledge (agnōsia) is ignorance, an irony for a church that prided itself on knowledge. That is the diagnosis under the error. Behind the denial is not a difficulty with biology but a God too small to raise the dead, which is to say not the God who made the world out of nothing. He breathed, and Adam stood up out of the dust; he called, and Lazarus walked out of the tomb. To deny the resurrection is to know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matthew 22:29).

The God who raised Jesus. In the New Testament God is named by what he did on the third day: the one “who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord” (Romans 4:24). To deny it leaves out the deed by which he has made himself known; to know God is to know him as the Father of the risen Son (John 17:3).

I say this to your shame. It is the second time in the letter Paul has used that phrase (6:5). A church full of knowledge, and some of its members do not know God.

How do I keep unbelieving friends without being pulled away? Be the influence rather than the influenced. Jesus ate with sinners, but set the direction of the conversation. Keep your roots deep: the word daily, church weekly, and Christian friends close enough to notice if you drift. Be open about your faith early in a friendship. Watch for the warning signs: finding your convictions embarrassing, laughing at what grieves God, wanting their approval more than Christ’s. And if a particular friendship is steadily dragging you into sin, love may require distance. The goal is to win them, not to become them.
verseByVerse.note: “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The resurrection body will be the same person, raised by God in a new and glorious form fitted for the age to come. Paul answers the sceptic’s question, how and with what body (v. 35), first from the field: a seed must die before it lives, and what comes up is far greater than what went down, yet still its own kind (vv. 36–38). Then from creation: God has made flesh and bodies and glories of many kinds, and is not short of designs (vv. 39–41). So the body sown perishable, dishonoured, weak and natural is raised imperishable, glorious, powerful and spiritual (vv. 42–44). Behind it all stand two men: we have borne the image of Adam, the man of dust, and shall bear the image of Christ, the man of heaven (vv. 45–49).
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The church has always confessed the resurrection of the body, not merely the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed holds both truths: continuity, since seed and plant are one living thing at different stages, and transformation, since the plant’s glory exceeds anything visible in the seed. Christ’s own resurrection is the pattern (see vv. 37–38 and v. 44).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul will not accept the Greek terms, that the body is the problem. The body is God’s good creation and is destined for resurrection; the problem is not having a body but mortality and corruption. Now: Whenever the goal of salvation is pictured as the soul leaving the body behind for ever, the Corinthian problem is back. The goal is the new creation: raised bodies on a renewed earth, in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How the dead can be raised is answered in every field: a seed must be buried and die before it comes to life, so burial is not the end of the story but a sowing. Paul lets the sceptic put the objection in his own words, and answers from the ground under his feet.

How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come? Not a stupid question. Bodies decay, are burned, are lost at sea and scattered so completely that not a molecule stays in place. Where is the body to be raised, and what would it be like? The same decaying body sounded absurd to Greeks.

You foolish person! Foolish (aphrōn) means without sense, and it is sharper in English than in Greek: someone reasoning without what he already knows, who has the answer in his own back garden and has not looked at it.

Unless it dies. The answer is a seed. You bury a hard dry seed in the ground: a funeral. Dig it up a fortnight later and it is soft and rotting. And out of that comes a green shoot, then a stalk carrying thirty seeds of its own. The seed refutes the objection in every field the objector has walked past: burial is sowing.

Evidence from a seed. Paul could have answered from revelation (2 Corinthians 12:2–4); he answers from a seed. God has arranged the world so that the hardest thing a person has to believe is acted out every spring in front of him, in mud: a pattern written into creation, applied at last to the thing that matters most.

A grain of wheat. Jesus said exactly this about himself, days before it happened: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). He meant his own burial, and a harvest that would include the man asking this question.

Supposing him to be the gardener. The God of the harvest is the God of the resurrection. Where he was crucified there was a garden, and in it a new tomb (John 19:41). The Seed went into that ground on Friday, and on Sunday Mary, weeping, supposed the man in front of her to be the gardener (John 20:15): the first of a crop that will cover the earth.

Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated? Not to God’s power; he will raise the cremated as surely as the buried. Burial pictures the sowing of a seed, but cremation is no wrong; what matters is respect for the body and a funeral that speaks plainly of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes up from the ground looks nothing like the seed that went in, yet it is the same life: God gives each its own body, as he chooses. The resurrection body is not an improved corpse, and it is still you.

A bare kernel. A seed looks nothing like the plant; if you had only seen the seed, you would think the plant a wild story. So part of the answer to “With what kind of body do they come?” is: not one you could work out from what goes into the ground. The resurrection body is to the buried body what the plant is to the seed: the same life, in a new and far greater form.

As he has chosen. God gives the new body, and that quietly settles the question of scattered atoms: the wheat plant is not built only out of the seed but of soil and rain and air. Continuity is not the same particles reassembled; it is the same God attending to the same person. A body ruined by illness, burned, or lost at sea is no obstacle. The God who made the first body out of the ground knows exactly where every one of his people is. He who knitted you together in your mother’s womb (Psalm 139:13) will clothe you in glory, and you will praise him with a body fit at last for praise.

To each kind of seed its own body. Wheat becomes wheat. Each person will be raised as himself: not one generic glorified shape issued to everybody, not a soul absorbed among souls, but his own. Barley does not come up wheat.

The body he has chosen. We need not guess; he has done it once already. The body laid in the garden tomb came out of it, leaving the linen behind; yet it stood among the disciples behind locked doors (John 20:19) and could never die again. The Lord will change our weak bodies to match his own body of glory (Philippians 3:21). The seed God has already raised is his own Son, and every believer’s harvest will be shaped like his.

Will I still be me? Yes. Not a new person who happens to carry your name, but you, body and soul, raised and made whole. Your soul, with Christ since death, will be reunited with your body, the same body, transformed; your history, relationships and the work of grace in you will not be erased. The risen Jesus was recognisably Jesus; he knew Mary by name and she knew him by his voice. So it will be with you, except that everything sin and death have spoiled will be gone.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has already made bodies of many kinds, each with its own glory, so a body raised in a new kind of glory is no difficulty for him. The objector assumed a resurrection body must be the same sort of thing as his own, and that assumption is his whole difficulty.

Not all flesh is the same. A second comparison: “body” need not mean only one kind of thing. The list echoes Genesis 1: a man’s flesh and a fish’s flesh are both flesh and not remotely alike; the bird that lives in the air and the fish that would drown in it are both embodied creatures.

Heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. Sun, moon and stars; plants, animals and people. Each has its own splendour (doxa, glory, brightness), of different orders altogether. A God with this much range will not be stuck for a design when he comes to raise the dead.

Star differs from star in glory. A tentmaker writing to a quarrelling church about a difficult doctrine stops to look up and notice that the stars are not alike. Difference is not a defect in God’s workmanship; it is his habit. He made a church of eyes and ears and feet (12:17), and a sky in which no two lights are matched. A congregation that had been ranking one another by a single measure is being shown a night sky.

Through him all things were made. “By him all things were created … all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16). The One who made flesh for fish and birds, and fixed every star in its own glory, is the Son, and the same Son “gives life to whom he will” (John 5:21). He has never yet run short of ideas.

What it does not mean. Not that believers will become stars, or that there will be ranks of glory among the saved based on merit: the illustration is about kinds, not ranks. Scripture does speak elsewhere of rewards that differ (3:12–15), but every raised believer will bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49).

In everyday life. Look at your church with the eyes you turn to the night sky: stop measuring your brothers and sisters by a single standard, and thank God for one person this week who is gloriously unlike you.

Will there be rewards in heaven? Yes, but not the kind that make anyone envious. Scripture speaks of reward for faithful service (3:14; Matthew 25:21), but every reward is itself grace, for even our good works were prepared by God (Ephesians 2:10). No one will be second-class in glory or begrudge another; the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Every vessel will be filled to the brim with joy, though the vessels may differ in size. The greatest reward of all is the same for everyone: Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The body buried in decay, humiliation and weakness will be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful. The comparisons stop and the promises begin: four contrasts (vv. 42–44), and each of the first three names something every reader has felt.

Perishable … imperishable. Perishable (phthora) is decay; imperishable (aphtharsia) is incorruption. The present body is on a schedule of decay. The knee goes, the eyes go, the name of somebody you have known for forty years will not come. Slow it as you may (and there is nothing wrong with slowing it), the direction is fixed. The resurrection body will have nothing in it that can wear out.

Sown in dishonor … raised in glory. This is the honest one, and anyone who has sat with the dying knows what Paul means. There is little dignity at the end: being washed by strangers, a mind that says the wrong word, a person once formidable now frightened of the stairs. Death does not merely end a life; it humiliates it first. Into that Paul writes “raised in glory”, the same word used of the splendour of God himself. The body that was carried out of a ward with a sheet over it comes back radiant (Matthew 13:43).

Raised in power. Weakness is the ceiling everyone lives under: wanting to help and being too tired, the body unable to carry the will that far. “Raised in power” means the body will at last be able to do all that the person longs to do.

Sown. The word used in every one of these contrasts is not “disposed of” or “lost” but “sown”: a thing done by a farmer, on purpose, with a harvest in mind. A grave, on Paul’s account, is not a full stop but a planting.

He was sown first. Every one of these contrasts happened first to Christ. He was sown in dishonour: stripped, mocked and hung naked on a cross, then laid in a borrowed grave. “He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4), and “being raised from the dead, will never die again” (Romans 6:9). What has already happened to one body, his people will follow.

In everyday life. Visit someone whose body is failing, in a hospital, a care home, or their own front room, and treat them with the honour due to one who will be raised in glory.

How should I care for my body now if it will be raised? With gratitude and respect, but without idolatry. Your body is not a prison to escape but a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19) and a seed of glory. Feed it, rest it, exercise it, and do not abuse it with drunkenness or sexual sin; and care for the bodies of the sick, the elderly and the disabled, because God will raise them. But do not worship youth or beauty, and do not despair as the body declines. The wrinkles and the aches are the dishonour of the sowing, and the harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The body that is raised is not a ghost but a real body, wholly alive with the Holy Spirit and governed by him. This fourth contrast is the most often misunderstood.

It is sown a natural body. Natural (psychikos, soulish) describes a body animated by ordinary human life and suited to this age (2:14): breath, blood, appetite, sleep.

It is raised a spiritual body. Not a ghost, a mist, or a soul escaped from its container. Spiritual (pneumatikos) describes what governs and empowers it, not what it is made of; Paul uses the same word of spiritual people (2:15), who are not made of spirit either. So the resurrection body is not less physical than the present one but, if anything, more: more solid, more alive, more capable, with everything that drags at the body removed.

One such body was examined. The risen Christ told them to touch him: “a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). He ate broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:42–43), and offered Thomas the wounds (John 20:27).

He kept the scars. The one resurrection body we know is marked permanently by what was done to it: the wounds healed, the marks kept. The risen life does not forget. The Lamb in heaven stands as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

A man with scarred hands on the throne. He did not leave his body in the grave like a shell but took it into heaven, where a man with scarred hands now sits on the throne of the universe, and the Spirit who raised him dwells in his people, the pledge that he will give life to our mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). Blessed be the Lord who redeems the body and does not discard it.

Will we know one another? The disciples knew him, sometimes at once, sometimes after a moment, always in the end; and Paul assumes that Christians will be reunited and will recognise each other (1 Thessalonians 4:17–18; 2 Corinthians 4:14). Love does not end (13:8), and the people we have loved in Christ will be ours to love forever, more truly than now.

What about bodies wrecked by disease, dementia or disability? Verse 38 has already answered it: God gives a body as he has chosen, and what is raised is raised imperishable, in glory, in power (vv. 42–43). Nothing the fall put into a body will be raised with it. The child who never walked will run; the mind lost to dementia will know and praise and remember; the body broken by illness will be strong. At what age? Scripture does not say, and we should not invent. What it does say is enough, and more than a description: the body will be like his (Philippians 3:21).

Where Christians differ: a physical resurrection? Some say the resurrection body is immaterial, a spirit body, and that Jesus’ resurrection was spiritual rather than physical. This commentary’s view: Christ’s resurrection body was physical: he ate, was touched, had flesh and bones and the marks of his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27). The tomb was empty. Ours will be like his (Philippians 3:21). The spiritual body is physical, but transformed and wholly governed by the Holy Spirit (Westminster Confession 32.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.2).
verseByVerse.note: A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam received life and handed on a natural body; Christ, the last Adam, gives life by the Spirit, and in God’s order the natural comes first and the spiritual afterwards. Paul grounds verse 44 in the two men who head the human race.

The first man Adam became a living being. Paul goes back to Genesis 2:7, where Adam becomes a living being (psychē zōsa, a living soul); from that word psychē comes the word translated “natural” in verse 44. Everything the first man had, he was given: he was made from dust he did not gather, given breath he did not take, and put in a garden he did not plant.

The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Not merely alive: a source. By his resurrection the head of the new humanity (Romans 5:12–21) became the giver of life through the Spirit. Adam received life; Christ gives it (John 5:21; 6:63). The first Adam was a vessel; the last is a spring. The resurrection of Jesus is not simply the best example of resurrection but its cause.

What life-giving spirit means. Not that Christ is no longer bodily, nor that he turned into the Holy Spirit; the two remain distinct persons (2 Corinthians 13:14). The risen Christ, in a body wholly alive with the Spirit, now gives life: he pours out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) and will raise his people by him. And he is the last Adam, so that no one need expect a third. Everything after Christ is a matter of which of the two you belong to.

First the natural, and then the spiritual. The order of history is first Adam and this age, then Christ and the age to come: dust before glory. That is a rebuke to the Corinthian error, which was to believe they had already arrived, already reigning (4:8).

Seed first, harvest afterwards. It is also a comfort to anyone who suspects his Christian life is too plain to be real. Plainness is the appointed order, and the Lord himself went through it (Hebrews 5:8): some thirty years in a carpenter’s shop came before about three years of ministry. The fountain of life was content to receive daily bread from his Father’s hand, to grow, and to wait. There is no shortcut past the natural into the spiritual, and God is not in a hurry.

My Christian life feels ordinary. Am I missing something? Probably not. Most of the Christian life is meant to be ordinary: prayer and Scripture, weekly worship, faithful work, patient love at home. That is not second-rate Christianity but the seed before the harvest; there is no secret level you are missing. Seek more of him, and do not settle for coldness. But beware of anyone who promises a shortcut to glory now. The glory is coming, and it is far greater than any experience this life can give.

parallels.desc: the man became a living creature

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As we have shared the likeness of Adam, mortal and made of dust, so all who belong to Christ will share the likeness of the risen Man from heaven. Two men, two origins, and two families that look like their heads.

The first man was from the earth, a man of dust. God formed the man of dust from the ground (Genesis 2:7), and told him after the fall that to dust he would return (Genesis 3:19). We are made of the soil, kept alive by it, and return to it.

The second man is from heaven. Not of different material: his body, born of a woman, got tired and hungry and bled. He is from heaven in origin: he existed before he was born and came here from heaven, which is true of no other human being, and his risen body belongs to the heavenly realm.

We shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. Image (eikōn): we were born in Adam’s likeness (Genesis 5:3), and know its features intimately: mortality, weakness, the pull toward what we know is wrong. The second likeness is as certain: “we shall also bear”, a plain statement of what will happen, with no condition attached. Those God foreknew he predestined, settled beforehand, to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29); “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The gap closes. The man you have wanted to be and the man you are have never once been the same; every Christian carries a record of the gap. On that day it closes, not by lowering the standard or by gradual improvement finally arriving, but because the likeness of Christ, worked into his people slowly and against resistance, will be completed in an instant and will hold. There will be nothing left in you that he would have to overlook.

The brothers of the King. The Son of God came down from heaven and bore our image all the way to the grave, so that we, the men of dust, might bear his. He wore Adam’s likeness, marked by death, and rose in a likeness death cannot touch. Glory to the Man from heaven, who has made the children of Adam the brothers of the King.

If I will bear his image then, why try to be like him now? Because the Spirit is already at work forming that image in you, and you are called to cooperate with him: “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The resurrection completes what sanctification, the Spirit’s patient remaking of a forgiven sinner, begins. The hope is itself a motive: “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). You do not become like Christ in order to be saved; you become like him because you are saved, and the finished likeness is promised.

Textual note. In verse 47 the KJV, following later manuscripts, reads “the second man is the Lord from heaven”; the earliest lack “the Lord”, so most modern Bibles omit it. In verse 49 many manuscripts, including most of the oldest, read “let us bear”, making it a call to action; the ESV note mentions this. The two Greek words differ by a single vowel that sounded much the same aloud, so copyists could easily confuse them. The future “we shall” fits the context of the resurrection better, and it is the reading the argument requires, which is why most translations print it.

parallels.desc: you are dust

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Christ comes, death itself will be swallowed up, and that victory, already won and given through him, makes every labour for him worth it. Our bodies as they are cannot inherit God’s kingdom, so Paul reveals a mystery: living and dead believers alike will be changed in an instant at the last trumpet (vv. 50–52). The perishable must put on the imperishable, and then Isaiah’s promise comes true, death swallowed up in victory (vv. 53–54). Paul taunts death, whose sting is sin, empowered by the law (vv. 55–56), then breaks into thanks to God, who gives us the victory through Christ (v. 57). So the chapter ends not in speculation but in work: stand firm and abound in the Lord’s work, for it is not in vain (v. 58).
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The chapter ends not with heaven but with work (see the note on v. 58). Herman Bavinck’s great theme was that grace restores nature: the resurrection does not cancel creation but redeems and glorifies it.

Anthony Hoekema makes the same point in his study of what the Bible teaches about the last things: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that their dead were not lost, that their own work was not futile, and that the God who raised Christ would finish what he had begun in them. This hope is what lets love bear all things and endure all things (13:7). Now: Every generation asks whether a life means anything beyond its short span. Paul’s answer is yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our bodies as they now are cannot enter God’s eternal kingdom, so every believer, whether dead or still alive when Christ returns, will be changed.

Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. A Hebrew phrase for human nature in its present weak, mortal state (Matthew 16:17; Galatians 1:16), not a slur on physical existence, which Paul has spent fifteen verses defending. It is not a moral judgment but a statement of what such a body is fit for. You do not go deep-sea diving in a jacket. (It does not mean the resurrection body is not flesh; see the note on v. 44.)

A mystery. In Paul a mystery is not a puzzle but a truth God had hidden and now makes known: the King is coming, and his people will be changed.

We shall not all sleep. Sleep means, as all through the chapter, to die. The new information: the generation of Christians alive when Christ returns will never be buried at all, but will reach the same transformation by a different road.

But we shall all be changed. All believers, dead and living: changed (allassō) is exchanged, as one garment is exchanged for another. Paul’s teaching here joins hands with 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17: the trumpet, the dead in Christ rising first, the living caught up together with them. Christians of every persuasion share nearly all of it: that Jesus Christ will return personally, visibly and bodily; that the dead in Christ will be raised and the living transformed, in an instant; and that no believer of any generation will be left out.

He shared our flesh and blood. The Son of God, who had always possessed the kingdom, took the very nature that cannot inherit it, “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). He entered mortal flesh, died in it, and was raised in it, changed, flesh and bone made imperishable (Luke 24:39). The change Paul announces is his people being made like him.

In everyday life. Live today as if he might come before evening, not in fear, but in readiness: with sins confessed, quarrels made up, and your face turned toward the sky.

Did Paul expect to be alive when Christ returned? He writes “we” as one of the living church, always to be ready; he did not know the day (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2), and he never set one.

Will believers who are alive at his coming miss anything by not dying? No, and the dead are not disadvantaged either: the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and both groups meet the Lord together, changed into his likeness. Whether he comes in your lifetime or you go to him first, you lose nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The change will happen in an instant, when the last trumpet sounds: the dead will be raised never to die again, and the living will be transformed.

In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. In a moment translates en atomō: in an uncuttable instant, the word from which we get atom. A slice of time too thin to have parts; the twinkling of an eye is the homelier version, over before it is noticed.

The slowest and the fastest work of God. Everything else in the Christian life is slow. Sanctification takes decades and moves backwards on many days; grief takes years; prayers are answered over a lifetime, or not visibly at all. Then this: no gradual improvement. A woman eleven years unable to leave her chair is in the next instant imperishable; a man in a churchyard since 1840, his stone illegible, is standing. The slowest work God does and the fastest work God does are both directed at the same person.

At the last trumpet. In Israel trumpets announced great acts of God, summoned the assembly, called the camp to move (Numbers 10:1–10) and announced a new king (1 Kings 1:34). This one does all of these at once (Matthew 24:31), and it is last because there will never again be anyone who needs calling.

The dead will be raised. They do not rise by their own power; they “will be raised”, as Christ “was raised” (v. 4), and nobody in that vast company contributes anything. They are called, and they come, because the voice that calls them is the voice of the Son of God: “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29), as once he called, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43).

Raised by the same voice. That morning does not rest on the strength of anyone’s faith. The believing dead of every age, apostles and martyrs, mothers and children, the forgotten saints of a thousand village churches, will be raised by the same voice, in a moment, imperishable, and look on the face of their King. He who was laid in a tomb will open every tomb.

Will there be one resurrection or two? One general resurrection, at Christ’s return. Jesus said that all in the tombs will come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). Paul spoke of a resurrection of the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). This chapter dwells on believers, for comfort and hope; but the same trumpet that raises the saints to glory summons all to judgment (Matthew 25:31–46). That is why the gospel is urgent now. Premillennial Christians see two resurrections a thousand years apart in Revelation 20:4–6; this commentary takes the first resurrection there as the believer’s new life with Christ now, with one bodily resurrection at his return.

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists (Christians who divide history into distinct eras and expect a separate future for national Israel) teach a secret rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers away before a seven-year tribulation, and then return again visibly later. Many of them read the Scriptures with great care, and point to promises that believers are not destined for wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9) and will be kept from the hour of trial (Revelation 3:10). Others see one coming: Paul ties this moment to the last trumpet, the public trumpet of Christ’s coming (Matthew 24:31), and to the resurrection that ends death (vv. 54–55); and the word for meeting the Lord in the air was used of citizens going out to meet an arriving king and escorting him into the city, not of being taken away from it. This commentary’s view: Paul says this happens at the last trumpet, which suggests the end, not a stage before further events. The New Testament describes one return of Christ, visible, public and glorious (Matthew 24:27, 30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7), at which the dead are raised, the living changed, and all are judged. There is no secret rapture. Believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, to welcome him as he comes, and then be with him forever. Even so, it is a poor use of a promise this size to make it the occasion of a quarrel among people who are all waiting for the same trumpet. (On the millennium, see the note on vv. 23–24.)
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This same mortal body will be clothed with immortality, and then God’s ancient promise will come true: death will be swallowed up in victory.

This perishable body must put on the imperishable. The verb is put on (endyō), the word for getting dressed. The perishable body is not discarded and a better one issued; it is clothed, and what is underneath is still there (2 Corinthians 5:2–4): resurrection, not replacement. And notice “this perishable body”: not bodies in general, but this one. One imagines him, with a scarred back and perhaps failing eyes, gesturing at himself as he dictated: this one.

Must. Necessity, not likelihood. God has determined that his people will live in a new creation, where a perishable body cannot; and he has bound himself by his promise. Paul repeats it, as a man repeats good news he can hardly believe he may tell.

Immortality. Immortality (athanasia) is deathlessness. Only God has immortality in himself (1 Timothy 6:16); he will give it to his people. How will mortals receive it? Through the One who is both: our Saviour Christ Jesus “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). The immortality the saints put on is not a quality they develop but the life of the risen Christ shared with them. On that day his people will be dressed in what he already wears.

Death is swallowed up in victory. The quotation is from Isaiah 25:8, and Isaiah is describing a feast: on his mountain the LORD will swallow up death forever, and wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). Swallowed up (katapinō) is gulped down, devoured. No negotiated settlement: the thing that has swallowed every human being who ever lived is itself swallowed at last. On a hill outside Jerusalem, death opened its mouth and swallowed the Son of God, and it could not keep him down. On the third day he came out of the grave, and death was the thing that had been swallowed.

The faces. The detail most people need is the faces. God is not described as issuing a decree about grief, but as coming close enough to wipe tears off individual faces with his own hand, which is what he is doing at the end of the Bible too (Revelation 21:4). Timothy Keller often pointed to the moment in Tolkien’s The Return of the King when Sam Gamgee wakes after the darkness is over and asks, “Is everything sad going to come untrue?” The resurrection is God’s answer, and the answer is yes: not that the sorrow never happened, but that it will be undone and turned into a joy that is greater for having passed through it.

In everyday life. If you know someone who is grieving this month, send them Isaiah 25:8 with one line telling them you are praying.

How do I hold on to this when I am grieving? Slowly, and with help. Grief does not obey arguments, and God does not ask you to stop grieving; he promises to wipe away tears, so there will be tears to wipe. Read these verses aloud, even when they feel far off. Let others pray for you when you cannot pray. Visit the grave, if it helps, and say there what Paul says here. The day is coming when the Lord will lift your face with his own hand, and the person you have lost in Christ will be at the table.

parallels.desc: he will swallow up death forever

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death has lost its power over believers, because its sting is sin, and Christ has taken that sting away. Paul taunts death to its face, then explains why he can.

O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? Paul is quoting Hosea 13:14, where the questions probably summon death’s plagues to punish unfaithful Israel; standing on the far side of the empty tomb, he turns them into a taunt song over defeated death, the sort of thing shouted after a beaten enemy being watched off the field. Death has never lost a single engagement in the history of the world; every person it has come for, it has taken. And Paul stands in front of it and asks what it has won.

The sting. The barb of a scorpion or a bee, the part that can kill you. A honeybee that has stung has left its sting behind; it can still clear a picnic, but a child who knows will stand still while it buzzes round his head. Death may still frighten, but it cannot destroy believers.

The sting of death is sin. Paul explains the picture. Death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). What makes it terrible is not that it ends the body (animals die, and it is sad, but not frightening in this way) but that it is the doorway to judgment for a guilty person. Sin gives death its barb.

And the power of sin is the law. The law gives sin its power by exposing it, condemning it, and even provoking it (Romans 7:7–13). The law is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12), but it puts our wrongdoing on record as the breaking of God’s known command, and pronounces the sentence.

Follow the chain backwards. Death is fearful because of sin; sin has its power from the law; and Christ has dealt with both: he kept the law we broke and bore the curse it pronounced (Galatians 3:13). And the religious person who hopes his good record will see him through is relying on the very law that accuses him. Only the One who kept the law for us and bore its curse can disarm it.

The sting stayed in him. Death drove its sting into the Son of God, and the sting stayed in him. He took into his body the curse of the law and the wages of sin, until no condemnation was left for anyone in him. O death, where is your sting? It was spent on Golgotha.

In everyday life. Say Paul’s taunt aloud at the end of a hard day, and again when you hear bad news from a doctor.

What about those who die without Christ? For them death keeps its sting, because their sin remains on their own account. Death is then not a doorway to rest but to judgment, and Scripture warns plainly of conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). That is why the gospel is the most urgent message in the world. The sting is drawn only for those in Christ. If you are not yet trusting him, come to him now, while death is still at a distance; he receives all who come. And if you are grieving someone who seemed to die without him, see the note on vv. 29–30.

Textual note. The KJV reads “O grave” in the second question, and puts “sting” first, following later manuscripts; the earliest have “death” twice.

parallels.desc: O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory over sin and death is God’s gift, given to us now through Jesus Christ, and the only fitting response is thanks. The proofs are finished, the objections answered, and Paul does the one thing left: he gives thanks (compare Romans 7:25).

Who gives us the victory. Nobody in the sentence wins anything. The victory is given, as a present, to people who were dead in trespasses and sins and had contributed nothing except the problem. And “gives” is in the present tense: God is giving us the victory now, to people still in perishable bodies, still burying their friends, still afraid of the diagnosis.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through his death, which removed sin’s sting, and his resurrection, which defeated death. Not through our grasp of the doctrine or the quality of our dying. Christians have died well and badly, frightened, confused, heavily medicated, and it makes no difference to the outcome, because the victory was won by somebody else: “we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

He said her name. He was dead, pronounced dead by soldiers who knew when a job was finished (John 19:33–34), and shut behind a stone by friends with no expectation of seeing him again. And on the first day of the week he rose, left the face cloth folded up in a place by itself, went out into a garden where a woman was crying, and said her name (John 20:7, 15–16). Thanks be to God.

What does victory look like on a hard day? Rarely like triumph, but like a believer who falls and gets up again, who confesses sin instead of hiding it, who keeps praying when prayer feels empty, who weeps at a graveside and still sings the hymn. Victory in Christ is not the absence of struggle but the certainty of the outcome. You may feel defeated and still be more than a conqueror, because the deciding battle has been won. On the hardest days, do not look for the feeling of victory; look at the One who gives it, and thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Christ is risen and death is beaten, stand firm and pour yourselves into the Lord’s work, for nothing done in him is ever wasted. Fifty-seven verses of the highest doctrine in the letter, and the conclusion is about Monday.

Therefore, my beloved brothers. After a letter of rebukes Paul calls them beloved, and says not “therefore look forward to heaven” but “therefore get on with it”. Chapter 16 opens with a collection for poor believers in Jerusalem (16:1): from the last trumpet Paul turns straight to the offering.

Steadfast, immovable. Steadfast (hedraios) is firmly seated; immovable (ametakinētos) is not to be moved: the answer to a church blown about by every teacher and every clever argument all through this letter.

Always abounding. Abounding (perisseuō) is an overflow word: not doing one’s bit, but spilling over the edge. A man is told to spend himself in a perishable body because it is going to be raised: the doctrine produces not detachment from this life but holy recklessness in it. Nor is the strength his own: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in him (Romans 8:11), and the overflow comes from that spring.

Your labor is not in vain. Labour (kopos) is toil to exhaustion. Not in vain (ou kenos, not empty) is the word that has haunted this chapter (vv. 10, 14).

In the Lord. These words carry the whole promise, and the Lord’s own story shows why. Isaiah gives the Servant of the LORD a sentence every tired believer has felt: “I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD” (Isaiah 49:4). Jesus lived that: on Friday evening, his friends scattered and his body in a tomb, it looked like the most wasted life in history. On Sunday the Father answered, and because his labour was not in vain, nothing done in him can be. Nor does the promise wait for flawless work, for none of ours is; it is offered in the One whose obedience was perfect and is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and God accepts it for his sake (1 Peter 2:5).

Not in vain, concretely. The mother who has prayed thirty years for a son who got worse. The man who taught eight children on Sundays for a decade and has no idea what became of them. The woman who nursed a husband through seven years of dementia, when he no longer knew her name. Each has looked at what they have to show for it and thought: that was nothing. Each has been wrong, on the authority of this verse: what is done in the Lord belongs to a world that is not going to be thrown away but raised. The God who did not let his Son’s body stay in the ground will not let his people’s work stay there either; he wastes nothing and forgets nothing.

The hunger for a legacy. When belief in a life to come fades, the hope of being remembered takes its place. The longing to leave a mark runs beneath a great deal of ambition, at work and even in ministry. But a legacy is a fragile kind of immortality. Few of us can name all eight great-grandparents; within a few generations nearly everyone is forgotten. The Preacher saw it long ago: “There is no remembrance of former things” (Ecclesiastes 1:11). A life built on being remembered must keep straining, and every failure feels like a small death. Paul offers something better. Your work is kept alive not by those who come after you, who will move on, but by the Lord, who will not: “For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10). You do not need history to remember you; he does, and that makes an unseen life worth spending.

In everyday life. Take the task that most feels like nothing, the one no one notices, and do it today as an offering to the risen Christ.
