What counts as the work of the Lord? Far more than church activities: any work done in the Lord, for his sake, in faith, by his strength. Changing a nappy, filling in a spreadsheet honestly, caring for an elderly parent, visiting a lonely neighbour, praying in secret, raising children in the faith. Paul told household slaves, whose work no one praised, to do it with all their heart as for the Lord, because the Lord himself would repay them (Colossians 3:23–24). The question is not whether the task is religious but whether it is done in him.

How do I stay steadfast? By staying where the ground is solid. The gospel is the thing “in which you stand” (v. 1), so keep coming back to it: learn verses 3 and 4 by heart, and let them answer the doubts of the day. Stay planted among God’s people; faith is usually lost in company (v. 33), and usually kept there too. Keep to the ordinary means God gives: his Word daily, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the gathering on the Lord’s Day. When a new idea unsettles you, weigh it slowly against Scripture before you let it move you (14:29, 36). And when your strength runs low, remember who is holding whom. It is Christ “who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:8), and the risen Shepherd does not lose one of those the Father has given him (John 6:39). You are immovable because he is.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand,<sup>2</sup>and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.<sup>3</sup>For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>4</sup>that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>5</sup>and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.<sup>6</sup>Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep.<sup>7</sup>Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.<sup>8</sup>Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.<sup>9</sup>For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.<sup>10</sup>But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.<sup>11</sup>Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.<sup>12</sup>Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?<sup>13</sup>But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.<sup>14</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.<sup>15</sup>We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.<sup>16</sup>For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised.<sup>17</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.<sup>18</sup>Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.<sup>19</sup>If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.<sup>20</sup>But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.<sup>21</sup>For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead.<sup>22</sup>For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.<sup>23</sup>But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ.<sup>24</sup>Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.<sup>25</sup>For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.<sup>26</sup>The last enemy to be destroyed is death.<sup>27</sup>For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him.<sup>28</sup>When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.<sup>29</sup>Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?<sup>30</sup>Why are we in danger every hour?<sup>31</sup>I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!<sup>32</sup>What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”<sup>33</sup>Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”<sup>34</sup>Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.<sup>35</sup>But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”<sup>36</sup>You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.<sup>37</sup>And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.<sup>38</sup>But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.<sup>39</sup>For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish.<sup>40</sup>There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another.<sup>41</sup>There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.<sup>42</sup>So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable.<sup>43</sup>It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.<sup>44</sup>It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.<sup>45</sup>Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.<sup>46</sup>But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.<sup>47</sup>The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven.<sup>48</sup>As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven.<sup>49</sup>Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.<sup>50</sup>I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.<sup>51</sup>Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,<sup>52</sup>in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.<sup>53</sup>For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality.<sup>54</sup>When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”<sup>55</sup>“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”<sup>56</sup>The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.<sup>57</sup>But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>58</sup>Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

keyVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this verse. Verses 12–19 hang on an “if”; here Paul steps out of it into what actually happened, and the word firstfruits makes Christ’s rising the pledge of a whole harvest. Every promise that follows, from the order of the resurrection to the body raised in glory and death swallowed up in victory, grows from this one sheaf.

15.reflection:
Paul calls Christ’s death for our sins, his burial and his resurrection “of first importance” (vv. 3–4). How would you put the gospel into a sentence or two for a friend, and why does it matter that it is news of what God has done rather than advice about what we must do?

Verses 12–19 list what would be lost if Christ had not been raised. Which of these strikes you most, and how does “But in fact Christ has been raised” (v. 20) change the way you face guilt, doubt or a Christian funeral?

Paul answers “With what kind of body do they come?” with a seed, the stars and the two Adams (vv. 35–49). What do these pictures teach about how the resurrection body is the same as ours and how it is different, and how should that shape the way we treat our own bodies and those of the sick and elderly now?

The chapter ends not with speculation but with work (v. 58). What labour in your life most feels as if it is in vain, and how does the resurrection of Christ answer that feeling?

16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16 closes the letter. The resurrection chapter has just ended with “your labor is not in vain” (15:58), and Paul now takes up the last question from the Corinthians’ letter before his plans, final commands and greetings.

The message. The hope of the resurrection is lived out in ordinary faithfulness: in money set aside for poor believers far away, plans held under the Lord’s permission, a warm welcome for those who serve, courage soaked in love, and above all love for the Lord Jesus and longing for his coming. Practical matters are not a step down from chapter 15; they are where its hope shows.

Why it was said. The Corinthians had asked about the collection (v. 1; see the introduction). A proud, divided church that graded leaders by eloquence and standing (1:12), they would show by how they received a timid Timothy, a prized Apollos and unglamorous servants like Stephanas whether the cross had really reshaped them.

How the chapter makes its case. Giving (vv. 1–4): regular, personal, proportionate and planned, carried to Jerusalem by messengers the church itself chooses. Plans (vv. 5–12): Paul hopes to winter with them, when sea travel stopped, but stays in Ephesus until Pentecost because a wide door has opened amid many adversaries; Timothy must be put at ease, and Apollos, the supposed rival, will come later. Commands (vv. 13–18): watch, stand firm, be courageous, be strong, do it all in love, and follow and honour servants like the household of Stephanas. Farewell (vv. 19–24): greetings from house churches, the holy kiss, Paul’s own signature, a solemn warning, the prayer Maranatha, and grace and love.

Where it leads. The giving echoes the One who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9); the open door with its adversaries is the road the Master walked; the servants Paul honours follow the one who is among us “as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27). And in his own hand Paul gathers the whole letter into love for the Lord and the oldest prayer of the church, “Our Lord, come!” (v. 22). Curse and hope stand side by side, and between them stands the cross, where Christ became a curse for us.

For us. The Christian life is lived not only on the summits of chapters 13 and 15 but in the diary, the bank account and the doorway on a Sunday morning. Ask what resurrection hope looks like in your giving, your plans and your welcome for the unimpressive, and, beneath them all, whether you love the Lord Jesus and long for him to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christian giving is a planned, shared act of grace, and it must be handled with visible honesty. As in the churches of Galatia, every believer is to set aside a share each Sunday, in proportion to income, so that there is no last-minute appeal when Paul comes (vv. 1–2). The gift will travel to Jerusalem in the hands of men the church itself has tested and approved, with Paul joining them only if it seems right (vv. 3–4), so that no one could doubt where the money went.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s fullest teaching on the collection, in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds generosity in the grace of Christ (see the note on vv. 1–2). The collection is not a tax but help given freely to those in need, across the lines of wealth and race (on the debt the Gentiles owed Jerusalem, see vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was poor, perhaps because of the famine of Acts 11:28, or because Jewish believers were cut off from the family and trade networks that had supported them. The collection was an act of solidarity across the deepest social divide of the ancient world. Now: Regular, proportionate, planned giving is still the wisest pattern for Christian giving (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer is to set aside a share of what God has given, week by week, for fellow believers in need.

The collection for the saints. “Now concerning” is how Paul takes up each topic from the Corinthians’ letter (7:1). After fifty-eight verses on the resurrection comes a hardship fund for a church some eight hundred miles away. The resurrection does not lift Christians above the practical; it sends them back into it with open hands.

As I directed the churches of Galatia. Corinth was not alone (2 Corinthians 8–9). One sentence follows with four marks of Christian giving.

On the first day of every week. It is regular. Sunday was when the church gathered (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and this is among the earliest evidence that the first day had become the Christian day of worship. It was the day the women found the tomb empty (Mark 16:2), so every coin set aside in Corinth was set aside on the day that proved labour in the Lord is not in vain (15:58). “Put something aside and store it up” is literally to lay it by “by himself”, and may mean the money was kept at home until Paul came.

Each of you. It is personal: not the wealthy patrons only, but everybody, deliberately and not on impulse.

As he may prosper. It is proportionate: the sum is scaled to income, not fixed. That single phrase protects the poor from a demand they cannot meet and stops the rich from discharging the duty with something they will not notice.

No collecting when I come. And it is planned. Paul does not want his visit remembered as a scramble or a high-pressure appeal, the week they were asked for money.

The setting. The collection was one of the great projects of Paul’s life. For years he gathered money from Gentile churches around the Aegean for a poor Jewish church most of them would never meet, and he risked his freedom delivering it (Romans 15:25–31). It was not for his own ministry; it expressed the unity of Gentile and Jewish believers in one body.

Why Paul names no figure. Here, and in two whole chapters on giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), Paul never names a figure. A fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten; a proportion has to be rethought whenever circumstances change. He moves people not by a rule but by a Person: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Lord of glory was laid in a manger and a borrowed tomb so that beggars might inherit a kingdom. Every gift we give is an echo of his: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15).

What it does not mean. Not that giving earns God’s favour; grace makes us generous. The religious heart gives to feel safe with God; the irreligious heart holds on to money because money feels like safety. The gospel frees both. In Christ you have a treasure that moth and rust cannot touch (Matthew 6:19–21), so you can give without trying to buy anything, and without fear of running out.

In everyday life. Sit down this week with your income in front of you, pray, and set a figure for your giving in proportion to what God has given you; and include in it something for believers in need beyond your own church.

What if I am in debt or can barely pay my bills? Give something, however small, and give it gladly; “as he may prosper” protects you from a demand you cannot meet, and the widow’s two coins were worth more in Christ’s eyes than the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44). But God does not want you to neglect your family or your honest debts in order to give (1 Timothy 5:8). Pay what you owe, live simply, get wise help with your budget if you need it, and let your giving rise as your circumstances improve. The habit matters more than the amount.

Where Christians differ: is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), hold that the fourth commandment still binds as moral law, the day changed to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection: the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept holy in worship and rest. Other Christians, including many Baptists and Reformed believers, see the Sabbath as a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17): the apostolic habit of meeting on the first day is wise and good, but no day binds the conscience as the Sabbath did (Romans 14:5–6). This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set the first day apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it. Here this commentary parts company with the 1689 Confession it follows on baptism; the first view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree that the Lord’s Day is the day of the church’s worship, a gift to be treasured rather than a burden to be minimised.

Where Christians differ: tithing. Some teach that Christians are bound to give exactly a tenth, as under the law; others that no standard applies. This commentary’s view: the New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It calls for regular, proportionate, generous, cheerful giving, in response to grace (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). The tithe is a helpful starting point and a biblical benchmark, and many Christians rightly give more. Giving is part of worship on the Lord’s Day.
verseByVerse.note: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The first day of the week is Sunday, the day Christians met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gift is to be carried by people the church itself has tested and chosen, so that its handling is honest and seen to be honest.

Those whom you accredit. Accredit (dokimazō) means to approve after testing. Paul, an apostle with every right to be trusted, will not carry the money alone. It travels with men the Corinthians have chosen and approved: their gift, with their escort.

Your gift. Gift (charis) is the word for grace (2 Corinthians 8:1, 6–7). Forgiven for nothing, the Corinthians pass on in coins a share of that kindness to believers who can never repay them.

If it seems advisable. Even whether the apostle travels with the delivery is left open. In the end Paul did go, with representatives from several churches (Acts 20:4; 24:17).

A debt to Jerusalem. “If the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings” (Romans 15:27). The greatest of those blessings is a Person: from Israel, “according to the flesh, is the Christ” (Romans 9:5). So Greek money travelling to a Jewish church was the thanks of the nations for a Jewish Messiah, and every coin said that the wall between Jew and Gentile was down (Ephesians 2:14).

Financial integrity. “We aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man” (2 Corinthians 8:21). A ministry must be honest before God, and visibly, checkably honest before people who are not obliged to think well of it. Many a scandal would have been prevented by Paul’s practice: more than one person responsible, audited accounts, a treasurer who is not the preacher, and no one, however trusted, ever alone with the cash. Not because Christians are suspect, but because the gospel is worth protecting from suspicion.

How can I know whether a ministry I give to is trustworthy? Ask the questions Paul’s practice answers. Is more than one person responsible for the money? Are the accounts audited and open to givers? Do the leaders live as they ask others to live? Is the ministry accountable to a church or board that can say no? Does it tell you plainly what your gift will do? A trustworthy ministry welcomes such questions, as Paul did. One that is offended by them, or pressures you to give quickly and emotionally, has given you your answer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every plan for the Lord’s work is held under the Lord’s permission and shaped by love for people. Paul hopes to come through Macedonia and stay, perhaps for the winter, not merely pass through (vv. 5–7), but for now he stays in Ephesus, where a wide door has opened along with many adversaries (vv. 8–9). Meanwhile Timothy must be welcomed without fear and sent back in peace (vv. 10–11), and Apollos, the man the factions set against Paul, has declined to come for now, a no Paul reports as a brother (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are more than logistics. The early churches were not independent congregations operating in isolation but a network bound together by the gospel, apostolic ministry, financial sharing and personal friendship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s care for Timothy’s welcome and his easy mention of Apollos as a brother show the warmth and shared work of early Christian ministry. Now: Christian ministry is easily treated as a competition; Paul’s warmth toward Apollos shows a heart shaped by the gospel (see the note on v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul plans to come and stay with them for a good while, but he holds every plan under the Lord’s permission.

Through Macedonia. Paul’s plan: from Ephesus, through Macedonia (northern Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica), then south to Corinth (Acts 19:21; 20:1–3).

Spend the winter. Sea travel stopped in winter; to winter somewhere was to be stuck there until spring. He did eventually spend three months in Greece (Acts 20:3). And there is warmth in it: Paul is proposing to be shut in for months with the most difficult church he has.

Help me on my journey. Help on my journey (propempō) means to provide for a missionary’s travel: food, money, companions. Paul accepted this help, though he refused payment for his preaching (9:15–18).

Not just in passing. That is what a man says about people he loves, not about a problem he is managing.

If the Lord permits. Paul makes detailed plans: a route, a season, a length of stay. There is nothing unspiritual about a diary, but every plan sits under a clause: “you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:15). Not a superstitious formula, but a settled awareness that the diary is a proposal and not a contract.

The Lord of the itinerary. In Paul the Lord is almost always Jesus, whose Spirit had once barred the road into Bithynia and sent Paul across to Macedonia (Acts 16:7–10). The one who may overrule the diary is not chance but the Good Shepherd, and a plan he changes is never a wasted winter. Nor did he visit us in passing: he came and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth (John 1:14), and he is with us always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20).

When plans change. In fact it did not go as written. Paul’s movements changed, and in his next letter he had to answer the charge of being unreliable (2 Corinthians 1:15–2:1). “If the Lord permits” has to be meant in advance, so that when the year goes differently there is something already in place to stand on.

How do I hold plans loosely without being unreliable? Plan carefully, keep your word wherever you can, and tell people honestly when circumstances change. “If the Lord permits” is not an escape clause for breaking promises lightly; Paul was grieved to be thought unreliable. It is a humble admission that God governs the future and you do not. When his providence closes a door, through illness, a change at work or a family need, accept it without bitterness, explain it kindly, and trust that his plan is better than yours.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stays where the gospel is advancing, and the opposition it stirs up is no reason to leave.

Until Pentecost. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover, in late spring. Paul wrote this letter in Ephesus, probably in the early months of the year.

A wide door. A door is an opportunity for the gospel (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3); wide and effective (energēs, active): work that works. Luke records what that looked like: two years of daily teaching, the word spreading through the province of Asia, sorcerers burning their books (Acts 19:9–10, 19–20).

Many adversaries. The same city, the same season: soon the silversmiths would fill the theatre with a riot (Acts 19:23–41). Paul does not write “but there are many adversaries”. He writes “and”: the adversaries are named in the same breath as the reason to stay.

The servant and his Master. “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). The widest door of all opened through the fiercest opposition of all: Herod and Pilate, the nations and the people, did what God’s hand had planned beforehand (Acts 4:27–28), and the cross they raised became the way of salvation for the world. An apostle with adversaries crowding round an open door is walking where his Master walked.

The riots of Ephesus came and went. Christ is the one “who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). The riots came and went, the temple of Artemis fell into ruins, and “the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily” (Acts 19:20).

Reading circumstances the right way round. Christians often reason like this: a door opens, resistance follows, so the door cannot have been from God. Paul assumes the opposite: where the gospel is advancing, something pushes back, and the absence of opposition may only mean that nothing has been disturbed.

How do I tell an open door with opposition from a closed door? The rule cuts both ways. Not every difficulty proves you are on the right road; some obstacles are God closing a door, and the Spirit once forbade Paul to go where he intended (Acts 16:6–7). But opposition alone never disqualified an opportunity. Ask not how big the difficulty is but what it is made of. Opposition from people who do not want the gospel to advance is evidence that it is advancing. A closed road, an exhausted body, a family that needs you at home, a door that will not open however hard it is pushed: those are different, and a wise Christian weighs them with prayer and the counsel of others.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must welcome the young and timid Timothy without making him afraid, because he does the Lord’s work, as Paul does.

Put him at ease. Paul is sending a young man into the hardest congregation he has, and he writes ahead. At ease (aphobōs) is without fear. Timothy was young (1 Timothy 4:12) and seems to have been prone to timidity (2 Timothy 1:7), and Corinth graded people by eloquence and presence (2 Corinthians 10:10).

The work of the Lord. Paul does not say Timothy is a fine preacher. He says: “he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am.” That is the whole credential (4:17), and it has nothing to do with confidence, accent or bearing.

Let no one despise him. Not for his youth, and not for his temperament; and send him back to Paul in peace, provided for.

The work of a crucified Lord. This letter has already said what kind of Lord that is. “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1:27), and the centre of the gospel is Christ crucified, who “had no form or majesty that we should look at him” (Isaiah 53:2). To despise Timothy for being unimpressive would be to despise the pattern of the gospel itself. Beneath the habit of grading preachers lies a quiet idol, the wish for leaders who make us look impressive; the gospel removes it, for our standing comes from Christ, and he is not ashamed of us.

A word for every Timothy. For anyone who has felt too young, too quiet, too unimpressive for the room: timidity is not a disqualification. It is a thing the family is supposed to make allowances for. The Lord Jesus does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20); he knows the frame of those who serve him, and remembers that they are dust (Psalm 103:14).

What does putting someone at ease actually look like? It is work, and somebody has to decide to do it: be the person who goes over first, who asks the question that lets a nervous newcomer talk about something he knows, who does not leave him at the edge of a room with a cup in his hand. Learn his name and use it. Introduce him to one other person. Thank a young preacher for something specific rather than offering a critique at the door. Pray for him, and tell him so. Every church has a Timothy in it on any given Sunday. The command is not to admire him but to go and put him at ease.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul calls Apollos his brother, has urged him to visit, and accepts his refusal without complaint: they are fellow servants, not rivals.

Now concerning our brother Apollos. A short verse, remarkable in three ways. Apollos is the other name in the faction fight (1:12), the eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24) whose admirers had used him as a stick to beat Paul with. And at the end of the same letter Paul calls him “our brother Apollos”.

I strongly urged him. First, Paul is actively trying to send his supposed rival to the church that prefers him (3:5–9).

Not his will to come now. Second, Apollos said no, and Paul reports it without complaint or appeal to his authority. Christian workers are fellow servants, not a chain of command (3:5). The likely reason is plain: a church divided into a Paul party and an Apollos party is not helped by the arrival of Apollos. Staying away may have been the most loving thing he could do.

When he has opportunity. Third, no coolness, no door shut: two servants of the same Lord disagree about timing, and the friendship stays intact. Much damage in churches would be avoided if Christians could let a no be a no without treating it as a verdict on the relationship.

Is Christ divided? How could the two men at the centre of a party quarrel stay friends? Because neither of them was the centre. When Corinth said “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos”, Paul answered: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1:13). One plants, another waters, but God gives the growth (3:6–7). The Lord Jesus never competed for a following; when the crowds would have made him king, he withdrew to the mountain by himself (John 6:15). “Our brother Apollos” is what the gospel sounds like when the Saviour, and not the preacher, is the one being followed.

In everyday life. If there is a Christian whose no you have taken personally, release it this week; let it be a no and not a verdict.

How do I find God’s will when Scripture does not settle a decision? The way Apollos did. He received no revelation; he weighed a request from a man he respected, formed a judgment and acted on it, and the New Testament records it without a hint that he should have waited for something more supernatural. Where Scripture commands, obey. Where it does not, you are free to reach a different conclusion even from someone you respect: pray, use the mind God gave you, take advice (Proverbs 15:22), weigh the good of others, and decide, trusting God’s providence to overrule your mistakes. You do not need a sign to do a wise and lawful thing.

Uncertain wording. The Greek says only that “it was not at all will” that he should come now, without saying whose. Most, with the ESV, take it as Apollos’s own will, which suits a man who has been urged and has declined; some read it as God’s will, which the bare word could also mean. Either way, Paul accepts the decision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A strong church is a loving church that follows its servants. Five short commands sum up the letter: watch, stand firm, be courageous, be strong, and do everything in love (vv. 13–14). Then Paul points to people who show what that looks like: the household of Stephanas, who posted themselves to serve the saints and are to be followed (vv. 15–16), and the three men whose visit refreshed him, who are to be honoured (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love in Christian Character

The commands of verses 13–14, watchful, firm, courageous, strong, and then loving, hold together what Paul has asked for all through the letter: the courage to stand for the truth, as he has done in every hard section, and the love that is patient and kind and bears all things (chapter 13). Neither is Christian without the other. Together they describe Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept on the way to Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed watchfulness, firmness, courage and strength, all held in love. Now: A church that is watchful and firm but unloving becomes a fortress, not a family; what each command becomes without love, and love without them, is drawn out in the note on vv. 13–14.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay alert, hold fast to the gospel, be brave and strong, and do it all in love.

Be watchful. Five commands, like an order of the day. Watchful (grēgoreō) is a sentry’s word: stay awake, keep looking, for Christ’s return (Matthew 24:42) and against false teaching. It is the verb Jesus used in Gethsemane to men who could not manage an hour (Mark 14:34–38).

Stand firm in the faith. Not in your faith: in the faith, the gospel handed over, especially as defended in chapter 15. The ground is not the church’s to renegotiate, and the pressure to move it is constant and usually reasonable-sounding.

Act like men. One word in Greek (andrizomai): be courageous, be mature. The Greek Old Testament uses it on the eve of battle, in the charge to Joshua to be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:6–7). Here it is addressed to the whole church, men and women: show the nerve of people whose God is with them wherever they go (Joshua 1:9).

Be strong. Be strong (krataioō) is in a form that means “be strengthened”. The strength is received from a Person: “be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10); “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is borrowed courage, and the lender never runs short.

The letter in five commands. The five sum up what Corinth needed: a church that slept through scandal (5:1–2), wavered over the resurrection (ch. 15), had to be called infants (3:1), thought itself strong already (4:10), and needed to learn that “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up (8:1).

Done in love. And then the fifth, which changes everything. Take the first four alone and you get a Christian everyone has met: watchful, immovable, courageous, strong, and impossible to be near. Without love vigilance becomes suspicion, firmness rigidity, and courage belligerence, the defender of the faith who is right about everything and has never comforted anyone. Take the fifth alone and you get a church so anxious to be loving that it will not stand anywhere or say a hard thing. Paul wants all four, soaked in the fifth.

Only Christ has held that balance. He was watchful in Gethsemane while his friends slept; he stood firm before the high priest and before Pilate; he set his face toward Jerusalem; and all of it was love. His perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and the love asked for here is the fruit of his Spirit, growing in us (Galatians 5:22).

Two scripts for manhood, both too small. Our culture argues loudly about men. One voice says the trouble is male strength itself, so courage is suspect and men are best softened. Another, louder online every year, says men should be hard, dominant and unashamed, and that kindness is weakness. Each is right about the other: the first has seen how often strength has crushed the weak; the second has seen young men given nothing worth being brave for. Paul overturns both. He calls the church to courage, which the first hardly dares to say, and then says what the second cannot bear: “Let all that you do be done in love.” Strength like Christ’s is not for winning. It is for carrying others.

In everyday life. Think of one place where you have gone quiet out of fear, and speak; and one place where you have been firm without kindness, and soften.

How do I keep watch and stand firm? Not by gritting your teeth, but by staying close to the One who has already stood firm for you. Stay awake to Christ. Begin each day with his word and a short prayer (Mark 14:38). Know where you stand. Learn the gospel well enough to say it in a few sentences, and test new ideas by it, especially reasonable-sounding ones that leave Christ smaller (Galatians 1:8). Watch your own heart. Confess the sin you have started to excuse before it settles in. Do not stand alone. Let a few believers in a faithful church know you well enough to warn you (Hebrews 3:13). Borrow strength. When you feel weak, say so to God and lean on his promise: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Your standing does not finally rest on your grip; Christ is the one “who is able to keep you from stumbling” (Jude 24).

What does it mean for a man, in particular, to act like a man? The command is to the whole church, but it lands with special weight on men, whom Scripture calls to lead their homes and, where qualified, the church (11:3; 1 Timothy 3:1–7). Biblical manhood is not swagger or control but courage in the service of others: standing firm in the truth, protecting the weak, taking responsibility instead of blaming, leading in prayer and repentance, and laying down your life as Christ did for his bride (Ephesians 5:25). A man who uses strength to dominate or harm has not acted like a man in Paul’s sense; he has acted like a child with a weapon. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and open every office to women; this commentary holds the complementarian reading (men and women equal in worth, with different callings in home and church) because Paul grounds the pattern not in the customs of his day but in creation (11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13), and it honours those who differ as brothers and sisters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow and defer to people like the household of Stephanas, who have proved themselves by serving.

Now I urge you. After fifteen chapters of problems, Paul points at some people who were getting it right.

The first converts in Achaia. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital. First converts is literally firstfruits (aparchē), the word used of Christ in 15:20: Stephanas and his household were God’s first sheaf in Achaia, with a whole province still to be gathered. Paul had baptised them (1:16), and they had been serving ever since.

Devoted to the service of the saints. Devoted (tassō) means they posted themselves to the duty. Nobody rostered them. They saw what the church needed and stepped into the gap, apparently for years and without a title.

Be subject to such as these. In a congregation that had spent the whole letter arguing about status, the unexpected instruction: follow those proved by serving, not the most gifted speaker or the most confident. The word for laborer means someone who works to the point of exhaustion: the qualification is that a person has worn himself out for the church.

Greatness turned upside down. Be subject to the servants: not a Corinthian idea, or a Roman one, but Christ’s. “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them … But I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:25–27). A church that follows people like Stephanas is adopting the Lord’s own standard, set by the one who served his people all the way to the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who serves automatically holds office. Elders are to be appointed according to the qualifications of Scripture (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). It means faithful servants deserve respect and should be followed.

Should I wait to be asked before serving? No. Stephanas did not wait. Many believers with real gifts never begin to serve because nobody asked and volunteering felt presumptuous; Paul commends a household that appointed themselves. See a need, speak to your elders, and fill it. And a warning for those already serving: Paul commends not the work but its direction. They devoted themselves to “the service of the saints”: to people, not to a programme, a building or a set of arrangements. You can be exhausted by church activity and never once have served a person.

Where Christians differ: does the household of Stephanas show that infants were baptised? Because Paul baptised the household (1:16), our paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) sometimes cite it, reading such households in the light of the covenant promise to believers and their children. This commentary’s view: the description here, a household that had “devoted themselves to the service of the saints”, describes believers, and nothing in either passage mentions children; the other household baptisms in Acts are likewise households that heard, believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:34; 18:8). With the 1689 London Baptist Confession, this commentary holds that baptism is for those who personally repent and believe, and it gladly labours alongside paedobaptist believers as honoured and beloved fellow servants.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three ordinary believers refreshed Paul simply by coming, and people like them deserve to be honoured.

Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul in Ephesus (7:1), a crossing of some two hundred and fifty miles by sea, and would carry his reply.

Made up for your absence. Their presence brought the church to him. He had missed not the letter or the news, but them.

They refreshed my spirit. Refreshed (anapauō) is to give someone rest, the way a weight is taken off. Paul carried “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28), and three men from a difficult congregation rested him. There is no record of Fortunatus preaching or Achaicus writing anything; what lifted the weight was some ordinary Christians turning up.

Give recognition to such people. Notice them, and say so out loud. Every congregation has its Stephanas, and the reason such people are rarely thanked is not unkindness but that quiet service is almost invisible by design: the work only becomes noticeable in the week it stops.

The traffic runs both ways. The letter has been a torrent of correction flowing from Ephesus to Corinth. Here it flows the other way: a half-grown church rested the apostle who was correcting it. Nobody is only a recipient in the body of Christ (Romans 1:12).

Refreshed in Christ. “Refresh my heart in Christ,” Paul asks Philemon (Philemon 20). The rest believers give one another is Christ’s own care passed from hand to hand, which is why the smallest visit can carry so much. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28): the Lord uses the same word, and gives rest to the weary apostle and the weary mother alike.

How can I refresh a pastor or missionary who is carrying too much? You do not need a gift for it. Go and see them, take something, and stay a while, but not too long. Say the encouraging thing you have thought and never said, and be specific: a sermon that helped, a visit that mattered. Pray for them and tell them so. Offer help that removes a burden rather than adds a meeting. Protect their day off. It sounds too small to matter, and Paul put three men’s names in Scripture for doing it.
verseByVerse.note: These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter ends with the family of God greeting one another, and with the one thing that matters most: love for the Lord Jesus. Greetings come from the churches of Asia and the church in Aquila and Prisca’s house, and the divided Corinthians are to greet one another with a holy kiss (vv. 19–20). Then Paul takes the pen himself (v. 21) to write a solemn curse on anyone who has no love for the Lord and the prayer Maranatha (v. 22), and he ends with grace and with his own love for them all (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Church’s Prayer for Christ’s Coming

The Aramaic is best read as a prayer, our Lord, come, as its place after the warning and before the blessing suggests (on the word and its echo in Revelation 22:20, see the note on v. 22). A church that has the cross at its centre and proclaims the resurrection lives with this prayer on its lips.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An Aramaic prayer kept untranslated in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small, moving piece of evidence that Jewish and Gentile believers prayed the same prayer in the same words. Now: Christians in every tradition and century have prayed for the Lord to come.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wider family of God sends its love, and the divided Corinthians are to show their own unity by greeting one another warmly.

The churches of Asia send you greetings. Asia here is the Roman province around Ephesus, in the west of modern Turkey, with churches at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4:13) that had not existed a few years earlier.

Aquila and Prisca. Aquila and Prisca (Priscilla in Acts), tentmakers like Paul expelled from Rome under Claudius, took him in at Corinth (Acts 18:1–3) and moved to Ephesus with him. There they took the eloquent Apollos aside and “explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26): two tentmakers correcting a brilliant preacher, privately, and he took it. They “risked their necks” for Paul’s life (Romans 16:4). Prisca is usually named first, which was not the ordinary order. They knew the Corinthians well, hence the hearty greetings.

The church in their house. For some two centuries there were no dedicated church buildings: a front room, some benches, and a family willing to have people tramping through every week.

A holy kiss. The family greeting of believers (Romans 16:16; 1 Peter 5:14), and after all the divisions the command is pointed: be reconciled and show it. In that room slave and slave-owner greeted each other this way, Jew and Greek, the rich patron and the dockworker who arrived late for the supper. It was holy because they had been set apart for God in Christ Jesus (1:2), bought with the same price (7:22–23). The cross had torn up the world’s seating plan, and the kiss showed it. Much of this letter’s fight comes down to whom you are willing to greet warmly on a Sunday morning.

Front rooms, then a city. The Father has gathered children from every nation into one household, and given them front rooms to meet in until he gives them a city. The Son “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and “God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6).

In everyday life. If you have a home, ask God how it might be opened to his people, for a meal, a Bible study, or a lonely student on a Sunday afternoon.

So what should I actually do in a culture that does not kiss? Greet people warmly, in whatever way your place counts as warm: a firm handshake, a hug where it is welcome, a smile and a name remembered. Greet especially the ones you would not naturally cross the room for: the visitor, the elderly widow, the awkward teenager, the person you quarrelled with last month. Be pure and considerate; holy means no one should feel uncomfortable or used. A congregation can be transformed by ten people obeying this for a month.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul takes the pen himself, so that the Corinthians know the letter is truly his and that he means every word of what follows.

With my own hand. Letters were normally dictated to a secretary (Romans 16:22). Now the apostle takes the pen himself, and the script on the papyrus would have visibly changed. He does this at the end of several letters as a signature (Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

The seal of a real correspondent. Forged letters were a real problem, and Paul had to warn one congregation not to be shaken by a letter “seeming to be from us” (2 Thessalonians 2:2). His handwriting was the seal, and a congregation that knew his hand could check.

What the last lines are. He has picked up the pen to write a warning, a prayer, and two declarations of love to a church that had given him as much grief as any. He did not save his own handwriting for the easy people.

The marks of Jesus. Signing Galatians, Paul added: “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (Galatians 6:17). The hand that signed this letter belonged to a man flogged, beaten with rods and stoned for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). His authority rested not on his pen or eloquence but on the risen Lord who had met him, sent him, and marked him as his own.

In everyday life. Write a note by hand this week to someone who has hurt you or whom you have found hard, with one line of genuine blessing, as Christ blessed you when you were hard to love.

Does it matter that Paul used a secretary? Not for the authority of the letter. The secretary wrote what Paul dictated, and Paul signed it; the words are Paul’s, and through Paul, the Lord’s (14:37). God inspired the Scriptures through the ordinary means of the ancient world, papyrus, ink, scribes and couriers, and kept every word he intended. Not a leather-bound book with gilt edges, but a roll of papyrus, dictated over days, carried across a sea, read aloud to a room of people who had been waiting for it, and at the bottom of the last sheet, larger and less tidy than the rest, the writing of a man they knew.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has no love at all for the Lord Jesus stands under God’s curse, and those who love him pray for him to come.

Let him be accursed. Love here is phileō, warm affection. Accursed is anathema: handed over to the judgment of God. Written in Paul’s own hand, it is a formal declaration that all who have no love for Christ, whatever their gifts or knowledge, are outside the kingdom. No one speaking in the Spirit, he said earlier, ever says “Jesus is accursed” (12:3); here the curse falls on whoever has no love for the Lord.

What the verse does not say. A tender conscience will misread it at once. It does not say “does not love the Lord perfectly”, or “whose love has grown cold”; every believer, the writer included, would fall under that. It says “has no love”. None. Paul means the person for whom Jesus Christ is a matter of complete indifference, who may be perfectly orthodox and enjoy the debates, and has no affection for him at all.

But it should not be softened. The letter was written to a congregation stuffed with knowledge and gifts, and at the end Paul names the one thing nothing can replace. Christianity is not merely agreeing with true statements; it is love for a Person. The Father wills “that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23), so indifference to Jesus is not neutral: it is a cold shoulder turned to the dearest treasure of heaven.

Our Lord, come! Then, at once, the other sentence, left in Aramaic: Marana tha, “our Lord, come!” In a Greek letter the phrase is left untranslated because everyone already knew it. It was probably a prayer of the earliest, Aramaic-speaking church, and shows Jewish believers, who would never pray to a mere man, praying to Jesus as Lord from the very beginning. The church has been praying it ever since, and one day, in the middle of the prayer, he will come.

Between them stands the cross. The prayer of the first believers is still the last prayer in the Bible: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). The One we pray to became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that no anathema remains for anyone who loves him. The curse and the hope sit side by side in this verse, and between them stands the cross.

In everyday life. Tell the Lord Jesus that you love him, in your own words, today, and pray for one person you know to whom he is a matter of complete indifference.

Is it not harsh to curse people simply for not loving Jesus? Not loving one teacher among many would hardly deserve it. But if Jesus is the Lord who gave himself for sinners, to have no love for him is to refuse the only rescue there is, and God’s judgment confirms what that person has chosen (John 3:18–19). Paul calls for no one to be harmed and speaks from no personal spite; he states how things stand, and in the same breath prays for the Lord’s coming. Meanwhile the door stays open: anyone who turns to Christ, however cold he has been, will find no curse left to bear.

I am afraid I do not love Christ enough. Am I under this curse? No, and the fear is itself the answer. Nobody who has no love for Christ is troubled by a verse about not loving him; the people it describes read it and feel nothing, which is precisely the diagnosis. Your love will always be smaller than it should be. Do not try to manufacture feeling; look at him. Read of his life and death, think on what he has forgiven you, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5). “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

Uncertain wording. The Aramaic letters can be divided two ways: Marana tha, “our Lord, come!”, a prayer, or Maran atha, “our Lord has come”, or “is coming”, a confession. The prayer of Revelation 22:20, “Come, Lord Jesus!”, and the place of the phrase between a warning and a blessing make the prayer the likelier reading, as the ESV takes it. The KJV prints “Anathema Maranatha” together as though one curse, but they are two separate sayings.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Our Lord, come!” translates Maranatha, an Aramaic prayer of the earliest church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends as he began, with grace, and adds what no other letter of his says: his own love for them all in Christ Jesus.

Grace at both ends. The letter opened with grace (1:3) and closes with it, and everything in between, rebuke and teaching alike, flows from it. Whatever this church was, it was a church, and Paul never once wrote as though it were not.

My love be with you all. No other letter of Paul ends like this, and it is written to a congregation that had split into parties, questioned his apostleship, tolerated a scandal that shocked pagans, sued one another, and got drunk at the Lord’s table while poor members went hungry. He answered every question, softening almost nothing, and then took the pen and wrote: “My love be with you all.” All, including the men who thought him a fool. Love, from chapter 13, is the last word.

In Christ Jesus. Such love does not grow in human ground. Paul had no natural stock of affection for people like this, and neither has anyone else. What he had was a share in the love of the One who had looked at a world exactly this arrogant, divided and ungrateful, and had not withheld himself from it.

How do I love someone I have had to correct? Let the correction serve the love, not replace it. Before you speak, pray for the person and remember the grace you have received. Correct what is wrong plainly, as Paul did, without exaggeration or contempt. Then show that you are still for them: stay in touch, speak well of them to others, and be quick to rejoice in any change. If they reject what you said, keep loving them, as Christ has kept loving you. A rebuke wrapped in grace and sealed with love is one of the kindest gifts one Christian can give another.

Textual note. “Amen” means “so be it”. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV and the ESV, end with it, while some early ones leave it out; either way it is the right last word.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do.<sup>2</sup>On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.<sup>3</sup>And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.<sup>5</sup>I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia,<sup>6</sup>and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go.<sup>7</sup>For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.<sup>8</sup>But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,<sup>9</sup>for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.<sup>10</sup>When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am.<sup>11</sup>So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.<sup>12</sup>Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.<sup>13</sup>Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.<sup>14</sup>Let all that you do be done in love.<sup>15</sup>Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints—<sup>16</sup>be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.<sup>17</sup>I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,<sup>18</sup>for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.<sup>19</sup>The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord.<sup>20</sup>All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>21</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.<sup>22</sup>If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!<sup>23</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.<sup>24</sup>My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

keyVerse.quote: Let all that you do be done in love.
keyVerse.note: Seven words gather up the whole letter. Every Corinthian trouble, from parties and lawsuits to idol meat and tongues, came from knowledge, gifts or freedom used without love, and chapter 13 has already shown what love is. Set beside the call to courage in verse 13, it describes the character of Christ himself, who stood firm to the cross and did it all for love of us.

16.reflection:
Paul turns from the resurrection (chapter 15) straight to a collection for the poor (vv. 1–4). What does regular, proportionate giving look like for you, and how does Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), change the spirit in which we give?

Paul makes detailed plans yet says “if the Lord permits” (v. 7), and he stays in Ephesus because of an open door with many adversaries (vv. 8–9). How do you tell an opportunity with opposition from a door God has closed, and how can we hold plans firmly enough to be reliable yet loosely enough to trust him?

Timothy was to be put at ease (vv. 10–11), and the church was to follow and honour quiet servants like Stephanas (vv. 15–18). Who in our church might feel unimpressive or overlooked, and what could we do this month to welcome, refresh or thank them?

Verse 22 sets a curse on those with no love for the Lord beside the prayer “Our Lord, come!” What does it mean to love the Lord Jesus, rather than only to agree with true things about him, and what would it look like for us to long for his coming?
